--- SOURCE 13: What is the EU Data Boundary? - Microsoft Privacy | Microsoft Learn ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/privacy/eudb/eu-data-boundary-learn

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Microsoft Learn documentation defines the **EU Data Boundary** — a geographically defined boundary within which Microsoft commits to store and process Customer Data and personal data for its enterprise online services, including Azure, Dynamics 365, Power Platform, and Microsoft 365. Professional Services Data will be stored at rest for these services. These commitments are subject to limited circumstances where data continues to be transferred outside the EU Data Boundary.

**Key definitions:**
- **Customer Data**: All data (including text, sound, video, image files, and software) provided to Microsoft by or on behalf of a Customer through use of the Online Service. It excludes Professional Services Data and configuration information (technical settings, resource names).
- **Personal data in system-generated logs**: Microsoft online services create system-generated logs as part of regular operation. Some logs contain fields that identify or can identify specific persons (e.g., product and service usage data, user activity logs).
- **Pseudonymization**: Per GDPR Article 4(5), pseudonymization replaces personally identifiable information with artificial identifiers/pseudonyms. Microsoft requires all personal data in system-generated logs to be pseudonymized using techniques including encryption, masking, tokenization, and data blurring. This enables authorized Microsoft personnel to work (e.g., DevOps identifying service issues across regions) without identifying or reidentifying users. Anonymization is not used because it would permanently alter data and compromise Microsoft's ability to ensure quality, reliability, and security of services.
- **Security controls for system-generated logs** include: data minimization via minimum retention policies, regular checks and scrubbing, limited usage solely for service operations, and access controls limiting rehydration/reidentification of personal data.
- **Professional Services Data**: All data provided to Microsoft through an engagement to obtain Professional Services (consulting services and technical support services).

**EU Data Boundary countries and datacenter locations:**
- Consists of EU countries (Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden) and EFTA countries (Liechtenstein, Iceland, Norway, Switzerland).
- Uses Microsoft datacenters announced/operating in Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland. Additional datacenters may be established in the future.

**How to configure services:**
- **Azure**: Regional services deployed in an EU Data Boundary region are in-scope. Non-regional services require configuration via Azure Resource Manager.
- **Dynamics 365 and Power Platform**: Requires BOTH (1) provisioning the tenant and all environments in the "European Union (EU) and European Free Trade Association (EFTA)" Macro Region Geography, AND (2) maintaining a billing address in an EU Data Boundary country. Meeting only one requirement doesn't place environments within the boundary.
- **Microsoft 365**: Customers with a sign-up location in an EU or EFTA country are in-scope; however, customers with Multi-Geo Capabilities are not in-scope even if their tenant is in an EU/EFTA country.

The documentation was last updated February 26, 2025, and reflects the current state of the EU Data Boundary as of the publication date.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Microsoft Q&A forum thread titled "Inquiry on Data Residency, Compliance, and Security for Microsoft Azure OpenAI Subscription." The original poster, Nikhil Bhatia, asked four questions about: (1) whether data/prompts submitted to Azure OpenAI via API remain in Switzerland, (2) how Microsoft handles data requests from US or foreign authorities, (3) what AI subscriptions are commonly used by law firms and how data is secured against training usage, and (4) Microsoft's GDPR/FDAP compliance framework and list of sub-processors.

Key answers provided across the thread:

**Data Residency in Switzerland:** Azure OpenAI Service is available in the Switzerland North region, allowing data residency within Switzerland when configured with regional deployment. However, for 'Global' deployment types, prompts and responses may be processed in any geography where the relevant model is deployed. For 'DataZone' deployments, data may be processed within the specified data zone. A Microsoft moderator (Manas R Mohanty) clarified that with Global Standard deployments, data at rest remains in the designated geography (e.g., Europe) but inference calls may route to any global location. DataZone deployments keep data at rest in the designated geography (e.g., Switzerland North) while inference may occur anywhere within that data zone.

**Government Data Requests:** Microsoft only responds to government or foreign authority data requests under applicable laws, following a rigorous legal review. Microsoft does not provide governments direct access to customer data, attempts to redirect requests to customers where legally possible, and notifies customers unless prohibited. Microsoft's process includes legal review, customer notification, challenging unlawful requests, transparency reports, escalation to legal/compliance teams, and documentation in the Data Protection Addendum (DPA).

**Service Provider Entity:** For EU customers, including Ireland, the service provider is Microsoft Ireland Operations Limited (MIOL), operating under Irish law. However, Microsoft remains a US-headquartered company subject to US legal obligations such as the CLOUD Act. US authorities can issue data requests, but Microsoft will challenge non-EU government requests and only comply if legally required under EU law, notifying customers where permissible. The DPA includes clauses on Data Transfers referencing the 2021 Standard Contractual Clauses, GDPR Article 46 safeguards, and Article 30(2) documentation.

**Law Firm Subscriptions:** Law firms typically use Standard, PTU (Provisioned Throughput Unit), or Batch API subscriptions for legal drafting, contract analysis, and e-discovery. EA (Enterprise Agreement) subscriptions offer higher quota and support. Azure OpenAI models are stateless—no prompts or completions are stored in the model, and they are not used to train, retrain, or improve base models by default. Data is encrypted at rest by default.

**Compliance:** Azure OpenAI is GDPR- and FDAP-compliant, offering encryption in transit and at rest, Customer-Managed Keys, and pseudonymization. Microsoft publishes a list of sub-processors through the Microsoft Trust Center. Compliance offerings for EMEA include EU Cloud CoC, EU GDPR, EU Model Clauses, Germany C5, and others. Microsoft offers Sovereign Cloud options and features like Data Guardian (Europe-based access approval) and External Key Management for maximum sovereignty.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Microsoft Azure OpenAI provides robust support for data residency, including the option to host and process data entirely within Switzerland. The Azure OpenAI Service is available in the Switzerland North region, allowing organizations to ensure that all data—including prompts, completions, and embeddings remain within Swiss borders when configured appropriately."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Google Cloud documentation page provides implementation guidance for FedRAMP (Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program) compliance on Google Cloud. The document is designed for security, compliance, and IT personnel responsible for FedRAMP implementation and compliance.

**Key Points:**

1. **About FedRAMP**: FedRAMP is a US federal program established to standardize security assessment, authorization, and continuous monitoring of cloud products across government agencies. Congress codified it in 2022. In 2025, FedRAMP launched the "FedRAMP 20x" initiative to adopt automated monitoring and move away from manually compiled documentation. FedRAMP is based on NIST SP 800-53, with impact levels (Low, Moderate, High). The FedRAMP Moderate baseline has 325 controls, while the High baseline has 421 controls.

2. **Google Cloud FedRAMP Authorization**: The FedRAMP Board (formerly JAB, including CIOs from DoD, DHS, and GSA) has issued a FedRAMP High Provisional Authority to Operate (P-ATO) to Google Cloud and its underlying Google Common Infrastructure (GCI). Following FedRAMP 20x improvements, the GSA became the authorizing agency for Google Cloud. The FedRAMP Moderate baseline is a subset of High, so High authorization covers all Moderate requirements.

3. **Services in Audit Scope**: Google Cloud's FedRAMP High P-ATO covers more than 150 cloud services, including ML/AI services (Generative AI on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Model Garden with 200+ LLMs). Individual LLMs are not independently FedRAMP-authorized; the cloud services hosting them are. Google-managed models (Gemini family, Anthropic partners) support Provisioned Throughput in FedRAMP High environments.

4. **Achieving FedRAMP ATO**: The path is the Rev. 5 Agency ATO, requiring collaboration with Google and a third-party assessment organization (3PAO). For FedRAMP High compliance, users must use Data Boundary for FedRAMP High via Assured Workloads. Google provides a Customer Responsibility Matrix (CRM) and System Security Plan (SSP) under NDA.

5. **Guidance and Automation**: Google provides service-specific Control Mapping Guides (CMGs) for services including BigQuery, Compute Engine, IAM, Cloud Logging, and Generative AI on Agent Platform. FedRAMP High implementation guides cover service-specific APIs for Apigee, GKE, Cloud Storage, Cloud KMS, and others—all under NDA.

6. **Data Residency and SA-9(5)**: Data residency requirements apply only to FedRAMP High baseline. Google offers data residency contractual commitments for regional services, ensuring FedRAMP High data stays in US regions. In July 2020, FedRAMP updated the SA-9(5) control restricting high-impact data to the US. Some Google Cloud services were flagged in the FedRAMP Marketplace with an asterisk as not meeting SA-9(5); Google is actively pursuing resubmission to remove these clarifications.

7. **Digital Sovereignty and Encryption**: Google emphasizes digital sovereignty via Assured Workloads and software-defined community cloud. Recommended mitigations include customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) via Cloud KMS, Cloud External Key Manager (Cloud EKM), Cloud HSM (FIPS 140 validated), envelope encryption, and data encryption in transit (MACsec at Layer 2, TLS at application layer, Cloud VPN for on-premises connections). FIPS 140 validation is required for FedRAMP authorization (SC-13 control).

8. **Key Assurances**: Google personnel cannot access unencrypted customer key material; decrypted key material can't be exported or viewed; HSMs are FIPS 140 validated; Google system operators are prevented from accessing customer key material.

- Data centers are geographically distributed, physically secure, with redundant power (UPS batteries + backup generators capable of running at full capacity for days), dual circuits/switches/networks.
- Servers use Linux-based customized implementations with proprietary algorithms for data security.
- Access requires electronic card keys with dual authentication, CCTV monitoring 24/7, and records retained up to 30 days.
- Personnel must undergo background checks, sign confidentiality agreements, and receive security training.
- Decommissioned disks are erased in a multi-step process verified by at least two independent validators, with results logged by serial number.
- Data is stored in a multi-tenant environment on Google-owned servers and replicated between geographically dispersed data centers.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 15: Last updated January 2023 ---
URL: https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/abs_googlecloud_mapping

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is Google Cloud's mapping of its security and compliance controls against the Monetary Authority of Singapore's (MAS) "Guideline on Outsourcing" control objectives, organized into three categories: A) Govern the Cloud, B) Design and Secure the Cloud, and C) Run the Cloud. It is last updated January 2023.

The document presents a table format pairing MAS guideline control objectives with Google Cloud's corresponding controls and notes whether each requirement is primarily the customer's responsibility or is satisfied by Google.

KEY POINTS BY CATEGORY:

**A) Govern the Cloud**
- Most governance requirements (oversight of cloud outsourcing, accountability, staff skills, empowered interface, compliance, testing, remediation, billing) are primarily customer responsibilities.
- Google provides: external security documentation and whitepapers, an internal ISMS certified under ISO 27001, SLAs publicly available, audits/access commitments under the Cloud Data Processing Addendum and Financial Services Addendum (FSCMA), an incident management process, Cloud Console for resource management/diagnostics, and cost management tools (cloud.google.com/cost-management).
- Google Cloud holds third-party certifications including MTCS Singapore Standard 584 Tier 3, ISO 27001, ISO 27017, ISO 27018, and SOC 1/2/3 (SSAE 16/ISAE 3402 Type II).

**B) Design and Secure the Cloud**
- Google offers financial services-specific solutions (cloud.google.com/solutions/financial-services/).
- Data isolation: Google logically isolates each customer's data; data centers use electronic card key access linked to system alarms with logged access attempts.
- Code development follows a structured, peer-reviewed release process with purpose-built code analysis tools and continuous post-production testing.
- Redundancy is embedded in architecture; essential hardware is hot swappable; status dashboards at status.cloud.google.com.
- IAM tools (Cloud IAM, Identity) provide centralized access management; defense-in-depth techniques documented.
- Encryption: Google maintains encryption at rest for customer data and security measures for data in transit; provides encryption whitepapers (Encryption in Transit, Encryption at Rest, G Suite Encryption).
- Key management: Google provides controls to manage encryption keys through their lifecycle; capabilities to manage keys on behalf of tenants.
- Third-party audits: SOC 1/2/3, ISO 27001, ISO 27017/27018, PCI-DSS, HIPAA; Access Transparency provides audit logs for GCP.
- Physical security: formal access procedures, 2-factor authentication for all production resources, need-to-know access restrictions, asset tracking via barcodes/asset tags from acquisition to destruction.
- Data retention: customers manage their own policies using storage features or Google Vault (G Suite).
- Penetration testing: Google performs fuzz testing, penetration testing, and vulnerability scanning; maintains a Vulnerability Rewards Program.
- Incident management: network and host-based detection tools, automated log collection, rigorous incident response process; Data Incident Response Whitepaper available.

**C) Run the Cloud**
- Change management: structured peer-reviewed code development and release process; customers can bring their own change/configuration management tools.
- Event management: rigorous incident management process prioritizing events that directly impact customers.
- Intrusion detection involves: (1) tightly controlling attack surface, (2) intelligent detection at data entry points, (3) automated remediation of dangerous situations.
- Patching: Google operates a homogeneous machine environment with custom software to minimize exposure; patches as quickly as vulnerabilities are addressed rather than on a scheduled basis.
- Capacity management: budget approvals and internal SLAs govern provisioning; customers can monitor service consumption.
- Disaster recovery: Google replicates data over multiple systems, maintains a Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Plan aligned with Alphabet Inc.'s plans, provides uptime metrics and certifications (ISO 27001, ISO 27018).

Across nearly all control objectives, the document emphasizes that it is "Primarily customer responsibility to satisfy this requirement" for configuration, compliance with jurisdiction-specific requirements, data retention, access management, and change management, while Google provides the underlying infrastructure, certifications, documentation, and tools.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Google provides comprehensive external documentation and whitepapers detailing our security infrastructure and operational model. Google also maintains an internal ISMS and evidence of its effectiveness is provided via ISO 27001 certification."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: How to Implement GDPR Data Processing Compliance Controls in Google Cloud ---
URL: https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-17-how-to-implement-gdpr-data-processing-compliance-controls-in-google-cloud/view

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a technical blog post from OneUptime (an open-source observability platform) providing a practical guide to implementing GDPR data processing compliance controls on Google Cloud. Published by Nawaz Dhandala on Feb 17, 2026, and technically validated on May 28, 2026.

The article covers the following key areas:

**Google's Data Processing Agreement (DPA):** A prerequisite before processing EU personal data on Google Cloud. Covers Google as data processor, sub-processor transparency, data deletion upon contract termination, and assistance with data subject requests. Accepted through Google Cloud Console under Organization Settings.

**Data Residency and Location Controls:** While GDPR doesn't strictly require EU data residency, many organizations choose it as a compliance simplification. The guide provides CLI commands for creating resources in EU regions (Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Cloud SQL) and enforcing EU-only locations via Organization Policies using the constraint `gcp.resourceLocations` with allowed value `in:eu-locations`.

**Personal Data Classification with Cloud DLP:** Use Cloud DLP inspection jobs to identify personal data (PERSON_NAME, EMAIL_ADDRESS, PHONE_NUMBER, DATE_OF_BIRTH, STREET_ADDRESS, IP_ADDRESS, CREDIT_CARD_NUMBER, IBAN_CODE, VAT_NUMBER) across data stores, including reusable inspection templates.

**Data Subject Rights Implementation:**
- Article 15 (Right of Access): Python code to export all personal data for a user across multiple BigQuery tables to GCS.
- Article 17 (Right to Erasure): Python/BigQuery code to delete user data across tables, with audit logging and consideration of crypto-shredding for large-scale data.
- Article 20 (Data Portability): Export data in machine-readable formats (CSV/JSON) using `bq extract` and query-based exports.

**Consent Management:** BigQuery schema for tracking consent records (consent_type, consent_given, timestamps, source, version, IP address) and SQL queries to verify active consent before processing.

**Data Retention:** Automated retention policies using BigQuery partition expiration (e.g., 730 days) and scheduled cleanup queries.

**Breach Detection:** Enable Event Threat Detection via SCC, create high-priority monitoring alerts for unusual data access (BigQuery scanned_bytes > 10GB threshold), and SCC notifications for DATA_EXFILTRATION and ANOMALOUS_ACCESS findings.

**DPIA Support:** Export Cloud Asset Inventory, IAM policies, and data flow logs (BigQuery InsertJob activity) for Data Protection Impact Assessment documentation.

**Terraform Infrastructure:** Terraform configuration for GDPR-compliant infrastructure including EU-only location org policies, EU-located BigQuery datasets with KMS encryption and partition expiration.

The article concludes that GDPR compliance requires both technical controls (well-supported by Google Cloud) and organizational processes (consent management, data subject request handling, DPIA workflows). It recommends starting with data classification to understand where personal data lives.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"GDPR compliance on Google Cloud requires a combination of technical controls and organizational processes. The technical side - encryption, access controls, data residency, and logging - is well-supported by Google Cloud services. The organizational side - consent management, data subject request handling, and DPIA processes - requires building workflows on top of those services. Start with data classification to understand what personal data you have and where it lives, then layer on the controls from there."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: GDPR Data Breach Notification: The 72-Hour Rule | ISpectra ---
URL: https://ispectratechnologies.com/hub/gdpr/gdpr-data-breach-notification.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a GDPR educational guide published by ISpectra Technologies (a cybersecurity and compliance firm serving 200+ enterprises) focusing on the GDPR Data Breach Notification 72-Hour Rule. The guide explains that a qualifying personal data breach must be reported to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of it (not after investigation is complete), unless the breach is unlikely to pose a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms.

Key content points:
- A personal data breach is broader than a hack, defined as a security breach leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, or unauthorized disclosure/access to personal data (e.g., lost laptops, missent emails, ransomware, unauthorized employee access).
- Three breach types: confidentiality (unauthorized disclosure/access), integrity (unauthorized alteration), and availability (loss of access/destruction); a single incident can involve multiple types (e.g., ransomware is often both availability and confidentiality).
- When risk to individuals is high, affected persons must be notified without undue delay in clear language (e.g., advise password changes, fraud awareness).
- Regulator notification must describe: nature of breach, categories and approximate number of affected individuals/records, likely consequences, measures taken/proposed, and a contact point (e.g., DPO).
- Phased notification is permitted — report what you know within 72 hours and provide further details as available.
- Processors must notify controllers without undue delay; the controller meets the 72-hour deadline.
- Every breach must be documented in a breach register (facts, effects, action taken), regardless of notifiability.
- Risk assessment determines whether to notify regulator, individuals, both, or neither; decisions not to notify must be justifiable.
- The 72-hour clock starts upon "awareness" — interpreted broadly once there is reasonable certainty a security incident compromised personal data, not when investigation completes.
- Common breach mistakes: failing to recognize an incident as a breach, starting the clock too late, missing the window while investigating, failing to notify individuals at high risk, and not documenting non-notified breaches.
- ISpectra offers services to build breach response plans, set up detection/escalation, prepare notification templates, run tabletop exercises, and maintain breach registers. The page includes an FAQ section and links to other GDPR Hub resources (complete guide, requirements, fines, ongoing compliance, controller vs processor, RoPA).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"When personal data is compromised, GDPR imposes one of its most time-pressured obligations: a qualifying breach must be reported to your supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of it."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Data Breach Notification Clause: Timelines & Drafting ---
URL: https://www.contractken.com/glossary/data-breach-notification-clause

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a comprehensive glossary entry on "Data Breach Notification Clause" from ContractKen's Contract Clauses Central repository, aimed at legal professionals reviewing and drafting contracts.

**Definition and Core Elements:**
A data breach notification clause is the contractual mechanism allocating the obligation to report, investigate, and coordinate response to security incidents affecting personal data. It typically appears in data processing agreements (controller-processor), master services agreements, or cybersecurity addenda. The clause addresses four core elements: (1) definition of a reportable incident, (2) notification trigger and timeline, (3) minimum content and method of notification, and (4) allocation of cooperation obligations.

**Key Regulatory Frameworks:**
- GDPR Article 33 requires controllers to notify supervisory authorities within 72 hours of awareness; Article 34 requires individual notification for high-risk breaches
- HIPAA Breach Notification Rule (45 CFR 164.400-414) requires 60-day notice to individuals, HHS, and media (for breaches affecting 500+ residents)
- All 50 U.S. states, DC, and Puerto Rico have breach notification statutes, with timelines ranging from 30 days (Texas) to 90 days (several states)

**Why It Matters:**
- The Identity Theft Resource Center reported 3,205 publicly disclosed data compromises in 2023 (78% increase over 2022), affecting over 353 million victim notices
- IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2024: global average cost USD 4.88 million; U.S. average USD 9.36 million; healthcare at USD 9.77 million; financial services at USD 6.08 million
- Notification-related costs alone average 35-40% of total breach costs
- CCPA/CPRA private right of action provides statutory damages of USD 100-750 per consumer
- Thomson Reuters Practical Law 2024 DPA Survey: 67% of enterprise customer-side DPAs demand breach notification within 24-48 hours

**Key Elements of a Well-Drafted Clause (10 items):** defined reportable event (aligned with GDPR Article 4(12)), notification trigger point, contractual notification window (typically 24-48 hours for processor-to-controller), minimum notice content (tracking GDPR Article 33(3)), ongoing updates/interim notices, cooperation on investigation and regulatory response, cost allocation, regulatory communication coordination, individual notice coordination, and ongoing security remediation.

**Market Positions:** Provider-favorable (no fixed hour commitment, narrow definitions, customer bears costs), Market Standard (48-72 hour notification, shared costs, 1-2 years credit monitoring), and Customer-favorable (24-hour notification, broad definitions including near-misses, provider bears all costs including 2-3 years credit monitoring).

**Common Contract Types:** DPAs, HIPAA Business Associate Agreements, SaaS/Cloud agreements, Payment Processor/PCI agreements, Healthcare IT/EHR vendor contracts, Financial Services Technology vendors (NYDFS Part 500 requires 72-hour notification), Government contracts (DFARS requires 72-hour reporting), and M&A Transition Services Agreements.

**Negotiation Playbook:** Calibrate notification clock to regulatory deadlines (working backward from the 72-hour GDPR clock), write broad definitions of reportable events, address near-misses explicitly, protect attorney-client privilege in investigations, align with cyber insurance notice provisions (typically 24-72 hours), and integrate with indemnification and super-caps.

**Jurisdiction Notes:** Includes detailed requirements for U.S. federal (HIPAA, SEC Form 8-K within 4 business days, NYDFS Part 500, DFARS), U.S. state laws, EU GDPR (max fines of €20M or 4% of global turnover), UK GDPR, Canada's PIPEDA, Brazil's LGPD, Australia's Notifiable Data Breaches scheme (30 days), Singapore's PDPA (72 hours), India's DPDPA, EU NIS2 Directive (effective 17 October 2024, 24-hour early warning/72-hour notification), and DORA (effective 17 January 2025).

The page also includes three sample clause languages (GDPR SaaS DPA, HIPAA BAA, and incident cooperation clause) and links to related clauses including DPA, Data Protection, Confidentiality, Indemnification, Limitation of Liability, Insurance, and Audit clauses.
</summary>

"The Identity Theft Resource Center reported 3,205 publicly disclosed data compromises in 2023, a new record, affecting over 353 million victim notices."

--- SOURCE 5: Data incident response process  |  Security  |  Google Cloud Documentation ---
URL: https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/security/incident-response

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Google Cloud documentation page (last updated June 2026) explains Google's Data Incident Response Process for protecting customer data in Google Cloud. It defines a data incident per the Cloud Data Processing Addendum as "a breach of Google's security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to, Customer Data on systems managed by or otherwise controlled by Google." Unsuccessful login attempts, pings, port scans, and denial of service attacks do not qualify as data incidents.

The incident response program involves expert teams including specialized incident response teams (including a machine-learning incident response team), product engineering, site reliability engineering, cloud security, digital forensics, detection and response, legal counsel, security response operations, privacy and trust response, trust and safety, and Cloud Customer Care. An incident commander is designated to coordinate response and assembles a response team.

The response process follows seven main steps: (1) Identification - detection via automated network/system log analysis, behavioral anomaly detection, penetration tests, internal code reviews, privileged access monitoring, and Google's vulnerability reward program, with AI-powered smart alert triaging; (2) Reporting; (3) Coordination/Triage - severity assessment based on potential harm, nature of incident, data type affected, service impact, and incident status; (4) Response team engagement; (5) Resolution - investigation, containment and recovery, and communication (including customer notification); (6) Closure - lessons learned and post-mortem analysis; and (7) Continuous improvement - program development and prevention.

AI is used throughout the process: machine-learning models analyze alert signals and correlate events during identification; AI agents suggest resolutions during investigation (strictly limited to suggestions); and during resolution, AI models are prohibited from executing commands directly—they generate structured action payloads requiring human-in-the-loop confirmation. All AI actions are recorded in immutable audit logs.

Customer notifications are sent via Essential Contacts and the Google Admin console, using @google.com email addresses from various senders. Notifications include affected services/projects, incident description, detection time, unique incident identifier, and links to resources. Customers should configure incident response group emails, grant the Advisory Notifications Viewer (roles/advisorynotifications.viewer) IAM role, and create Cloud Monitoring alerts.

Google aligns its incident response with regulatory frameworks including EU's Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) and Network and Information Systems Directive 2.0 (NIS2), and products undergo certification for ISO-27017, ISO-27018, ISO-27001, PCI-DSS, SOC 2, and FedRAMP. Further reading includes O'Reilly's "Building secure and reliable systems" Chapter 17 and the Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"a breach of Google's security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to, Customer Data on systems managed by or otherwise controlled by Google"

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Google Cloud documents the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) provisional authorizations (PAs) granted to Google Cloud and Google Workspace by the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA). Key points include:

- **DoD PA Levels**: Google Cloud holds DoD provisional authorizations at Impact Levels 2 (IL2), 4 (IL4), and 5 (IL5), allowing it to process and store controlled unclassified information (CUI). In 2022, Google Cloud was the first hyperscaler to receive a DoD IL5 PA for a software-defined community cloud. Google Distributed Cloud air-gapped and air-gapped appliance maintain a DoD IL6 PA (for information classified up to SECRET level).

- **Compliance Framework**: DISA manages the DoD Cloud Service Provider Security Requirements Guide (SRG), which defines baseline security requirements based on the DoD Risk Management Framework (RMF), CNSSI 1253 Security Categorization, and NIST SP 800-53 controls. DoD ILx authorization packages are based on FedRAMP High packages with additional DoD-specific controls.

- **IL2 Requirements**: Covers data cleared for public release and some low-confidentiality unclassified data (L-M-x categorization per CNSSI 1253). DoD allows full reciprocity with FedRAMP Moderate or High P-ATO. IL2 data is permitted only in U.S. data centers authorized for the CSO; workloads must be deployed using Data Boundary via Assured Workloads.

- **IL4 and IL5 Requirements**: Accommodate CUI up to moderate confidentiality, moderate integrity (M-M-x). Customers must deploy using Data Boundary via Assured Workloads, which provides compliance monitoring and implements key DoD IL4/IL5 controls by default. Google Cloud's storage and network infrastructure maintain IL4/IL5 PAs; data at rest is automatically encrypted with FIPS 140 validated encryption, and data in transit within a VPC is automatically encrypted. Google was the first hyperscale provider to achieve IL4/IL5 PAs for a public cloud offering.

- **U-NNPI Compliance**: Google Cloud has verified compliance with all 17 extra Unclassified Naval Nuclear Propulsion Information (U-NNPI) security controls through an accredited third-party assessment organization (3PAO) letter of attestation. U-NNPI is categorized as CUI, with access restricted to U.S. citizens who need to know; Google employees don't access IL5 Customer Data.

- **Google Workspace**: Google Workspace Enterprise Plus supports DoD IL2 workloads and has achieved a DoD IL4 PA, requiring Assured Controls Plus for IL4 deployment. Includes built-in security controls and feature sets to help customers obtain their own Authority to Operate (ATO).

- **IL6**: Google Distributed Cloud air-gapped (rack-based) and air-gapped appliance (portable standalone device) support IL6 at H-H-x categorization, enabling direct connectivity to the DoD Secret Internet Protocol Router Network (SIPRNet). Neither requires connectivity to Google Cloud.

- **Access to Documentation**: DoD ILx packages are shared only by DISA (not Google) and must be requested through the DoD Enterprise Mission Assurance Support Service (eMASS). Google Workspace DoD IL4 documentation is also accessed via eMASS or DISA liaison.

--- SOURCE 14: Overview of Assured Workloads ---
URL: https://docs.cloud.google.com/assured-workloads/docs/overview

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Google Cloud documentation page provides an overview of Assured Workloads, a service that enables organizations in the private and public sectors to configure a sovereign data and access boundary with residency, access, and personnel controls for sensitive workloads in the cloud. The service allows users to apply predefined control packages to folders to simplify management and configuration of regulated workloads while maintaining the scale, cost, and service availability benefits of commercial cloud infrastructure.

**Use cases:** Organizations with strict regulations for data storage, key management, and access (financial services, healthcare, governmental bodies); organizations that must store data within certain regions/countries; and organizations that must control Google Cloud personnel access to their data.

**Key capabilities:**
- **Control packages** (foundation for compliance enforcement) available in three types: regional data boundaries, regulatory data boundaries, and Sovereign Controls by Partners.
- **Regional data boundaries** restrict resource storage to specified geographic regions (e.g., EU Data Boundary restricts to EU-only regions).
- **Regulatory data boundaries** address specific compliance requirements including CJIS, FedRAMP Moderate/High, Healthcare and Life Sciences Controls (HIPAA/HITRUST), IL2/IL4/IL5, ITAR, and IRS Publication 1075.
- **Sovereign Controls by Partners** lets users use a local, trusted partner to manage encryption keys, access justification, and audits.
- **Personnel access control** via Assured Support (available with Enhanced or Premium Support), requiring Google support personnel to adhere to geographical and background check requirements (e.g., FedRAMP High requires US-located personnel with enhanced background checks).
- **Key management** controls vary by package — ITAR requires customer-managed encryption keys (CMEKs) with separate key management projects; support also includes Google-owned/managed keys (FIPS-140-2), Cloud EKM, and key import.
- **Workload updates** allow evaluation and maintenance of control package configurations, applying upgrades when newer versions are available.
- **Violation monitoring** tracks organization policy constraint violations and resource violations, with email notification options.

**Related access control services:** Access Approval (customer approval before Google personnel access), Access Transparency (logs of Google personnel activity), and Key Access Justifications (approve/deny key access requests).

**Control package renaming notice (effective June 2025):** Control package names in the console and APIs changed as of June 2025, reflected in the ComplianceRegime enums used in the Assured Workloads API. Only names changed, not underlying functionality. Examples include: "EU Data Boundary" became "EU Regions," "US Data Boundary" became "US Regions," "Data Boundary for ITAR" became "International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR)," and various "Regions" names replaced previous naming conventions. A complete mapping table of old to new names is provided.

The page also links to pricing information, available control packages, supported products, a free trial program, and Audit Manager for environment auditing. Last updated 2026-07-17 UTC.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Assured Workloads enables organizations in the private and public sectors to configure a sovereign data and access boundary with residency, access, and personnel controls for sensitive workloads in the cloud."

You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
Search

AWS Blogs

## [AWS Security Blog](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/)

# AWS Digital Sovereignty Pledge: Control without compromise

[French](#French) | [German](#German) | [Indonesian](#Indonesian) | [Italian](#Italian)  | [Japanese](#Japanese) | [Korean](#Korean) | [Portuguese](#Portuguese) | [Spanish](#Spanish) | [Arabic](https://aws.amazon.com/ar/security/blogs/aws-digital-sovereignty-pledge-control-without-compromise/)

We’ve always believed that for the cloud to realize its full potential it would be essential that customers have control over their data. Giving customers this sovereignty has been a priority for AWS since the very beginning when we were the only major cloud provider to allow customers to control the location and movement of their data. The importance of this foundation has only grown over the last 16 years as the cloud has become mainstream, and governments and standards bodies continue to develop security, data protection, and privacy regulations.

Today, having control over digital assets, or digital sovereignty, is more important than ever.

As we’ve innovated and expanded to offer the world’s most capable, scalable, and reliable cloud, we’ve continued to prioritize making sure customers are in control and able to meet regulatory requirements anywhere they operate. What this looks like varies greatly across industries and countries. In many places around the world, like in Europe, digital sovereignty policies are evolving rapidly. Customers are facing an incredible amount of complexity, and over the last 18 months, many have told us they are concerned that they will have to choose between the full power of AWS and a feature-limited sovereign cloud solution that could hamper their ability to innovate, transform, and grow. We firmly believe that customers shouldn’t have to make this choice.

This is why today we’re introducing the AWS Digital Sovereignty Pledge—our commitment to offering all AWS customers the most advanced set of sovereignty controls and features available in the cloud.

AWS already offers a range of [data protection](https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/data-protection/) features, accreditations, and contractual commitments that give customers control over where they locate their data, who can access it, and how it is used. We pledge to expand on these capabilities to allow customers around the world to meet their digital sovereignty requirements without compromising on the capabilities, performance, innovation, and scale of the AWS Cloud. At the same time, we will continue to work to deeply understand the evolving needs and requirements of both customers and regulators, and rapidly adapt and innovate to meet them.

### Sovereign-by-design

Our approach to delivering on this pledge is to continue to make the AWS Cloud sovereign-by-design—as it has been from day one. Early in our history, we received a lot of input from customers in industries like financial services and healthcare—customers who are among the most security- and data privacy-conscious organizations in the world—about what data protection features and controls they would need to use the cloud. We developed AWS encryption and key management capabilities, achieved compliance accreditations, and made contractual commitments to satisfy the needs of our customers. As customers’ requirements evolve, we evolve and expand the AWS Cloud. A couple of recent examples include the [data residency guardrails](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2021/11/aws-control-tower-controls-data-residency-requirements/) we added to [AWS Control Tower](https://aws.amazon.com/controltower/) (a service for governing AWS environments) late last year, which give customers even more control over the physical location of where customer data is stored and processed. In February 2022, we announced AWS services that adhere to the [Cloud Infrastructure Service Providers in Europe (CISPE) Data Protection Code of Conduct](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/aws-cloud-services-adhere-to-cispe-data-protection-code-of-conduct/), giving customers an independent verification and an added level of assurance that our services can be used in compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). These capabilities and assurances are available to all AWS customers.

We pledge to continue to invest in an ambitious roadmap of capabilities for data residency, granular access restriction, encryption, and resilience:

**1. Control over the location of your data**

Customers have always controlled the location of their data with AWS. For example, currently in Europe, customers have the choice to deploy their data into any of eight existing Regions. We commit to deliver even more services and features to protect our customers’ data. We further commit to expanding on our existing capabilities to provide even more fine-grained data residency controls and transparency. We will also expand data residency controls for operational data, such as identity and billing information.

**2. Verifiable control over data access**

We have designed and delivered first-of-a-kind innovation to restrict access to customer data. The [AWS Nitro System](https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/nitro/), which is the foundation of AWS computing services, uses specialized hardware and software to protect data from outside access during processing on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2). By providing a strong physical and logical security boundary, Nitro is designed to enforce restrictions so that nobody, including anyone in AWS, can access customer workloads on EC2. We commit to continue to build additional access restrictions that limit all access to customer data unless requested by the customer or a partner they trust.

**3. The ability to encrypt everything everywhere**

Currently, we give customers features and controls to encrypt data, whether in transit, at rest, or in memory. All AWS services already support encryption, with most also supporting encryption with customer managed keys that are inaccessible to AWS. We commit to continue to innovate and invest in additional controls for sovereignty and encryption features so that our customers can encrypt everything everywhere with encryption keys managed inside or [outside the AWS Cloud](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/announcing-aws-kms-external-key-store-xks/).

**4. Resilience of the cloud**

It is not possible to achieve digital sovereignty without resiliency and survivability. Control over workloads and high availability are essential in the case of events like supply chain disruption, network interruption, and natural disaster. Currently, AWS delivers the highest network availability of any cloud provider. Each AWS Region is comprised of multiple [Availability Zones](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/global-infrastructure/regions_az/) (AZs), which are fully isolated infrastructure partitions. To better isolate issues and achieve high availability, customers can partition applications across multiple AZs in the same AWS Region. For customers that are running workloads on premises or in intermittently connected or remote use cases, we offer services that provide specific capabilities for offline data and remote compute and storage. We commit to continue to enhance our range of sovereign and resilient options, allowing customers to sustain operations through disruption or disconnection.

### Earning trust through transparency and assurances

At AWS, earning customer trust is the foundation of our business. We understand that protecting customer data is key to achieving this. We also know that trust must continue to be earned through transparency. We are [transparent](https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/privacy-features/) about how our services process and transfer data. We will continue to challenge requests for customer data from law enforcement and government agencies. We provide guidance, compliance evidence, and contractual commitments so that our customers can use AWS services to meet compliance and regulatory requirements. We commit to continuing to provide the transparency and business flexibility needed to meet evolving privacy and sovereignty laws.

### Navigating changes as a team

Helping customers protect their data in a world with changing regulations, technology, and risks takes teamwork. We would never expect our customers to go it alone. Our trusted partners play a prominent role in bringing solutions to customers. For example, in Germany, T-Systems (part of Deutsche Telekom) offers [Data Protection as a Managed Service on AWS](https://www.t-systems.com/de/en/newsroom/news/data-protection-as-managed-service-498622). It provides guidance to ensure data residency controls are properly configured, offering services for the configuration and management of encryption keys and expertise to help guide their customers in addressing their digital sovereignty requirements in the AWS Cloud. We are doubling down with local partners that our customers trust to help address digital sovereignty requirements.

We are committed to helping our customers meet digital sovereignty requirements. We will continue to innovate sovereignty features, controls, and assurances within the global AWS Cloud and deliver them without compromise to the full power of AWS.

# AWS Digital Sovereignty Pledge: le contrôle sans compromis

Nous avons toujours pensé que pour que le cloud révèle son entier potentiel, il était essentiel que les clients aient le contrôle de leurs données. Garantir à nos clients cette souveraineté a été la priorité d’AWS depuis l’origine, lorsque nous étions le seul grand fournisseur de cloud à permettre aux clients de contrôler la localisation et le flux de leurs données. L’importance de cette démarche n’a cessé de croître ces 16 dernières années, à mesure que le cloud s’est démocratisé et que les gouvernements et les organismes de régulation ont développé des réglementations en matière de sécurité, de protection des données et de confidentialité.

Aujourd’hui, le contrôle des ressources numériques, ou souveraineté numérique, est plus important que jamais.

Tout en innovant et en nous développant pour offrir le cloud le plus performant, évolutif et fiable au monde, nous avons continué à ériger comme priorité la garantie que nos clients gardent le contrôle et soient en mesure de répondre aux exigences réglementaires partout où ils opèrent. Ces exigences varient considérablement selon les secteurs et les pays. Dans de nombreuses régions du monde, comme en Europe, les politiques de souveraineté numérique évoluent rapidement. Les clients sont confrontés à une incroyable complexité. Au cours des dix-huit derniers mois, ils nous ont rapporté qu’ils craignaient de devoir choisir entre les vastes possibilités offertes par les services d’AWS et une solution aux fonctionnalités limitées qui pourrait entraver leur capacité à innover, à se transformer et à se développer. Nous sommes convaincus que les clients ne devraient pas avoir à faire un tel choix.

C’est pourquoi nous présentons aujourd’hui l’*AWS Digital Sovereignty Pledge –* notre engagement à offrir à tous les clients AWS l’ensemble le plus avancé d’outils et de fonctionnalités de contrôle disponibles dans le cloud au service de la souveraineté.

AWS propose déjà une série de fonctionnalités de [protection des données](https://aws.amazon.com/fr/compliance/data-protection/), de certifications et d’engagements contractuels qui donnent à nos clients le plein contrôle de la localisation de leurs données, de leur accès et de leur utilisation. Nous nous engageons à développer ces capacités pour permettre à nos clients du monde entier de répondre à leurs exigences en matière de souveraineté numérique, sans faire de compromis sur les capacités, les performances, l’innovation et la portée du cloud AWS. En parallèle, nous continuerons à travailler pour comprendre en profondeur l’évolution des besoins et des exigences des clients et des régulateurs, et nous nous adapterons et innoverons rapidement pour y répondre.

### Souverain dès la conception

Pour respecter *l’AWS Digital Sovereignty Pledge*, notre approche est de continuer à rendre le cloud AWS souverain dès sa conception, comme il l’a été dès le premier jour. Aux débuts de notre histoire, nous recevions de nombreux commentaires de nos clients de secteurs tels que les services financiers et la santé – des clients qui comptent parmi les organisations les plus soucieuses de la sécurité et de la confidentialité des données dans le monde – sur les fonctionnalités et les contrôles de protection des données dont ils auraient besoin pour leur utilisation du cloud. Nous avons développé des compétences en matière de chiffrement et de gestion des données, obtenu des certifications de conformité et pris des engagements contractuels pour répondre aux besoins de nos clients. Nous développons le cloud AWS à mesure que les exigences des clients évoluent. Nous pouvons citer, parmi les exemples récents, les [*data residency guardrails*](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2021/11/aws-control-tower-controls-data-residency-requirements/) (les *garde-fous de la localisation des données*) que nous avons ajoutés en fin d’année dernière à l’[*AWS Control Tower*](https://aws.amazon.com/controltower/) (un service de gestion des environnements AWS) et qui donnent aux clients davantage de contrôle sur l’emplacement physique de leurs données, où elles sont stockées et traitées. En février 2022, nous avons annoncé de nouveaux services AWS adhérant au [Code de Conduite sur la protection des données de l’association CISPE](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/aws-cloud-services-adhere-to-cispe-data-protection-code-of-conduct/) (*Cloud Infrastructure Service Providers in Europe (CISPE)*). Ils apportent à nos clients une vérification indépendante et un niveau de garantie supplémentaire attestant que nos services peuvent être utilisés conformément au Règlement général sur la protection des données (RGPD). Ces capacités et ces garanties sont disponibles pour tous les clients d’AWS.

Nous nous engageons à poursuivre nos investissements conformément à une ambitieuse feuille de route pour le, , développement de capacités au service de la localisation des données, de la restriction d’accès granulaire (pratique consistant à accorder à des utilisateurs spécifiques différents niveaux d’accès à une ressource particulière), de chiffrement et de résilience :

**1. Contrôle de l’emplacement de vos données**

AWS a toujours permis à ses clients de contrôler l’emplacement de leurs données. Aujourd’hui en Europe, par exemple, les clients ont le choix de déployer leurs données dans l’une des huit Régions existantes. Nous nous engageons à fournir encore plus de services et de capacités pour protéger les données de nos clients. Nous nous engageons également à développer nos capacités existantes pour fournir des contrôles de localisation des données encore plus précis et transparents. Nous allons également étendre les contrôles de localisation des données pour les données opérationnelles, telles que les informations relatives à l’identité et à la facturation.

**2. Contrôle fiable de l’accès aux données**

Nous avons conçu et fourni une innovation unique en son genre pour restreindre l’accès aux données clients. Le [système AWS Nitro](https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/nitro/), qui constitue la base des services informatiques d’AWS, utilise du matériel et des logiciels spécialisés pour protéger les données contre tout accès extérieur pendant leur traitement sur les serveurs EC2. En fournissant une solide barrière de sécurité physique et logique, Nitro est conçu pour empêcher, y compris au sein d’AWS, l’accès à ces données sur EC2. Nous nous engageons à continuer à développer des restrictions d’accès supplémentaires qui limitent tout accès aux données de nos clients, sauf indication contraire de la part du client ou de l’un de ses prestataires de confiance.

**3. La possibilité de tout chiffrer, partout**

Aujourd’hui, nous offrons à nos clients des fonctionnalités et des outils de contrôle pour chiffrer les données, qu’elles soient en transit, au repos ou en mémoire. Tous les services AWS prennent déjà en charge le chiffrement, la plupart permettant également le chiffrement sur des clés gérées par le client et inaccessibles à AWS. Nous nous engageons à continuer d’innover et d’investir dans des outils de contrôle au service de la souveraineté et des fonctionnalités de chiffrement supplémentaires afin que nos clients puissent chiffrer l’ensemble de leurs données partout, avec des clés de chiffrement gérées à l’intérieur ou [à l’extérieur du cloud AWS](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/announcing-aws-kms-external-key-store-xks/).

**4. La résilience du cloud**

La souveraineté numérique est impossible sans résilience et sans capacités de continuité d’activité lors de crise majeure. Le contrôle des charges de travail et la haute disponibilité de réseau sont essentiels en cas d’événements comme une rupture de la chaîne d’approvisionnement, une interruption du réseau ou encore une catastrophe naturelle. Actuellement, AWS offre la plus haute disponibilité de réseau de tous les fournisseurs de cloud. Chaque Région AWS est composée de plusieurs [zones de disponibilité](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/global-infrastructure/regions_az/) (AZ), qui sont des portions d’infrastructure totalement isolées. Pour mieux isoler les difficultés et obtenir une haute disponibilité de réseau, les clients peuvent répartir les applications sur plusieurs zones dans la même Région AWS. Pour les clients qui exécutent des charges de travail sur place ou dans des cas d’utilisation à distance ou connectés par intermittence, nous proposons des services qui offrent des capacités spécifiques pour les données hors ligne, le calcul et le stockage à distance. Nous nous engageons à continuer d’améliorer notre gamme d’options souveraines et résilientes, permettant aux clients de maintenir leurs activités en cas de perturbation ou de déconnexion.

### Gagner la confiance par la transparence et les garanties

Chez AWS, gagner la confiance de nos clients est le fondement de notre activité. Nous savons que la protection des données de nos clients est essentielle pour y parvenir. Nous savons également que leur confiance s’obtient par la transparence. Nous sommes [transparents](https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/privacy-features/) sur la manière dont nos services traitent et transfèrent leurs données. Nous continuerons à nous contester les demandes de données des clients émanant des autorités judiciaires et des organismes gouvernementaux. Nous fournissons des conseils, des preuves de conformité et des engagements contractuels afin que nos clients puissent utiliser les services AWS pour répondre aux exigences de conformité et de réglementation. Nous nous engageons à continuer à fournir la transparence et la flexibilité commerciale nécessaires pour répondre à l’évolution du cadre réglementaire relatif à la confidentialité et à la souveraineté des données.

### Naviguer en équipe dans un monde en perpétuel changement

Aider les clients à protéger leurs données dans un monde où les réglementations, les technologies et les risques évoluent nécessite un travail d’équipe. Nous ne pouvons-nous résoudre à ce que nos clients relèvent seuls ces défis. Nos partenaires de confiance jouent un rôle prépondérant dans l’apport de solutions aux clients. Par exemple, en Allemagne, T-Systems (qui fait partie de Deutsche Telekom) propose la [protection des données en tant que service géré sur AWS](https://www.t-systems.com/de/en/newsroom/news/data-protection-as-managed-service-498622). L’entreprise fournit des conseils pour s’assurer que les contrôles de localisation des données sont correctement configurés, offrant des services pour la configuration en question, la gestion des clés de chiffrements et une expertise pour aider leurs clients à répondre à leurs exigences de souveraineté numérique dans le cloud AWS. Nous redoublons d’efforts avec les partenaires locaux en qui nos clients ont confiance pour les aider à répondre à ces exigences de souveraineté numérique.

Nous nous engageons à aider nos clients à répondre aux exigences de souveraineté numérique. Nous continuerons d’innover en matière de fonctionnalités, de contrôles et de garanties de souveraineté dans le cloud mondial d’AWS, tout en fournissant sans compromis et sans restriction la pleine puissance d’AWS.

# AWS Digital Sovereignty Pledge: Kontrolle ohne Kompromisse

Wir waren immer der Meinung, dass die Cloud ihr volles Potenzial nur dann erschließen kann, wenn Kunden die volle Kontrolle über ihre Daten haben. Diese Datensouveränität des Kunden genießt bei AWS schon seit den Anfängen der Cloud Priorität, als wir der einzige große Anbieter waren, bei dem Kunden sowohl Kontrolle über den Speicherort als auch über die Übertragung ihrer Daten hatten. Die Bedeutung dieser Grundsätze hat über die vergangenen 16 Jahre stetig zugenommen: Die Cloud ist im Mainstream angekommen, sowohl Gesetzgeber als auch Regulatoren entwickeln ihre Vorgaben zu IT-Sicherheit und Datenschutz stetig weiter.

Kontrolle bzw. Souveränität über digitale Ressourcen ist heute wichtiger denn je.

Unsere Innovationen und Entwicklungen haben stets darauf abgezielt, unseren Kunden eine Cloud zur Verfügung zu stellen, die skalierend und zugleich verlässlich global nutzbar ist. Dies beinhaltet auch unseren Kunden die Kontrolle zu gewährleisten die sie benötigen, damit sie alle ihre regulatorischen Anforderungen erfüllen können. Regulatorische Anforderungen sind länder- und sektorspezifisch. Vielerorts – wie auch in Europa – entstehen neue Anforderungen und Regularien zu digitaler Souveränität, die sich rasant entwickeln. Kunden sehen sich einer hohen Anzahl verschiedenster Regelungen ausgesetzt, die eine enorme Komplexität mit sich bringen. Innerhalb der letzten achtzehn Monate haben sich viele unserer Kunden daher mit der Sorge an uns gewandt, vor eine Wahl gestellt zu werden: Entweder die volle Funktionalität und Innovationskraft von AWS zu nutzen, oder auf funktionseingeschränkte „souveräne“ Cloud-Lösungen zurückzugreifen, deren Kapazität für Innovation, Transformation, Sicherheit und Wachstum aber limitiert ist. Wir sind davon überzeugt, dass Kunden nicht vor diese „Wahl“ gestellt werden sollten.

Deswegen stellen wir heute den „AWS Digital Sovereignty Pledge“ vor – unser Versprechen allen AWS Kunden, ohne Kompromisse die fortschrittlichsten Souveränitäts-Kontrollen und Funktionen in der Cloud anzubieten.

AWS bietet schon heute eine breite Palette an [Datenschutz](https://aws.amazon.com/de/compliance/data-protection/?nc1=h_ls)-Funktionen, Zertifizierungen und vertraglichen Zusicherungen an, die Kunden Kontrollmechanismen darüber geben, wo ihre Daten gespeichert sind, wer darauf Zugriff erhält und wie sie verwendet werden. Wir werden diese Palette so erweitern, dass Kunden überall auf der Welt, ihre Anforderungen an Digitale Souveränität erfüllen können, ohne auf Funktionsumfang, Leistungsfähigkeit, Innovation und Skalierbarkeit der AWS Cloud verzichten zu müssen. Gleichzeitig werden wir weiterhin daran arbeiten, unser Angebot flexibel und innovativ an die sich weiter wandelnden Bedürfnisse und Anforderungen von Kunden und Regulatoren anzupassen.

### **Sovereign-by-design**

Wir werden den „AWS Digital Sovereignty Pledge“ so umsetzen, wie wir das seit dem ersten Tag machen und die AWS Cloud gemäß unseres „sovereign-by-design“ Ansatz fortentwickeln. Wir haben von Anfang an, durch entsprechende Funktions- und Kontrollmechanismen für spezielle IT-Sicherheits- und Datenschutzanforderungen aus den verschiedensten regulierten Sektoren Lösungen gefunden, die besonders sensiblen Branchen wie beispielsweise dem Finanzsektor oder dem Gesundheitswesen frühzeitig ermöglichten, die Cloud zu nutzen. Auf dieser Basis haben wir die AWS Verschlüsselungs- und Schlüsselmanagement-Funktionen entwickelt, Compliance-Akkreditierungen erhalten und vertragliche Zusicherungen gegeben, welche die Bedürfnisse unserer Kunden bedienen. Dies ist ein stetiger Prozess, um die AWS Cloud auf sich verändernde Kundenanforderungen anzupassen. Ein Beispiel dafür sind die [Data Residency Guardrails](https://aws.amazon.com/de/about-aws/whats-new/2021/11/aws-control-tower-controls-data-residency-requirements/), um die wir [AWS Control Tower](https://aws.amazon.com/de/controltower/) Ende letzten Jahres erweitert haben. Sie geben Kunden die volle Kontrolle über die physikalische Verortung ihrer Daten zu Speicherungs- und Verarbeitungszwecken. Dieses Jahr haben wir einen Katalog von AWS Diensten veröffentlicht, die den [Cloud Infrastructure Service Providers in Europe (CISPE)](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/aws-cloud-services-adhere-to-cispe-data-protection-code-of-conduct/) erfüllen. Damit verfügen Kunden über eine unabhängige Verifizierung und zusätzliche Versicherung, dass unsere Dienste im Einklang mit der DSGVO verwendet werden können. Diese Instrumente und Nachweise stehen schon heute allen AWS Kunden zur Verfügung.

Wir haben uns ehrgeizige Ziele für unsere Roadmap gesetzt und investieren kontinuierlich in Funktionen für die Verortung von Daten (Datenresidenz), granulare Zugriffsbeschränkungen, Verschlüsselung und Resilienz:

**1. Kontrolle über den Ort der Datenspeicherung**

Bei AWS hatten Kunden immer schon die Kontrolle über Datenresidenz, also den Ort der Datenspeicherung. Aktuell können Kunden ihre Daten z.B. in 8 bestehenden Regionen innerhalb Europas speichern, von denen 6 innerhalb der Europäischen Union liegen. Wir verpflichten uns dazu, noch mehr Dienste und Funktionen zur Verfügung zustellen, die dem Schutz der Daten unserer Kunden dienen. Ebenso verpflichten wir uns, noch granularere Kontrollen für Datenresidenz und Transparenz auszubauen. Wir werden auch zusätzliche Kontrollen für Daten einführen, die insbesondere die Bereiche Identitäts- und Abrechnungs-Management umfassen.

**2. Verifizierbare Kontrolle über Datenzugriffe**

Mit dem [AWS Nitro System](https://aws.amazon.com/de/ec2/nitro/) haben wir ein innovatives System entwickelt, welches unberechtigte Zugriffsmöglichkeiten auf Kundendaten verhindert: Das Nitro System ist die Grundlage der AWS Computing Services (EC2). Es verwendet spezialisierte Hardware und Software, um den Schutz von Kundendaten während der Verarbeitung auf EC2 zu gewährleisten. Nitro basiert auf einer starken physikalischen und logischen Sicherheitsabgrenzung und realisiert damit Zugriffsbeschränkungen, die unautorisierte Zugriffe auf Kundendaten auf EC2 unmöglich machen – das gilt auch für AWS als Betreiber. Wir werden darüber hinaus für weitere AWS Services zusätzliche Mechanismen entwickeln, die weiterhin potentielle Zugriffe auf Kundendaten verhindern und nur in Fällen zulassen, die explizit durch Kunden oder Partner ihres Vertrauens genehmigt worden sind.

**3. Möglichkeit der Datenverschlüsselung überall und jederzeit**

Gegenwärtig können Kunden Funktionen und Kontrollen verwenden, die wir zur Verschlüsselung von Daten während der Übertragung, persistenten Speicherungen oder Verarbeitung in flüchtigem Speicher anbieten. Alle AWS Dienste unterstützen schon heute Datenverschlüsselung, die meisten davon auf Basis der Customer Managed Keys – d.h. Schlüssel, die von Kunden verwaltet werden und für AWS nicht zugänglich sind. Wir werden auch in diesem Bereich weiter investieren und Innovationen vorantreiben. Es wird zusätzliche Kontrollen für Souveränität und Verschlüsselung geben, damit unsere Kunden alles jederzeit und überall verschlüsseln können – [und das mit Schlüsseln, die entweder durch AWS oder durch den Kunden selbst bzw. ausgewählte Partner verwaltet werden können](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/announcing-aws-kms-external-key-store-xks/).

**4. Resilienz der Cloud**

Digitale Souveränität lässt sich nicht ohne Ausfallsicherheit und Überlebensfähigkeit herstellen. Die Kontrolle über Workloads und hohe Verfügbarkeit z.B. in Fällen von Lieferkettenstörungen, Netzwerkausfällen und Naturkatastrophen ist essenziell. Aktuell bietet AWS die höchste Netzwerk-Verfügbarkeit unter allen Cloud-Anbietern. Jede AWS Region besteht aus mehreren [Availability Zones (AZs)](https://aws.amazon.com/de/about-aws/global-infrastructure/regions_az/), die jeweils vollständig isolierte Partitionen unserer Infrastruktur sind. Um Probleme besser zu isolieren und eine hohe Verfügbarkeit zu erreichen, können Kunden Anwendungen auf mehrere AZs in derselben Region verteilen. Kunden, die Workloads on-premises oder in Szenarien mit sporadischer Netzwerk-Anbindung betreiben, bieten wir Dienste an, welche auf Offline-Daten und Remote Compute und Storage Anwendungsfälle angepasst sind. Wir werden unser Angebot an souveränen und resilienten Optionen ausbauen und fortentwickeln, damit Kunden den Betrieb ihrer Workloads auch bei Trennungs- und Disruptionsszenarien aufrechterhalten können.

### Vertrauen durch Transparenz und Zusicherungen

Der Aufbau eines Vertrauensverhältnisses mit unseren Kunden, ist die Grundlage unserer Geschäftsbeziehung bei AWS. Wir wissen, dass der Schutz der Daten unserer Kunden der Schlüssel dazu ist. Wir wissen auch, dass Vertrauen durch fortwährende Transparenz verdient und aufgebaut wird. Wir bieten schon heute [transparenten](https://aws.amazon.com/de/compliance/privacy-features/) Einblick, wie unsere Dienste Daten verarbeiten und übertragen. Wir werden auch in Zukunft Anfragen nach Kundendaten durch Strafverfolgungsbehörden und Regierungsorganisationen konsequent anfechten. Wir bieten Rat, Compliance-Nachweise und vertragliche Zusicherungen an, damit unsere Kunden AWS Dienste nutzen und gleichzeitig ihre Compliance und regulatorischen Anforderungen erfüllen können. Wir werden auch in Zukunft die Transparenz und Flexibilität an den Tag legen, um auf sich weiterentwickelnde Datenschutz- und Soveränitäts-Regulierungen passende Antworten zu finden.

### Den Wandel als Team bewältigen

Regulatorik, Technologie und Risiken sind stetigem Wandel unterworfen: Kunden dabei zu helfen, ihre Daten in diesem Umfeld zu schützen, ist Teamwork. Wir würden nie erwarten, dass unsere Kunden das alleine bewältigen müssen. Unsere Partner genießen hohes Vertrauen und spielen eine wichtige Rolle dabei, Lösungen für Kunden zu entwickeln. Zum Beispiel bietet T-Systems in Deutschland [Data Protection as a Managed Service auf AWS](https://www.t-systems.com/de/de/newsroom/news/data-protection-as-managed-service-498756) an. Das Angebot umfasst Hilfestellungen bei der Konfiguration von Kontrollen zur Datenresidenz, Zusatzdienste im Zusammenhang mit der Schlüsselverwaltung für kryptographische Verfahren und Rat bei der Erfüllung von Anforderungen zu Datensouveränität in der AWS Cloud. Wir werden die Zusammenarbeit mit lokalen Partnern, die besonderes Vertrauen bei unseren gemeinsamen Kunden genießen, intensivieren, um bei der Erfüllung der Digitalen Souveräntitätsanforderungen zu unterstützen.

Wir verpflichten uns dazu unseren Kunden bei der Erfüllung ihre Anforderungen an digitale Souveränität zu helfen. Wir werden weiterhin Souveränitäts-Funktionen, Kontrollen und Zusicherungen für die globale AWS Cloud entwickeln, die das gesamte Leistungsspektrum von AWS erschließen.

# Janji Kedaulatan Digital AWS: Kontrol tanpa kompromi

Kami selalu percaya bahwa agar *cloud* dapat merealisasi potensi sepenuhnya, penting bagi pelanggan untuk memiliki kontrol atas data mereka.
