**Key Points:**

**NERC Overview:** NERC is a not-for-profit regulatory authority ensuring reliability of the North American bulk power system, subject to oversight by the US FERC and Canadian authorities. FERC granted NERC the Electric Reliability Organization (ERO) designation in 2006 under the Energy Policy Act of 2005. NERC develops and enforces CIP reliability standards (first approved by FERC in 2007).

**Azure vs. Azure Government:** Both provide multi-tenant cloud platforms with logical isolation for customer data. Azure Government is a US government community cloud, physically separated from Azure, available only in the US to US-based registered entities, with contractual commitments limiting access to screened US persons. Azure is available to NERC entities in both the US and Canada. Both are suitable for registered entities deploying certain NERC CIP-compliant workloads.

**NERC CIP Data Categorization:** CIP standards apply to the Bulk Electric System (BES) (generally 100 kV and above; 20MVA+ generating units; 75MVA+ generating plants; Control Centers), not to distribution (with exceptions like UFLS, UVLS, Blackstart Resources). Key definitions include Cyber Asset, BES Cyber Asset (BCA), BES Cyber System (BCS), Electronic Security Perimeter (ESP), Protected Cyber Asset (PCA), Electronic Access Point (EAP), Electronic Access Control or Monitoring Systems (EACMS), and Control Center. Current NERC CIP definitions emphasize physical assets ("in those devices") and lack provisions for cloud concepts like virtualization and multi-tenancy. Workloads not subject to the 15-minute rule include transmission planning, SCADA historical data, AI/analytics, IoT monitoring, and NERC CIP audit evidence. BES Cyber System Information (BCSI) can be deployed in cloud if proper security controls are in place.

**Compliance Audits:** Azure and Azure Government maintain three relevant independent third-party audits: CSA STAR Certification and Attestation, AICPA SOC 2 Type 2 Attestation, and FedRAMP High P-ATOs (issued by the JAB) plus over 250 Moderate and High ATOs. The FedRAMP Moderate control baseline (325 controls) encompasses all NERC CIP requirements. NERC reviewed Azure controls and FedRAMP evidence for CIP-004-6 and CIP-011-2 (applicable to BCSI), concluding no extra guidance is needed for cloud BCSI deployment.

**Isolation and Security:** Both platforms provide logical isolation across identity (Microsoft Entra ID with RBAC), compute (Hyper-V virtualization, plus Azure Dedicated Host/Isolated VMs for physical isolation), networking (Azure VNet), and storage (encrypted at rest with Microsoft-managed or customer-managed keys via Azure Key Vault with FIPS 140 validated HSMs). Microsoft engineers have no default access to customer data. Azure Government requires US persons verification for operations personnel.

**Additional Considerations:** Nuclear electric utilities may face DoE 10 CFR Part 810 export control requirements. Registered entities are ultimately responsible for NERC CIP compliance. Microsoft offers a "Cloud implementation guide for NERC audits" (downloadable under NDA from the Service Trust Portal) with pre-filled Reliability Standard Audit Worksheets (RSAWs) narratives and control mappings between NERC CIP standards and FedRAMP Moderate baseline.
</summary>

<summary>
This webpage is Microsoft's official documentation page for "System and Organization Controls (SOC) 2 Type 2" compliance offering for Azure and other Microsoft cloud services.

**Overview:** SOC reports are internal control reports created by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) designed to examine services provided by a service organization so end users can assess and address risk associated with outsourced services. A SOC 2 Type 2 attestation is performed under SSAE No. 18 (including AT-C sections 105 and 205), the SOC 2 Reporting guide, and TSP section 100 (2017 Trust Services Criteria covering security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy). At the conclusion of a SOC 2 audit, the auditor renders an opinion in a SOC 2 Type 2 report describing the CSP's system, assessing the fairness of its controls description, and evaluating whether controls were designed appropriately, in operation, and operating effectively over a specified period.

**Azure and SOC 2 Type 2:** Microsoft Azure, Dynamics 365, and other Microsoft cloud services undergo independent third-party SOC 2 Type 2 audits conducted by a CPA firm. The Azure SOC 2 Type 2 attestation report also addresses the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM) version 4 and Germany's C5:2020 (Cloud Computing Compliance Criteria Catalogue by the German Federal Office for Information Security BSI).

**Audit reports:** The Azure SOC 2 Type 2 report covers Azure, Dynamics 365, Power Platform, and select Microsoft 365 services, accessible from the Service Trust Portal (STP) SOC reports section.

- SOC reports are based on a rolling 12-month audit period with new reports issued semi-annually (period ends 31-Mar and 30-Sep), taking about six weeks to publish. Bridge letters are issued the first week of each quarter covering the prior three-month period.

- Azure publishes a combined attestation report (C5:2020, SOC 2 Type 2, CSA STAR Attestation).

--- SOURCE 1: Breach Notification - Microsoft GDPR | Microsoft Learn ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/compliance/regulatory/gdpr-breach-notification

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Microsoft Learn documentation page on GDPR Breach Notification. It outlines Microsoft's approach to complying with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) regarding personal data breach notifications for organizations offering goods/services to EU residents or collecting/analyzing EU resident data.

**Key definitions**: A personal data breach is "a breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to, personal data transmitted, stored, or otherwise processed." Personal data refers to any information that can identify an individual directly or indirectly.

**Microsoft's breach notification obligations**: As a data processor, Microsoft ensures service customers can meet GDPR breach notification requirements as data controllers. Microsoft notifies customers of any personal data breach, except where personal data is confirmed unintelligible (e.g., encrypted data with confirmed key integrity). Initial notifications include a description of the breach's nature, approximate user impact, and mitigation steps. Data controllers are responsible for assessing privacy risks and determining whether a breach requires notification of their DPA.

**Product-specific breach notification details**:
1. **Office 365**: Microsoft invests in systems, processes, and personnel to reduce breach likelihood and mitigate consequences. Customers can contact Microsoft Support to report suspected breaches.
2. **Azure and Dynamics 365**: Microsoft operates a global 24x7 incident response service. Azure employs a shared responsibility model — Microsoft doesn't monitor security incidents within the customer's realm of responsibility. Microsoft determines breach priority/severity by investigating functional impact, recoverability, and information impact, working with global legal advisors. Customer notifications are delivered within 72 hours of breach declaration, except when notification would increase risk to other customers or when the 72-hour timeline limits available incident details.
3. **Microsoft Support and Professional Services**: Some data protection incidents may fall within the customer's realm of responsibility; Microsoft follows a documented industry-standard response plan.
4. **Windows**: The Windows diagnostic data processor configuration uses cloud infrastructure and built-in security features, backed by Microsoft's 24x7 global incident response service.

**Admin tools**: Tenant Administrators can set their organization's privacy contact via the Microsoft Entra admin center. The page also links to the Microsoft Trust Center for more GDPR information. Page last updated 2026-05-05.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A personal data breach is 'a breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to, personal data transmitted, stored, or otherwise processed.'", "As a data processor, Microsoft ensures that service customers can meet the GDPR's breach notification requirements as data controllers. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Microsoft Learn documentation page titled "Microsoft Support and Professional Services and Breach Notification Under the GDPR." It describes how Microsoft Professional Services (a team of over 21,000 consultants, Digital Advisors, engineers, and sales professionals across 191 countries and regions, supporting 46 languages) handles data protection incidents and GDPR breach notification requirements.

Key points covered:

- **Data protection incident definition**: A breach of security leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to Personal Data or Professional Services Data while processed by Microsoft.
- **Scope and limits**: Microsoft only responds to incidents within its realm of responsibility. Customer-driven incidents (e.g., customers inadvertently sending passwords, fraud against customers) are classified as "events" rather than Microsoft data protection incidents, though Microsoft will inform and assist customers.
- **Incident types**: The response team has identified various scenarios, from misdirected emails (requiring little investigation) to malicious personnel activity (requiring full forensic investigation).
- **Incident response process**: A triage process involving assessing the event, determining scope, assessing maliciousness, preliminary investigation with severity assignment, and stakeholder coordination. Detection methods include automated alerts, customer reports, external reports, anomaly observation, and malicious activity indicators.
- **Training and drills**: Annual data protection incident response drills are conducted with security, legal, and communications teams. All personnel must complete mandatory training on privacy fundamentals and GDPR regulations.
- **Notification requirements**: Microsoft targets notification to customers within 72 hours of declaring a data protection incident. Initial notifications may not include complete details, and some details may be withheld if disclosure would increase risk to others or interfere with law enforcement. Microsoft recognizes that customers, as data processors, are responsible for notifying Data Protection Authorities and their own data subjects.
- **Notification contents**: Nature of the breach, mitigation measures, product/service involved, exposure duration, volume of affected records, and sub-processor/supplier details (if known and applicable).
- **Post-mortems**: Internal post-mortems are conducted for higher-severity incidents, are highly confidential, and are reviewed by external auditors. Commercial customers with Unified Support or ISD should refer to the Microsoft Products and Services Data Protection Addendum (DPA).

The page notes that access requires authorization and was last updated on 2026-05-05. Additional resources link to Microsoft Professional Services trust information at https://aka.ms/pstrust.

--- SOURCE 5: Azure, Dynamics 365, and Power Platform breach ... ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/regulatory/gdpr-breach-azure-dynamics

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Microsoft Learn documentation page describes how Microsoft Azure, Dynamics 365, and Power Platform handle data breach notification under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). 

**Key Topics:**

**Security Approach:** Microsoft uses a "assume breach" security strategy built on defense-in-depth, incorporating privacy-by-design and privacy-by-default via the Security Development Lifecycle. Microsoft has a dedicated global, 24/7 incident response service, with data center protections including video monitoring, smart cards, and biometric controls.

**Shared Responsibility Model:** Microsoft doesn't monitor or respond to security incidents within the customer's realm of responsibility. A customer-only security compromise isn't a Microsoft security incident. Customers can use services like Microsoft Defender for Cloud for their own incident response.

**Five-Stage Incident Response Process:**
1. **Detect** - First indication of a potential incident
2. **Assess** - Incident response team member evaluates impact and severity
3. **Diagnose** - Technical/forensic investigation; if customer data may be exposed, Customer Incident Notification begins in parallel
4. **Stabilize and Recover** - Recovery plan created; crisis containment (e.g., quarantining systems) may happen immediately
5. **Close and Post-mortem** - Post-mortem created to revise policies and prevent recurrence

**Detection Triggers:** Automated system alerts, first-party reports, MSRC vulnerability reports, customer reports via support portals, Red Team/Blue Team security activity, and escalations by Microsoft service operators.

**Incident Classifications:** False positive, Security event, Security Incident/Customer Reportable Security/Privacy Incident (CRSPI), Privacy Event, and Privacy Incident/CRSPI. A CRSPI is declared when unauthorized access to customer data happened or likely happened, or when legal/contractual commitments require notification.

**Customer Notification:** Microsoft notifies impacted customers and regulatory authorities without undue delay, and in no more than 72 hours from declaring a breach, except in limited circumstances (e.g., notification might increase risk to other customers, or details are not yet available). Notifications are delivered via the Azure service health notifications blade (as Security Advisory), and/or email to Azure Subscription Administrators/Owners, Microsoft Entra Global Tenant Administrators, and Microsoft Entra tenant Technical Contacts. For Dynamics 365 and Power Platform, notifications go through the Microsoft 365 admin center Message Center with a Data Privacy tag.

**Dynamics 365/Power Platform:** These services follow the same technical and organizational measures as Azure for breach security, with built-in features covering secure identity, data protection, role-based security, and threat management.

**Important recommendation:** Microsoft recommends using roles with the fewest permissions, and minimizing the number of users with Global Administrator role to improve security.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Microsoft delivers customer notices without undue delay, and in any event in no more than 72 hours from the time it declared a breach except in some limited circumstances."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 11: Azure AI Foundry: Modified Abuse Monitoring, EU data residency, retention, and least-privilege RBAC for runtime agent - Microsoft Q&A ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/5966351/azure-ai-foundry-modified-abuse-monitoring-eu-data

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Microsoft Q&A forum post from a nonprofit organization (using an Azure Nonprofit Sponsorship subscription) asking for guidance on configuring Azure AI Foundry / Azure OpenAI with Microsoft Entra ID authentication and RBAC (no API keys) for a runtime-only agent identity. The question covers four areas, and a detailed moderator answer (by Manish Deshpande, Microsoft External Staff) addresses each:

**1. European Data Zone Processing (answered first as it changes priorities):** The Global Standard deployment is the issue. Data residency documentation states that global deployment types may process data in any Azure region, while Data Zone types (EU, US, APAC) process only within the specified zone, and Standard single-region types process in the deployment region. The EU Data Zone follows the Azure EU Data Boundary, which can include EFTA countries like Switzerland. However, an EU Data Zone deployment does not keep processing in Switzerland specifically — if Swiss residency is required, a single-region Standard in Switzerland North would be needed (with narrower model availability). A documented caveat notes that Global deployments may process prompts/completions outside the EU even for EU-based resources. Recommended action: apply Azure Policy to disable global deployments, verify the deployment SKU reads DataZoneStandard, and confirm the parent Foundry resource is in an EU region.

**2. Data Retention, Storage, and Human Review:** Data storage applies only to the abuse-monitoring path; automated path prompts/completions are not stored or used for training. The abuse-monitoring store is logically separated per customer and located in the Azure geography of the Foundry resource. Human review occurs only when automated review fails confidence thresholds or is unavailable, accessed via Secure Access Workstations (SAWs) with Just-In-Time (JIT) approval. For models sold by Azure in the EEA, authorized reviewers are located in the EEA. The moderator explicitly refused to give a default retention number, noting that while a "30 days" figure circulates in forums, it is absent from the current authoritative documentation and should not be used in compliance files without a written contractual answer under the Microsoft Products and Services Data Protection Addendum. After Modified Abuse Monitoring approval: "the data storage and human review process described above is not performed. However, automated review may still be conducted."

**3. Modified Abuse Monitoring:** Being a nonprofit does not itself qualify — eligibility is limited to customers managed by a Microsoft account team or under an eligible program. However, non-managed customers are invited to apply anyway via the same forms. Review time is 5-10 business days. The form is linked from the Abuse monitoring and Limited access pages. Caveats: approval is per model class (not blanket), and disabling human review may make abuse detection less accurate. Verification after approval: check the Foundry resource JSON view or run `az cognitiveservices account show` and look for `{"name":"ContentLogging","value":"false"}` in Capabilities — absence of the property means storage is still on.

**4. Least-Privilege RBAC:** The moderator explicitly says NOT to use Cognitive Services OpenAI User or Azure AI Developer roles for Foundry scenarios (these are for direct AI Services resource access). The recommended role is **Foundry Agent Consumer** — the least-privilege role for principals that only interact with agents, with exactly one of eight capabilities (interact with agent endpoints). GUIDs should be used instead of display names due to recent role renames. Scope should be narrowed to a single agent. However, Foundry Agent Consumer doesn't grant access to Agent Applications — Foundry User or a custom role would be needed if the agent is published as an Agent Application. Notably, Owner and Contributor roles cannot interact with agent endpoints at all (ARM control-plane only). The moderator also emphasized that role-based enforcement only works if key-based authentication is disabled (set disableLocalAuth on the Foundry account), since API keys bypass role assignments entirely.

A second, shorter answer by user "Nithin" suggests somewhat different guidance: using Modified Abuse Monitoring to disable "30-day human review data retention," provisioning resources in EU regions (Sweden Central or France Central), and assigning the Cognitive Services OpenAI User role at resource group level — though this conflicts with the moderator's explicit guidance against that role for Foundry scenarios.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Data residency for all deployment types: Data stored at rest remains in the designated Azure geography. However, inferencing data is processed as follows: Global types: May be processed in any Azure region. Data Zone types: The service processes data only within the Microsoft-specified data zone (US, EU, or Asia Pacific (APAC)). Standard (single region) types: The service processes data in the deployment region."

--- SOURCE 13: What is the EU Data Boundary? - Microsoft Privacy | Microsoft Learn ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/privacy/eudb/eu-data-boundary-learn

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Microsoft Learn documentation defines the **EU Data Boundary** — a geographically defined boundary within which Microsoft commits to store and process Customer Data and personal data for its enterprise online services, including Azure, Dynamics 365, Power Platform, and Microsoft 365. Professional Services Data will be stored at rest for these services. These commitments are subject to limited circumstances where data continues to be transferred outside the EU Data Boundary.

**Key definitions:**
- **Customer Data**: All data (including text, sound, video, image files, and software) provided to Microsoft by or on behalf of a Customer through use of the Online Service. It excludes Professional Services Data and configuration information (technical settings, resource names).
- **Personal data in system-generated logs**: Microsoft online services create system-generated logs as part of regular operation. Some logs contain fields that identify or can identify specific persons (e.g., product and service usage data, user activity logs).
- **Pseudonymization**: Per GDPR Article 4(5), pseudonymization replaces personally identifiable information with artificial identifiers/pseudonyms. Microsoft requires all personal data in system-generated logs to be pseudonymized using techniques including encryption, masking, tokenization, and data blurring. This enables authorized Microsoft personnel to work (e.g., DevOps identifying service issues across regions) without identifying or reidentifying users. Anonymization is not used because it would permanently alter data and compromise Microsoft's ability to ensure quality, reliability, and security of services.
- **Security controls for system-generated logs** include: data minimization via minimum retention policies, regular checks and scrubbing, limited usage solely for service operations, and access controls limiting rehydration/reidentification of personal data.
- **Professional Services Data**: All data provided to Microsoft through an engagement to obtain Professional Services (consulting services and technical support services).

**EU Data Boundary countries and datacenter locations:**
- Consists of EU countries (Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden) and EFTA countries (Liechtenstein, Iceland, Norway, Switzerland).
- Uses Microsoft datacenters announced/operating in Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland. Additional datacenters may be established in the future.

**How to configure services:**
- **Azure**: Regional services deployed in an EU Data Boundary region are in-scope. Non-regional services require configuration via Azure Resource Manager.
- **Dynamics 365 and Power Platform**: Requires BOTH (1) provisioning the tenant and all environments in the "European Union (EU) and European Free Trade Association (EFTA)" Macro Region Geography, AND (2) maintaining a billing address in an EU Data Boundary country. Meeting only one requirement doesn't place environments within the boundary.
- **Microsoft 365**: Customers with a sign-up location in an EU or EFTA country are in-scope; however, customers with Multi-Geo Capabilities are not in-scope even if their tenant is in an EU/EFTA country.

The documentation was last updated February 26, 2025, and reflects the current state of the EU Data Boundary as of the publication date.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The EU Data Boundary is a geographically defined boundary within which Microsoft has committed to store and process Customer Data and personal data for our Microsoft enterprise online services, including Azure, Dynamics 365, Power Platform, and Microsoft 365.
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Microsoft Q&A forum thread titled "Inquiry on Data Residency, Compliance, and Security for Microsoft Azure OpenAI Subscription." The original poster, Nikhil Bhatia, asked four questions about: (1) whether data/prompts submitted to Azure OpenAI via API remain in Switzerland, (2) how Microsoft handles data requests from US or foreign authorities, (3) what AI subscriptions are commonly used by law firms and how data is secured against training usage, and (4) Microsoft's GDPR/FDAP compliance framework and list of sub-processors.

Key answers provided across the thread:

**Data Residency in Switzerland:** Azure OpenAI Service is available in the Switzerland North region, allowing data residency within Switzerland when configured with regional deployment. However, for 'Global' deployment types, prompts and responses may be processed in any geography where the relevant model is deployed. For 'DataZone' deployments, data may be processed within the specified data zone. A Microsoft moderator (Manas R Mohanty) clarified that with Global Standard deployments, data at rest remains in the designated geography (e.g., Europe) but inference calls may route to any global location. DataZone deployments keep data at rest in the designated geography (e.g., Switzerland North) while inference may occur anywhere within that data zone.

**Government Data Requests:** Microsoft only responds to government or foreign authority data requests under applicable laws, following a rigorous legal review. Microsoft does not provide governments direct access to customer data, attempts to redirect requests to customers where legally possible, and notifies customers unless prohibited. Microsoft's process includes legal review, customer notification, challenging unlawful requests, transparency reports, escalation to legal/compliance teams, and documentation in the Data Protection Addendum (DPA).

**Service Provider Entity:** For EU customers, including Ireland, the service provider is Microsoft Ireland Operations Limited (MIOL), operating under Irish law. However, Microsoft remains a US-headquartered company subject to US legal obligations such as the CLOUD Act. US authorities can issue data requests, but Microsoft will challenge non-EU government requests and only comply if legally required under EU law, notifying customers where permissible. The DPA includes clauses on Data Transfers referencing the 2021 Standard Contractual Clauses, GDPR Article 46 safeguards, and Article 30(2) documentation.

**Law Firm Subscriptions:** Law firms typically use Standard, PTU (Provisioned Throughput Unit), or Batch API subscriptions for legal drafting, contract analysis, and e-discovery. EA (Enterprise Agreement) subscriptions offer higher quota and support. Azure OpenAI models are stateless—no prompts or completions are stored in the model, and they are not used to train, retrain, or improve base models by default. Data is encrypted at rest by default.

**Compliance:** Azure OpenAI is GDPR- and FDAP-compliant, offering encryption in transit and at rest, Customer-Managed Keys, and pseudonymization. Microsoft publishes a list of sub-processors through the Microsoft Trust Center. Compliance offerings for EMEA include EU Cloud CoC, EU GDPR, EU Model Clauses, Germany C5, and others. Microsoft offers Sovereign Cloud options and features like Data Guardian (Europe-based access approval) and External Key Management for maximum sovereignty.
</summary>

URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/regulatory/gdpr-breach-office365

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Microsoft Learn documentation page explains Office 365's breach notification obligations and practices under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). As a data processor, Microsoft commits to: (1) allowing customers to designate a dedicated privacy contact via the Privacy reader role in Message Center; (2) notifying customers of personal data breaches within 72 hours of a breach being declared, published to Message Center and accessible through the Microsoft 365 admin center; and (3) including in the initial notification the nature of the breach, an approximation of user impact, and applicable mitigation steps. Microsoft notifies customers of any personal data breach except those where personal data is confirmed to be unintelligible (e.g., encrypted data with verified key integrity).

The page details Office 365's investments in data security, including: access control systems with a "zero-standing access" policy and least-privilege principles; real-time security monitoring systems with automatic threat resolution and red-team penetration testing exercises; and personnel/processes including a detailed privacy breach Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) shared across teams, plus regular training on data classification and personal data handling.

In the event of a breach, customers can expect a consistent incident response lifecycle, consistent notification criteria (focusing on confidentiality, integrity, and availability of customer data), and consistent notification details (timing of breach and awareness, approximate number of users impacted, type of user data breached, and mitigation actions needed). Office 365, as a data processor, does not determine breach risk — data controllers must assess breach severity, decide whether users need notification, whether regulators (DPAs) need notification, and what mitigation steps the controller should take. Customers wishing to notify Microsoft should contact Microsoft Support, which interfaces with engineering teams. Microsoft recommends customers designate Message Center Privacy readers through the Microsoft 365 admin center to receive breach notifications. The page was last updated on May 5, 2026.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Microsoft announced the completion of the EU Data Boundary for the Microsoft Cloud in February 2025, an industry-leading solution that stores and processes public sector and commercial customer data within the EU and European Free Trade Association (EFTA) regions. This milestone, announced by Julie Brill (Corporate Vice President and Chief Privacy Officer) and Paul Lorimer (Corporate Vice President, Microsoft 365), enables European commercial and public sector customers to store and process customer data and pseudonymized personal data for Microsoft core cloud services—including Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, Power Platform, and most Azure services—within the EU and EFTA regions. Additionally, professional services data from technical support interactions for core cloud services is now stored within these regions.

The EU Data Boundary was delivered in three phases:
- Phase 1 (January 2023): Enabled storage and processing of customer data for core services including Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, Power Platform, and Azure.
- Phase 2 (January 2024): Expanded scope to include pseudonymized personal data.
- Phase 3 (February 2025): Ensured professional services data (customer logs and Microsoft-generated support case notes) for Microsoft 365, Power Platform, and Dynamics 365 support interactions are stored within EU/EFTA regions. Certain Azure services may require additional customer action for this commitment.

Microsoft's commitment to Europe spans more than 40 years, with over $20 billion invested in AI and cloud infrastructure across the continent over the past 16 months. Additional offerings include Microsoft 365 Advanced Data Residency for granular data location controls, Microsoft Cloud for Sovereignty for public sector customers, and the European Cloud Principles for transparency and accountability. Microsoft also highlighted its Secure Future Initiative (SFI) for cybersecurity, noting that in limited security instances requiring coordinated global response, essential data may be transferred with robust protections including encryption, strict access controls, and other security measures, with transparent information provided to customers.

<summary>
This is a Microsoft Security Community Blog post (updated December 2023/January 2024) providing a comprehensive FAQ about the EU Data Boundary for the Microsoft Cloud. The EU Data Boundary is a phased solution announced for rollout beginning January 1, 2023, that enables commercial and public sector customers in the EU and European Free Trade Association (EFTA) to store and process their customer data within the region for Microsoft 365, Azure, Power Platform, and Dynamics 365 services. The phased rollout includes three phases with completion projected for December 31, 2024. Phase 1 focuses on Customer Data storage and processing; Phase 2 adds pseudonymized personal data as an additional focus area.

Key points covered in the FAQ include:
- The EU Data Boundary reduces data flows out of Europe and builds on industry-leading data residency solutions, with Microsoft's cloud services already complying with or exceeding EU requirements.
- There is no loss of functionality and no additional cost (price increase) for customers adopting the EU Data Boundary.
- Microsoft publishes transparency documentation on the EU Data Boundary Trust Center webpage detailing any limited continuing transfers of Customer Data outside the EU.
- Subprocessors may still require access to Customer Data but are screened, background-checked, and subject to strict access controls via secure remote workstations.
- Support Data plans include storage of Professional Services Data in the EU Data Boundary, secure remote access, and an optional paid offering ensuring first technical support contact is located in the EU.
- The EU Data Boundary is distinct from but complementary to Microsoft 365 Advanced Data Residency and Microsoft Cloud for Sovereignty.
- Microsoft remains certified under the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework and will continue investing in the EU Data Boundary.
- Microsoft commits to defending customer data against government requests, directing requests to customers, challenging unlawful demands, and providing monetary compensation for GDPR violations causing harm.
- Security measures include encryption, access controls, pseudonymization, and robust global threat analysis; limited data transfers outside the EU for security analysis are integral to maintaining defenses against globally coordinated cyber threats.

# How to Enforce Data Sovereignty with Google Cloud Regions

Learn how to enforce data sovereignty requirements on Google Cloud using region restrictions, organization policies, and resource location constraints.

![Nawaz Dhandala](https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/nawazdhandala?s=64 "Nawaz Dhandala")

By @nawazdhandala

• Feb 17, 2026 •  Reading time

[GCP](/blog/tag/gcp)   [Data Sovereignty](/blog/tag/data-sovereignty)   [Organization Policies](/blog/tag/organization-policies)   [Compliance](/blog/tag/compliance)   [Cloud Governance](/blog/tag/cloud-governance)

## On this page

---

Data sovereignty laws are getting stricter around the world. Whether it is GDPR in Europe, LGPD in Brazil, or data localization requirements in India and Russia, the mandate is clear: certain data must stay within specific geographic boundaries. On Google Cloud, enforcing this is not just about choosing the right region when you create a resource. You need guardrails that prevent anyone in your organization from accidentally or deliberately storing data in the wrong place.

This guide covers how to set up those guardrails using organization policies, resource location constraints, and monitoring.

## Understanding GCP's Region and Zone Structure

Google Cloud resources exist in regions and zones. A region is a specific geographic area like us-central1 (Iowa) or europe-west1 (Belgium). Zones are isolated locations within a region. Multi-regional locations like "US" or "EU" span multiple regions within a geographic boundary.

For data sovereignty, you care about regions because, for supported data-containing services, a resource's location reflects where that resource's data is stored. When a regulation says data must stay in the EU, you need to ensure supported resources only get created in EU regions and that service-specific replication, backup, and export settings do not move data to non-EU locations.

## Step 1: Define Your Location Requirements

Start by mapping your regulatory requirements to GCP regions. Here is a typical mapping for an organization that operates in Europe and the US:

| Data Category | Allowed Regions | Regulation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EU Customer PII | europe-west1, europe-west3, europe-west4 | GDPR |
| US Financial Data | us-central1, us-east1, us-east4 | SOX |
| General Internal | Any US or EU region | Internal Policy |

## Step 2: Apply Resource Location Restrictions

The `gcp.resourceLocations` organization policy constraint restricts where resources can be created. Apply it at the organization, folder, or project level.

```
# Set the organization policy to restrict resource creation to EU regions only # Apply this to the folder containing EU customer data projects gcloud resource-manager org-policies set-policy \ --folder=EU_FOLDER_ID \ policy-eu-only.yaml
```

Create the policy file:

```
# policy-eu-only.yaml # This restricts all resource creation to EU locations only constraint: constraints/gcp.resourceLocations listPolicy: allowedValues: - "in:eu-locations" # All EU regions deniedValues: []
```

For more granular control, specify individual regions:

```
# policy-specific-eu-regions.yaml # Allow only specific EU regions that meet your requirements constraint: constraints/gcp.resourceLocations listPolicy: allowedValues: - "in:europe-west1-locations" # Belgium - "in:europe-west3-locations" # Frankfurt - "in:europe-west4-locations" # Netherlands
```

```
# Apply the specific regions policy gcloud resource-manager org-policies set-policy \ --folder=EU_FOLDER_ID \ policy-specific-eu-regions.yaml # Verify the policy is applied gcloud resource-manager org-policies describe \ gcp.resourceLocations \ --folder=EU_FOLDER_ID
```

## Step 3: Restrict Service-Specific Locations

Some services have their own location settings that you should also constrain.

### BigQuery

```
# Create a BigQuery dataset that can only exist in the EU bq mk --dataset \ --location=EU \ --default_table_expiration=0 \ --description="EU-only customer data" \ project_id:eu_customer_data
```

### Cloud Storage

```
# Create a bucket in a specific EU region gcloud storage buckets create gs://eu-customer-data-bucket \ --location=europe-west1 \ --uniform-bucket-level-access # Set a retention policy to prevent deletion of compliance data gcloud storage buckets update gs://eu-customer-data-bucket \ --retention-period=2592000 # 30 days in seconds
```

### Cloud SQL

```
# Create a Cloud SQL instance in an EU region gcloud sql instances create eu-postgres \ --database-version=POSTGRES_15 \ --tier=db-custom-4-16384 \ --region=europe-west1 \ --availability-type=REGIONAL
```

## Step 4: Prevent Data Replication to Wrong Regions

Even with location restrictions, data can move through replication, backups, exports, or cross-region operations. Lock these down too. The resource locations constraint helps prevent creation of supported resources, including multi-region and dual-region Cloud Storage buckets, outside the allowed boundary. You still need to configure service-specific replication and backup settings for each service you use.

```
# policy-disable-non-eu-locations.yaml # Prevent supported resources from being created outside EU locations constraint: constraints/gcp.resourceLocations listPolicy: allowedValues: - "in:eu-locations"
```

For Spanner, which can be configured with multi-region instances:

```
# Create a Spanner instance using an EU-only multi-region config gcloud spanner instances create eu-spanner \ --config=eur3 \ --description="EU-only Spanner instance" \ --nodes=3
```

## Step 5: Set Up Custom Organization Policies

Beyond the built-in location constraint, create custom organization policies for more specific controls.

```
# custom-policy-eu-bigquery-location.yaml # Require BigQuery datasets covered by this policy to use the EU multi-region name: organizations/ORG_ID/customConstraints/custom.bigquery.requireEuLocation resourceTypes: - bigquery.googleapis.com/Dataset methodTypes: - CREATE - UPDATE condition: "resource.location == 'EU'" actionType: ALLOW displayName: "Require EU BigQuery dataset location" description: "Only allows BigQuery datasets in the EU multi-region"
```

```
# Create the custom constraint gcloud org-policies set-custom-constraint custom-policy-eu-bigquery-location.yaml
```

Then create the policy file that enforces the custom constraint:

```
# custom-policy-enforcement.yaml name: organizations/ORG_ID/policies/custom.bigquery.requireEuLocation spec: rules: - enforce: true
```

```
# Apply it to the organization gcloud org-policies set-policy \ custom-policy-enforcement.yaml
```

## Step 6: Monitor for Compliance Violations

Set up monitoring to detect any resources created in unauthorized locations, even if someone manages to bypass the policies.

```
from google.cloud import asset_v1 def find_resources_in_wrong_locations(org_id, allowed_regions): """Scan for resources that exist outside allowed regions.""" client = asset_v1.AssetServiceClient() parent = f"organizations/{org_id}" # Search for all compute and storage resources request = asset_v1.SearchAllResourcesRequest( scope=parent, asset_types=[ "compute.googleapis.com/Instance", "storage.googleapis.com/Bucket", "bigquery.googleapis.com/Dataset", "sqladmin.googleapis.com/Instance", ], ) violations = [] for resource in client.search_all_resources(request=request): # Check if the resource location matches allowed regions location = resource.location if location and not any( location.startswith(region) for region in allowed_regions ): violations.append({ "resource": resource.name, "type": resource.asset_type, "location": location, "project": resource.project, }) return violations # Check for EU compliance eu_regions = ["europe-west1", "europe-west3", "europe-west4", "EU", "eu"] violations = find_resources_in_wrong_locations("123456789", eu_regions) for v in violations: print(f"VIOLATION: {v['type']} in {v['location']}: {v['resource']}")
```

## Step 7: Automate Remediation

When a violation is detected, automatically tag it and notify the responsible team.

```
import base64 import json def remediate_location_violation(event, context): """Respond to resources created in unauthorized locations.""" # Parse the Cloud Asset Inventory Pub/Sub notification. asset = json.loads(base64.b64decode(event["data"]).decode("utf-8")) resource_name = asset.get("asset", {}).get("name", "") location = asset.get("asset", {}).get("resource", {}).get("location", "") # Check against allowed locations for this folder/project allowed = get_allowed_locations(asset.get("asset", {}).get("ancestors", [])) if location not in allowed: # Send alert to security team send_alert( channel="security-alerts", message=f"Data sovereignty violation detected: {resource_name} " f"created in {location}. Allowed locations: {allowed}" ) # Tag the resource as non-compliant tag_resource_non_compliant(resource_name) # Optionally, delete the resource if policy allows # delete_resource(resource_name)
```

## Using Assured Workloads for Stronger Guarantees

For stronger data residency and personnel access controls, use Assured Workloads. This creates a managed environment where the selected control package applies data location controls and, where supported by that package, support and personnel access controls.

```
# Create an Assured Workloads environment for EU sovereignty gcloud assured workloads create \ --organization=ORG_ID \ --location=europe-west1 \ --display-name="EU Sovereign Workload" \ --compliance-regime=eu-regions-and-support \ --billing-account=billingAccounts/BILLING_ACCOUNT_ID \ --enable-sovereign-controls=true \ --next-rotation-time="2026-03-01T00:00:00Z" \ --rotation-period="2592000s"
```

This is a OneUptime blog post (by Nawaz Dhandala, Feb 17, 2026, technically validated May 28, 2026) titled "How to Enforce Data Sovereignty with Google Cloud Regions." It provides a comprehensive guide for enforcing data sovereignty requirements on Google Cloud using organization policies, resource location constraints, and monitoring.

Key content:
- Data sovereignty laws (GDPR, LGPD, India, Russia) require data to stay within specific geographic boundaries.
- GCP resources exist in regions/zones; a resource's location reflects where its data is stored.
- Step-by-step guide:
  1. Define location requirements by mapping regulatory needs to GCP regions (e.g., EU Customer PII → europe-west1/3/4 for GDPR; US Financial Data → us-central1/us-east1/us-east4 for SOX).
  2. Apply resource location restrictions using the `gcp.resourceLocations` organization policy constraint (at organization, folder, or project level), using listPolicy with allowedValues like "in:eu-locations" or specific regions.
  3. Restrict service-specific locations for BigQuery (--location=EU), Cloud Storage (e.g., europe-west1, with retention policies), and Cloud SQL (--region=europe-west1).
  4. Prevent data replication to wrong regions via resource location constraints and service-specific configs (e.g., Spanner EU-only multi-region config `eur3`).
  5. Set up custom organization policies for specific controls (e.g., custom.bigquery.requireEuLocation constraint requiring BigQuery datasets in EU multi-region).
  6. Monitor for compliance violations using Google Cloud Asset Inventory (SearchAllResourcesRequest) to scan compute, storage, BigQuery, and SQL resources outside allowed regions.
  7. Automate remediation via Cloud Asset Inventory Pub/Sub notifications that tag non-compliant resources and alert security teams.
- For stronger guarantees, use Assured Workloads with EU compliance regime (`eu-regions-and-support`) and sovereign controls enabled.
- Conclusion: Data sovereignty requires defense-in-depth—organization policies for prevention, asset inventory scans for detection, and automated remediation for response.

## Objective

This reference document provides information about where F5® Distributed Cloud Services process and store customer data, including persistent storage locations, non-persistent processing locations, and the sub-processors used by each supported service.

This document helps you understand the geographic locations where customer data may reside or be processed, helping you evaluate data residency, data localization, and compliance requirements for your deployments.

See [F5 Privacy Statements](https://www.f5.com/company/policies#privacy) for a description of the data that is processed for each service.

* **Non-Persistent Storage Location** is a location where data is stored in memory for the purpose of immediate or imminent processing, and is cleared or overwritten from the memory after the processing is complete. For example, an F5 Distributed Cloud WAF, running at a Regional or Customer Edge, may process an HTTP request in main memory. After processing the request, WAF may clear the memory or overwrite the memory with a new request.
* **Persistent Storage Location** means a location where data is stored for processing that is necessary to provide the service(s) that a customer subscribes to, but may not be immediate nor imminent. For example, an F5 Distributed Cloud service may store data for a customer at a selected location for 30 days. During that time, the customer may execute queries or generate reports based on that data. F5 SOC team may also query that data to identify malicious traffic or attack campaigns against that customer.

## **How GCP Regions and Zones work?**

Google Cloud Platform (GCP) organizes its infrastructure into regions and zones to ensure high availability, redundancy, and low-latency performance for users worldwide.

**Regions** are specific geographical locations where GCP resources are deployed. Each region consists of multiple **zones**. A zone is an isolated data center within a region. The separation into regions and zones allows GCP to provide high availability and fault tolerance. If one zone experiences an outage, other zones within the same region can continue to operate, minimizing disruptions to services.

Each region is identified by a specific name, such as “us-central1” for the central United States or “asia-east1” for East Asia. These regions are strategically distributed across the globe, enabling users to deploy resources close to their customers, reducing latency and improving performance.

**Zones**, on the other hand, are designated with additional identifiers, like “us-central1-a” or “asia-east1-b”. Each zone is a collection of GCP resources isolated from others within the same region. This isolation means that zones have independent power, cooling, and networking, reducing the risk of simultaneous failures.

GCP users can deploy their resources across multiple zones within a region to ensure redundancy. For example, by setting up a cloud storage system in two different zones within the same region, users can achieve high availability. If one zone goes down, the other can take over, ensuring continuous service.

Furthermore, GCP offers various tools and services, such as multi-region storage and global load balancing, to help users seamlessly manage their applications across multiple regions and zones. This architecture not only boosts performance but also provides a robust disaster recovery framework, making GCP a reliable choice for businesses with critical uptime requirements.

## **Google cloud Regions and Zones expansion**

In recent years, GCP has significantly ramped up its global presence. For example, in 2023, [GCP opened new regions in Berlin (Germany), Doha (Qatar), Dammam (Saudi Arabia), Johannesburg (South Africa)](https://cloud.google.com/about/locations#lightbox-regions-map) each comprising multiple zones. This expansion allows businesses in these regions to run applications closer to their customers, reducing latency and improving performance.

Google has invested billions of dollars in its cloud infrastructure. For instance, the company committed to investing $10 billion in 2020 alone to expand data centers and renewable energy projects. Each new region represents a substantial financial commitment, often ranging from hundreds of millions to over a billion dollars, depending on the complexity and scale of the data centers.

The Jakarta region, for example, involved a significant investment to build state-of-the-art facilities that comply with local regulations and meet the high standards of performance and security expected by GCP customers. Additionally, investments in undersea cables, such as the Dunant and Curie cables, further enhance connectivity between regions, ensuring faster and more reliable global communications.

Google Cloud announced that they will further expand into the following regions: Mexico, Malaysia, Thailand, New Zealand, Greece, Norway, Austria, and Sweden.

## **Wrap Up: Optimizing Your GCP Footprint**

Understanding Google Cloud Platform (GCP) regions and zones is crucial for optimizing your cloud environment. Considerations like latency, data residency regulations, and cost can all influence your choice of location. For example, deploying resources closer to your users can minimize latency, while some regions might offer more competitive pricing.

While GCP provides default regions, zones and virtual private clouds (VPCs) with each account, managing numerous resources across diverse locations can quickly become complex. This can lead to “shadow IT” or hidden costs associated with unused resources. Here’s where [Holori](https://holori.com/) steps in.

Holori acts as your GCP cartographer, automatically generating a visual representation of your entire cloud infrastructure. This includes pinpointing your resources across regions and zones, alongside valuable cost insights. By visualizing your GCP environment, Holori helps you identify underutilized resources (“zombie resources”) and optimize your overall cloud spend. # Google Expands Sovereign Cloud to Address EU Data Sovereignty Requirements

![Google Expands Sovereign Cloud to Address EU Data Sovereignty Requirements](https://futurumgroup.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Google-Expands-Sovereign-Cloud-to-Address-EU-Data-Sovereignty-Requirements.png.webp)

Analyst(s): Daniel Newman  
Publication Date: June 10, 2025

Google Cloud expands its sovereign cloud portfolio with enhanced data control capabilities, new validation services, and in-region operational models. These additions aim to address growing customer concerns over data residency, regulatory compliance, and geopolitical risk, particularly in Europe.

## What is Covered in this Article:

**The News:** Google Cloud has introduced major enhancements to its sovereign cloud offerings, focused on delivering more stringent data location control, independent security validation, and national compliance support for enterprise customers. New capabilities include an upgraded Google Cloud Data Boundary, the launch of User Data Shield, and expanded Google Cloud Dedicated deployments with local operators in Europe.

The company also confirmed that Google Cloud Air-Gapped, designed for high-security environments, is now authorized to handle classified US government workloads. These updates come as geopolitical friction and EU regulatory scrutiny continue to intensify pressure on US hyperscalers to adapt to local data sovereignty expectations.

## Google Expands Sovereign Cloud to Address EU Data Sovereignty Requirements

**Analyst Take:** Google’s latest updates to its sovereign cloud offering come at a time when European customers are increasingly focused on keeping their data within national borders and under local control. These moves show Google is trying to meet that demand by combining strong technical features with region-specific operational models. Instead of offering a one-size-fits-all solution, Google is building a flexible framework that can support both security and compliance across multiple jurisdictions.

## Reinforced Data Boundary Empowers Customers

Google’s updated Cloud Data Boundary now allows customers to choose exactly where their data is stored and processed, even down to the country level. They can also hold onto their own encryption keys and decide who can access their data or block access entirely if needed. For users of Google Workspace, there’s an option to limit data handling to the US or EU and to use encryption that even Google can’t bypass. These features help customers meet strict regional data rules while still using Google’s powerful cloud tools, including AI, Confidential Computing, and External Key Management. The flexibility ensures organizations can stay compliant without giving up performance or reach.

## Built-In Security Testing Raises Confidence

The new User Data Shield service adds an extra layer of security by regularly testing the applications built on Google’s sovereign cloud systems. Mandiant, a well-known cybersecurity firm, powers these tests. User Data Shield introduces recurring security testing capabilities to customer applications built on sovereign infrastructure, leveraging Mandiant’s frontline expertise. This allows businesses to prove to regulators and stakeholders that their systems remain secure and compliant over time. Rather than just setting up controls and hoping they hold, companies now have an active way to monitor and validate their data protection efforts, building long-term trust in Google’s platform.

## Dedicated Partnerships Enhance Regional Alignment

Google’s ongoing execution of its Dedicated Cloud model, including its Trusted Cloud deployment with Thales via S3NS in France and its upcoming rollout with T-Systems in Germany, creates an operational structure that aligns directly with national standards such as France’s SecNumCloud. These deployments bring Google Cloud’s full capabilities – including GPU-based support for AI – to customers under local operational control. This approach ensures that data remains under national jurisdiction, a critical factor for regulated sectors in Europe, and positions Google as a cooperative partner rather than an external provider imposing foreign infrastructure standards.

## Air-Gapped Architecture Addresses the Highest Sensitivity Needs

Google offers a fully air-gapped cloud environment for organizations handling the most sensitive information, such as defense and intelligence agencies. This means the systems can run without any connection to external networks, reducing the risk of data leaks. These environments can be operated by Google, its partners, or the customer, and they are already cleared to handle classified US government data. The offering is built on open tools but is designed for continuity even during disruptions, making it suitable for the most demanding use cases.

# EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications

This page describes the set of controls that are applied on EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications workloads in Assured Workloads. It provides detailed information about [data residency](/assured-workloads/docs/data-residency), [supported Google Cloud products](#products_endpoints) and their API endpoints, and any applicable [restrictions or limitations](#restrictions_limitations) on those products.

The following additional information applies to EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications:

* **Data residency**: The EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications control package sets data location controls to support [EU-only regions](/assured-workloads/docs/locations#europe). For more information, see the [Google Cloud-wide organization policy constraints](#org_cloud) section.
* **Support**: Technical support services for EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications workloads are available with Enhanced or Premium [Cloud Customer Care](/support) subscriptions. EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications workloads support cases are routed to EU personnel located in the EU. For more information, see [Getting support](/assured-workloads/docs/getting-support#eu-data-boundary-access-justifications).
* **Pricing**: The EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications control package is included in Assured Workloads' *Premium tier*, which incurs a 5% additional charge. For more information, see [Assured Workloads pricing](https://cloud.google.com/assured-workloads/pricing).

## Prerequisites

Verify that you meet and have completed the following prerequisites before deploying workloads to EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications:

* Create an EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications folder using Assured Workloads and deploy your workloads only in that folder.
* Don't change the default organization policy constraint values unless you understand and are willing to accept the data residency risks that might occur.
* Don't use [Google Cloud MCP servers](/mcp/overview) unless otherwise noted. EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications doesn't provide data residency controls for in-use data and in-transit data with Google Cloud MCP servers. To block unwanted Google Cloud MCP servers access, see the [Control Google Cloud MCP servers use with IAM page](/mcp/control-mcp-use-iam) page.
* When accessing the Google Cloud console for EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications workloads, you must use one of the following EU-specific [Jurisdictional Google Cloud console](/assured-workloads/docs/jurisdictional-console) URLs:
  + [console.eu.cloud.google.com](https://console.eu.cloud.google.com)
  + [console.eu.cloud.google](https://console.eu.cloud.google) for federated identity users
* Consider adopting the general security best practices provided in the [Google Cloud security best practices center](https://cloud.google.com/security/best-practices).

## Supported products and API endpoints

Unless otherwise noted, users can access all supported products through the Google Cloud console. Restrictions or limitations that affect the features of a supported product, including those that are enforced through [organization policy constraint settings](/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/overview#how_organization_policy_works), are listed in the following table.

If a product is not listed, that product is unsupported and has not met the control requirements for EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications. Unsupported products are not recommended for use without due diligence and a thorough understanding of your responsibilities in the [shared responsibility model](/assured-workloads/docs/shared-responsibility). Before using an unsupported product, ensure that you are aware of and are willing to accept any associated risks involved, such as negative impacts to data residency or data sovereignty.

## Restrictions and limitations

The following sections describe Google Cloud-wide or product-specific restrictions or limitations for features, including any organization policy constraints that are set by default on EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications folders. Other applicable organization policy constraints—even if not set by default—can provide additional defense-in-depth to further protect your organization's Google Cloud resources.

### Google Cloud-wide

#### Affected Google Cloud-wide features

| Feature | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Google Cloud console | To access the Google Cloud console when using the EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications control package, you must use one of the following URLs:   * [console.eu.cloud.google.com](https://console.eu.cloud.google.com) * [console.eu.cloud.google](https://console.eu.cloud.google) for federated identity users |

#### Google Cloud-wide organization policy constraints

The following [organization policy constraints](/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/org-policy-constraints) apply across Google Cloud.

| Organization policy constraint | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [`gcp.resourceLocations`](/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/defining-locations) | Set to the following locations in the `allowedValues` list:  * `europe-central2` * `europe-north1` * `europe-north2` * `europe-southwest1` * `europe-west1` * `europe-west10` * `europe-west12` * `europe-west3` * `europe-west4` * `europe-west8` * `europe-west9`  This value restricts creation of new resources to the selected values. When set, no resources can be created in any other regions, multi-regions, or locations outside of the selection. See [Resource locations supported services](/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/defining-locations-supported-services) for a list of resources that can be restricted by the Resource Locations organization policy constraint, as some resources may be out of scope and cannot be restricted.   Changing this value by making it less restrictive potentially undermines data residency by allowing data to be created or stored outside of a compliant data boundary. |
| `gcp.restrictCmekCryptoKeyProjects` | Set to `under:organizations/your-organization-name`, which is your Assured Workloads organization. You can further restrict this value by specifying a project or folder.   Limits the scope of approved folders or projects that can provide [Cloud KMS keys](/kms/docs/algorithms) for encrypting at-rest data using CMEK. This constraint prevents unapproved folders or projects from providing encryption keys, thus helping to guarantee data sovereignty for in-scope services' at-rest data. |
| [`gcp.restrictNonCmekServices`](/kms/docs/cmek-org-policy#require-cmek) | Set to a list of all in-scope [API service names](/iam/docs/full-resource-names), including:  * `aiplatform.googleapis.com` * `artifactregistry.googleapis.com` * `bigquery.googleapis.com` * `bigquerydatatransfer.googleapis.com` * `bigtable.googleapis.com` * `cloudfunctions.googleapis.com` * `composer.googleapis.com` * `compute.googleapis.com` * `container.googleapis.com` * `dataflow.googleapis.com` * `dataproc.googleapis.com` * `documentai.googleapis.com` * `integrations.googleapis.com` * `logging.googleapis.com` * `notebooks.googleapis.com` * `pubsub.googleapis.com` * `run.googleapis.com` * `secretmanager.googleapis.com` * `spanner.googleapis.com` * `sqladmin.googleapis.com` * `storage.googleapis.com` * `workstations.googleapis.com`  Some features may be affected for each of the services listed above.    Each listed service requires [Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)](/kms/docs/cmek). CMEK encrypts at-rest data with a key managed by you, not Google's default encryption mechanisms.    Changing this value by removing one or more in-scope services from the list may undermine data sovereignty, because new at-rest data will be automatically encrypted using Google's own keys instead of yours. Existing at-rest data will remain encrypted by the key you provided. |
| [`gcp.restrictServiceUsage`](/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/restricting-resources) | Set to allow all [supported products and API endpoints](#products_endpoints).   Determines which services can be used by restricting runtime access to their resources. For more information, see [Restricting resource usage](/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/restricting-resources). |
| [`gcp.restrictTLSVersion`](/docs/security/compliance/restrict-tls-versions) | Set to deny the following TLS versions:   * `TLS_1_0` * `TLS_1_1`  For more information, see [Restrict TLS versions](/docs/security/compliance/restrict-tls-versions). |

### BigQuery

#### Affected BigQuery features

| Feature | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Enabling BigQuery on a new folder | BigQuery is supported, but it isn't automatically enabled when you create a new Assured Workloads folder due to an internal configuration process. This process normally finishes in ten minutes, but can take much longer in some circumstances. To check whether the process is finished and to enable BigQuery, complete the following steps:   1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the **Assured Workloads** page. [Go to Assured Workloads](https://console.eu.cloud.google.com/compliance/assuredworkloads) 2. Select your new Assured Workloads folder from the list. 3. On the **Folder Details** page in the **Allowed services** section, click **Review Available Updates**. 4. In the **Allowed services** pane, review the services to be added to the [Resource Usage Restriction](/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/restricting-resources) organization policy for the folder. If BigQuery services are listed, click **Allow Services** to add them.   If BigQuery services are not listed, wait for the internal process to complete. If the services are not listed within 12 hours of folder creation, contact [Cloud Customer Care](/support).   After the enablement process is completed, you can use BigQuery in your Assured Workloads folder.  Gemini in BigQuery is not supported by Assured Workloads. |
| Unsupported features | The following BigQuery features are not supported and should not be used in the BigQuery CLI. It is your responsibility not to use them in BigQuery for Assured Workloads.   * Interaction with remote data sources * [Externally-trained BQML models](/bigquery/docs/bqml-introduction#externally_trained_models) are not supported.  [Internally-trained BQML models](/bigquery/docs/bqml-introduction#internally_trained_models) are supported. * [Data masking with policy tags](/bigquery/docs/column-data-masking#mask_data_with_policy_tags) is not supported. [Data masking by applying data policies directly to columns](/bigquery/docs/column-data-masking#data-policies-on-column) is supported. * GDrive export * [Remote functions](/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/remote-functions#overview) * [Saved queries](/bigquery/docs/work-with-saved-queries) * Workflow scheduling * For BigQuery Studio, [notebooks](/bigquery/docs/create-notebooks) are unsupported. * Gemini in BigQuery is not supported. |
| [BigQuery CLI](/bigquery/docs/bq-command-line-tool) | The BigQuery CLI is supported. |
| Google Cloud SDK | You must use Google Cloud SDK version 403.0.0 or newer to maintain data regionalization guarantees for technical data. To verify your current Google Cloud SDK version, run `gcloud --version` and then `gcloud components update` to update to the newest version. |
| Administrator controls | BigQuery will disable unsupported APIs but administrators with sufficient permissions to create Assured Workloads folders can enable an unsupported API. If this occurs, you will be notified of potential non-compliance through the [Assured Workloads monitoring dashboard](/assured-workloads/docs/monitor-folder). |
| Loading data | [BigQuery Data Transfer Service connectors](/bigquery/docs/dts-introduction#supported_data_sources) for Google Software as a Service (SaaS) apps, external cloud storage providers, and data warehouses are not supported. It is your responsibility not to use BigQuery Data Transfer Service connectors for EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications workloads. |
| [Third-party transfers](/bigquery/docs/third-party-transfer) | BigQuery doesn't verify support for third-party transfers for the BigQuery Data Transfer Service. It is your responsibility to verify support when using any third-party transfer for the BigQuery Data Transfer Service. |
| Non-compliant BQML models | [Externally-trained BQML models](/bigquery/docs/bqml-introduction#externally_trained_models) are not supported. |
| Query jobs | Query jobs should only be created within Assured Workloads folders. |
| Queries on datasets in other projects | BigQuery doesn't prevent Assured Workloads datasets from being queried from non-Assured Workloads projects. You should ensure that any query that has a read or a join on Assured Workloads data be placed in Assured Workloads folders. You can specify a [fully-qualified table name](/bigquery/docs/reference/bq-cli-reference#bq_query) for their query result using `projectname.dataset.table` in the BigQuery CLI. |
| Cloud Logging | BigQuery utilizes Cloud Logging for some of your log data. You should disable your `_default` logging buckets or restrict `_default` buckets to in-scope regions to maintain compliance using the following command:   `gcloud alpha logging settings update --organization=ORGANIZATION_ID --disable-default-sink`   For more information, see [Regionalize your logs](/logging/docs/regionalized-logs). |

This constraint provides fine-grained permissions for buckets and their contents.   If a bucket is created while this constraint is enabled, access to it can never be managed by using ACLs. In other words, the access control method for a bucket is permanently set to using IAM policies instead of Cloud Storage ACLs. |

This page is Google Cloud documentation describing the "EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications" control package in Assured Workloads. This control package provides data residency controls supporting EU-only regions and is included in Assured Workloads' Premium tier, which incurs a 5% additional charge. Technical support is available with Enhanced or Premium Cloud Customer Care subscriptions, with support cases routed to EU personnel located in the EU.

Key prerequisites include creating an EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications folder via Assured Workloads, deploying workloads only in that folder, not changing default organization policy constraint values, avoiding Google Cloud MCP servers (no data residency controls for in-use/in-transit data), and using EU-specific Jurisdictional Google Cloud console URLs (console.eu.cloud.google.com, or console.eu.cloud.google for federated identity users).

The page includes a comprehensive table of supported products and their API endpoints, including BigQuery, Bigtable, Cloud Storage, Compute Engine, Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud KMS, Cloud SQL, Spanner, Pub/Sub, and many others. Products not listed are unsupported and not recommended without due diligence under the shared responsibility model.

Major restrictions and limitations include:
- Google Cloud-wide organization policy constraints: gcp.resourceLocations (restricted to 11 European regions), gcp.restrictCmekCryptoKeyProjects, gcp.restrictNonCmekServices (requiring CMEK for 22 listed services), gcp.restrictServiceUsage, and gcp.restrictTLSVersion (denying TLS 1.0 and 1.1).
- BigQuery: not auto-enabled on new folders (internal process takes ~10 minutes, contact support if not done within 12 hours); unsupported features include externally-trained BQML models, data masking with policy tags, GDrive export, remote functions, saved queries, workflow scheduling, notebooks, and Gemini in BigQuery; requires Google Cloud SDK 403.0.0+; Data Transfer Service connectors for SaaS apps/external providers not supported.
- Bigtable: ListHotTablets API methods unsupported; Data Boost disabled; split boundaries accessible by Google personnel.
- Cloud Build: build provenance generation unsupported.
- Cloud Interconnect: HA VPN must be enabled.
- Cloud KMS: only EXTERNAL and EXTERNAL_VPC protection levels allowed.
- Cloud Logging: log-based alerts, shortened URLs, saved queries, and SQL-based alerting policies disabled; filters shouldn't contain Customer Data.
- Cloud Monitoring: Synthetic Monitor, uptime checks, log panel widgets, error reporting panel widgets, EventAnnotation filters, and SqlCondition in alertPolicies disabled.
- Cloud Run: Cloud Trace integration, Cloud Run functions, and Eventarc triggers unsupported.
- Cloud SQL: restrictNoncompliantDiagnosticDataAccess and restrictNoncompliantResourceCreation set to True.
- Cloud Storage: HMAC authentication prevented; uniform bucket-level access set to True; jurisdictional console prevents uploads/downloads (use in-scope regional endpoints).
- Cloud VPN: not available in console (use API/CLI); endpoints must be in in-scope regions.
- Compute Engine: VM suspend/resume and Local SSDs disabled (cannot be CMEK-encrypted); serial port output and screenshot APIs disabled; SSH-in-browser disabled; compliance memory protection enabled; global Cloud Armor policy disabled; health checks and network endpoint groups not in console.
- Knowledge Catalog: Attribute Store, Data Catalog, Discovery, data insights, and Lakes/Zones features deprecated or disabled.
- Managed Service for Apache Spark: doesn't support jurisdictional console; use CLI or API.
- GKE: container.restrictNoncompliantDiagnosticDataAccess set to True; avoid unsupported service resources in cluster config.
- Pub/Sub: Single Message Transforms disabled for subscriptions and topics.
- Spanner: split boundaries accessible by Google personnel; assuredWorkloadsAdvancedServiceControls set to True; multi-region instances disabled.

The page was last updated 2026-08-11 UTC.

# Google Cloud’s Commitment to EU International Data Transfers and the CJEU Ruling

##### Pablo Chavez

Vice President, Government Affairs & Public Policy, Google Cloud

On July 16, 2020,  the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) issued a ruling invalidating the [EU US Privacy Shield Framework](https://www.privacyshield.gov/welcome), but upholding the validity of EU Model Contract Clauses (MCCs), also known as Standard Contractual Clauses. Both of these mechanisms were created for the lawful transfer of personal data from the European Union (EU) to countries outside of the EU under the EU Directive, and then the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). **Given the CJEU has upheld the MCCs, it is important to know that your use of** [**G Suite**](https://support.google.com/a/team/answer/6366832?hl=en) **and** [**Google Cloud Platform**](https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/6329727?hl=en) **meets GDPR’s standards for transfer of personal data outside of the EU.**

Google Cloud has always been committed to compliance with EU privacy legislation since we began offering our first Google Cloud services in 2006.  We have ensured our products and services are built with the highest standards of security and privacy, enabling not only our customers in Europe—but all of our customers—to meet regulatory and compliance frameworks, even as legislation evolves. Millions of organizations rely on our cloud services to run their businesses, and we’re committed to helping them directly address global privacy and data protection requirements by offering industry-leading security, third-party audits and certifications, legal commitments, and products and services to support compliance needs.

Beginning in 2012, Google Cloud began [offering](https://cloud.googleblog.com/2012/06/google-apps-to-offer-additional.html) MCCs as a data transfer mechanism, and in 2017, the Article 29 Working Party, the predecessor of the [European Data Protection Board](https://edpb.europa.eu/about-edpb/about-edpb_en), [concluded](https://www.blog.google/products/google-cloud/eu-data-protection-authorities-confirm-compliance-google-cloud-commitments-international-data-flows/) that Google’s agreements for international transfers of data for [G Suite](https://cloud.google.com/files/2016-12-30_Common_Opinion_for_G-Suite.pdf) and [Google Cloud Platform](https://cloud.google.com/files/2016-12-30_Common_Opinion_for_Google_Cloud_Platform.pdf) are in alignment with the European Commission’s [MCCs](http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=OJ:L:2010:039:0005:0018:EN:PDF). Our customers have been able to rely on Google Cloud MCCs for the international transfer of their data, and this continues today.

Regardless of the location of the data, data protection remains a priority for Google. We will continue to follow and be certified against internationally-recognized privacy standards such as [ISO 27018](https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/iso-27018) and [ISO 27701](https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/iso-27701).

We have been closely monitoring the developments around the evolution of the international data transfer mechanisms permitted under GDPR. We are currently studying the ruling, as well as related developments, and will keep you updated as things evolve.
