###### EMEA | ALL INDUSTRIES

# EU Standard Contractual Clauses

In 2010, the European Commission (EC) approved model contract clauses as a means of complying with the requirements of the EU Data Protection Directive, which in May 2018 was replaced by the [General Data Protection Regulation](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02016R0679-20160504&qid=1532348683434) (GDPR). For years, Google Cloud customers who are subject to European data protection laws relied on our 2010 Standard Contractual Clauses (also known as Model Contract Clauses), as previously [approved](https://www.blog.google/products/google-cloud/eu-data-protection-authorities-confirm-compliance-google-cloud-commitments-international-data-flows/) by regulators, to legitimize overseas transfers of their customer personal data when using our services.

On 4 June 2021 the EC published [new Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32021D0915&from=EN) to help safeguard personal data. These new SCCs replaced the SCCs previously adopted by the EC in 2010 and can be used to facilitate lawful transfers of data under certain conditions. By imposing various contractual obligations, SCCs allow personal data subject to the GDPR to flow to recipients outside the European Economic Area (EEA).

We have updated our data processing terms for [Google Cloud Platform](https://cloud.google.com/terms/data-processing-terms), and [Google Workspace (including Workspace for Education) and Cloud Identity](https://workspace.google.com/terms/dpa_terms.html), to incorporate the [new SCCs](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32021D0915&from=EN).

For all Google Cloud customers, this new approach:

For customers located in Europe (i.e. in the EEA, UK and Switzerland), Google has further simplified data transfer compliance by assuming all the responsibilities imposed by the new SCCs.

Our [whitepaper](https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/gc_new_eu_scc.pdf) outlines the European legal rules for data transfers and explains our approach to implementing the new EU SCCs - as well as separate UK SCCs - so that our customers can better understand what our updated terms mean for them and their privacy compliance.

This is a Google Cloud webpage explaining the EU Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) and how Google has implemented them for its cloud services. Key points include:

- In 2010, the European Commission (EC) approved model contract clauses to comply with the EU Data Protection Directive, which was replaced by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in May 2018.
- Google Cloud customers relied on the 2010 SCCs (also known as Model Contract Clauses) to legitimize overseas transfers of customer personal data.
- On 4 June 2021, the EC published new Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) to safeguard personal data, replacing the 2010 versions. These new SCCs allow personal data subject to GDPR to flow to recipients outside the European Economic Area (EEA).
- Google has updated its data processing terms for Google Cloud Platform and Google Workspace (including Workspace for Education) and Cloud Identity to incorporate the new SCCs.
- For customers located in Europe (EEA, UK, and Switzerland), Google has simplified data transfer compliance by assuming all the responsibilities imposed by the new SCCs.
- Google provides a whitepaper outlining European legal rules for data transfers and its approach to implementing the new EU SCCs, as well as separate UK SCCs.
- Quick links are provided for related resources including GDPR, EU Data Protection Board, SCCs blog, SCCs whitepaper, and Schrems 2 blog.

**GDPR Transfer Restrictions** refer to rules under Chapter V of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 governing the transfer of European personal data to third countries outside the European Economic Area (EUR-Lex, 2016). GDPR does not prohibit US cloud hyperscalers. Rather, it requires that transfers rely on an approved legal mechanism, such as an adequacy decision or Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs). Specifically, certified US providers process data under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, while SCCs provide a continuous contractual fallback. Furthermore, decisions from the [Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU)](https://curia.europa.eu) confirm that SCCs remain valid when combined with strong encryption controls. In our experience, hosting production workloads in EU cloud regions (such as AWS Frankfurt `eu-central-1`) satisfies European enterprise buyers without requiring platform migrations.

### 1. The EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF)

The European Commission adopted the EU-US Data Privacy Framework on July 10, 2023, establishing an adequacy decision for certified US entities (EUR-Lex, 2023). AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure are all certified under the DPF. On September 3, 2025, the EU General Court dismissed the Latombe challenge, upholding the framework while an appeal continues at the CJEU.

### 2. Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs)

Standard Contractual Clauses serve as an essential legal fallback under Article 46. The CJEU explicitly confirmed in the 2020 Schrems II ruling that SCCs remain valid transfer mechanisms when paired with appropriate security controls.

### 3. Regional Data Isolation

Under the DPF, certified US companies can process European personal data without requiring extra transfer authorization. Specifically, AWS, Azure, and GCP execute standard Data Processing Addendums (DPAs) incorporating DPF certification and SCCs. For example, signing a hyperscaler's standard DPA satisfies European legal requirements. Consequently, your compliance setup requires zero custom legal negotiations. For broader context on security standards, see our comparison of [SOC 2 vs GDPR overlap](/blog/soc2-vs-gdpr-overlap).

`+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

For instance, processing German health data under DigiG requires BSI C5 Type 2 attestation. ## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does GDPR require US startups to host data exclusively in Europe?

No. GDPR allows data transfers to the US under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework or Standard Contractual Clauses, though hosting in EU regions simplifies buyer procurement.

### Are AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud certified under the DPF?

Yes. AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud are all certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, providing a valid legal basis for cross-border data processing.

### What is the US CLOUD Act risk for European data?

The US CLOUD Act allows US law enforcement to compel US-parented companies to provide data. However, encryption, legal challenge rights, and DPF safeguards manage this risk effectively for standard B2B SaaS.

### When is sovereign cloud required in Germany?

Sovereign cloud setups are required primarily in specialized sectors like healthcare (DigiG BSI C5), federal government contracts, or strict financial auditing under DORA.

# EU-US data transfer: what European companies should know

![EU-US Data Privacy Framework cover: Two semi-transparent spheres in space symbolizing transatlantic data transfers—one with swirling blue-gold particles and 12-star EU pattern, the other with U.S. ribbon motifs—connected by a selective membrane allowing lawful glowing data flows under DPF, Schrems II, and GDPR compliance.](https://taggrs.io/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/what-is-data-privacy-framework.webp)

By: ![](https://taggrs.io/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/ate-70x70.webp) [Ate Keurentjes](https://taggrs.io/author/ate/) | 9 July 2024 | Last updated:

Schrems II ruling was introduced in 2020. And ever since, data transfers to U.S. services like Google Analytics have faced legal uncertainty. The new EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF) aims to restore a lawful basis for these transfers. But an important question remains, **is US data processing now truly GDPR‑compliant?** And, can European businesses safely continue using American marketing or analytics tools?

Transferring personal data to the US is **still possible, but not risk-free**. The Data Privacy Framework simplifies compliance for certified organizations, yet legal uncertainty persists due to ongoing scrutiny by European courts.

In this article, we explain what the Data Privacy Framework means in practice, how to verify compliance, and why TAGGRS Server‑Side Tracking offers a safer and more future‑proof GDPR‑compliant alternative.

## What is the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF)?

The DPF is a formal agreement that allows organizations in the European Economic Area (EEA) to transfer personal data to U.S. companies certified under the framework. Overseas, American companies can voluntarily join the framework by self‑certifying with the U.S. Department of Commerce. To stay compliant, certified participants must:

* Publish and maintain a clear, public privacy policy that aligns with DPF principles
* Put internal monitoring and enforcement measures in place
* Respond to complaints and provide independent dispute resolution options.

Once certified, these **organizations can legally receive personal data from the EEA** without extra contractual or technical safeguards. But non‑compliance has consequences… the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) can take enforcement action, and violators risk being removed from the DPF list.

If a U.S. company isn’t DPF‑certified, data transfers are still possible but require other legal tools, such as Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs), supported by additional safeguards like encryption or pseudonymization.

Want to learn more? Check out the [Data Privacy Framework program](https://www.dataprivacyframework.gov/).

### Examples of personal data commonly transferred

* IP addresses
* Email addresses
* Device IDs and cookies
* Usernames or login data
* Customer metadata and CRM fields
* Birth dates or location data

Expert Tip

Even if your company “only” shares an IP address or hashed identifier with a U.S. service, this can qualify as personal data under the GDPR.

## Why is the DPF still under review in the EU?

On one hand, the DPF brings more transparency and strengthens individual rights, but on the other its **long‑term legal stability remains uncertain**. Privacy advocates like NOYB have already challenged it, claiming that U.S. surveillance laws could still allow disproportionate government data access to European data. A future ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union could – once again – reshape how EU-US data transfers work.

For European companies, this means relying exclusively on the DPF may not be a sustainable, long-term compliance strategy.

## How to check if your data is protected (3-step verification)

Before sharing user data with any U.S. service provider, you can easily check if they are certified:

1. Visit the [official DPF list](https://www.dataprivacyframework.gov/list)
2. Search for the company name (e.g., “Google LLC”)
3. Confirm that the company’s status is “Active” and check whether the specific service (e.g., Google Analytics or Google Ads) is covered.

Now, you are presented with 2 possible scenarios:

1. If covered, you may transfer data under DPF without additional measures.
2. If not covered, you must implement supplementary safeguards.

## Supplementary safeguards for companies that are *not* DPF-certified

If your U.S. partner isn’t certified under the Data Privacy Framework, there are still ways to stay compliant. Here are three main options:

### 1) Use a transfer tool

You can rely on recognized legal instruments for data transfers outside the EEA, such as the [Standard Contractual Clauses](https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/international-dimension-data-protection/standard-contractual-clauses-scc_en) under Article 46 GDPR or Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) for multinational organizations. These form the legal basis for sending data abroad while staying within GDPR limits.

### 2) Add technical and organizational measures

If needed, you can take additional measures to protect personal data.

The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) outlines several practical steps in its

[Recommendations for Measures Supplemental to Transfer Instruments](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2022-04/edpb_recommendations_202001vo.2.0_supplementarymeasurestransferstools_nl.pdf), such as:

* End-to-end encryption before transfer
* Pseudonymization of data
* Data minimization and strict access control.

You should consider on a case-by-case basis what measure or combination of measures is necessary to properly protect personal data.

### 3) Move data handling to EU territories

Another sustainable approach is to keep data processing within the EU itself. Hosting, anonymizing, or handling data through EU‑based servers (for example, with a Server‑side Tracking setup) helps minimize cross‑border risks altogether.

Learn more about [European Data Sovereignty with UpCloud and TAGGRS](https://taggrs.io/data-sovereignty-eu-compliant-cloud-services/).

## Why EU Server-side Tracking is often the more resilient strategy

Server-side Tracking inside the EU gives you:

* Control exactly what data is shared with third-party vendors through filtering or pseudonymisation before any transfer
* Ability to keep raw or sensitive data inside EU jurisdictions, reducing cross-border transfer risk
* Easier GDPR compliance and simplified breach/DSAR procedures because your organization stays in charge of data handling and retention.

By keeping tracking logic and user data within EU borders, companies gain a scalable setup that’s less dependent on uncertain legal frameworks such as the DPF. It futureproofs your data infrastructure and builds stronger trust with privacy‑aware customers. It’s important, though, to verify any provider’s claims by checking the actual hosting locations, subcontractors, and Data Processing Agreements (DPA).

In a nutshell: Server‑side Tracking with EU hosting is not only about compliance. It’s about putting data ownership and responsibility back in your hands, where it belongs.

## How TAGGRS ensures that personal data is protected

TAGGRS offers [hosting for Google Tag Manager Server-side Tracking](https://taggrs.io/gtm-server-side-tagging-hosting/) and privacy‑enhancing tools like PII hashing and anonymization, designed to let marketing teams, DPOs, or data-driven professionals maintain both technical and legal control.

We help organizations stay GDPR compliant through several key features:

* **Enhanced control over third‑party data:** Server‑Side GTM lets you decide exactly which data points are shared with external services like Meta or Google, ensuring vendors only receive the information you approve.  
  Learn why minimizing third‑party dependencies helps future‑proof your business: [Cookies, privacy concerns and a future‑proof solution](https://taggrs.io/first-party-vs-third-party-cookies/#cookie-and-privacy)
* **Effective data management:** Server‑Side GTM supports advanced data handling, like hashing user information according to platform standards or cleaning URLs before sending them to ad or analytics tools, protecting sensitive data from exposure. Learn more in our [Google Ads enhanced conversions documentation](https://taggrs.io/docs/server-side-tracking/google-ads/enhanced-conversions#hash)
* **Proprietary server locations:** TAGGRS operates on [its own EU‑based infrastructure](https://taggrs.io/infrastructure/), meaning data stays within European borders. Keeping hosting local adds an extra layer of legal and technical security, helping your organization meet both GDPR and national compliance standards.  
  Explore more insights in our blog post on [GDPR and Server‑Side Tracking.](https://taggrs.io/server-side-tracking/gdpr/)
* **Secure processing of sensitive information and PII with the** [**TAGGRS GDPR tool:**](https://taggrs.io/gdpr-tool/) sensitive data such as email addresses or identifiers are anonymized or hashed before being processed, helping you align with GDPR obligations.  
  Discover more about privacy rules for PII and personal data.

Check the [server status](https://status.taggrs.io/). Anytime, everywhere.

Enter our [legal hub](https://dashboard.taggrs.io/legal) to read our DPA and SLA per product.

## FAQ: Data Privacy Framework & U.S. Data Transfers

### **Who can use the DPF?**

Only those U.S. organizations that self-certify with the U.S. Department of Commerce and appear on the official DPF list may legally receive such data without additional safeguards. EU-based companies cannot participate; they can only transfer data to certified U.S. partners.

### **Why is TAGGRS not part of the DPF?**

The DPF applies only to U.S. entities. TAGGRS is an EU-based provider that keeps data within European borders.

### **Is Google part of the DPF?**

Yes, Google LLC participates under “Google Cloud,” “Google Ads,” and “Google Analytics.” Verify coverage for your service.

### **Are Transfer Impact Assessments still required under DPF?**

While the DPF provides an adequate basis for transfers, EU regulators and privacy authorities recommend that European companies still perform a Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA) as part of their accountability obligations. TIAs help document risks, confirm DPF coverage for the specific service, and outline mitigation measures for sensitive data.

### **What if DPF is invalidated again?**

Use SCCs plus supplementary safeguards like encryption and pseudonymization.

### **Should EU businesses rely exclusively on DPF or combine with supplementary measures?**

Businesses should not rely solely on the DPF, given ongoing legal and regulatory uncertainty. The most resilient approach is to combine DPF usage (where unavoidable) with technical, organizational, and contractual safeguards — and implement EU-hosted Server-side Tracking wherever possible to minimize risk and simplify compliance.

### **Why choose EU Server-side Tracking?**

EU-based Server-side Tracking (such as TAGGRS) keeps all user data within European-controlled environments, ensuring full GDPR compliance and eliminating dependence on international transfer frameworks. Businesses retain direct technical and legal control over personal data, reducing potential exposure to foreign surveillance or regulatory shifts.

### **Is the Data Privacy Framework GDPR-compliant?**

The European Commission considers the DPF to offer adequate protection, but critics argue U.S. surveillance laws still pose risks. The NOYB privacy group and others continue to challenge its validity. If invalidated again, businesses must fall back on Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) and supplementary safeguards like encryption and pseudonymization.

This article from TAGGRS explains the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF) and what European companies should know about transferring personal data to the US following the Schrems II ruling (2020). The DPF is a formal agreement allowing EEA organizations to transfer personal data to US companies certified through self-certification with the US Department of Commerce. Certified participants must publish a public privacy policy aligned with DPF principles, implement internal monitoring and enforcement, and provide independent dispute resolution. The FTC can take enforcement action against non-compliant companies.

Key points covered include:
- Common personal data transferred includes IP addresses, email addresses, device IDs, cookies, usernames, CRM fields, birth dates, and location data. Even a shared IP address or hashed identifier can qualify as personal data under GDPR.
- The DPF remains legally uncertain — NOYB has challenged it, arguing US surveillance laws could allow disproportionate government access to European data. A future CJEU ruling could reshape EU-US data transfers.
- 3-step verification process: visit the official DPF list, search for the company name (e.g., "Google LLC"), and confirm the status is "Active" and the specific service is covered.
- For companies NOT DPF-certified, three main options exist: (1) use transfer tools like Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) under Article 46 GDPR or Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs); (2) add technical/organizational measures per EDPB recommendations (end-to-end encryption, pseudonymization, data minimization, strict access control); (3) move data handling to EU territories (e.g., EU-hosted server-side tracking).
- TAGGRS promotes EU-based Server-side Tracking as a more resilient strategy, offering control over data shared with third parties, keeping raw data in EU jurisdictions, and simplifying GDPR compliance. TAGGRS operates on its own EU-based infrastructure with features like PII hashing and anonymization via its GDPR tool.
- Google LLC participates in the DPF under "Google Cloud," "Google Ads," and "Google Analytics."
- FAQ highlights: EU companies cannot join DPF (only US organizations can); Transfer Impact Assessments are still recommended despite DPF; if DPF is invalidated again, businesses should fall back on SCCs plus supplementary safeguards; businesses should not rely exclusively on the DPF.
args.key_excerpts: "Transferring personal data to the US is still possible, but not risk-free. The Data Privacy Framework simplifies compliance for certified organizations, yet legal uncertainty persists due to ongoing scrutiny by European courts."

# EU Standard Contractual Clauses

In 2010, the European Commission (EC) approved model contract clauses as a means of complying with the requirements of the EU Data Protection Directive, which in May 2018 was replaced by the [General Data Protection Regulation](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02016R0679-20160504&qid=1532348683434) (GDPR). For years, Google Maps Platform customers who are subject to European data protection laws relied on our 2010 Standard Contractual Clauses (also known as Model Contract Clauses), to legitimize overseas transfers of their customer personal data when using our services.

On 4 June 2021 the EC published [new Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32021D0915&from=EN) to help safeguard personal data. These new SCCs replaced the SCCs previously adopted by the EC in 2010 and can be used to facilitate lawful transfers of data under certain conditions. By imposing various contractual obligations, SCCs allow personal data subject to the GDPR to flow to recipients outside the European Economic Area (EEA).

We have updated our Controller-Controller Data Protection Terms for [Google Maps Platform](https://business.safety.google/controllerterms/) to incorporate the [new SCCs](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32021D0915&from=EN).

For all Google Maps Platform customers, this new approach:

* offers clear and transparent support for their compliance with applicable European data protection laws
* simplifies the entities involved in contracting by no longer requiring any customer to deal with an additional Google entity only for SCC purposes
* aligns more closely with potential flows of data within the services.

For customers located in Europe (i.e. in the EEA, UK and Switzerland), Google has further simplified data transfer compliance by assuming all the responsibilities imposed by the new SCCs.

# Hunterdon Healthcare: Achieving higher-quality, more cost-effective care

![Hunterdon Healthcare logo](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/Dq5L9cpuhOrJPlfouz51Iskls4W6VMW8KJLwsFY-pKYvo2np4ICbB3_N52cXKZJeTrmLTC51OGk6Y6pVbQWAe65VPEOeRorCn9y4tg)

# About Hunterdon Healthcare

Hunterdon Healthcare is a non-profit healthcare organization providing a full range of quality health and medical services to communities in northwest New Jersey.

#### Tell us your challenge. We're here to help.

![SADA Systems logo](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/d6CwiiUMwv5zoFZzbGXDDtQWOuh0xQX3soXsJF0NPifd35jOAXk-QfIwivxBWcwt5nax0NMxLsfi6nxD6zwOCmieGoY6ry-Y3cTWAXk0wIqcAI1-B-M)

## About SADA Systems

SADA Systems is a Google Cloud Premier Partner with proven expertise in Google Workspace assessment and consultation, migration and deployment, user adoption, and change management. Premier Partners help businesses of all sizes run better on Google Cloud, from building custom applications to offering managed services.

# Hunterdon Healthcare uses Google Workspace to improve collaboration and efficiency, reclaiming 30% of caregivers’ time for patient interactions while reducing costs by $1.3 million over 3 years.

## Google Cloud Results

Over 80% employee satisfaction after only a few months

Between New York City and Philadelphia lies bucolic Hunterdon County, New Jersey, home to more than 120,000 residents. Serving the county’s healthcare needs is [Hunterdon Healthcare](https://www.hunterdonhealthcare.org/), a health system with a 178-bed hospital, 65 ambulatory locations, and more than 25 care facilities. The organization provides a full range of preventive, diagnostic, and therapeutic inpatient and outpatient hospital and community health services. Its medical center, Hunterdon Medical Center, treats over 8,600 inpatients annually, with 33,000 emergency department visits and over 292,000 outpatient visits per year.

To keep quality high and enable caregivers to spend more time with patients, Hunterdon Healthcare is adopting cloud-based collaboration tools that help the organization’s medical and IT professionals work faster and smarter. Several years ago, the IT team decided to replace Hunterdon’s aging email system, which had limitations with file size, required external products for archiving, and presented challenges around security and usability. After an extensive review of cloud solutions, the organization began transitioning to [Google Workspace](https://workspace.google.com/), first moving its 3,000 employees to [Gmail](https://workspace.google.com/products/gmail/) and [Calendar](https://workspace.google.com/products/calendar/).

“We wanted to present the organization with a modern toolset to stimulate and enable collaboration,” says Daniel Morreale, CIO at Hunterdon Healthcare. “Google Workspace was the right solution for us because many employees were already using it in their personal lives, and it’s so easy to use that we were confident they would adopt it organically over time.”

“SADA Systems has been absolutely awesome. They helped us realize the importance of ongoing Google Workspace training and we continue to work together to help people increase their productivity by discovering and adopting new workflows.”

## Driving user adoption

To help employees get the most out of Google Workspace, Hunterdon Healthcare worked with [SADA Systems](https://sadasystems.com/), a Google Cloud Premier Partner, to provide group-based and one-on-one training. Together, the organizations took a focused, department-by-department approach to change management, using webinars, live auditorium sessions, and YouTube videos to engage and educate users. SADA Systems and Hunterdon IT provided customized training to help users transition faster, and a mobile classroom with 40 Google [Chromebooks](https://cloud.google.com/chrome-enterprise/chromebooks/) provides hands-on instruction to users at remote locations.

“SADA Systems has been absolutely awesome,” says Daniel. “They helped us realize the importance of ongoing Google Workspace training and we continue to work together to help people increase their productivity by discovering and adopting new workflows.”

SADA’s collaborative approach toward workforce training was instrumental in helping employees get over the hump of change. After just a few months, Hunterdon Healthcare user surveys indicated over 80 percent satisfaction rate with Google Workspace — impressive for a new piece of software replacing an entrenched legacy system.

“As they learned more about Google Workspace, people began to see how much more effective they could be every day,” says Denise Amiano, Manager of Customer Service, who oversees Hunterdon Healthcare’s IT Help Desk and works closely with SADA Systems on user training. “As people started digging deeper into Google Workspace, we began to see some real successes.”

Adds Daniel: “Google has a forward-looking vision for collaboration and communication, as well as a strong partner network that helped us manage change and drive user adoption.”

## Helping secure productivity for nursing and IT

Information security is a major priority for Hunterdon, which must comply with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and other regulations. Hunterdon opted for a Google Workspace Enterprise license, which replaced three separate security solutions with its enhanced customization and controls. Google Workspace apps also support HIPAA compliance, allowing Hunterdon Medical Center’s nursing department to automate processes that were previously manual to help nurses spend more time with patients.

For example, nurses use [Forms](https://workspace.google.com/products/forms/) to immediately record patient safety incidents and track them in [Sheets](https://workspace.google.com/products/sheets/). The hospital’s risk manager is automatically notified via the notification feature in Sheets, allowing investigations to begin immediately to improve overall patient safety. Budgeting processes are likewise streamlined because multiple stakeholders across all departments can co-edit documents in real time on [Drive](https://workspace.google.com/products/drive/), eliminating the need to re-enter information.

IT staff have seen similar benefits from Google Workspace. Instead of filing formal requests in the help desk system for small tasks, they use Sheets to track help desk calls and streamline incident management, allowing IT employees to respond faster.

“Google Workspace has been great for our help desk because it gives us the ability to share documents and information in real time, without sending emails back and forth,” says Jason Tahaney, Director of IT, Hunterdon Healthcare. “It’s much easier for us to communicate and resolve issues faster.”

“By enabling our caregivers to be more effective and efficient administratively with Google Workspace, we’re reclaiming approximately 30 percent of their time for face-to-face patient interactions, which is what we always want.”

## Connecting caregivers and teams

Before Google Workspace, videoconferencing was limited at Hunterdon Healthcare. Today, IT staff use [Google Meet](https://workspace.google.com/products/meet/) every day to communicate with each other on live video while solving problems and also to assist people face-to-face. Employees now have a seamless video experience on their laptops and mobile devices, which are managed using the built-in mobile device management capabilities of Google Workspace.

“We’re averaging approximately 160 Google Meet per week organization-wide,” says Jason. “Our ability to work on critical IT issues has greatly improved. The ability to pull the team together, instantaneously with mobile face-to-face communication, has been a great success to our department and our customers. Our IT department relies heavily on Google Chat and Meet for immediate communication.”

The benefits of video collaboration extend to clinicians and caregivers as well. During educational meetings and brainstorming sessions, teams use [Jamboard](https://workspace.google.com/products/jamboard/) interactive whiteboards to sketch out ideas and save meeting minutes.

“Google Workspace has become an integral part of how we connect our organization,” says Daniel. “So much of what happens in healthcare is a team effort, and having the capacity to collaborate, collect data, and make informed decisions has had a very positive impact for us.”

## Reclaiming 30% of caregivers’ time

When new employees start with Hunterdon Healthcare, it’s easy for them to get onboarded and started immediately with Google Workspace, as most have previous experience with the toolset. Once onboard, employees have fast access to critical information and learning resources hosted on [Sites](https://workspace.google.com/products/sites/), helping them do their jobs better.

“Administrative tasks and patient care are always going to be interconnected,” says Daniel. “By enabling our caregivers to be more effective and efficient administratively with Google Workspace, we’re reclaiming approximately 30 percent of their time for face-to-face patient interactions, which is what we always want.”

“Moving to Google Workspace reduced our IT costs by $1.3 million over three years while enhancing our security posture and contributing to improved quality of care. We definitely took a step forward.”

## Saving $1.3 million over 3 years

# Expanding the reach of Google Cloud Platform’s HIPAA-compliant offerings for healthcare

##### Rohit Talreja

Technical Program Manager, Healthcare & Life Sciences Compliance, Google Cloud Platform

##### Joe Corkery, M.D.

Director of Product Management, Healthcare & Life Sciences, Google Cloud

At Google Cloud, we strive to create innovative and elegant solutions to help you address the unique challenges of your industries. In particular, we have a strong and growing focus on making Google Cloud the best platform for the healthcare industry as has been evidenced at numerous events over the past year, including [HIMSS](https://www.blog.google/topics/google-cloud/google-cloud-himss-engaging-healthcare-and-health-it-community/), [RSNA](https://www.blog.google/topics/google-cloud/google-cloud-rsna-engaging-medical-imaging-community/) and [Google Cloud Next](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wdFo_CtQNfA). We’ve showcased a number of [solutions](http://cloud.google.com/health), including a clinical data warehouse, integration with multiple radiology workflows, an API-enabling an entire country’s healthcare system, as well as a petabyte-scale genomics processing capabilities.

Of course, no solution, whether it be for handling patient data or billing records, can be considered complete without proper consideration of the relevant data security and compliance requirements. [Google Cloud Platform](https://cloud.google.com/) (GCP) offers market-leading security technologies, such as encryption by default, both [at rest](https://cloud.google.com/security/encryption-at-rest/) and [in transit](https://cloud.google.com/security/encryption-in-transit/), [trusted server boot](https://cloudplatform.googleblog.com/2017/08/Titan-in-depth-security-in-plaintext.html) and [data loss prevention tools](https://cloud.google.com/security/data-loss-prevention/preventing-data-exfiltration), which can help our customers jumpstart their compliance journeys. We've been steadily increasing the number of services covered by the Google Cloud Platform [HIPAA Business Associate Agreement](https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/hipaa/#covered-products) (BAA) in line with the overall growth of the product suite. Currently, we have around 75% of applicable GCP services covered under our BAA.

Today we're excited to announce a new addition to our HIPAA BAA, [Google App Engine](https://cloud.google.com/appengine/). App Engine offers customers the ability to build highly scalable web and mobile applications without having to worry about managing the underlying infrastructure and other overhead that comes from managing large-scale web applications. With this release, customers will now be able to leverage App Engine to build applications serving the healthcare sector. Many of our customers, for example [CSG Actuarial, LLC](https://www.csgactuarial.com/), are already taking advantage of these additions:

#### CSG Actuarial, LLC utilizes Google Cloud Platform to quickly design and implement innovative solutions for producers in the insurance industry. We are excited to be introducing a multi-carrier Medicare Supplement online enrollment tool in February, where we will be able to securely store personal health information with Google App Engine under the Google Cloud Platform HIPAA BAA

— Bryan Neary, Principal, CSG Actuarial, LLC

In addition, GCP’s [AI and machine learning capabilities](https://cloud.google.com/products/machine-learning/), including the Speech, Translation, Vision, and Natural Language APIs, as well as Cloud Machine Learning Engine, are covered by the HIPAA BAA. These products allow customers to leverage pre-trained models in the form of APIs and custom trained models with Cloud Machine Learning Engine. Cloud Machine Learning Engine provides a managed solution for the popular TensorFlow open source machine learning framework, allowing customers to develop, train, and run custom models on HIPAA-covered data on Google Cloud.

#### The ability to train robust machine learning models in a secure, privacy-respecting and HIPAA compliant manner is central to our business. We found Google Cloud Platform to go beyond our expectations in terms of supporting infrastructure enabling us to focus on developing our core application and building on top of the stack that GCP provides.

—John Axerio-Cilies, CTO, Arterys

While there's no formal certification process recognized by the US Department of Health and Human Services for HIPAA compliance, and complying with HIPAA is a shared responsibility between the customer and Google, GCP has undergone several independent audits to assess the controls present in our systems, facilities and operations. This includes the ISO 27018 international standard of practice for protection of personally identifiable information in public cloud services. More information on GCP’s security and compliance efforts, as well as the complete list of services covered by our HIPAA BAA, can be found on our comprehensive compliance site [here](https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance).

In addition to supporting healthcare, we have also developed industry guidance for life sciences customers working to deploy and validate “good practices” (commonly referred to as GxP) on GCP. Please [contact](https://cloud.google.com/contact/) a Google Cloud representative for details. Our [recently announced partner](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/flex-expands-digital-health-capabilities-launches-brightinsight-connected-health-solution-on-google-cloud-platform-300606563.html), Flex, just launched its BrightInsight platform, built on GCP, that enables pharmaceutical and medical technology companies to optimize therapies through better data management and analysis from Class I, II and III medical devices and combination products. BrightInsight will accelerate the R&D and go-to-market timelines for these companies by delivering a secure, managed infrastructure service for regulated medical devices and therapies, and provides a platform for the development of advanced machine learning and analytics capabilities to deliver real-time actionable insights to its customers.

#### Flex saw the need for a secure cloud platform designed to support highly-regulated connected drug delivery and medical devices, going beyond simple connectivity to deliver real-time intelligence and actionable insights. Through our strategic partnership with Google, we will be able to deliver a new level of intelligence to healthcare all built within a regulated, managed services framework that is designed to comply with the varying privacy and security laws around the world.

— Kal Patel, MD, Senior Vice President of Digital Health, Flex

To learn more about what we’re doing in the healthcare and life sciences space, visit us at HIMSS this week. In particular, come learn the basics of how to set up a project in the Developer Innovation Lab that can support HIPAA compliance so that you can take advantage of our comprehensive infrastructure, analytics and machine learning capabilities.

###### U.S. | Healthcare and life sciences

# HIPAA

The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) is a federal law that establishes data privacy and security requirements for organizations that are charged with safeguarding individuals' protected health information (PHI). These organizations meet the definition of “covered entities” or “business associates” under HIPAA.

Customers that are subject to HIPAA and want to utilize any Google Cloud products in connection with PHI must review and accept Google's Business Associate Agreement (BAA). Google ensures that the Google products covered under the BAA meet the requirements under HIPAA and align with our ISO/IEC 27001, 27017, and 27018 certifications and SOC 2 report.

The Google Cloud BAA covers Google Cloud’s entire infrastructure (all regions, all zones, all network paths, all points of presence), and the services listed below.

#### What is the purpose of the BAA (Business Associate Agreement) with Google and how is it executed?

The BAA allows covered entities and business associates to enter into an agreement with Google that governs the processing of PHI through Google Cloud.

In order to execute a BAA, organizations that use Google Cloud should talk to their account managers about entering into a BAA with us.

#### Is having a BAA with Google Cloud sufficient to ensure my organization’s compliance with HIPAA?

The covered entity that enters into the BAA with Google Cloud is responsible for building a HIPAA compliant solution using the approved Google Cloud services. After the solution is built, the covered entity is responsible for the implementation of compliance controls.

# HIPAA

The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) is a federal law that establishes data privacy and security requirements for organizations that are charged with safeguarding individuals' protected health information (PHI). These organizations meet the definition of “covered entities” or “business associates” under HIPAA.

Customers that are subject to HIPAA and want to utilize any Google Cloud products in connection with PHI must review and accept Google's Business Associate Agreement (BAA). Google ensures that the Google products covered under the BAA meet the requirements under HIPAA and align with our ISO/IEC 27001, 27017, and 27018 certifications and SOC 2 report.

The Google Cloud BAA covers Google Cloud’s entire infrastructure (all regions, all zones, all network paths, all points of presence), and the services listed below.

#### What is the purpose of the BAA (Business Associate Agreement) with Google and how is it executed?

The BAA allows covered entities and business associates to enter into an agreement with Google that governs the processing of PHI through Google Cloud.

In order to execute a BAA, organizations that use Google Cloud should talk to their account managers about entering into a BAA with us.

#### Is having a BAA with Google Cloud sufficient to ensure my organization’s compliance with HIPAA?

The covered entity that enters into the BAA with Google Cloud is responsible for building a HIPAA compliant solution using the approved Google Cloud services. After the solution is built, the covered entity is responsible for the implementation of compliance controls.

#### Can my organization request to modify the BAA?

The BAA is not subject to modification.

<webpage_content>
# Google Cloud VMware Engine now HIPAA compliant

##### Krishna Chengavalli

Product Management, Google Cloud

##### Sai Gopalan

Product Management, Google Cloud

We are excited to announce that as of April 1, 2021, [**Google Cloud VMware Engine**](https://cloud.google.com/vmware-engine) **is covered under the Google Cloud Business Associate Agreement (BAA)**, meaning it has achieved HIPAA compliance. Healthcare organizations can now migrate and run their HIPAA-compliant VMware workloads in a fully compatible VMware Cloud Verified stack running natively in Google Cloud with Google Cloud VMware Engine, without changes or re-architecture to tools, processes, or applications.

Healthcare organizations increasingly use cloud platforms to personalize patient care, analyze large datasets more effectively, enhance research and development collaboration, and share medical knowledge. Leveraging cloud platforms can also help healthcare organizations increase the privacy and security of information systems, including protected health information (PHI), and, as a result, better comply with applicable laws and regulations while reducing the burden of compliance. For PHI, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) set standards in the United States to protect individually identifiable health information. HIPAA applies to health plans, most healthcare providers, and healthcare clearinghouses that manage PHI electronically, and to persons or entities that perform certain functions on their behalf.

With Google Cloud, organizations can leverage solutions that enable secure, continuous patient care and data-driven clinical and operational decisions with ease, while being empowered with collaboration and productivity tools. Further, [Google Cloud Platform supports HIPAA compliance](https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/hipaa-compliance). We offer [HIPAA-regulated customers](https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/hipaa) the same products at the same pricing that is available to all customers, unlike many other cloud providers.

For healthcare organizations that leverage VMware on-premises, having a consistent, cloud-integrated platform that provides seamless access to native cloud services unlocks the opportunity to extend, migrate, and modernize healthcare IT infrastructure and applications in a fast, low-risk manner at their own pace. This is especially important for mission-critical healthcare provider workloads, where having a low-risk way to adopt the cloud is important. Google Cloud VMware Engine offers that solution. By achieving coverage under Google Cloud’s BAA, Google Cloud VMware Engine enables healthcare organizations to realize the benefits of cloud computing and stay on track with their HIPAA compliance efforts without additional complexity. This is very relevant in hybrid scenarios, where customers would like to leverage other native cloud services such as analytics and big data processing, without having to enter into multiple BAAs.

Google Cloud VMware Engine offers dedicated, isolated software-defined datacenter environments with fully redundant and dedicated 100 Gbps networking that are suitable for healthcare organizations to run applications storing and processing PHI data. Customers have the ability to [encrypt their virtual storage area network (vSAN)](https://cloud.google.com/vmware-engine/docs/vmware-ecosystem/howto-vsan-encryption) using an external key management server. Healthcare customers can run their workloads in a [native VMware environment](https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/digital_google_vmware_data_sheet_ga.pdf)—vSphere, vCenter, vSAN, NSX-T, and HCX—while benefiting from Google Cloud’s highly performant infrastructure to meet the needs of their workloads. Customers can connect their VMware applications to native Google Cloud services such as [BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/) and [artificial intelligence](https://cloud.google.com/products/ai/) (AI) to derive new insights from existing data and quickly make informed decisions.

Protecting against and mitigating the impact of [ransomware attacks](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/5-pillars-of-protection-to-prevent-ransomware-attacks) is top-of-mind for Healthcare organizations. This requires building a cyber resilience program and back-up strategy to prepare for how users can restore core systems or assets affected by a security (in this case, ransomware) incident. This is a critical function for supporting recovery timelines and lessening the impact of a cyber event so organizations can get back to operating their business.  Google Cloud VMware Engine in combination with Google Cloud first party solutions such as [Actifio Go](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/storage-data-transfer/using-actifio-with-google-cloud-vmware-engine-for-dr), or partner solutions such as [NetApp CVO](https://cloud.google.com/netapp) can provide an efficient way to recover incremental point-in-time backups along with on-demand provisioning of new compute to  recover both data and infrastructure from Ransomware attacks quickly and efficiently.

Healthcare customers can also use Google Cloud VMware Engine as a [disaster recovery (DR) target](https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/google_vmware_ecosystem_brief.pdf) for their on-premises VMware workloads. Healthcare organizations also need a business continuity plan for their mission critical applications. When a disaster occurs, hospitals need their data protected so they can quickly get back to treating patients. It is a HIPAA requirement that healthcare organizations must be able to recover from a natural disaster. Google Cloud VMware Engine offers a like-for-like [cost-effective](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/storage-data-transfer/using-actifio-with-google-cloud-vmware-engine-for-dr) DR target for these customers. The DR environment can be operated without new training using the same tools as their on-premises deployment. Google Cloud VMware Engine is currently available in [12 regions](https://cloud.google.com/about/locations) across the globe including three regions in the US, which means our regional and multi-national customers can take advantage of this service for geographic diversification as well.

If you are interested in understanding more and taking advantage of Google Cloud VMware Engine, contact your [Google sales team](https://cloud.google.com/contact/?form=vmwareengine) now.

For details, see [HIPAA compliance on Google Cloud Platform](https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/hipaa).

*Note: This post has been contributed to by Manish Lohani, Product Management, Google Cloud and Wade Holmes, Solution Management, Google Cloud*

URL: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/powering-hipaa-compliant-workloads-using-aws-serverless-technologies

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This AWS Compute Blog post (written by Mayank Thakkar, AWS Senior Solutions Architect) discusses how AWS Serverless technologies can be used to power HIPAA-compliant workloads in the healthcare and life sciences industry. The post announces that AWS Step Functions has achieved HIPAA-eligibility status and been added to the AWS Business Associate Addendum (BAA), joining most other serverless AWS services in the HIPAA program. The BAA is a required contract under HIPAA rules that ensures AWS appropriately safeguards protected health information (PHI).

The post examines three common healthcare use cases with reference architectures:

1. **Provider directory web application**: A serverless architecture using Amazon S3 for static file hosting, Amazon CloudFront for content delivery with caching at the edge, AWS Lambda@Edge for customizing delivered content, Amazon API Gateway for API management, AWS WAF for web protection, and Lambda functions that can access VPC or on-premises resources via VPN/Direct Connect. All services are HIPAA-eligible, pay-as-you-go, and scale automatically to handle enrollment-season spikes.

2. **Medical device telemetry**: IoT medical devices (infusion pumps, dialysis machines) connect via edge nodes/collectors using the Kinesis Producer Library to stream data to Amazon Kinesis Streams (with server-side encryption support). Lambda processes data in real-time, storing insights in Amazon DynamoDB to power near-real-time health dashboards. Historical analysis uses AWS Batch, Amazon EMR, EC2, or serverless MapReduce with Lambda. Lambda can also load data into Amazon Redshift for petabyte-scale data warehousing.

3. **Mobile diagnostics**: Mobile devices with biosensors (otoscopes, thermometers, heart rate monitors) authenticate via Amazon Cognito (which also provides data sync and offline features) and access APIs through API Gateway. Lambda handles CRUD operations storing data in DynamoDB, which caregivers access through browser interfaces. DynamoDB Streams integration with Lambda enables near-real-time reactions to incoming data, and Amazon SNS delivers secure alerts to smart devices.

The post concludes that Lambda is a powerful, event-driven, stateless, on-demand compute platform offering scalability, agility, security, and reliability with fine-grained cost structure, and AWS is committed to making more services HIPAA-eligible. It references the Serverless Application Developer Tooling page and the HIPAA Eligible Services Reference for more details.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is AWS's official compliance page for the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). It explains how AWS enables covered entities and their business associates to use AWS cloud services to process, maintain, and store protected health information (PHI) in a HIPAA-compliant manner.

Key content includes:
- HIPAA is a 1996 federal law protecting the privacy and security of PHI, modified with rules for Privacy (2003), Security (2005), Enforcement (2006), and Breach Notification (2009). It applies to covered entities (health plans, healthcare clearinghouses, and healthcare providers transmitting health information electronically) and their business associates.
- The HIPAA Privacy Rule requires protection of PHI on any medium; the Security Rule requires administrative, physical, and technical controls for confidentiality, integrity, and availability of PHI.
- AWS considers cloud service providers (CSPs) like itself as "business associates" under HIPAA. AWS signs a standard Business Associate Addendum (BAA) with customers, which can be accepted and managed via AWS Artifact in the AWS Management Console.
- AWS is not "HIPAA certified" (no such certification exists for CSPs); instead, AWS aligns its HIPAA risk management program with FedRAMP and NIST 800-53, which are higher security standards mapping to the HIPAA Security Rule.
- Customers with a BAA may use any AWS service in a HIPAA-designated account but should only process PHI in HIPAA-eligible services as defined in the BAA (see the HIPAA Eligible Services Reference).
- HITECH (2009) expanded HIPAA rules; together they establish federal standards for PHI protection under the "Administrative Simplification" rules.
- HITRUST CSF is described as a certifiable framework unifying security controls from federal law (HIPAA/HITECH), state law, and non-governmental frameworks (e.g., PCI) tailored for healthcare.
- For AWS SaaS partners with a BAA selling to healthcare providers, covered entities only need to sign a BAA with the SaaS partner (not AWS), unless they are also direct AWS customers for HIPAA-related systems.
</summary>

"The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) is a federal law that includes provisions designed to protect the privacy and security of PHI."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This AWS News Blog post announces that four AWS services have been added to the AWS Business Associate Addendum (BAA), making them HIPAA-eligible for use with Protected Health Information (PHI). The newly eligible services are: Amazon API Gateway, AWS Direct Connect, AWS Database Migration Service (DMS), and Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS).

The post was written by Patrick Combes (Healthcare and Life Sciences Global Technical Leader at AWS) and Aaron Friedman (Healthcare and Life Sciences Partner Solutions Architect at AWS), and published by Ana Visneski.

Key details about each newly HIPAA-eligible service:
- **Amazon API Gateway**: Enables secure creation, publishing, monitoring, and securing of APIs at any scale. Can be used for patient/provider directories, patient dashboards, medical device telemetry, HL7 message processing, and notably FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) specification — expected to become the next-generation standard for health information exchange due to its RESTful architecture support.
- **AWS Direct Connect**: Provides private connectivity between AWS and on-premises infrastructure (datacenter, office, or colocation), reducing network costs and increasing bandwidth throughput. Useful for hybrid architectures (as used by Johnson & Johnson) and secure migration of data to AWS for use with HIPAA-eligible storage/processing services like Amazon S3 and Amazon EMR. Also supports connecting to third-party/partner solutions and cloud-based Electronic Medical Record systems.
- **AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)**: Over 20,000 databases have been migrated to AWS via DMS. It enables secure migration of core databases containing PHI (patient directories, payment/transaction records, revenue management databases) while keeping the source database fully operational to minimize downtime.
- **Amazon SQS**: Message queueing service for distributed components and microservices. Can buffer requests passing HL7 or FHIR messages between application components. SQS FIFO ensures PHI-containing messages are delivered in order and available until processed and deleted — important for patient record updates and hospital payment processing.

Important compliance note: As with all HIPAA-eligible services under the AWS BAA, PHI must be encrypted while at-rest and in-transit. AWS references its HIPAA compliance whitepaper for configuration guidance, and notes that non-PHI application components can use any of AWS's 90+ services.

--- SOURCE 7: FedRAMP Compliance - Amazon Web Services (AWS) ---
URL: https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/fedramp

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from AWS provides comprehensive information about the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) and AWS's compliance with it. AWS is described as the world's most comprehensive cloud platform, and the page details how the US Federal Government uses AWS cloud services to process, store, and transmit federal government data.

Key points covered:

**What is FedRAMP?** FedRAMP is a US government-wide program that standardizes security assessment, certification, and continuous monitoring for cloud products and services used by federal agencies. It is governed by the FedRAMP Board, Program Management Office (PMO), Technical Advisory Group (TAG), and Federal Secure Cloud Advisory Committee (FSCAC). CSPs must demonstrate FedRAMP compliance using NIST SP 800 series and complete an independent security assessment by a FedRAMP Recognized Independent Assessment Service (formerly 3PAO), compliant with FISMA 2002.

**Why FedRAMP matters:** Established in response to the federal government's Cloud First Policy (now Cloud Smart Strategy) via the OMB FedRAMP Policy Memo, FedRAMP is mandatory for all US federal agencies and cloud services.

**FedRAMP 20x Initiative:** The PMO, industry stakeholders, and agency experts are redesigning the FedRAMP assessment process to streamline and enhance compliance.

**FedRAMP Consolidated Rules for 2026 (CR26):** These published regulations modernize how CSPs communicate changes and maintain ongoing compliance. Key changes include:
- Significant Change Notifications (SCN) for communicating reportable changes to agency customers
- Collaborative Continuous Monitoring (CCM) for ongoing compliance reporting
- "FedRAMP Authorized" renamed to "FedRAMP Certified"

**AWS FedRAMP Certification details:**
- AWS has achieved FedRAMP Certification for AWS GovCloud (US) as Class D (formerly High baseline) and AWS US East-West as Class C (formerly Moderate baseline)
- No increase in AWS service costs due to FedRAMP compliance
- FedRAMP IDs: AWS US East-West = AGENCYAMAZONEW; AWS GovCloud (US) = F1603047866
- AWS maintains continuous monitoring through quarterly Ongoing Certification Reports (OCR) and Quarterly Review briefings
- AWS supports high-impact workloads on AWS GovCloud (US), which is authorized for high impact level

**Key distinctions:**
- FedRAMP Certification is issued by the FedRAMP PMO (congressionally mandated under the FedRAMP Authorization Act)
- The JAB Provisional Authority to Operate (P-ATO) previously issued to AWS is a legacy designation superseded by FedRAMP Certification
- Agencies must issue their own ATO through the Risk Management Framework (RMF) for systems incorporating FedRAMP Certified services
- FedRAMP is the process for CSPs; RMF is the process for agencies authorizing their IT systems

**Accessing FedRAMP packages:** US Government employees/contractors can request the AWS FedRAMP Certification Package via a Package Access Request Form submitted to package-access@fedramp.gov. Commercial customers can access the AWS FedRAMP Partner Package via AWS Artifact. AWS FedRAMP Security Artifacts are also available through AWS Artifact in the AWS Management Console.

**Related compliance programs:** FedRAMP relates to FISMA (built on NIST SP 800-53 controls), DoD CSP SRG (Impact Levels requiring FIPS 140-3 for certain encryption controls), DFARS (requires NIST SP 800-171 for CUI protection), and NIST SP 800-171.

**Government usage:** Many US government agencies and entities use AWS services, with case studies available on the AWS Customer Success webpage and AWS for Government webpage.
</summary>

**ISO 9001:2015**: Quality management system certification covering quality manual documentation, management responsibilities, resource management, service development, customer satisfaction, and QMS measurement/improvement. Supports customers developing quality-controlled IT systems and industry-specific programs like GxP in life sciences and ISO 13485 in medical devices.

**ISO/IEC 27001:2013**: A widely-adopted global security standard requiring systematic evaluation of information security risks, implementation of comprehensive security controls, and ongoing management processes. **ISO/IEC 27017:2015**: Provides cloud-specific information security controls supplementing ISO 27002 and ISO 27001 standards, specific to cloud service providers.

**HITRUST CSF**: Leverages standards like GDPR, ISO, NIST, PCI, and HIPAA to create baseline security and privacy controls. Certain AWS services have been certified under the HITRUST CSF Assurance Program, valid for two years.

**CSA STAR**: A free, publicly accessible registry documenting security controls of cloud offerings. AWS participates in the STAR Self-Assessment and publishes its completed Consensus Assessments Initiative Questionnaire (CAIQ).

--- SOURCE 1: GitHub - ramimac/aws-customer-security-incidents: A repository of breaches of AWS customers · GitHub ---
URL: https://github.com/ramimac/aws-customer-security-incidents

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the GitHub repository "aws-customer-security-incidents" by user ramimac, which serves as a comprehensive, publicly-available catalog of security incidents that impacted AWS customers. The repository's stated purpose is that "cloud security must be threat-informed" and it compiles public data on security incidents to guide prioritized security investment. It seeks to index all publicly disclosed AWS customer security incidents with a known root cause, while explicitly excluding incidents involving exposed data stores (e.g., S3 bucket leaks, exposed managed/hosted databases), which are cataloged elsewhere. The author notes the repository is intended in the spirit of "blameless postmortems" and not as criticism of listed companies.

The main content consists of two detailed tables:

**1. Catalog of AWS Customer Security Incidents** — A chronological table (2014–2026) of ~80 incidents with columns for Name, Date, Root Cause, Escalation Vector(s), Impact, and Link to details. Key incidents include:
- **Uber (2014 & 2016):** GitHub Gist with AWS credentials led to 50,000 records exposed; later 600k driver records and PII of 57 million users.
- **Code Spaces (2014):** AWS Console credentials compromised via phishing led to wiped S3 buckets, EC2 instances, AMIs, and EBS snapshots (putting the company out of business).
- **Capital One (2019):** Misconfigured WAF enabling SSRF attack via over-privileged EC2 Role affected 100 million credit applications.
- **DNC Hack by GRU (2016):** EC2 Snapshots copied to attacker AWS accounts.
- **Lastpass (2022):** Compromised developer account (IAM User) with later compromise of privileged engineer's machine for decryption keys; broadly compromised internal/customer data.
- **Bybit / Safe{Wallet} (2025):** Compromised developer machine with malicious JavaScript via S3 bucket write access led to $1.5 billion stolen.
- **Medibank (2022):** Compromised credentials led to data exfiltration from Redshift.
- **Reddit (2018):** Employee SMS intercepted for 2FA bypass.
- **Capital One (2019), OneLogin (2017), Imperva (2019), Twilio (2020), Dropbox Sign (2024), Cisco (2020), Cloudflare (2023), and many others.**

Common root causes across incidents include: exposed/committed AWS credentials (GitHub, source code, APK, JS files), compromised employee credentials (stale accounts, former employees, insider threats), SSRF attacks, cryptojacking, exposed Kubernetes/Docker consoles, third-party compromise, supply chain attacks (Trivy, Jenkins, OAuth tokens), and infostealer malware. Common impacts include: data exfiltration (S3, RDS, Redshift), cryptojacking/cryptomining, ransomware, phishing/SES abuse, LLMJacking, service outages, and identity theft data exposure.

**2. Vendor-reported AWS Customer Security Incident Case Studies** — A table of ~50 case studies (2020–2025) from vendors including Mandiant, TeamTNT, Expel, CrowdStrike, Sysdig, Unit42 (Palo Alto), Datadog, Wiz, Permiso, Rapid7, Darktrace, and others. These document attack patterns such as credential theft from GitHub, cryptojacking worms (TeamTNT), IAM privilege escalation, IMDS credential theft, SIM-swap attacks, SSRF exploitation, LLMJacking, and S3 ransomware (e.g., SSE-C encryption abuse by Halcyon's Codefinger research).

The repository also includes supporting documentation files: ACTORS.md, DISCLOSURE.md, KEYLEAKS.md, LICENSE, README.md, REPORTS.md, RESEARCH_NOTES.md, SSRF.md, USAGES.md, and a Claude skill folder (.claude/skills/aws-incidents-solver). The repository has 815 stars, 61 forks, and 328 commits.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Cloud security must be threat-informed. This repository compiles public data on security incidents impacting AWS customers, to guide prioritized security investment."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: AWS Security Incident Response: The customer’s journey to accelerating the incident response lifecycle | AWS Security Blog ---
URL: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/aws-security-incident-response-the-customers-journey-to-accelerating-the-incident-response-lifecycle

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This AWS Security Blog post (republished August 1, 2024, to remove incorrect references to AWS WAF and Shield) describes how AWS Security Incident Response—a Tier 1 AWS-native service launched in December 2024—accelerates the incident response lifecycle. The post walks through a real-world scenario to demonstrate the service's capabilities.

KEY STATISTICS AND CONTEXT:
- Over 50% of security alerts go unaddressed due to resource constraints and alert fatigue; false positives consume 30% of investigation time.
- Organizations take an average of 258 days to identify and contain security events (2024 IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report).
- Nearly half of SOC teams report increased detection/response times over the past two years; 80% say manual threat investigation significantly impacts response times.
- Organizations with mature incident response capabilities achieve 50% reduction in mean time to resolution (MTTR) and cost savings of up to 58% per incident.

SERVICE CAPABILITIES:
- Addresses three challenges: alert fatigue (via automated monitoring and intelligent triage), fragmented access/communications, and security skills gaps (via 24/7 access to AWS CIRT experts).
- Integrates with GuardDuty and Security Hub (detection), Systems Manager (management/governance), and third-party solutions through Security Hub integrations and the AWS Security Incident Response Partner Specialization program.
- Provides expert knowledge from AWS Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT), tools via APIs and console, and streamlined processes.

SETUP REQUIREMENTS:
- Configure IAM permissions (AWSSecurityIncidentResponseFullAccess for admins; AWSSecurityIncidentResponseCaseFullAccess and AWSSecurityIncidentResponseReadOnlyAccess for role-based access in dev/test environments).
- Establish incident response team contacts and notification channels.
- Optionally enable GuardDuty and Security Hub, and deploy CloudFormation StackSets for automated containment actions.

WALKTHROUGH SCENARIO (incident at 2:00 AM):
1. DETECTION: GuardDuty detects anomalous IAM behavior, unusual API calls from unknown IPs, and a surge of EC2 instance creations with SSH keys and internet-accessible security groups—matching known threat behaviors via GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection.
2. TRIAGE: The service automatically analyzes GuardDuty findings (including historical baseline, finding types, correlation patterns) and opens an AWS Security Incident Response case when a true positive is identified, notifying the configured team. It correlates disparate events (e.g., CloudTrail log deletion, unauthorized access key creation, suspicious S3 object access) and maps signals to MITRE ATT&CK tactics/techniques/procedures, revealing a potential ransomware threat.
3. AWS CIRT ENGAGEMENT: The team opens a one-click escalation to AWS CIRT through the incident case, with a 15-minute acknowledgement timeframe. AWS CIRT provides conference bridge calls, advanced artifact analysis, technical guidance, and recommendations—even in environments with limited logging.
4. RESOURCE TAGGING: The team tags affected resources using the incident case ID as the primary tag key, enabling targeted access controls, containment measures, cost tracking, and post-incident analysis.
5. CONTAINMENT (via Systems Manager): Using pre-deployed CloudFormation StackSets, the service performs three-step containment: Isolate (remove instances from security groups), Preserve (create snapshots), and Investigate (collect system info via Systems Manager). Actions are reversible.
6. RESOLUTION: Verification of containment, threat alleviation, service restoration, and access control normalization. The service compiles a comprehensive incident timeline for reporting to executives, regulators, and cyber insurance providers.

LESSONS LEARNED AND LONG-TERM IMPROVEMENTS: Enhanced logging based on AWS CIRT recommendations, updated security controls, and improved incident response processes.

ADDITIONAL RESOURCES: AWS Customer Playbook Framework, Assisted Log Enabler, Athena Security Analytics Bootstrap, and five publicly available AWS CIRT workshops.

The post concludes that AWS Security Incident Response delivers measurable benefits through continuous threat monitoring, reduced response times, enhanced investigation via AWS CIRT collaboration, streamlined containment, and comprehensive documentation—with cost savings up to 58% per incident.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Organizations with mature incident response capabilities demonstrate a 50 percent reduction in mean time to resolution (MTTR) and achieve cost savings of up to 58 percent per incident."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: DPA - AWS Data Processing Addendum - awsstatic.com ---
URL: https://d1.awsstatic.com/legal/aws-gdpr/aws-gdpr-dpa-online.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the AWS Data Processing Addendum (DPA), a legal document that supplements the AWS Customer Agreement and governs how AWS processes Customer Data on behalf of its customers. The DPA establishes AWS as a data processor and the Customer as either a controller or processor of Customer Data.

Key provisions include:
- **Data Processing Roles**: AWS acts as processor; Customer acts as controller or processor. The subject matter is Customer Data, with duration determined by the Customer.
- **Customer Instructions**: The DPA and Agreement constitute documented instructions for AWS's processing. Additional instructions require prior written agreement.
- **Confidentiality**: AWS will not access, use, or disclose Customer Data except as necessary to provide Services or comply with law/governmental orders. AWS will redirect governmental demands to Customer where possible.
- **Security Measures**: AWS maintains technical and organizational measures including network security, physical security of facilities, access controls for personnel, and regular testing/evaluation per the AWS Security Standards (Annex 1).
- **Sub-processors**: AWS has general authorization to use sub-processors, which are listed at https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/sub-processors/. AWS must notify Customers at least 30 days before engaging a new sub-processor and remains responsible for sub-processor compliance.
- **Data Subject Requests**: AWS assists via Service Controls and forwards data subject requests to Customer promptly.
- **Security Incidents**: AWS must notify Customer without undue delay after becoming aware of a Security Incident. Unsuccessful incidents (e.g., port scans, failed logins, denial of service attacks) are excluded.
- **Certifications and Audits**: AWS holds ISO 27001, 27017, 27018, and 27701 certifications and SOC 1, 2, and 3 reports. External audits are performed at least annually per ISO 27001 standards.
- **Data Transfers**: Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) apply to GDPR-protected data transferred to Third Countries. Controller-to-Processor Clauses apply when Customer is a controller; Processor-to-Processor Clauses apply when Customer is a processor. SCCs do not apply if AWS has adopted Binding Corporate Rules or alternative compliance standards.
- **Return/Deletion**: AWS returns or deletes Customer Data upon request up to 90 days post-termination, after which Customer must close all AWS accounts.
- **Termination**: The DPA remains in force until the Agreement terminates. In case of conflict, the DPA controls over the Agreement, except Service Terms control over the DPA.

The document also includes Annex 1 (AWS Security Standards) detailing the information security program, network security controls (firewalls, authentication), physical security measures (nondescript facilities, photo-ID badges, video surveillance, intrusion detection), limited employee/contractor access, and continued security evaluation.
</summary>

URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/navigating-gdpr-compliance/aws-data-processing-addendum-dpa.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage describes AWS's Data Processing Addendum (DPA), which is designed to help AWS customers comply with GDPR contractual obligations. Key points include:

- The AWS DPA is incorporated into the AWS Service Terms and applies automatically to all customers globally whenever they use AWS services to process customer data, regardless of applicable data protection laws.
- AWS uses Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) as a data transfer tool for transfers of customer data outside the EU to countries not recognized by the European Commission as providing adequate protection. The SCCs are part of AWS Service Terms, incorporated by reference into the AWS DPA, and apply automatically.
- In February 2021, AWS adopted strengthened contractual commitments for protecting customer data through a Supplementary Addendum to the AWS DPA, which applies to all customer data processed by AWS, regardless of whether it is transferred outside the EEA. No additional customer action is required.
- Key commitments in the Supplementary Addendum include: redirecting governmental requests for customer data directly to customers whenever possible; promptly notifying customers if AWS is compelled to disclose customer data (unless prohibited by law); actively challenging overly broad or inappropriate governmental requests that conflict with EU laws; and disclosing only minimal necessary customer data when legally compelled.
- AWS outlines a structured framework clarifying division of responsibilities under a shared responsibility model: customers assess and implement technical/organizational measures to secure data transfers, while AWS maintains contractual and infrastructure-level safeguards.
- A practical six-step process based on European Data Protection Board (EDPB) guidance helps customers: (1) map data transfers; (2) identify the legal transfer mechanism (such as SCCs); (3) assess destination country laws and practices; (4) implement supplementary safeguards where necessary; (5) document procedural steps; and (6) reassess risk periodically.
- AWS offers safeguards including encryption, data residency controls, and legal commitments to resist overreaching governmental requests.
</summary>
