SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Microsoft Learn article explains how electric power utilities and registered entities subject to North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) standards can use Microsoft Azure and Azure Government for cloud computing compliance.

**Key Points:**

**NERC Overview:** NERC is a not-for-profit regulatory authority ensuring reliability of the North American bulk power system, subject to oversight by the US FERC and Canadian authorities. FERC granted NERC the Electric Reliability Organization (ERO) designation in 2006 under the Energy Policy Act of 2005. NERC develops and enforces CIP reliability standards (first approved by FERC in 2007).

**Azure vs. Azure Government:** Both provide multi-tenant cloud platforms with logical isolation for customer data. Azure Government is a US government community cloud, physically separated from Azure, available only in the US to US-based registered entities, with contractual commitments limiting access to screened US persons. Azure is available to NERC entities in both the US and Canada. Both are suitable for registered entities deploying certain NERC CIP-compliant workloads.

**NERC CIP Data Categorization:** CIP standards apply to the Bulk Electric System (BES) (generally 100 kV and above; 20MVA+ generating units; 75MVA+ generating plants; Control Centers), not to distribution (with exceptions like UFLS, UVLS, Blackstart Resources). Key definitions include Cyber Asset, BES Cyber Asset (BCA), BES Cyber System (BCS), Electronic Security Perimeter (ESP), Protected Cyber Asset (PCA), Electronic Access Point (EAP), Electronic Access Control or Monitoring Systems (EACMS), and Control Center. Current NERC CIP definitions emphasize physical assets ("in those devices") and lack provisions for cloud concepts like virtualization and multi-tenancy. Workloads not subject to the 15-minute rule include transmission planning, SCADA historical data, AI/analytics, IoT monitoring, and NERC CIP audit evidence. BES Cyber System Information (BCSI) can be deployed in cloud if proper security controls are in place.

**Compliance Audits:** Azure and Azure Government maintain three relevant independent third-party audits: CSA STAR Certification and Attestation, AICPA SOC 2 Type 2 Attestation, and FedRAMP High P-ATOs (issued by the JAB) plus over 250 Moderate and High ATOs. The FedRAMP Moderate control baseline (325 controls) encompasses all NERC CIP requirements. NERC reviewed Azure controls and FedRAMP evidence for CIP-004-6 and CIP-011-2 (applicable to BCSI), concluding no extra guidance is needed for cloud BCSI deployment.

**Isolation and Security:** Both platforms provide logical isolation across identity (Microsoft Entra ID with RBAC), compute (Hyper-V virtualization, plus Azure Dedicated Host/Isolated VMs for physical isolation), networking (Azure VNet), and storage (encrypted at rest with Microsoft-managed or customer-managed keys via Azure Key Vault with FIPS 140 validated HSMs). Microsoft engineers have no default access to customer data. Azure Government requires US persons verification for operations personnel.

**Additional Considerations:** Nuclear electric utilities may face DoE 10 CFR Part 810 export control requirements. Registered entities are ultimately responsible for NERC CIP compliance. Microsoft offers a "Cloud implementation guide for NERC audits" (downloadable under NDA from the Service Trust Portal) with pre-filled Reliability Standard Audit Worksheets (RSAWs) narratives and control mappings between NERC CIP standards and FedRAMP Moderate baseline.
</summary>

"Both Azure and Azure Government are suitable for registered entities deploying certain workloads subject to compliance with NERC CIP standards."

--- SOURCE 9: Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) - Azure Compliance ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/compliance/offerings/offering-fedramp

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Microsoft Learn page provides detailed information about the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) compliance for Microsoft Azure and Azure Government cloud services.

**FedRAMP Overview**: FedRAMP was established in December 2011 to provide a standardized approach for assessing, monitoring, and authorizing cloud computing products and services under FISMA, and to accelerate secure cloud adoption by US federal agencies. Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) can demonstrate compliance via three paths: (1) earning a Provisional Authorization to Operate (P-ATO) from the FedRAMP Joint Authorization Board (JAB), (2) receiving an Authorization to Operate (ATO) from a federal agency, or (3) independently developing a CSP Supplied Package. All paths require assessment by an accredited independent third-party assessment organization (3PAO) and technical review by the FedRAMP Program Management Office (PMO). FedRAMP is based on NIST SP 800-53 and offers three impact levels: Low, Moderate (325 controls), and High (421 controls). The JAB comprises representatives from DoD, DHS, and GSA.

**Azure and FedRAMP**: Both Azure and Azure Government maintain FedRAMP High P-ATOs issued by the JAB, plus more than 400 Moderate and High ATOs from individual federal agencies. Azure Government provides additional customer assurances through controls limiting access to systems processing customer data to screened US persons. Microsoft provides Azure Policy regulatory compliance built-in initiatives for FedRAMP High and Moderate on both Azure and Azure Government.

**Key Facts**:
- All Azure public US regions are in scope for the Azure FedRAMP High P-ATO; non-US regions aren't formally authorized but run the same security controls.
- Azure Government regions in scope: US Gov Arizona, US Gov Texas, and US Gov Virginia.
- FISMA's process was replaced by FedRAMP in 2011; FedRAMP is mandatory for federal agency cloud deployments.
- Customers can use Azure's FedRAMP High P-ATO as the foundation for their own agency ATOs but must achieve authorizations for components outside these services.
- FedRAMP documentation (SSP, continuous monitoring reports, POA&M) is available via the FedRAMP Marketplace (requires .gov or .mil email), Service Trust Portal (requires sign-in and Azure subscription or free trial).
- Azure penetration tests are conducted annually by an accredited 3PAO, with reports typically due in September and uploaded to STP by December or shortly after.
- FedRAMP is not a point-in-time certification but an ongoing assessment and authorization program with continuous monitoring provisions.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Breach Notification - Microsoft GDPR | Microsoft Learn ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/compliance/regulatory/gdpr-breach-notification

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Microsoft Learn documentation page on GDPR Breach Notification. It outlines Microsoft's approach to complying with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) regarding personal data breach notifications for organizations offering goods/services to EU residents or collecting/analyzing EU resident data.

**Key definitions**: A personal data breach is "a breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to, personal data transmitted, stored, or otherwise processed." Personal data refers to any information that can identify an individual directly or indirectly.

**Microsoft's breach notification obligations**: As a data processor, Microsoft ensures service customers can meet GDPR breach notification requirements as data controllers. Microsoft notifies customers of any personal data breach, except where personal data is confirmed unintelligible (e.g., encrypted data with confirmed key integrity). Initial notifications include a description of the breach's nature, approximate user impact, and mitigation steps. Data controllers are responsible for assessing privacy risks and determining whether a breach requires notification of their DPA.

**Product-specific breach notification details**:
1. **Office 365**: Microsoft invests in systems, processes, and personnel to reduce breach likelihood and mitigate consequences. Customers can contact Microsoft Support to report suspected breaches.
2. **Azure and Dynamics 365**: Microsoft operates a global 24x7 incident response service. Azure employs a shared responsibility model — Microsoft doesn't monitor security incidents within the customer's realm of responsibility. Microsoft determines breach priority/severity by investigating functional impact, recoverability, and information impact, working with global legal advisors. Customer notifications are delivered within 72 hours of breach declaration, except when notification would increase risk to other customers or when the 72-hour timeline limits available incident details.
3. **Microsoft Support and Professional Services**: Some data protection incidents may fall within the customer's realm of responsibility; Microsoft follows a documented industry-standard response plan.
4. **Windows**: The Windows diagnostic data processor configuration uses cloud infrastructure and built-in security features, backed by Microsoft's 24x7 global incident response service.

**Admin tools**: Tenant Administrators can set their organization's privacy contact via the Microsoft Entra admin center. The page also links to the Microsoft Trust Center for more GDPR information. Page last updated 2026-05-05.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A personal data breach is 'a breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to, personal data transmitted, stored, or otherwise processed.'", "As a data processor, Microsoft ensures that service customers can meet the GDPR's breach notification requirements as data controllers. <summary>
This webpage is a Microsoft Learn documentation page titled "Microsoft Support and Professional Services and Breach Notification Under the GDPR." It describes how Microsoft Professional Services (a team of over 21,000 consultants, Digital Advisors, engineers, and sales professionals across 191 countries and regions, supporting 46 languages) handles data protection incidents and GDPR breach notification requirements.

Key points covered:

- **Data protection incident definition**: A breach of security leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to Personal Data or Professional Services Data while processed by Microsoft.
- **Scope and limits**: Microsoft only responds to incidents within its realm of responsibility. Customer-driven incidents (e.g., customers inadvertently sending passwords, fraud against customers) are classified as "events" rather than Microsoft data protection incidents, though Microsoft will inform and assist customers.
- **Incident types**: The response team has identified various scenarios, from misdirected emails (requiring little investigation) to malicious personnel activity (requiring full forensic investigation).
- **Incident response process**: A triage process involving assessing the event, determining scope, assessing maliciousness, preliminary investigation with severity assignment, and stakeholder coordination. Detection methods include automated alerts, customer reports, external reports, anomaly observation, and malicious activity indicators.
- **Training and drills**: Annual data protection incident response drills are conducted with security, legal, and communications teams. All personnel must complete mandatory training on privacy fundamentals and GDPR regulations.
- **Notification requirements**: Microsoft targets notification to customers within 72 hours of declaring a data protection incident. Initial notifications may not include complete details, and some details may be withheld if disclosure would increase risk to others or interfere with law enforcement. Microsoft recognizes that customers, as data processors, are responsible for notifying Data Protection Authorities and their own data subjects.
- **Notification contents**: Nature of the breach, mitigation measures, product/service involved, exposure duration, volume of affected records, and sub-processor/supplier details (if known and applicable).
- **Post-mortems**: Internal post-mortems are conducted for higher-severity incidents, are highly confidential, and are reviewed by external auditors. Commercial customers with Unified Support or ISD should refer to the Microsoft Products and Services Data Protection Addendum (DPA).

**Key Topics:**

**Security Approach:** Microsoft uses a "assume breach" security strategy built on defense-in-depth, incorporating privacy-by-design and privacy-by-default via the Security Development Lifecycle. Microsoft has a dedicated global, 24/7 incident response service, with data center protections including video monitoring, smart cards, and biometric controls.

**Shared Responsibility Model:** Microsoft doesn't monitor or respond to security incidents within the customer's realm of responsibility. A customer-only security compromise isn't a Microsoft security incident. Customers can use services like Microsoft Defender for Cloud for their own incident response.

**Five-Stage Incident Response Process:**
1. **Detect** - First indication of a potential incident
2. **Assess** - Incident response team member evaluates impact and severity
3. **Diagnose** - Technical/forensic investigation; if customer data may be exposed, Customer Incident Notification begins in parallel
4. **Stabilize and Recover** - Recovery plan created; crisis containment (e.g., quarantining systems) may happen immediately
5. **Close and Post-mortem** - Post-mortem created to revise policies and prevent recurrence

**Detection Triggers:** Automated system alerts, first-party reports, MSRC vulnerability reports, customer reports via support portals, Red Team/Blue Team security activity, and escalations by Microsoft service operators.

**Incident Classifications:** False positive, Security event, Security Incident/Customer Reportable Security/Privacy Incident (CRSPI), Privacy Event, and Privacy Incident/CRSPI. A CRSPI is declared when unauthorized access to customer data happened or likely happened, or when legal/contractual commitments require notification.

**Customer Notification:** Microsoft notifies impacted customers and regulatory authorities without undue delay, and in no more than 72 hours from declaring a breach, except in limited circumstances (e.g., notification might increase risk to other customers, or details are not yet available). Notifications are delivered via the Azure service health notifications blade (as Security Advisory), and/or email to Azure Subscription Administrators/Owners, Microsoft Entra Global Tenant Administrators, and Microsoft Entra tenant Technical Contacts. For Dynamics 365 and Power Platform, notifications go through the Microsoft 365 admin center Message Center with a Data Privacy tag.

**Dynamics 365/Power Platform:** These services follow the same technical and organizational measures as Azure for breach security, with built-in features covering secure identity, data protection, role-based security, and threat management.

**Important recommendation:** Microsoft recommends using roles with the fewest permissions, and minimizing the number of users with Global Administrator role to improve security.

--- SOURCE 11: Azure AI Foundry: Modified Abuse Monitoring, EU data residency, retention, and least-privilege RBAC for runtime agent - Microsoft Q&A ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/5966351/azure-ai-foundry-modified-abuse-monitoring-eu-data

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Microsoft Q&A forum post from a nonprofit organization (using an Azure Nonprofit Sponsorship subscription) asking for guidance on configuring Azure AI Foundry / Azure OpenAI with Microsoft Entra ID authentication and RBAC (no API keys) for a runtime-only agent identity. The question covers four areas, and a detailed moderator answer (by Manish Deshpande, Microsoft External Staff) addresses each:

**1. European Data Zone Processing (answered first as it changes priorities):** The Global Standard deployment is the issue. Data residency documentation states that global deployment types may process data in any Azure region, while Data Zone types (EU, US, APAC) process only within the specified zone, and Standard single-region types process in the deployment region. The EU Data Zone follows the Azure EU Data Boundary, which can include EFTA countries like Switzerland. However, an EU Data Zone deployment does not keep processing in Switzerland specifically — if Swiss residency is required, a single-region Standard in Switzerland North would be needed (with narrower model availability). A documented caveat notes that Global deployments may process prompts/completions outside the EU even for EU-based resources. Recommended action: apply Azure Policy to disable global deployments, verify the deployment SKU reads DataZoneStandard, and confirm the parent Foundry resource is in an EU region.

**2. Data Retention, Storage, and Human Review:** Data storage applies only to the abuse-monitoring path; automated path prompts/completions are not stored or used for training. The abuse-monitoring store is logically separated per customer and located in the Azure geography of the Foundry resource. Human review occurs only when automated review fails confidence thresholds or is unavailable, accessed via Secure Access Workstations (SAWs) with Just-In-Time (JIT) approval. For models sold by Azure in the EEA, authorized reviewers are located in the EEA. The moderator explicitly refused to give a default retention number, noting that while a "30 days" figure circulates in forums, it is absent from the current authoritative documentation and should not be used in compliance files without a written contractual answer under the Microsoft Products and Services Data Protection Addendum. After Modified Abuse Monitoring approval: "the data storage and human review process described above is not performed. However, automated review may still be conducted."

**3. Modified Abuse Monitoring:** Being a nonprofit does not itself qualify — eligibility is limited to customers managed by a Microsoft account team or under an eligible program. However, non-managed customers are invited to apply anyway via the same forms. Review time is 5-10 business days. The form is linked from the Abuse monitoring and Limited access pages. Caveats: approval is per model class (not blanket), and disabling human review may make abuse detection less accurate. Verification after approval: check the Foundry resource JSON view or run `az cognitiveservices account show` and look for `{"name":"ContentLogging","value":"false"}` in Capabilities — absence of the property means storage is still on.

**4. Least-Privilege RBAC:** The moderator explicitly says NOT to use Cognitive Services OpenAI User or Azure AI Developer roles for Foundry scenarios (these are for direct AI Services resource access). The recommended role is **Foundry Agent Consumer** — the least-privilege role for principals that only interact with agents, with exactly one of eight capabilities (interact with agent endpoints). GUIDs should be used instead of display names due to recent role renames. Scope should be narrowed to a single agent. However, Foundry Agent Consumer doesn't grant access to Agent Applications — Foundry User or a custom role would be needed if the agent is published as an Agent Application. Notably, Owner and Contributor roles cannot interact with agent endpoints at all (ARM control-plane only). The moderator also emphasized that role-based enforcement only works if key-based authentication is disabled (set disableLocalAuth on the Foundry account), since API keys bypass role assignments entirely.

A second, shorter answer by user "Nithin" suggests somewhat different guidance: using Modified Abuse Monitoring to disable "30-day human review data retention," provisioning resources in EU regions (Sweden Central or France Central), and assigning the Cognitive Services OpenAI User role at resource group level — though this conflicts with the moderator's explicit guidance against that role for Foundry scenarios.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 13: What is the EU Data Boundary? - Microsoft Privacy | Microsoft Learn ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/privacy/eudb/eu-data-boundary-learn

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Microsoft Learn documentation defines the **EU Data Boundary** — a geographically defined boundary within which Microsoft commits to store and process Customer Data and personal data for its enterprise online services, including Azure, Dynamics 365, Power Platform, and Microsoft 365. Professional Services Data will be stored at rest for these services. These commitments are subject to limited circumstances where data continues to be transferred outside the EU Data Boundary.

**Key definitions:**
- **Customer Data**: All data (including text, sound, video, image files, and software) provided to Microsoft by or on behalf of a Customer through use of the Online Service. It excludes Professional Services Data and configuration information (technical settings, resource names).
- **Personal data in system-generated logs**: Microsoft online services create system-generated logs as part of regular operation. Some logs contain fields that identify or can identify specific persons (e.g., product and service usage data, user activity logs).
- **Pseudonymization**: Per GDPR Article 4(5), pseudonymization replaces personally identifiable information with artificial identifiers/pseudonyms. Microsoft requires all personal data in system-generated logs to be pseudonymized using techniques including encryption, masking, tokenization, and data blurring. This enables authorized Microsoft personnel to work (e.g., DevOps identifying service issues across regions) without identifying or reidentifying users. Anonymization is not used because it would permanently alter data and compromise Microsoft's ability to ensure quality, reliability, and security of services.
- **Security controls for system-generated logs** include: data minimization via minimum retention policies, regular checks and scrubbing, limited usage solely for service operations, and access controls limiting rehydration/reidentification of personal data.
- **Professional Services Data**: All data provided to Microsoft through an engagement to obtain Professional Services (consulting services and technical support services).

**EU Data Boundary countries and datacenter locations:**
- Consists of EU countries (Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden) and EFTA countries (Liechtenstein, Iceland, Norway, Switzerland).
- Uses Microsoft datacenters announced/operating in Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland. Additional datacenters may be established in the future.

**How to configure services:**
- **Azure**: Regional services deployed in an EU Data Boundary region are in-scope. Non-regional services require configuration via Azure Resource Manager.
- **Dynamics 365 and Power Platform**: Requires BOTH (1) provisioning the tenant and all environments in the "European Union (EU) and European Free Trade Association (EFTA)" Macro Region Geography, AND (2) maintaining a billing address in an EU Data Boundary country. Meeting only one requirement doesn't place environments within the boundary.
- **Microsoft 365**: Customers with a sign-up location in an EU or EFTA country are in-scope; however, customers with Multi-Geo Capabilities are not in-scope even if their tenant is in an EU/EFTA country.

The documentation was last updated February 26, 2025, and reflects the current state of the EU Data Boundary as of the publication date.
</summary>

When a resource's data location is set to a European country/region in scope of EUDB, all processing and storage of personal data remains within the European Union.

Key details per service:
- **Calling**: Defines key participant roles (Organizer, Initiator, Guest) and terms (Call, Real Time Text/RTT, Resource). For calling resources located in a European data boundary country, when the organizer, initiator, or a guest joins from a location inside the boundary, all personal data (PII) is processed and stored in facilities within EU boundary countries/regions. RTT is noted as an EU accessibility compliance requirement (Directive 2019/882).
- **SMS**: Data is processed and stored in the Netherlands, Ireland, or Switzerland regions, ensuring no unauthorized transfer outside the EEA. Advanced security measures including encryption protect SMS data at rest and in transit. Customers can select data residency within EUDB. Note: ACS is regulated in EU and UK as a provider of interpersonal communications services (ICS) and complies with each member state's national laws (licensing, reporting, regulatory fees, security, CLI restrictions, data retention, anti-spam/anti-fraud, etc.).
- **SMS EUDB FAQ**: UK data is processed within the EUDB (Netherlands, Ireland, or Switzerland regions) despite no longer being in the EU. For recipients outside the EU, core processing/storage remains in EUDB, but messages may be routed through non-EU networks for delivery purposes only. Data can be transferred to non-EU regions solely to deliver SMS to recipients outside the EU, but processing and storage at rest still comply with EUDB.
- **Messaging**: All threads created from an EU resource process and store personal data in the EU.

A related resource is the Microsoft EU Data Boundary Overview in Microsoft's Trust Center.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Microsoft Q&A forum thread titled "Inquiry on Data Residency, Compliance, and Security for Microsoft Azure OpenAI Subscription." The original poster, Nikhil Bhatia, asked four questions about: (1) whether data/prompts submitted to Azure OpenAI via API remain in Switzerland, (2) how Microsoft handles data requests from US or foreign authorities, (3) what AI subscriptions are commonly used by law firms and how data is secured against training usage, and (4) Microsoft's GDPR/FDAP compliance framework and list of sub-processors.

Key answers provided across the thread:

**Data Residency in Switzerland:** Azure OpenAI Service is available in the Switzerland North region, allowing data residency within Switzerland when configured with regional deployment. However, for 'Global' deployment types, prompts and responses may be processed in any geography where the relevant model is deployed. For 'DataZone' deployments, data may be processed within the specified data zone. A Microsoft moderator (Manas R Mohanty) clarified that with Global Standard deployments, data at rest remains in the designated geography (e.g., Europe) but inference calls may route to any global location. DataZone deployments keep data at rest in the designated geography (e.g., Switzerland North) while inference may occur anywhere within that data zone.

**Government Data Requests:** Microsoft only responds to government or foreign authority data requests under applicable laws, following a rigorous legal review. Microsoft does not provide governments direct access to customer data, attempts to redirect requests to customers where legally possible, and notifies customers unless prohibited. Microsoft's process includes legal review, customer notification, challenging unlawful requests, transparency reports, escalation to legal/compliance teams, and documentation in the Data Protection Addendum (DPA).

**Service Provider Entity:** For EU customers, including Ireland, the service provider is Microsoft Ireland Operations Limited (MIOL), operating under Irish law. However, Microsoft remains a US-headquartered company subject to US legal obligations such as the CLOUD Act. US authorities can issue data requests, but Microsoft will challenge non-EU government requests and only comply if legally required under EU law, notifying customers where permissible. The DPA includes clauses on Data Transfers referencing the 2021 Standard Contractual Clauses, GDPR Article 46 safeguards, and Article 30(2) documentation.

**Law Firm Subscriptions:** Law firms typically use Standard, PTU (Provisioned Throughput Unit), or Batch API subscriptions for legal drafting, contract analysis, and e-discovery. EA (Enterprise Agreement) subscriptions offer higher quota and support. Azure OpenAI models are stateless—no prompts or completions are stored in the model, and they are not used to train, retrain, or improve base models by default. Data is encrypted at rest by default.

**Compliance:** Azure OpenAI is GDPR- and FDAP-compliant, offering encryption in transit and at rest, Customer-Managed Keys, and pseudonymization. Microsoft publishes a list of sub-processors through the Microsoft Trust Center. Compliance offerings for EMEA include EU Cloud CoC, EU GDPR, EU Model Clauses, Germany C5, and others. Microsoft offers Sovereign Cloud options and features like Data Guardian (Europe-based access approval) and External Key Management for maximum sovereignty.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Office 365 Breach Notification Under the GDPR - Microsoft GDPR | Microsoft Learn ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/regulatory/gdpr-breach-office365

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Microsoft Learn documentation page explains Office 365's breach notification obligations and practices under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). As a data processor, Microsoft commits to: (1) allowing customers to designate a dedicated privacy contact via the Privacy reader role in Message Center; (2) notifying customers of personal data breaches within 72 hours of a breach being declared, published to Message Center and accessible through the Microsoft 365 admin center; and (3) including in the initial notification the nature of the breach, an approximation of user impact, and applicable mitigation steps. Microsoft notifies customers of any personal data breach except those where personal data is confirmed to be unintelligible (e.g., encrypted data with verified key integrity).

The page details Office 365's investments in data security, including: access control systems with a "zero-standing access" policy and least-privilege principles; real-time security monitoring systems with automatic threat resolution and red-team penetration testing exercises; and personnel/processes including a detailed privacy breach Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) shared across teams, plus regular training on data classification and personal data handling.

In the event of a breach, customers can expect a consistent incident response lifecycle, consistent notification criteria (focusing on confidentiality, integrity, and availability of customer data), and consistent notification details (timing of breach and awareness, approximate number of users impacted, type of user data breached, and mitigation actions needed). Office 365, as a data processor, does not determine breach risk — data controllers must assess breach severity, decide whether users need notification, whether regulators (DPAs) need notification, and what mitigation steps the controller should take. Customers wishing to notify Microsoft should contact Microsoft Support, which interfaces with engineering teams. Microsoft recommends customers designate Message Center Privacy readers through the Microsoft 365 admin center to receive breach notifications. The page was last updated on May 5, 2026.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Microsoft announced the completion of the EU Data Boundary for the Microsoft Cloud in February 2025, an industry-leading solution that stores and processes public sector and commercial customer data within the EU and European Free Trade Association (EFTA) regions. This milestone, announced by Julie Brill (Corporate Vice President and Chief Privacy Officer) and Paul Lorimer (Corporate Vice President, Microsoft 365), enables European commercial and public sector customers to store and process customer data and pseudonymized personal data for Microsoft core cloud services—including Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, Power Platform, and most Azure services—within the EU and EFTA regions. Additionally, professional services data from technical support interactions for core cloud services is now stored within these regions.

The EU Data Boundary was delivered in three phases:
- Phase 1 (January 2023): Enabled storage and processing of customer data for core services including Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, Power Platform, and Azure.
- Phase 2 (January 2024): Expanded scope to include pseudonymized personal data.
- Phase 3 (February 2025): Ensured professional services data (customer logs and Microsoft-generated support case notes) for Microsoft 365, Power Platform, and Dynamics 365 support interactions are stored within EU/EFTA regions. Certain Azure services may require additional customer action for this commitment.

Microsoft's commitment to Europe spans more than 40 years, with over $20 billion invested in AI and cloud infrastructure across the continent over the past 16 months. Additional offerings include Microsoft 365 Advanced Data Residency for granular data location controls, Microsoft Cloud for Sovereignty for public sector customers, and the European Cloud Principles for transparency and accountability. Microsoft also highlighted its Secure Future Initiative (SFI) for cybersecurity, noting that in limited security instances requiring coordinated global response, essential data may be transferred with robust protections including encryption, strict access controls, and other security measures, with transparent information provided to customers.

- **Azure AI Bot Service**: Bot data plane data stored/processed in the EU.
- **Azure Communication Services**: Specify geography; Europe geography ensures EU Data Boundary compliance.
- **Azure Kubernetes Service on Azure Local**: Data sent to region selected during cluster configuration.
- **Azure Migrate**: Geography selected at project creation; EU geography ensures EU Data Boundary storage.
- **Azure Resource Manager**: Can be configured via tenant-level data boundary configuration for newly provisioned tenants only (no existing subscriptions/resources); configuration cannot be removed or modified once set; resource deployments restricted to EU regions.

- **Azure VM Image Builder**: EU region templates store/process data in EU.
- **Cloud Shell**: Can create storage within EU Data Boundary by selecting an EU Cloud Shell region.
- **Microsoft Entra ID and Azure AD B2C**: Specify geography; EU location ensures EU Data Boundary compliance (with residual transfers documented).
- **Microsoft Fabric**: Geo determined by first sign-up user; configure tenant and all capacities in EU datacenter locations; region selection option available for capacity.
- **Power BI Embedded**: Select Azure region for workspace data; home region default option.
- **Translator**: Provides a European endpoint (api-eur.cognitive.microsofttranslator.com); all requests processed only in EU datacenters, with errors returned if no EU datacenter available.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Microsoft Q&A forum thread titled "Request for Clarification on Azure OpenAI Global Standard Deployment – Data Residency & Processing." The original poster, Zoey Azimi (from a Germany-based company), asks about data residency and processing for Azure OpenAI Service's Global Standard deployment mode, given strict GDPR and EU AI Act compliance requirements.

Key questions raised by the poster:
1. Which countries/data centers may process data (prompts, completions, telemetry, logs) in Global Standard mode for core model inference, abuse detection, and telemetry/moderation.
2. Whether any Microsoft or third-party services outside the EU/US (e.g., Asia, Latin America, Africa) are involved in data routing, logging, abuse monitoring, health monitoring, or diagnostics.
3. Whether Microsoft provides a detailed Data Flow Diagram or Architecture Document.
4. What contractual safeguards (SCCs, DPA, BAA) apply for GDPR compliance.
5. Whether logging/abuse monitoring can be opted out of, or additional protections like Azure Private Link or customer-managed keys can be used.

Community responses provided the following clarifications:
- In Global Standard mode, core model inference occurs in the selected Azure region (e.g., EU or US), but prompts and completions may be processed in any geography where the relevant Azure OpenAI model is deployed.
- Abuse detection samples are stored in the Azure geography where the customer's resource is deployed.
- Azure OpenAI models are deployed across various global regions including Australia East, Japan East, South India, and Sweden Central, among others.
- Microsoft relies on Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) and the Data Protection Addendum (DPA) for GDPR compliance and data transfers outside the EU/US.
- Abuse monitoring can be turned off upon approval, verifiable via the ContentLogging flag.
- Data is not shared with OpenAI or used for model training, which is important for GDPR alignment.
- Specific documentation on data flow diagrams, third-party vendor involvement in non-EU/US locations, and specific regional processing lists were not fully detailed; the responder suggested contacting Microsoft directly for precise details.
- A reference link to Microsoft's data privacy documentation was provided: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/legal/cognitive-services/openai/data-privacy?tabs=azure-portal

The thread contains follow-up exchanges (March 25 – April 7, 2025) where the poster acknowledged some clarity was achieved and raised final remaining questions about specific non-EU/US regions, third-party vendor involvement, and explicit legal bases for data transfers. The thread includes unanswered follow-up requests from the responder asking whether a resolution was reached.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In Global Standard deployment mode, core model inference occurs in the selected Azure region (e.g., EU or US). However, prompts and completions may be processed in any geography where the relevant Azure OpenAI model is deployed."

--- SOURCE 13: What are Azure Availability Zones? ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/reliability/availability-zones-overview

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an official Microsoft Learn documentation page explaining Azure availability zones. Availability zones are separated groups of datacenters within an Azure region, each with independent power, cooling, and networking infrastructure, so that if one zone experiences an outage, regional services and high availability are supported by remaining zones. An availability zone is a logical grouping of one or more physically separate datacenters, typically separated by several kilometers but within about 100 kilometers of each other, providing low-latency connectivity while reducing the impact of local outages or weather events.

The page describes three types of availability zone support for Azure services: (1) Zone-redundant resources, which are replicated or distributed across multiple zones by the service (with Microsoft managing spreading requests and data replication, and automatic failover in the event of an outage); (2) Zonal resources, which are deployed to a single zone selected by the user and do not automatically provide resiliency (users must design multi-zone architectures themselves and are responsible for failover); and (3) Nonzonal/regional deployments, where resources are not configured to use zones and Azure may place them across any zones, potentially causing downtime if an affected zone experiences an outage. A resource is considered "zone-resilient" if it uses two or more zones.

Key technical details include: physical zones are mapped to logical zones per-subscription with potentially different mapping orders (determinable via Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, or Azure Resource Manager APIs such as List Locations and Check Zone Peers); Microsoft aims to deploy updates to a single zone at a time to reduce workload impact; inter-zone networking within a region targets round-trip latency of less than approximately 2 milliseconds; and Azure does not charge for data transfer between availability zones in the same region.

Architectural guidance recommends that production workloads use multiple availability zones if supported by the region, and that mission-critical workloads consider both multiregion and multi-zone solutions. For single-region workloads constrained by data residency, multi-zone deployment is the primary recommended way to maximize availability. Availability zones do not protect against full-region outages.

The page includes a table listing regions supporting availability zones across the Americas (e.g., Brazil South, Canada Central, Central US, East US, East US 2, Mexico Central, South Central US, West US 2, West US 3), Europe (e.g., Austria East, Belgium Central, Denmark East, France Central, Germany West Central, Italy North, North Europe, Norway East, Poland Central, Spain Central, Sweden Central, Switzerland North, UK South, West Europe), Middle East (Israel Central, Qatar Central, UAE North), Africa (South Africa North), and Asia Pacific (Australia East, Central India, East Asia, India South Central, Indonesia Central, Japan East, Japan West, Korea Central, Malaysia West, New Zealand North, Southeast Asia). The page was last updated on 2026-06-26.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Many Azure regions provide availability zones, which are separated groups of datacenters within a region. Each availability zone has independent power, cooling, and networking infrastructure, so that if one zone experiences an outage, then regional services, capacity, and high availability are supported by the remaining zones."
</key_excerpts>

- Azure Form Recognizer to read handwriting on forms dating back 10-20 years
- Azure Blob Storage for secure document storage
- Azure AI Search for keyword-based search across the document repository

**Results:**
- 2 million documents digitized and indexed into 50 document types
- Compliance case processing reduced from 80 to 20 minutes (75% less time on regulatory review)
- Employees freed up for higher-value work (compliance strategy and risk mitigation)
- AI-powered digital assistant introduced into the mobile app, guiding customers directly to features (e.g., blocking a credit card in stressful situations), processing queries in multiple languages

This AWS video tutorial (posted February 1, 2022, with 5,357 views) demonstrates how to enable data residency controls using AWS Control Tower guardrails. Guardrails are pre-packaged rules that automate security and operational controls across a multi-account environment. The tutorial walks through three types of guardrails:

1. **Preventive guardrail (region deny)**: Denies access to AWS services in non-governed (non-government) regions. The user modifies landing zone settings to enable the region deny feature, which prohibits access across all regions except the five governed regions controlled by Control Tower. The tutorial demonstrates that attempting to create a VPC in a non-governed region results in an "unauthorized to perform this action" error, while governed regions allow normal operations.

2. **Detection guardrail (S3 public access)**: Detects whether Amazon S3 settings block public access. Applied to a "data resident OU," this guardrail identifies non-compliant resources. The tutorial shows an account with S3 public access enabled, and after disabling public access in S3, the guardrail no longer reports the resource as non-compliant.

3. **Preventive guardrail (VPC internet access)**: Disables internet access for new Amazon VPCs, but does not apply to existing VPCs. Attempting to create a VPC with internet access results in an error message and automatic rollback of the operation's resources, though VPCs without internet/public access can still be created.

Key benefits highlighted: better control over data residency, reduced project delays, and the ability to match guardrails to specific business needs. The tutorial also shows how to view guardrail policy templates in AWS Organizations, including templatized parameters restricting region access and global AWS resources excluded from deny lists.

# Architecting for data residency with AWS Outposts rack and landing zone guardrails

*This blog post was written by Abeer Naffa’, Sr. Solutions Architect, Solutions Builder AWS, David Filiatrault, Principal Security Consultant, AWS and Jared Thompson, Hybrid Edge SA Specialist, AWS.*

In this post, we will explore how organizations can use [AWS Control Tower landing zone](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/controltower/latest/userguide/planning-your-deployment.html) and [AWS Organizations](https://aws.amazon.com/organizations/) custom guardrails to enable compliance with data residency requirements on [AWS Outposts rack](https://aws.amazon.com/outposts/rack/?nc=sn&loc=2). We will discuss how custom guardrails can be leveraged to limit the ability to store, process, and access data and remain isolated in specific geographic locations, how they can be used to enforce security and compliance controls, as well as, which prerequisites organizations should consider before implementing these guardrails.

Data residency is a critical consideration for organizations that collect and store sensitive information, such as Personal Identifiable Information (PII), financial, and healthcare data. With the rise of cloud computing and the global nature of the internet, it can be challenging for organizations to make sure that their data is being stored and processed in compliance with local laws and regulations.

One potential solution for addressing [data residency](https://d1.awsstatic.com/product-marketing/Outposts/AWS%20Outposts%20Data%20Residency%20eBook.pdf) challenges with AWS is to use Outposts rack, which allows organizations to run AWS infrastructure on premises and in their own data centers. This lets organizations store and process data in a location of their choosing. An Outpost is seamlessly connected to an [AWS Region](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/global-infrastructure/regions_az/) where it has access to the full suite of AWS services managed from a single plane of glass, the [AWS Management Console](https://aws.amazon.com/console/) or the AWS Command Line Interface ([AWS CLI](https://aws.amazon.com/cli/)).  Outposts rack can be configured to utilize landing zone to further adhere to data residency requirements.

The landing zones are a set of tools and best practices that help organizations establish a secure and compliant multi-account structure within a cloud provider. A landing zone can also include Organizations to set policies – guardrails – at the root level, known as [Service Control Policies (SCPs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html)) across all member accounts. This can be configured to enforce certain data residency requirements.

When leveraging Outposts rack to meet data residency requirements, it is crucial to have control over the in-scope data movement from the Outposts. This can be accomplished by implementing landing zone best practices and the suggested guardrails. The main focus of this blog post is on the custom policies that restrict data snapshots, prohibit data creation within the Region, and limit data transfer to the Region.

## Prerequisites

Landing zone best practices and custom guardrails can help when data needs to remain in a specific locality where the Outposts rack is also located.  This can be completed by defining and enforcing policies for data storage and usage within the landing zone organization that you set up. The following prerequisites should be considered before implementing the suggested guardrails:

1. **AWS Outposts rack**

AWS has installed your Outpost and handed off to you. An Outpost may comprise of one or more racks connected together at the site. This means that you can start using AWS services on the Outpost, and you can manage the Outposts rack using the same tools and interfaces that you use in AWS Regions.

2. **AWS Control Tower landing zone**

Control Tower is a managed service that provides a pre-packaged set of best-practice blueprints for setting up and governing multi-account AWS environments. You’ll need to have Control Tower fully implemented in your environment before you can deploy custom guardrails.

Control Tower launches a key resource associated with your account, called a landing zone, which serves as a home for your organizations and their accounts.

Note that Control Tower relies on Organizations to create and manage multi-account structures. You’ll need to have Organizations set up and configured as well.

3. **Set up the data residency guardrails**

Using Organizations, you must make sure that the Outpost is ordered within a workload account in the landing zone.

[![Figure 1 Landing Zone Accelerator Outposts workload on AWS high level Architecture](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/1b6453892473a467d07372d45eb05abc2031647a/2023/03/14/Figure-1-Landing-Zone-Accelerator-Outposts-workload-on-AWS-high-level-Architecture.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/1b6453892473a467d07372d45eb05abc2031647a/2023/03/14/Figure-1-Landing-Zone-Accelerator-Outposts-workload-on-AWS-high-level-Architecture.png)

![Figure 1 Landing Zone Accelerator Outposts workload on AWS high level Architecture](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/1b6453892473a467d07372d45eb05abc2031647a/2023/03/14/Figure-1-Landing-Zone-Accelerator-Outposts-workload-on-AWS-high-level-Architecture.png)

Figure 1: Landing Zone Accelerator – Outposts workload on AWS high level Architecture

## **Utilizing Outposts rack for regulated components**

When local regulations require regulated workloads to stay within a specific boundary, or when an AWS Region or [AWS Local Zone](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/global-infrastructure/localzones/) isn’t available in your jurisdiction, you can still choose to host your regulated workloads on Outposts rack for a consistent cloud experience. When opting for Outposts rack, note that, as part of the [shared responsibility model](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/outposts/latest/userguide/security.html), [customers are responsible](https://aws.amazon.com/outposts/rack/faqs/#Security_.26_compliance) for attesting to physical security, access controls, and [compliance validation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/outposts/latest/userguide/compliance-validation.html) regarding the Outposts, as well as, environmental requirements for the facility, networking, and power. Utilizing Outposts rack requires that you procure and manage the data center within the city, state, province, or country boundary for your applications’ regulated components, as required by local regulations.

Procuring two or more racks in the diverse data centers can help with the [high availability](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/pdfs/whitepapers/latest/aws-outposts-high-availability-design/aws-outposts-high-availability-design.pdf#aws-outposts-high-availability-design) for your workloads. This is because it provides redundancy in case of a single rack or server failure. Additionally, having redundant network paths between Outposts rack and the parent Region can help make sure that your application remains connected and continue to operate even if one network path fails.

However, for regulated workloads with strict service level agreements (SLA), you may choose to spread Outposts racks across two or more isolated data centers within regulated boundaries. This helps make sure that your data remains within the designated geographical location and meets local data residency requirements.

In this post, we consider a scenario with one data center, but consider the specific requirements of your workloads and the regulations that apply to determine the most appropriate [high availability](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/pdfs/whitepapers/latest/aws-outposts-high-availability-design/aws-outposts-high-availability-design.pdf#aws-outposts-high-availability-design) configurations for your case.

## Outposts rack workload data residency guardrails

Organizations provide central governance and management for multiple accounts. Central security administrators use SCPs with Organizations to establish controls to which all [AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)](https://aws.amazon.com/iam/) principals (users and roles) adhere.

Now, you can use SCPs to set permission guardrails.  A suggested preventative controls for **data residency on Outposts rack** that leverage the implementation of SCPs are shown as follows. SCPs enable you to set permission guardrails by defining the maximum available permissions for IAM entities in an account. If an SCP denies an action for an account, then none of the entities in the account can take that action, even if their IAM permissions let them. The guardrails set in SCPs apply to all IAM entities in the account, which include all users, roles, and the account root user.

Upon finalizing these prerequisites, you can [create the guardrails](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-use-service-control-policies-to-set-permission-guardrails-across-accounts-in-your-aws-organization/) for the Outposts Organization Unit (OU).

|  |
| --- |
| Note that while the following guidelines serve as helpful guardrails – SCPs – for data residency, you should consult internally with legal and security teams for specific organizational requirements. |

To exercise better control over workloads in the Outposts rack and prevent data transfer from Outposts to the Region or data storage outside the Outposts, consider implementing the following guardrails. Additionally, local regulations may dictate that you set up these additional guardrails.

a. Deny copying data from Outposts to the Region for [Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2](https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/)), [Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS](https://aws.amazon.com/rds/)), [Amazon ElastiCache](https://aws.amazon.com/elasticache/) and data sync “DenyCopyToRegion”.

b. Deny [Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3](https://aws.amazon.com/s3/)) put action to the Region “DenyPutObjectToRegionalBuckets”.

|  |
| --- |
| If your data residency requirements mandate restrictions on data storage in the Region,  consider implementing this guardrail to prevent  the use of S3 in the Region.  Note: You can use [Amazon S3 for Outposts](https://aws.amazon.com/s3/outposts/). |

If your data residency requirements mandate restrictions on data storage in the Region,  consider implementing this guardrail to prevent  the use of S3 in the Region.

Note: You can use [Amazon S3 for Outposts](https://aws.amazon.com/s3/outposts/).

c. If your data residency requirements mandate restrictions on data storage in the Region, consider implementing “DenyDirectTransferToRegion” guardrail.

|  |
| --- |
| Out of Scope is metadata such as tags, or operational data such as KMS keys. |

Out of Scope is metadata such as tags, or operational data such as KMS keys.

This AWS Compute Blog post explores how organizations can use AWS Control Tower landing zones and AWS Organizations custom guardrails (Service Control Policies or SCPs) to enable compliance with data residency requirements on AWS Outposts rack. Authored by Abeer Naffa' (Sr. Solutions Architect), David Filiatrault (Principal Security Consultant), and Jared Thompson (Hybrid Edge SA Specialist).

Key topics covered:

**Background:** Data residency is critical for organizations handling PII, financial, and healthcare data. Outposts rack allows organizations to run AWS infrastructure on-premises in their own data centers, seamlessly connected to an AWS Region with access to the full AWS service suite. Landing zones provide a secure, compliant multi-account structure, and SCPs can enforce data residency requirements at the root level across all member accounts.

**Prerequisites:**
1. AWS Outposts rack must be installed and handed off (one or more racks connected at the site).
2. AWS Control Tower landing zone must be fully implemented, which requires AWS Organizations to be set up and configured.
3. The Outpost must be ordered within a workload account in the landing zone.

**Regulated components on Outposts rack:** Customers are responsible (under the shared responsibility model) for physical security, access controls, compliance validation, and environmental requirements (facility, networking, power) for Outposts. Procuring two or more racks in diverse data centers helps with high availability and redundancy. For regulated workloads with strict SLAs, Outposts racks may be spread across two or more isolated data centers within regulated boundaries.

**Suggested SCP guardrails for data residency:**
- a) "DenyCopyToRegion" — denies copying data from Outposts to the Region for EC2, RDS, ElastiCache, and DataSync (actions include ec2:CopyImage, ec2:CreateImage, ec2:ExportImage, ec2:ImportImage, rds:CreateDBSnapshot, elasticache:CreateSnapshot, datasync:Create*, etc.).
- b) "DenyPutObjectToRegionalBuckets" — denies S3 PutObject action to the Region to prevent S3 storage in the Region (Amazon S3 for Outposts can still be used).
- c) "DenyDirectTransferToRegion" — denies direct data transfer to the Region (covers DynamoDB, EC2 Traffic Mirror, RDS Global Cluster, SageMaker, Redshift, SES, SQS, MQ, CloudFront, ECR, RAM, etc.). Metadata such as tags and operational data such as KMS keys are out of scope.
- d) "DenySnapshotsToRegion" — denies creating snapshots of Outpost data in the Region (requires updating the outpost ARN pattern).
- e) "DenySnapshotsNotOutposts" — denies copying or modifying Outposts snapshots outside Outposts.
- f) "DenyNotOutpostSubnet" — denies running EC2 instances or creating network interfaces outside Outpost subnets (requires updating outpost subnet ARNs).

Full JSON policy examples are provided for each SCP guardrail.

**Additional considerations:** Organizations should implement backup and disaster recovery strategies that are compliant with data residency regulations and tested regularly. The provided SCPs do not block "logs:PutLogEvents," meaning applications may log data to CloudWatch Logs in the Region (though application-level logs are not automatically sent by default). If blocking is desired, this action should be added to the first recommended guardrail; specific role allowances can be combined with an ArnNotLike condition.

**Conclusion:** The combined use of Outposts rack and SCP guardrails via AWS Organizations enables better control over data movement, keeping data within specific geographic locations as required by data residency regulations. Thorough review of policies, procedures, and configurations is essential, along with regular testing and monitoring for ongoing compliance.

# AWS Control Tower Introduces Data Residency Guardrails for Enhanced Compliance

![Xiaotian Cheng](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*Qg3KBqW_cFgVg_mHaoKNrQ.png)

--

![]()

## Introduction

In response to the growing demand for data residency control, AWS has launched new features within AWS Control Tower. These features, referred to as guardrails, empower customers, especially those in highly regulated industries and the public sector, to have more control over where their data is stored and processed. This blog will provide an overview of these new capabilities and how they can be utilized to ensure compliance with local laws and regulations.

## Data Residency Guardrails with AWS Control Tower

AWS Control Tower now offers data residency guardrails to prevent and detect potential breaches of data residency requirements. These guardrails, implemented as Service Control Policies (SCPs) and AWS Config rules, prohibit the provisioning of resources in undesired AWS Regions by restricting access to AWS APIs.

## Preventive Guardrails

Preventive guardrails, implemented as SCPs, can deny access to AWS services in specific Regions, ensuring that content remains within selected Regions at the infrastructure level. For instance, customers in Germany can restrict access to AWS services outside of Frankfurt while allowing exceptions for global services like AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and AWS Organizations.

## Additional Preventive Measures

AWS Control Tower extends preventive measures to underlying AWS service options, such as blocking cross-region replication in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or preventing the creation of internet gateways.

## Enabling Data Residency Guardrails

To utilize these guardrails, users must have created a landing zone using AWS Control Tower. The guardrails can be accessed through the AWS Control Tower console under the “Guardrails” section, specifically in the “Data Residency” category.

## Configuring Region Deny Settings

One notable guardrail involves denying access to AWS based on the requested Region. This guardrail affects all Organizational Units (OUs) and must be activated in the landing zone settings. Users can update landing zone settings to enable Region deny, specifying the AWS Regions governed by the landing zone.

## **Testing Region Deny in a Sandbox Account**

The blog provides a step-by-step demonstration of testing Region deny settings in a sandbox account. It showcases attempts to create an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance in both governed and non-governed Regions, highlighting the effectiveness of the guardrail in restricting unauthorized access.

## **Detective Guardrails**

AWS Control Tower also introduces detective guardrails, implemented through AWS Config rules. These guardrails detect unexpected configuration changes and provide insights into potential compliance issues. The blog demonstrates testing detective guardrails by creating non-compliant resources and observing how the system identifies and reports these issues.

## Availability and Pricing

The data residency guardrails feature is available for use at no additional cost. Users only incur costs associated with other services used, such as AWS Config. The blog emphasizes the flexibility of the framework, allowing users to choose specific guardrails based on their data residency requirements.

## Conclusion

AWS Control Tower’s new data residency guardrails provide a simplified yet powerful way for customers to enforce data residency requirements in single- and multi-account environments. With preventive and detective measures, users gain enhanced control over where their data is stored and processed, ensuring compliance with local regulations and laws.

## [AWS News Blog](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/)

# New for AWS Control Tower – Region Deny and Guardrails to Help You Meet Data Residency Requirements

|  |
| --- |
| [Voiced by Polly](https://aws.amazon.com/polly/) |

![Voiced by Polly](https://a0.awsstatic.com/aws-blog/images/Voiced_by_Amazon_Polly_EN.png)

***April 11, 2023** – At AWS re:Invent, AWS Control Tower [introduced Comprehensive Controls Management](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/new-for-aws-control-tower-comprehensive-controls-management-preview/) to help you apply managed controls based on service, control objective, or compliance framework. Data residency controls can now be found in the Controls library. For detailed instructions, you can follow the [Controls that enhance data residency protection](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/controltower/latest/userguide/data-residency-controls.html) section of the documentation.*

Many customers, such as those in highly regulated industries and the public sector, want to have control over where their data is stored and processed. AWS already offers many tools and features to comply with local laws and regulations, but we want to provide a simplified way to translate **data residency** requirements into controls that can be applied to single- and multi-account environments.

Starting today, you can use [AWS Control Tower](https://aws.amazon.com/controltower/) to deploy data residency **preventive** and **detective** controls, referred to as [guardrails](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/controltower/latest/userguide/guardrails.html). These guardrails will prevent provisioning resources in unwanted AWS Regions by restricting access to AWS APIs through [service control policies (SCPs)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html) built and managed by AWS Control Tower. In this way, content cannot be created or transferred outside of your selected Regions at the infrastructure level. In this context, content can be software (including machine images), data, text, audio, video, or images hosted on AWS for processing or storage. For example, AWS customers in Germany can deny access to AWS services in Regions outside of Frankfurt with the exception of global services such as [AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)](https://aws.amazon.com/iam/) and [AWS Organizations](https://aws.amazon.com/organizations/).

AWS Control Tower also offers guardrails to further control data residency in underlying AWS service options, for example, blocking [Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3)](https://aws.amazon.com/s3/) cross-region replication or blocking the creation of internet gateways.

The AWS account used for managing AWS Control Tower is not restricted by the new Region deny settings. That account can be used for remediation if you have data in an unwanted Region before enabling Region deny.

Detective guardrails are implemented via [AWS Config](https://aws.amazon.com/config/) rules and can further detect unexpected configuration changes that should not be allowed.

You still retain a shared responsibility model for data residency at the application level, but these controls can help you restrict what infrastructure and application teams can do on AWS.

**Using Data Residency Guardrails in AWS Control Tower** To use the new data residency guardrails, you need to have created a landing zone using AWS Control Tower. See [Plan your AWS Control Tower landing zone](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/controltower/latest/userguide/planning-your-deployment.html) for more information.

To see all the new controls that are available, I select **Guardrails** on the left pane of the [AWS Control Tower console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/controltower/) and then find those in the **Data Residency** category. I sort results by **Behavior**. Guardrails that have a **Prevention** behavior are implemented as SCPs. Those that have a **Detection** behavior are implemented as AWS Config rules.

[![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/19/control-tower-data-residency-guardrails-1024x641.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/19/control-tower-data-residency-guardrails.png)

![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/19/control-tower-data-residency-guardrails-1024x641.png)

The most interesting guardrail is probably the one denying access to AWS based on the requested AWS Region. I choose it from the list and find that it is different from the other guardrails because it affects all [Organizational Units (OUs)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_ous.html) and cannot be activated here but must be activated in the landing zone settings.

[![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-region-deny-guardrail-1024x160.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-region-deny-guardrail.png)

![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-region-deny-guardrail-1024x160.png)

Below the **Overview**, in the **Guardrail components**, there is a link to the full SCP for this guardrail, and I can see the list of the AWS APIs that, when this setting is enabled, are still going to be allowed towards non-governed Regions. Depending on your requirements, some of those services, such as [Amazon CloudFront](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudfront/) or [AWS Global Accelerator](https://aws.amazon.com/global-accelerator/), can be further limited by a custom SCP.

In the **Landing zone settings**, the Region deny guardrail is currently not enabled. I choose **Modify settings** and then enable the **Region deny settings.**

[![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/23/control-tower-region-deny-settings-1-1024x758.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/23/control-tower-region-deny-settings-1.png)

![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/23/control-tower-region-deny-settings-1-1024x758.png)

Below the Region deny settings, there is the list of AWS Regions governed by the landing zone. Those will be the regions allowed when I enable Region deny.

[![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-governed-regions-1024x697.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-governed-regions.png)

![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-governed-regions-1024x697.png)

In my case, I have four governed Regions, two in the US and two in Europe:

I choose **Update landing zone** at the bottom. The update of the landing zone takes a few minutes to complete. Now, the vast majority of the AWS APIs are blocked if they are not directed to one of those governed Regions. Let’s do a few tests.

**Testing Region Deny in a Sandbox Account** I follow the instructions to [configure the AWS CLI to use AWS Single Sign-On](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-configure-sso.html). Now, I can use the the sandbox account with `AWSAdministratorAccess` permissions to run commands with the AWS CLI.

`AWSAdministratorAccess`

[![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-sso-sandbox-account-1024x649.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-sso-sandbox-account.png)

![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-sso-sandbox-account-1024x649.png)

I try to start a new [Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2)](https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/) instance in US East (Ohio), one of the non-governed Regions. In a landing zone, [the default VPC is replaced by a VPC managed by AWS Control Tower](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/controltower/latest/userguide/vpc-concepts.html). To start the instance, I need to specify a VPC subnet. Let’s find a subnet ID that I can use.

`aws ec2 describe-subnets --query 'Subnets[0].SubnetId' --region us-east-2
An error occurred (UnauthorizedOperation) when calling the DescribeSubnets operation:
You are not authorized to perform this operation.`

As expected, I am not authorized to perform this operation in US East (Ohio). Let’s try to start an EC2 instance without passing the subnet ID.

`aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0dd0ccab7e2801812 --region us-east-2 \
--instance-type t3.small                                     
An error occurred (UnauthorizedOperation) when calling the RunInstances operation:
You are not authorized to perform this operation.
Encoded authorization failure message: <ENCODED MESSAGE>`

Again, I am not authorized. More information is included in the encoded authorization failure message that I can decode as [described in this article](https://aws.amazon.com/premiumsupport/knowledge-center/ec2-not-auth-launch/):

`aws sts decode-authorization-message --encoded-message <ENCODED MESSAGE>`

The decoded message (that I have omitted for brevity) tells me that there was an explicit deny to my request and includes the full SCP that caused the deny. This information is really useful for debugging these kind of errors.

Now, let’s try in US East (N. Virginia), one of the four governed regions.

`aws ec2 describe-subnets --query 'Subnets[0].SubnetId' --region us-east-1
"subnet-0f3580c0c5e56c210"`

This time, the command returns the subnet ID of the first subnet returned by the request. Let’s start an instance in US East (N. Virginia) using this subnet.

`aws ec2 run-instances --image-id  ami-04ad2567c9e3d7893 --region us-east-1 \
--instance-type t3.small --subnet-id subnet-0f3580c0c5e56c210`

As expected, it works, and I can see the EC2 instance running in the console.

[![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-ec2-instance-running-1024x144.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-ec2-instance-running.png)

![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-ec2-instance-running-1024x144.png)

Similarly, APIs for other AWS services are limited by the Region deny settings. For example, I can’t create an S3 bucket in a non-governed Region.

[![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-s3-create-not-governed-1024x557.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-s3-create-not-governed.png)

![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-s3-create-not-governed-1024x557.png)

When I try to create the bucket, I get an access denied error.

[![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-s3-access-denied-1024x304.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-s3-access-denied.png)

![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-s3-access-denied-1024x304.png)

As expected, the creation of an S3 bucket works in a governed Region.

[![](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-s3-create-governed-1024x233.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-s3-create-governed.png)

![](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-s3-create-governed-1024x233.png)

Even if someone gives this account access to a bucket in a non-governed Region, I would not be able to copy any data into that bucket.

Other preventive guardrails can enforce data residency, for example:

Now, let’s see how detective guardrails work.

**Testing Detective Guardrails in a Sandbox Account**
  
I enable the following guardrails for all accounts in the sandbox OU:

Now, I want to see what happens if I go against these guardrails. In the [EC2 console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/ec2/), I create an EBS snapshot for the volume of the EC2 instance I started before. Then, I modify permissions to share it with all AWS accounts.

[![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-ebs-snaphot-public-1024x798.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-ebs-snaphot-public.png)

![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-ebs-snaphot-public-1024x798.png)

Then, in the [VPC console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/vpc), I create an internet gateway, attach it to the AWS Control Tower managed VPC, and update the route table of one of the private subnets to use the internet gateway.

[![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-igw-route-table-1024x344.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-igw-route-table.png)

![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-igw-route-table-1024x344.png)

After a few minutes, the noncompliant resources in the sandbox account are found by the detective guardrails.

[![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-noncompliant-resources-1024x408.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-noncompliant-resources.png)

![Console screenshot.](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2021/11/18/control-tower-noncompliant-resources-1024x408.png)

I look at the information provided by the guardrails and update my configuration to fix the issues. In a multi-account setup I’d contact the account owner and ask for remediation.

**Availability and Pricing** You can use data-residency guardrails to control resources in any AWS Region. To create a landing zone, you should start from one of the Regions where [AWS Control Tower](https://aws.amazon.com/controltower/) is offered. For more information, see the [AWS Regional Services List](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/global-infrastructure/regional-product-services/). There is no additional cost for this feature. You pay the costs of other services used, such as [AWS Config](https://aws.amazon.com/config/).

This feature provides you with a framework of controls and guidance for setting up a multi-account environment that addresses data residency requirements. Depending on your use case, you may use any subset of the new data residency guardrails.

**[Set up guardrails based on your data residency requirements with AWS Control Tower.](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/controltower/latest/userguide/getting-started-with-control-tower.html)**

— [Danilo](https://x.com/danilop)

![Danilo Poccia](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2018/11/22/danilo.png)
