# New Zealand moves to a cloud-based identity solution for its 4.9 million residents

[Share the story](#customers-share-modal-dialog)

## Share this story

![](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/image/microsoftcorp/New%20Zealand%20Department%20of%20Internal%20Affairsrealme%20Header%20Image?resMode=sharp2&op_usm=1.5,0.65,15,0&wid=1900&hei=550&qlt=100&fmt=png-alpha&fit=crop)

The New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs partnered with UNIFY Solutions to migrate the country’s RealMe identity service—more than 6 million sign-ins and authentications spanning 163 government services and 56 agencies—to Microsoft Azure Active Directory B2C, part of Microsoft Entra.

![New Zealand Department of Internal Affairsrealme](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/image/microsoftcorp/New%20Zealand%20Department%20of%20Internal%20Affairsrealme%20Story%20Thumbnail?resMode=sharp2&op_usm=1.5,0.65,15,0&wid=250&qlt=100)

“We needed to create authentication and identity verification services that could be used by both our private and public sector agencies and be easily scaled up as needed.”

Tim Waldron, Business and Market Development Manager for RealMe Services, New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs

In 2006, the [New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs](https://www.govt.nz/organisations/department-of-internal-affairs/) (DIA) decided to create a centralized online platform where residents can affirm their legal identities and easily access services—a voluntary opt-in digital ID used by government agencies and private companies. Called [RealMe](https://www.realme.govt.nz/), this sign-in service made it possible for people to use a single username and password to access 163 government services across 56 public agencies, and it had a fairly high adoption across New Zealand’s population of 4.9 million residents.

## New Zealand's RealMe Portal Screenshot

The RealMe homepage reads, "The easiest and most secure way to prove your identity online. RealMe allows you to access multiple online services with one username and password, and securely prove who you are online," next to an image of an individual on a cellphone.

---

![New Zealand's RealMe Portal Screenshot](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/image/microsoftcorp/New%20Zealand%20Department%20of%20Internal%20Affairsrealme%20Image%203?resMode=sharp2&op_usm=1.5,0.65,15,0&wid=1280&qlt=100&fit=constrain)

Figure 1: New Zealand’s RealMe portal

[More about this diagram](#asset_id_1436704192009435290)

To accomplish this, the team at RealMe built a bespoke solution using partner products and custom code to meet each client agency’s needs. Because of its complexity, however, the system had limited adaptability, meaning that it couldn’t keep up with the next generation of personalized digital services. Maintaining the old system was costly, and upgrades required time-consuming custom builds. Additionally, the entire network infrastructure needed an upgrade to meet modern security requirements at a cost of millions.

“We needed to create an identity verification service that could be used by both our private and public sector agencies and be easily scaled up as needed,” says Tim Waldron, Business and Market Development Manager for RealMe Services at the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs. “The policy was actually in place before the solution. We were working from a broad government directive to help New Zealanders do more online by creating a digital passport for access to services.”

Meanwhile, public cloud technology had raced ahead in the intervening 14 years, offering a plethora of off-the-shelf solutions at an attractive price point. Waldron recognized that the time was right to take advantage of these external innovations to create a more scalable, cost-efficient service that could keep up with changing needs.

### Defining the solution

Identity data is the crown jewel of any government. An updated version of RealMe would still have to provide maximum protection for more than 6 million customer records. And the new system had to provide the greater flexibility and personalized service that today’s users have come to expect.

Partnering with DIA, Waldron and his team settled on three requirements for a new cloud-based RealMe. First, the updated system would have to continue providing simple digital access—a sign-in service that gives a single authenticator for access to government services while helping ensure privacy. Second, the system would need to provide a trusted identity, binding that to the trusted authenticator. Third, it would need to take that trusted base identity and build a model where the system can link in people’s information, allowing users to share more consent-based information with other agencies and organizations.

After an exhaustive search that began in 2017, DIA chose [Microsoft Azure Active Directory B2C, part of Microsoft Entra](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/services/active-directory/external-identities/b2c/) because of its built-in security, scalability, and ease of integration with apps and databases. It was also impressed by its [Log Analytics](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/logs/log-analytics-overview) and easy integration with [Azure Sentinel](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sentinel/overview), enabling a monitoring and alert system that cuts down on false positives. “We’re looking at moving away from managing our security with on-premises solutions toward using that kind of cloud-based solution where security is built in and has all the accreditations,” adds Waldron.

“Microsoft has been great at sharing product details and doing workshops with us to help us understand why this is the right platform,” Waldron explains. “We saw that Azure AD B2C is far better than what we had.” He recalls that the [smart lockout](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/authentication/howto-password-smart-lockout) feature was an attractive, built-in security feature. “We wanted to reduce our total cost of ownership. If the security function is already implemented, that’s one more reason to go with the Microsoft solution.”

After DIA finalized its requirements for the business case and platform, it began a selection process to finalize a supplier who could help it achieve its desired outcome. In the end, DIA chose to partner with UNIFY Solutions.

### Establishing trust

DIA’s selection team did a full options analysis with the organization’s general managers and others, explaining that if DIA decided to upgrade its existing on-premises systems, its operating expense would remain high. If it moved services to the cloud with Azure AD B2C, however, DIA could actually lower its total cost of ownership (TCO) over the next five years, all while creating more solutions and adding feature enhancements. As an added bonus, the new system would be faster.

“We articulated to stakeholders and general managers what data we would move and what we would keep on-premises,” recalls Venkat Maddali, Identity and RealMe Architect at the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs. His team explained to agency leaders that users would access RealMe through Azure AD B2C, but their verified identity data, such as name, birthday, gender, and place of birth, would remain on-premises. The team demonstrated that architecturally, Azure AD B2C could support that pattern while easily scaling as a future-proof solution that would lower costs.

When UNIFY came onboard, one of the big challenges that it and the RealMe team faced was building government agencies’ trust in the cloud as a secure option for services. Fortunately, they were able to point to UNIFY’s successful track record of managing [Microsoft Azure](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/) cloud services for New Zealand’s Ministry of Education and New Zealand Police. And Microsoft had already partnered with the government for other cloud services, with the adoption of [Microsoft 365](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365), Azure, and [Dynamics 365](https://dynamics.microsoft.com/en-us/) becoming increasingly widespread.

Though Ireland had been the first country to move its citizen identity service to the cloud, the Irish government was able to keep their directory data onshore. New Zealand was the first to cross the next threshold, deciding that based on its risk assessment and successful history with Microsoft solutions, New Zealanders’ authentication data could safely reside offshore in the Azure public cloud.

### Making the move

After being in place for roughly 14 years, the earlier RealMe system was already integrated with many organizations and agencies. The teams at UNIFY and DIA needed an approach that could seamlessly transition data for millions of sign-ins to the cloud. That meant being able to replicate the earlier on-premises RealMe system within Azure AD B2C without extended downtime. Supported by Microsoft product engineering teams, they began the move in December 2019.

They began by mapping the RealMe interface to Azure, mirroring customer flows such as sign-ins, password management, and sign-ups so they’d be consistent across government agency sites. The RealMe team was clear that it didn’t want to use Azure AD B2C just as a directory service, but rather, to create a more integrated approach. “We wanted to make it an orchestration engine to guide the user’s journey through the customer identity framework,” explains Maddali.

Many government agencies and vendors who were still providing some existing services had to be integrated into a single Azure service managed by UNIFY. More than 6 million sign-in and authentication records then had to be migrated to the new platform in one big lift to avoid disrupting services. “Six million is actually higher than the population of New Zealand because RealMe allows for multiple identities for each user,” says Waldron. Though each user is allowed only a single verified identity record, notes Waldron, they’re allowed to create multiple identities or pseudonyms that are decoupled from their verified record.

Moving 163 government services across 56 public agencies was no small task. Despite a global pandemic, the UNIFY and DIA teams managed to get the new cloud-based RealMe platform up and running in just 18 months, completing the final data migration within 48 hours and launching the new system in July 2021.

“A big part of the journey was holding ourselves to using out-of-the-box Azure AD capabilities,” Waldron recalls. “That meant not falling into the trap of, ‘We’ll do it exactly the way we’ve been doing it—with our own code.’” In the end, the team at UNIFY only needed to customize some help desk functions for New Zealand users.

### Results

The RealMe team is pleased to have achieved its primary goals: to reduce TCO and create a more flexible solution that easily adapts as services grow. “There’s been a huge cost drop from the previous on-premises platform to the current Microsoft cloud solution,” says Maddali. “Also, we can implement enhancements faster while providing a better user experience.”

In addition to smart lockout, the team points at [self-service password reset](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/business-video/set-up-self-serve-password-reset?view=o365-worldwide) as another built-in feature that helped lower TCO. “We used to have people resetting passwords manually,” adds Mike Jones, Project Manager for RealMe at the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs. “So, besides the cost savings, we’ve improved the user experience as well.”

The new cloud-based RealMe has also helped improve security and trust for frontline workers who are dealing with the ongoing pandemic. New Zealand’s Ministry of Health frequently sends text messages with COVID-19 updates, and using RealMe as the authentication layer provides the necessary level of security.

Currently, RealMe has verified 905,000 New Zealand residents, and the number is growing.

### Strengthening partnerships, looking ahead

All three of the teams involved—DIA, UNIFY, and Microsoft—are proud of their accomplishments in future-proofing the new RealMe for New Zealanders in years to come. Maddali describes moving 6 million identities to Azure AD B2C as “relatively pain-free considering the scale. And it’s been very successful in terms of the flexibility, scalability, and minimal impact to users.”

Other jurisdictions are now looking at how DIA implemented Azure AD B2C, making it a showcase solution for more government agencies to emulate. Going forward, the team at DIA is committed to expanding the [Zero Trust approach](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/security/zero-trust/) to provide end-to-end security across the entire RealMe platform—from devices to data. It’s also looking forward to establishing [passwordless authentication](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/authentication/concept-authentication-passwordless) for a simple, highly secure user experience.

Everyone agrees that the collaborative relationship between RealMe, Microsoft, and UNIFY helped make this massive undertaking go smoothly. “Microsoft issued features and functional enhancements to help us,” explains Peter Tiernan, Chief Customer Success Officer at UNIFY Solutions. “Our three teams made up three legs of the stool. Along with building trust with your stakeholders, that kind of partnership and collaboration are vital elements of success.”

This is a Microsoft Customer Story (published November 10, 2021) about the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) migrating the country's national identity service, RealMe, to Microsoft Azure Active Directory B2C (part of Microsoft Entra), with partner UNIFY Solutions.

RealMe is a voluntary opt-in digital ID service that allows New Zealand's 4.9 million residents to use a single username and password to access 163 government services across 56 public agencies. The original system, built in 2006 with bespoke partner products and custom code, had limited adaptability, was costly to maintain, and required time-consuming custom builds and a multi-million-dollar network infrastructure upgrade.

After an exhaustive search beginning in 2017, DIA chose Azure AD B2C for its built-in security (including smart lockout), scalability, ease of integration, Log Analytics, and easy integration with Azure Sentinel. The team defined three core requirements: simple digital access, a trusted identity binding, and a model for linking consent-based information sharing.

Key milestones:
- Migration began in December 2019, supported by Microsoft product engineering teams
- More than 6 million sign-in and authentication records (higher than NZ's population because users can create multiple pseudonymous identities decoupled from one verified record) were migrated in a single lift
- The new platform was completed in 18 months despite the global pandemic, with final data migration finished within 48 hours
- Launched in July 2021
- New Zealand was the first country to allow citizen authentication data to reside offshore in the Azure public cloud (Ireland was first to move its citizen identity service to cloud but kept directory data onshore)

Results: Reduced total cost of ownership (TCO), faster feature enhancements, improved user experience (including self-service password reset and smart lockout), improved security for frontline workers during the pandemic (e.g., Ministry of Health COVID-19 text notifications use RealMe as authentication layer). As of publication, RealMe had verified 905,000 New Zealand residents.

Looking ahead, DIA is expanding its Zero Trust approach and exploring passwordless authentication. Other jurisdictions are examining DIA's implementation as a showcase for government cloud identity adoption. Key personnel quoted include Tim Waldron (Business and Market Development Manager for RealMe), Venkat Maddali (Identity and RealMe Architect), Mike Jones (Project Manager for RealMe), and Peter Tiernan (Chief Customer Success Officer at UNIFY Solutions).
args.key_excerpts: "We needed to create authentication and identity verification services that could be used by both our private and public sector agencies and be easily scaled up as needed." — Tim Waldron, Business and Market Development Manager for RealMe Services, NZ Department of Internal Affairs

# Ally Financial empowers customer service associates to focus on human engagement by using Azure OpenAI Service

[Share the story](#customers-share-modal-dialog)

## Share this story

![](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/image/microsoftcorp/Ally%20Financial%20Header%20Image-1?resMode=sharp2&op_usm=1.5,0.65,15,0&wid=1900&hei=550&qlt=100&fmt=png-alpha&fit=crop)

Digital financial services firm Ally Financial (Ally) is using Microsoft Azure and Azure OpenAI Service to reduce manual tasks for its customer service associates, freeing up time for them to engage with customers. Ally is committed to delivering a seamless customer experience, and its associates are its human face. Previously, they had to take notes and write summaries after calls, which competed with the amount of time and attention they could give customers. By using generative AI to automate manual tasks, Ally empowered its associates to deliver a better, more personal experience while protecting vital customer data. Now they are more productive and engaged than ever.

![Ally Financial](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/image/microsoftcorp/Ally%20Financial%20Story%20Thumbnail-1?resMode=sharp2&op_usm=1.5,0.65,15,0&wid=250&qlt=100)

Pioneering digital financial services firm Ally Financial (Ally) wanted to enhance the customer experience its call-center associates provided while producing detailed documentation for each call. Every moment that associates spent taking notes was time away from connecting with customers, so Ally set out to reduce their effort and enhance the human connection. The firm has a history of innovation, and it looked to generative AI technology for its solution. “As widespread adoption of generative AI began in early 2023, we were already thinking about the best way to use the technology to support our teammates and our business,” says Sathish Muthukrishnan, Chief Information, Data, and Digital Officer at Ally. “We believe magic happens at the intersection of business impact, customer experience, and the right technology.”

After evaluating several options, Ally launched a collaborative project to develop a pilot built on [Microsoft Azure](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/) using [Azure OpenAI Service](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/ai-services/openai-service). It sought to complete the pilot within six weeks and have the first use case in eight, an exceptionally short timeline for the banking sector. By incorporating feedback from customer service associates, Ally addressed employees’ questions about AI and improved the new solution. Now more than 700 associates have real-time access to summaries of tens of thousands of customer service calls per week and can edit them as needed. The integration with AI empowers associates to focus on answering customer questions and saves them valuable minutes in servicing customer inquiries.

“It’s been very exciting to watch this technology empower our associates and give them a better tool to serve customers,” says Diane Morais, President of Consumer and Commercial Banking at Ally.

### Delivering a generative-AI solution in eight weeks with Azure OpenAI Service

Ally’s customer experience associates provide the human touch that customers expect. When the firm saw an opportunity to use generative AI to help it deliver enhanced value and personal service, it evaluated many vendor offerings. Ally found that Azure OpenAI Service was the best solution for its use case. “The massive investment Microsoft has made in OpenAI helped move things forward, but the key thing is that Microsoft really understands our need to implement robust, reliable, and secure capabilities,” says Scott Richardson, Chief Information Officer of Enterprise Data and Analytics at Ally.

To deliver value quickly, Ally set up a collaborative development effort. Business, technical, and customer service teams worked together to define needs, provide feedback, and fine-tune the AI. Ally identified three keys to successful development. First, it would learn from employees before implementing new technology for customers. Second, Ally would keep a human in the middle of all AI interactions and have oversight of all outputs. Finally, the company’s data would stay within its own firewalls, so the foundational model would not learn from Ally’s data. Following these guidelines, and with support from Microsoft, Ally’s technology group delivered a production-ready solution in just eight weeks.

### Targeting a 50 percent reduction in post-call effort with conversational AI

Ally customer service associates no longer take extensive notes while interacting with a customer or write detailed call summaries afterward. With the conversational-AI capabilities of Azure OpenAI Service, they simply review an automatically generated summary and confirm that it contains all the necessary information. The new solution has cut associates’ post-call effort by 30 percent—with the expectation of a 50 percent reduction—while capturing key details automatically. “Our associates say that as they read through the summaries, they often find information from the call that they had forgotten,” says Wendy Dempsey, Executive Director of Customer Experience at Ally.

Ally leaders attribute the accuracy of its solution to collaboration between its technology and customer service teams. The company kept things simple: after viewing the AI-generated call summary, associates gave either a thumbs-up or a thumbs-down rating. Based on their feedback, the technology team fine-tuned its models and prompts to deliver better results. Today, accuracy is over 85 percent, and Ally is still improving the solution.

Ally also took a proactive approach to addressing worries about AI in the call center. When employees voiced concerns about losing work, Ally assured them that the technology would be empowering. “The goal was to free up associates to truly focus on the customer and support that customer-obsessed mentality they have,” says Dempsey. “When they saw how beneficial the call summaries were, it alleviated their concerns.” Call-center associates are now enjoying a more meaningful work experience with less paperwork and more human interaction.

Ally teams are proud of the work they have done to tackle an industry-wide challenge. Banking and financial services are highly regulated, but Ally delivered a secure, responsible, and effective AI solution in an exceptionally short time frame. The firm emphasizes the importance of behind-the-scenes work in accelerating delivery. “If we didn’t have our data in a centralized place, we would not be able to take advantage of generative AI,” says Muthukrishnan. “It’s the work that goes on behind the scenes, where you invest patience, money, technology, and strategic thinking, that pays off when you launch a solution like our Ally.ai platform alongside a partner like Microsoft.”

### Advancing the future of secure AI with Microsoft

Ally remains focused on its customers and creating and capturing value through innovation to better serve them. Its technology organization has the ambitious goal of launching a new project each month as it looks to harness more new uses for AI. Ally is also committed to protecting data privacy and security throughout its journey with AI, and it collaborates with Microsoft to advance that goal. “Microsoft understands our desire for responsible, secure AI,” says Richardson. “They addressed our major concerns in advance, which made it easy to collaborate with them.”

Ultimately, Ally’s embrace of AI is about empowering employees and serving its customers. “For us, it’s about a relentless focus on our customers’ financial well-being and supporting our employees who are interacting with them every day,” says Muthukrishnan. “Microsoft understands these core principles and has helped us make our associates’ work experience more efficient and productive, so they can continue to serve customers at the highest level.”

“As widespread adoption of generative AI began in early 2023, we were already thinking about the best way to use the technology to support our teammates and our business. We believe magic happens at the intersection of business impact, customer experience, and the right technology.”

Sathish Muthukrishnan, Chief Information, Data, and Digital Officer, Ally Financial

This is a Microsoft customer story (published December 21, 2023) about how Ally Financial, a digital financial services firm based in the United States, used Microsoft Azure and Azure OpenAI Service to reduce manual tasks for its customer service associates and enhance human engagement with customers.

Key facts:
- Ally developed a pilot using Azure OpenAI Service with the goal of completing it in six weeks, and had a production-ready solution in just eight weeks—an exceptionally short timeline for the banking sector.
- More than 700 associates now have real-time access to AI-generated summaries of tens of thousands of customer service calls per week, which they can review and edit as needed.
- The solution has cut associates' post-call effort by 30 percent, with expectations of a 50 percent reduction.
- AI summary accuracy is over 85 percent and continues to improve.
- Previously, associates had to take notes during calls and write detailed summaries afterward, which reduced time spent with customers.

Development approach (three keys to success):
1. Learn from employees before implementing new technology for customers.
2. Keep a human in the middle of all AI interactions with oversight of all outputs.
3. Keep company data within its own firewalls so the foundational model would not learn from Ally's data.

Ally addressed employee concerns about AI by positioning it as empowering rather than displacing workers. Associates rate AI-generated summaries with thumbs-up/thumbs-down feedback, which the technology team uses to fine-tune models and prompts. Ally plans to launch a new AI project each month and emphasizes data centralization as critical to its success. The company continues to collaborate with Microsoft on responsible, secure AI.

Key people quoted:
- Sathish Muthukrishnan, Chief Information, Data, and Digital Officer at Ally
- Diane Morais, President of Consumer and Commercial Banking at Ally
- Scott Richardson, Chief Information Officer of Enterprise Data and Analytics at Ally
- Wendy Dempsey, Executive Director of Customer Experience at Ally

Industry context: Financial services, organization size 10,000+ employees, business need: modern infrastructure, country: United States.

# Digital Manufacturing Platform: ZF plants are now more efficient thanks to the smart factory solution based on Microsoft Azure

[Share the story](#customers-share-modal-dialog)

## Share this story

![](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/image/microsoftcorp/ZF%20Group%20Header%20Image-4?resMode=sharp2&op_usm=1.5,0.65,15,0&wid=1900&hei=550&qlt=100&fmt=png-alpha&fit=crop)

**Full transparency for all data to create maximum plant efficiency: ZF Group applies this basic concept to ensure that all the steps in the manufacturing process work seamlessly together. To this end, the mobility and technology company uses its own Digital Manufacturing Platform (DMP) and follows a cloud strategy built on Microsoft Azure. Today, this data platform and its applications provide ZF with a consistent, data-driven overview of its manufacturing activities. As a result, the company can optimize work steps such as maintenance and repair, make better use of resources, and increase production flexibility. This marks the first step toward establishing a globally connected, digital manufacturing network.**

![ZF Group](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/image/microsoftcorp/ZF%20Group%20Story%20Thumbnail-4?resMode=sharp2&op_usm=1.5,0.65,15,0&wid=250&qlt=100)

### **The challenge: Making better use of the efficiency benefits of digital transformation**

At [ZF](https://www.zf.com/mobile/en/homepage/homepage.html)’s 188 production sites, the various departments work closely together. ZF employees keep production running as smoothly as possible in the company’s four technology domains—Vehicle Motion Control, Integrated Safety, Automated Driving, and Electric Mobility. To do so, they must adhere to clearly defined workflows. For the 400-strong production team at ZF’s Diepholz pilot plant in northwestern Germany, such workflows used to include going to the machine control consoles to manually collate the number of parts produced and any machine downtimes during a given shift and entering that data into a central PC. On average, this took up around five minutes of everybody’s time at the end of every shift. Tooling—in other words, setting up a machine for a particular processing step—also requires a certain degree of documentation work. It was a similar story for the maintenance team: work orders and notifications from the SAP system had to be printed out. Loaded with these printouts, employees would go over to the malfunctioning machine, for instance to connect a diagnostics device to find the source of the error. Once identified, it was a case of fixing the problem and then reporting the outcome. Printing out the information, attending to the machine, and feeding the new data into SAP would occupy a member of the maintenance team for around 15 minutes. After all, having to physically move from place to place, and the formalities that go along with that, eat up time that would be better spent on more beneficial tasks.

At first, each ZF plant came up with its own IT solution for this kind of challenge—a consequence of the Group’s rapid growth. “From a Group perspective, it was inefficient. It clashed with the whole ethos of production, which is to continuously improve efficiency,” says Joachim Sprinz, Program Manager IIoT – Digital Manufacturing Platform at ZF. “Digital transformation allows us to generate more value from our data, which in turn raises the efficiency and performance of our plants. At the same time, this transformation ensures company-wide connectivity along the entire value chain.” What was needed was a solution that connected data from different sources and brought together the full potential of digital transformation on a single platform. It was crucial that this standard solution could be expanded to cover all plants to create data transparency and lean processes both throughout the company and at each individual plant. This was the root idea that grew into the DMP.

![](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/image/microsoftcorp/ZF%20Group%20Image%202-1?resMode=sharp2&op_usm=1.5,0.65,15,0&wid=1280&qlt=100&fit=constrain)

### **The solution: A platform in Microsoft Azure for data-driven efficiency at all plants**

“The first step toward raising efficiency across all plants is to achieve a synergy of people and data,” Sprinz says. “This is the only way to accelerate our production’s digital transformation and establish a global digital production network.” [Microsoft Azure](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/) provides the basis for all of this. “Our Group follows a cloud strategy built on Azure. Since our partnership with Microsoft was already well established and we were familiar with its products, Azure was the most sensible choice as the basis for our DMP,” he adds.

Today, ZF collects production machine data with [Azure IoT](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/solutions/iot/) connectivity components, stores it in [Azure Data Lake](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/solutions/data-lake/), and then uses [Azure Data Explorer](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/data-explorer/) to prepare and provide it for analysis. User management is through [Azure Active Directory](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/active-directory/): users open DMP web applications in the front end to view the KPIs presented on easily understandable [Power BI](https://powerbi.microsoft.com/en-us/) dashboards. The DMP is being upgraded all the time and parts if it are already being used at 18 plants, including Diepholz.

![](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/image/microsoftcorp/ZF%20Group%20Image%203-4?resMode=sharp2&op_usm=1.5,0.65,15,0&wid=1280&qlt=100&fit=constrain)

ZF’s DMP also established a connectivity stack, which enables employees to connect machines automatically to the cloud via a self-service app. “It’s often difficult to integrate older existing machines into a new landscape. Their programs tend not to be annotated and it’s rarely possible to get hold of the original programmers and manufacturers,” says Thorsten Schulze, Project Manager at ZF’s pilot plant in Diepholz. “In the past, this kind of integration called for major IT and business projects. But with our connectivity board, employees can simply connect their machines themselves, more or less at the push of a button, provided the machines in question have already been added to the network.”

“Thanks to cloud-based connectivity, it’s now much easier for us to integrate machines into our landscape. Processes are becoming more transparent and are revealing their optimization potential. At the end of the day, this allows us to raise efficiency, both of the machines and the entire plant.”

Thorsten Schulze, Project Manager, Diepholz pilot plant, ZF

The Diepholz plant is among those striving to raise machine efficiency, improve its management of material stocks and flows, and make better use of resources. Today, employees there are aided by the applications Worker Cockpit, OEE Analyzer, and Condition Monitoring. Worker Cockpit helps them log production losses during a given shift, almost in real time. Machines are equipped with a display that allows employees to see at any time which order is currently being filled, where losses in quality have occurred, and where a machine was idle. Machines automatically document when and why they malfunction and send this information to the DMP. “Smart algorithms speed up the process, making the information more transparent and available sooner,” Schulze says. “This also makes the tooling process more comprehensible, for instance. The status and overall process time are displayed immediately.” Next, experts and planners evaluate the Worker Cockpit data using OEE Analyzer; the results provide the basis for optimization. “This is how, for example, we see if a machine isn’t running as well as it could, and we can intervene directly. Once optimized, the machine runs more efficiently and performs better. But before all that, we have to be able to see the problem, which is precisely what our Azure-based DMP allows us to do,” Schulze says.

### **Preventing production downtimes and optimizing inventory**

Using Condition Monitoring, the Diepholz maintenance team can now identify and rectify problems with the machines faster than before. If the data generated by a machine exceeds a particular threshold, a push notification is automatically sent to the team. This notification contains all the information required to tell at a glance which machine and which parameters are affected. Experienced staff can then decide which tools or spare parts they will need for the repair before they have even left their desk. “This saves them unnecessary trips between their desk, the spare parts store, and the machine,” Schulze says. “Impending downtimes are also detected in advance. Let’s say there’s a machine fitted with two drilling tools and the data analysis shows that one is running at a significantly higher temperature than the other. We look over the details and order any spares in good time. This allows us to prevent unscheduled downtimes that, in the current supply situation, could potentially last several weeks.” In the future, ZP plans to introduce automatic anomaly detection to supplement its employees’ expertise.

“The DMP program has had a profound impact on how our company works. Business and IT collaborate more closely, we’ve set up expert forums, and we’re sharing expertise across all levels,” Sprinz says. “We’ve established the processes, mindset, and structures we need to flexibly scale the technology and how we manage it.” After all, the idea was for the DMP to be more than merely a Group reporting platform, but rather an IIoT platform that doubled as a central data and application hub for all 188 ZF production locations around the world—a single point of information for flexible, efficient management of all factories. This also paves the way for achieving yet more optimization, eliminating tasks that don’t add value, and driving forward company-wide connectivity in the future.

“With our Azure-based DMP, we’ve established the processes, mindset, and structures we need to flexibly scale the technology and how we manage it, and to leverage the potential of our digital transformation.”

Joachim Sprinz, Program Manager IIoT – Digital Manufacturing Platform, ZF

This is a Microsoft Customer Story (published February 22, 2023) detailing how ZF Group, a German mobility and technology company with 188 production sites and over 10,000 employees, implemented a Digital Manufacturing Platform (DMP) built on Microsoft Azure to increase plant efficiency and establish a globally connected digital manufacturing network.

**The Challenge:** At ZF's 188 production sites across four technology domains (Vehicle Motion Control, Integrated Safety, Automated Driving, Electric Mobility), manual processes were inefficient. At the Diepholz pilot plant in northwestern Germany, a 400-strong production team manually collected parts production and machine downtime data at machine control consoles, spending about five minutes per person per shift. The maintenance team printed SAP work orders and physically moved to machines, spending around 15 minutes per task on documentation and manual processes. Each plant had developed its own disparate IT solutions due to the Group's rapid growth, which conflicted with the ethos of continuous efficiency improvement.

**The Solution:** ZF built its DMP on Microsoft Azure following a group-wide cloud strategy. The platform uses:
- Azure IoT connectivity components to collect production machine data
- Azure Data Lake for data storage
- Azure Data Explorer for data preparation and analysis
- Azure Active Directory (Microsoft Entra ID) for user management
- Power BI dashboards for KPI visualization

The DMP established a self-service connectivity stack enabling employees to connect machines to the cloud automatically "at the push of a button," including older legacy machines. Parts of the DMP were already deployed at 18 plants, including Diepholz.

**Applications at Diepholz:**
1. **Worker Cockpit** - Helps employees log production losses in near real-time; machines automatically document malfunctions with smart algorithms making information more transparent and available sooner.
2. **OEE Analyzer** - Experts and planners evaluate Worker Cockpit data to identify optimization opportunities and intervene directly.
3. **Condition Monitoring** - Maintenance team receives automatic push notifications when machine data exceeds thresholds, including which machine and parameters are affected. This allows staff to prepare tools/spare parts before leaving their desks, detect impending downtimes in advance (e.g., detecting a drilling tool running at higher temperature), and prevent unscheduled downtimes that could last weeks given supply chain constraints.

**Future Plans:** ZF plans to introduce automatic anomaly detection and aims for the DMP to serve as an IIoT platform and central data/application hub for all 188 production locations worldwide—a single point of information for flexible, efficient management of all factories.

**Key People:**
- Joachim Sprinz, Program Manager IIoT – Digital Manufacturing Platform at ZF
- Thorsten Schulze, Project Manager at ZF's Diepholz pilot plant

**Details:** Customer: ZF Group (Germany, Vehicle Suppliers industry); Business needs: Modern infrastructure and cloud-scale analytics; Products: Azure, Azure Data Explorer, Azure IoT Hub, Microsoft Entra ID, Power BI.
args.key_excerpts: "From a Group perspective, it was inefficient. It clashed with the whole ethos of production, which is to continuously improve efficiency," says Joachim Sprinz, Program Manager IIoT – Digital Manufacturing Platform at ZF. "Digital transformation allows us to generate more value from our data, which in turn raises the efficiency and performance of our plants."

--- SOURCE 1: Powering HIPAA-compliant workloads using AWS Serverless technologies | AWS Compute Blog ---
URL: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/powering-hipaa-compliant-workloads-using-aws-serverless-technologies

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This AWS Compute Blog post (written by Mayank Thakkar, AWS Senior Solutions Architect) discusses how AWS Serverless technologies can be used to power HIPAA-compliant workloads in the healthcare and life sciences industry. The post announces that AWS Step Functions has achieved HIPAA-eligibility status and been added to the AWS Business Associate Addendum (BAA), joining most other serverless AWS services in the HIPAA program. The BAA is a required contract under HIPAA rules that ensures AWS appropriately safeguards protected health information (PHI).

The post examines three common healthcare use cases with reference architectures:

1. **Provider directory web application**: A serverless architecture using Amazon S3 for static file hosting, Amazon CloudFront for content delivery with caching at the edge, AWS Lambda@Edge for customizing delivered content, Amazon API Gateway for API management, AWS WAF for web protection, and Lambda functions that can access VPC or on-premises resources via VPN/Direct Connect. All services are HIPAA-eligible, pay-as-you-go, and scale automatically to handle enrollment-season spikes.

2. **Medical device telemetry**: IoT medical devices (infusion pumps, dialysis machines) connect via edge nodes/collectors using the Kinesis Producer Library to stream data to Amazon Kinesis Streams (with server-side encryption support). Lambda processes data in real-time, storing insights in Amazon DynamoDB to power near-real-time health dashboards. Historical analysis uses AWS Batch, Amazon EMR, EC2, or serverless MapReduce with Lambda. Lambda can also load data into Amazon Redshift for petabyte-scale data warehousing.

3. **Mobile diagnostics**: Mobile devices with biosensors (otoscopes, thermometers, heart rate monitors) authenticate via Amazon Cognito (which also provides data sync and offline features) and access APIs through API Gateway. Lambda handles CRUD operations storing data in DynamoDB, which caregivers access through browser interfaces. DynamoDB Streams integration with Lambda enables near-real-time reactions to incoming data, and Amazon SNS delivers secure alerts to smart devices.

The post concludes that Lambda is a powerful, event-driven, stateless, on-demand compute platform offering scalability, agility, security, and reliability with fine-grained cost structure, and AWS is committed to making more services HIPAA-eligible. It references the Serverless Application Developer Tooling page and the HIPAA Eligible Services Reference for more details.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: HIPAA Compliance - Amazon Web Services (AWS) ---
URL: https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/hipaa-compliance

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is AWS's official compliance page for the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). It explains how AWS enables covered entities and their business associates to use AWS cloud services to process, maintain, and store protected health information (PHI) in a HIPAA-compliant manner.

Key content includes:
- HIPAA is a 1996 federal law protecting the privacy and security of PHI, modified with rules for Privacy (2003), Security (2005), Enforcement (2006), and Breach Notification (2009). It applies to covered entities (health plans, healthcare clearinghouses, and healthcare providers transmitting health information electronically) and their business associates.
- The HIPAA Privacy Rule requires protection of PHI on any medium; the Security Rule requires administrative, physical, and technical controls for confidentiality, integrity, and availability of PHI.
- AWS considers cloud service providers (CSPs) like itself as "business associates" under HIPAA. AWS signs a standard Business Associate Addendum (BAA) with customers, which can be accepted and managed via AWS Artifact in the AWS Management Console.
- AWS is not "HIPAA certified" (no such certification exists for CSPs); instead, AWS aligns its HIPAA risk management program with FedRAMP and NIST 800-53, which are higher security standards mapping to the HIPAA Security Rule.
- Customers with a BAA may use any AWS service in a HIPAA-designated account but should only process PHI in HIPAA-eligible services as defined in the BAA (see the HIPAA Eligible Services Reference).
- HITECH (2009) expanded HIPAA rules; together they establish federal standards for PHI protection under the "Administrative Simplification" rules.
- HITRUST CSF is described as a certifiable framework unifying security controls from federal law (HIPAA/HITECH), state law, and non-governmental frameworks (e.g., PCI) tailored for healthcare.
- For AWS SaaS partners with a BAA selling to healthcare providers, covered entities only need to sign a BAA with the SaaS partner (not AWS), unless they are also direct AWS customers for HIPAA-related systems.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) is a federal law that includes provisions designed to protect the privacy and security of PHI."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Roundup of AWS HIPAA Eligible Service Announcements | AWS News Blog ---
URL: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/roundup-of-aws-hipaa-eligible-service-announcements

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This AWS News Blog post announces that four AWS services have been added to the AWS Business Associate Addendum (BAA), making them HIPAA-eligible for use with Protected Health Information (PHI). The newly eligible services are: Amazon API Gateway, AWS Direct Connect, AWS Database Migration Service (DMS), and Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS).

The post was written by Patrick Combes (Healthcare and Life Sciences Global Technical Leader at AWS) and Aaron Friedman (Healthcare and Life Sciences Partner Solutions Architect at AWS), and published by Ana Visneski.

Key details about each newly HIPAA-eligible service:
- **Amazon API Gateway**: Enables secure creation, publishing, monitoring, and securing of APIs at any scale. Can be used for patient/provider directories, patient dashboards, medical device telemetry, HL7 message processing, and notably FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) specification — expected to become the next-generation standard for health information exchange due to its RESTful architecture support.
- **AWS Direct Connect**: Provides private connectivity between AWS and on-premises infrastructure (datacenter, office, or colocation), reducing network costs and increasing bandwidth throughput. Useful for hybrid architectures (as used by Johnson & Johnson) and secure migration of data to AWS for use with HIPAA-eligible storage/processing services like Amazon S3 and Amazon EMR. Also supports connecting to third-party/partner solutions and cloud-based Electronic Medical Record systems.
- **AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)**: Over 20,000 databases have been migrated to AWS via DMS. It enables secure migration of core databases containing PHI (patient directories, payment/transaction records, revenue management databases) while keeping the source database fully operational to minimize downtime.
- **Amazon SQS**: Message queueing service for distributed components and microservices. Can buffer requests passing HL7 or FHIR messages between application components. SQS FIFO ensures PHI-containing messages are delivered in order and available until processed and deleted — important for patient record updates and hospital payment processing.

Important compliance note: As with all HIPAA-eligible services under the AWS BAA, PHI must be encrypted while at-rest and in-transit. AWS references its HIPAA compliance whitepaper for configuration guidance, and notes that non-PHI application components can use any of AWS's 90+ services.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: FedRAMP Compliance - Amazon Web Services (AWS) ---
URL: https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/fedramp

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from AWS provides comprehensive information about the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) and AWS's compliance with it. AWS is described as the world's most comprehensive cloud platform, and the page details how the US Federal Government uses AWS cloud services to process, store, and transmit federal government data.

Key points covered:

**What is FedRAMP?** FedRAMP is a US government-wide program that standardizes security assessment, certification, and continuous monitoring for cloud products and services used by federal agencies. It is governed by the FedRAMP Board, Program Management Office (PMO), Technical Advisory Group (TAG), and Federal Secure Cloud Advisory Committee (FSCAC). CSPs must demonstrate FedRAMP compliance using NIST SP 800 series and complete an independent security assessment by a FedRAMP Recognized Independent Assessment Service (formerly 3PAO), compliant with FISMA 2002.

**Why FedRAMP matters:** Established in response to the federal government's Cloud First Policy (now Cloud Smart Strategy) via the OMB FedRAMP Policy Memo, FedRAMP is mandatory for all US federal agencies and cloud services.

**FedRAMP 20x Initiative:** The PMO, industry stakeholders, and agency experts are redesigning the FedRAMP assessment process to streamline and enhance compliance.

**FedRAMP Consolidated Rules for 2026 (CR26):** These published regulations modernize how CSPs communicate changes and maintain ongoing compliance. Key changes include:
- Significant Change Notifications (SCN) for communicating reportable changes to agency customers
- Collaborative Continuous Monitoring (CCM) for ongoing compliance reporting
- "FedRAMP Authorized" renamed to "FedRAMP Certified"

**AWS FedRAMP Certification details:**
- AWS has achieved FedRAMP Certification for AWS GovCloud (US) as Class D (formerly High baseline) and AWS US East-West as Class C (formerly Moderate baseline)
- No increase in AWS service costs due to FedRAMP compliance
- FedRAMP IDs: AWS US East-West = AGENCYAMAZONEW; AWS GovCloud (US) = F1603047866
- AWS maintains continuous monitoring through quarterly Ongoing Certification Reports (OCR) and Quarterly Review briefings
- AWS supports high-impact workloads on AWS GovCloud (US), which is authorized for high impact level

**Key distinctions:**
- FedRAMP Certification is issued by the FedRAMP PMO (congressionally mandated under the FedRAMP Authorization Act)
- The JAB Provisional Authority to Operate (P-ATO) previously issued to AWS is a legacy designation superseded by FedRAMP Certification
- Agencies must issue their own ATO through the Risk Management Framework (RMF) for systems incorporating FedRAMP Certified services
- FedRAMP is the process for CSPs; RMF is the process for agencies authorizing their IT systems

**Accessing FedRAMP packages:** US Government employees/contractors can request the AWS FedRAMP Certification Package via a Package Access Request Form submitted to package-access@fedramp.gov. Commercial customers can access the AWS FedRAMP Partner Package via AWS Artifact. AWS FedRAMP Security Artifacts are also available through AWS Artifact in the AWS Management Console.

**Related compliance programs:** FedRAMP relates to FISMA (built on NIST SP 800-53 controls), DoD CSP SRG (Impact Levels requiring FIPS 140-3 for certain encryption controls), DFARS (requires NIST SP 800-171 for CUI protection), and NIST SP 800-171.

**Government usage:** Many US government agencies and entities use AWS services, with case studies available on the AWS Customer Success webpage and AWS for Government webpage.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) is a US government-wide program intended to standardize the security assessment, certification, and continuous monitoring for cloud products and services used by federal agencies."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: GitHub - ramimac/aws-customer-security-incidents: A repository of breaches of AWS customers · GitHub ---
URL: https://github.com/ramimac/aws-customer-security-incidents

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the GitHub repository "aws-customer-security-incidents" by user ramimac, which serves as a comprehensive, publicly-available catalog of security incidents that impacted AWS customers. The repository's stated purpose is that "cloud security must be threat-informed" and it compiles public data on security incidents to guide prioritized security investment. It seeks to index all publicly disclosed AWS customer security incidents with a known root cause, while explicitly excluding incidents involving exposed data stores (e.g., S3 bucket leaks, exposed managed/hosted databases), which are cataloged elsewhere. The author notes the repository is intended in the spirit of "blameless postmortems" and not as criticism of listed companies.

The main content consists of two detailed tables:

**1. Catalog of AWS Customer Security Incidents** — A chronological table (2014–2026) of ~80 incidents with columns for Name, Date, Root Cause, Escalation Vector(s), Impact, and Link to details. Key incidents include:
- **Uber (2014 & 2016):** GitHub Gist with AWS credentials led to 50,000 records exposed; later 600k driver records and PII of 57 million users.
- **Code Spaces (2014):** AWS Console credentials compromised via phishing led to wiped S3 buckets, EC2 instances, AMIs, and EBS snapshots (putting the company out of business).
- **Capital One (2019):** Misconfigured WAF enabling SSRF attack via over-privileged EC2 Role affected 100 million credit applications.
- **DNC Hack by GRU (2016):** EC2 Snapshots copied to attacker AWS accounts.
- **Lastpass (2022):** Compromised developer account (IAM User) with later compromise of privileged engineer's machine for decryption keys; broadly compromised internal/customer data.
- **Bybit / Safe{Wallet} (2025):** Compromised developer machine with malicious JavaScript via S3 bucket write access led to $1.5 billion stolen.
- **Medibank (2022):** Compromised credentials led to data exfiltration from Redshift.
- **Reddit (2018):** Employee SMS intercepted for 2FA bypass.
- **Capital One (2019), OneLogin (2017), Imperva (2019), Twilio (2020), Dropbox Sign (2024), Cisco (2020), Cloudflare (2023), and many others.**

Common root causes across incidents include: exposed/committed AWS credentials (GitHub, source code, APK, JS files), compromised employee credentials (stale accounts, former employees, insider threats), SSRF attacks, cryptojacking, exposed Kubernetes/Docker consoles, third-party compromise, supply chain attacks (Trivy, Jenkins, OAuth tokens), and infostealer malware. Common impacts include: data exfiltration (S3, RDS, Redshift), cryptojacking/cryptomining, ransomware, phishing/SES abuse, LLMJacking, service outages, and identity theft data exposure.

**2. Vendor-reported AWS Customer Security Incident Case Studies** — A table of ~50 case studies (2020–2025) from vendors including Mandiant, TeamTNT, Expel, CrowdStrike, Sysdig, Unit42 (Palo Alto), Datadog, Wiz, Permiso, Rapid7, Darktrace, and others. These document attack patterns such as credential theft from GitHub, cryptojacking worms (TeamTNT), IAM privilege escalation, IMDS credential theft, SIM-swap attacks, SSRF exploitation, LLMJacking, and S3 ransomware (e.g., SSE-C encryption abuse by Halcyon's Codefinger research).

The repository also includes supporting documentation files: ACTORS.md, DISCLOSURE.md, KEYLEAKS.md, LICENSE, README.md, REPORTS.md, RESEARCH_NOTES.md, SSRF.md, USAGES.md, and a Claude skill folder (.claude/skills/aws-incidents-solver). The repository has 815 stars, 61 forks, and 328 commits.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Cloud security must be threat-informed. This repository compiles public data on security incidents impacting AWS customers, to guide prioritized security investment."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: AWS Security Incident Response: The customer’s journey to accelerating the incident response lifecycle | AWS Security Blog ---
URL: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/aws-security-incident-response-the-customers-journey-to-accelerating-the-incident-response-lifecycle

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This AWS Security Blog post (republished August 1, 2024, to remove incorrect references to AWS WAF and Shield) describes how AWS Security Incident Response—a Tier 1 AWS-native service launched in December 2024—accelerates the incident response lifecycle. The post walks through a real-world scenario to demonstrate the service's capabilities.

KEY STATISTICS AND CONTEXT:
- Over 50% of security alerts go unaddressed due to resource constraints and alert fatigue; false positives consume 30% of investigation time.
- Organizations take an average of 258 days to identify and contain security events (2024 IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report).
- Nearly half of SOC teams report increased detection/response times over the past two years; 80% say manual threat investigation significantly impacts response times.
- Organizations with mature incident response capabilities achieve 50% reduction in mean time to resolution (MTTR) and cost savings of up to 58% per incident.

SERVICE CAPABILITIES:
- Addresses three challenges: alert fatigue (via automated monitoring and intelligent triage), fragmented access/communications, and security skills gaps (via 24/7 access to AWS CIRT experts).
- Integrates with GuardDuty and Security Hub (detection), Systems Manager (management/governance), and third-party solutions through Security Hub integrations and the AWS Security Incident Response Partner Specialization program.
- Provides expert knowledge from AWS Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT), tools via APIs and console, and streamlined processes.

SETUP REQUIREMENTS:
- Configure IAM permissions (AWSSecurityIncidentResponseFullAccess for admins; AWSSecurityIncidentResponseCaseFullAccess and AWSSecurityIncidentResponseReadOnlyAccess for role-based access in dev/test environments).
- Establish incident response team contacts and notification channels.
- Optionally enable GuardDuty and Security Hub, and deploy CloudFormation StackSets for automated containment actions.

WALKTHROUGH SCENARIO (incident at 2:00 AM):
1. DETECTION: GuardDuty detects anomalous IAM behavior, unusual API calls from unknown IPs, and a surge of EC2 instance creations with SSH keys and internet-accessible security groups—matching known threat behaviors via GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection.
2. TRIAGE: The service automatically analyzes GuardDuty findings (including historical baseline, finding types, correlation patterns) and opens an AWS Security Incident Response case when a true positive is identified, notifying the configured team. It correlates disparate events (e.g., CloudTrail log deletion, unauthorized access key creation, suspicious S3 object access) and maps signals to MITRE ATT&CK tactics/techniques/procedures, revealing a potential ransomware threat.
3. AWS CIRT ENGAGEMENT: The team opens a one-click escalation to AWS CIRT through the incident case, with a 15-minute acknowledgement timeframe. AWS CIRT provides conference bridge calls, advanced artifact analysis, technical guidance, and recommendations—even in environments with limited logging.
4. RESOURCE TAGGING: The team tags affected resources using the incident case ID as the primary tag key, enabling targeted access controls, containment measures, cost tracking, and post-incident analysis.
5. CONTAINMENT (via Systems Manager): Using pre-deployed CloudFormation StackSets, the service performs three-step containment: Isolate (remove instances from security groups), Preserve (create snapshots), and Investigate (collect system info via Systems Manager). Actions are reversible.
6. RESOLUTION: Verification of containment, threat alleviation, service restoration, and access control normalization. The service compiles a comprehensive incident timeline for reporting to executives, regulators, and cyber insurance providers.

LESSONS LEARNED AND LONG-TERM IMPROVEMENTS: Enhanced logging based on AWS CIRT recommendations, updated security controls, and improved incident response processes.

ADDITIONAL RESOURCES: AWS Customer Playbook Framework, Assisted Log Enabler, Athena Security Analytics Bootstrap, and five publicly available AWS CIRT workshops.

The post concludes that AWS Security Incident Response delivers measurable benefits through continuous threat monitoring, reduced response times, enhanced investigation via AWS CIRT collaboration, streamlined containment, and comprehensive documentation—with cost savings up to 58% per incident.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Organizations with mature incident response capabilities demonstrate a 50 percent reduction in mean time to resolution (MTTR) and achieve cost savings of up to 58 percent per incident."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://d1.awsstatic.com/legal/aws-gdpr/aws-gdpr-dpa-online.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the AWS Data Processing Addendum (DPA), a legal document that supplements the AWS Customer Agreement and governs how AWS processes Customer Data on behalf of its customers. The DPA establishes AWS as a data processor and the Customer as either a controller or processor of Customer Data.

Key provisions include:
- **Data Processing Roles**: AWS acts as processor; Customer acts as controller or processor. The subject matter is Customer Data, with duration determined by the Customer.
- **Customer Instructions**: The DPA and Agreement constitute documented instructions for AWS's processing. Additional instructions require prior written agreement.
- **Confidentiality**: AWS will not access, use, or disclose Customer Data except as necessary to provide Services or comply with law/governmental orders. AWS will redirect governmental demands to Customer where possible.
- **Security Measures**: AWS maintains technical and organizational measures including network security, physical security of facilities, access controls for personnel, and regular testing/evaluation per the AWS Security Standards (Annex 1).
- **Sub-processors**: AWS has general authorization to use sub-processors, which are listed at https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/sub-processors/. AWS must notify Customers at least 30 days before engaging a new sub-processor and remains responsible for sub-processor compliance.
- **Data Subject Requests**: AWS assists via Service Controls and forwards data subject requests to Customer promptly.
- **Security Incidents**: AWS must notify Customer without undue delay after becoming aware of a Security Incident. Unsuccessful incidents (e.g., port scans, failed logins, denial of service attacks) are excluded.
- **Certifications and Audits**: AWS holds ISO 27001, 27017, 27018, and 27701 certifications and SOC 1, 2, and 3 reports. External audits are performed at least annually per ISO 27001 standards.
- **Data Transfers**: Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) apply to GDPR-protected data transferred to Third Countries. Controller-to-Processor Clauses apply when Customer is a controller; Processor-to-Processor Clauses apply when Customer is a processor. SCCs do not apply if AWS has adopted Binding Corporate Rules or alternative compliance standards.
- **Return/Deletion**: AWS returns or deletes Customer Data upon request up to 90 days post-termination, after which Customer must close all AWS accounts.
- **Termination**: The DPA remains in force until the Agreement terminates. In case of conflict, the DPA controls over the Agreement, except Service Terms control over the DPA.

The document also includes Annex 1 (AWS Security Standards) detailing the information security program, network security controls (firewalls, authentication), physical security measures (nondescript facilities, photo-ID badges, video surveillance, intrusion detection), limited employee/contractor access, and continued security evaluation.
</summary>

This webpage describes AWS's Data Processing Addendum (DPA), which is designed to help AWS customers comply with GDPR contractual obligations. Key points include:

- The AWS DPA is incorporated into the AWS Service Terms and applies automatically to all customers globally whenever they use AWS services to process customer data, regardless of applicable data protection laws.
- AWS uses Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) as a data transfer tool for transfers of customer data outside the EU to countries not recognized by the European Commission as providing adequate protection. The SCCs are part of AWS Service Terms, incorporated by reference into the AWS DPA, and apply automatically.

- AWS outlines a structured framework clarifying division of responsibilities under a shared responsibility model: customers assess and implement technical/organizational measures to secure data transfers, while AWS maintains contractual and infrastructure-level safeguards.
- A practical six-step process based on European Data Protection Board (EDPB) guidance helps customers: (1) map data transfers; (2) identify the legal transfer mechanism (such as SCCs); (3) assess destination country laws and practices; (4) implement supplementary safeguards where necessary; (5) document procedural steps; and (6) reassess risk periodically.
- AWS offers safeguards including encryption, data residency controls, and legal commitments to resist overreaching governmental requests.

--- SOURCE 10: In detail - Navigating GDPR Compliance on AWS ---
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/navigating-gdpr-compliance/in-detail.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This AWS whitepaper provides a detailed guide for AWS customers on how to conduct a Data Transfer Assessment (DTA) as part of their GDPR compliance obligations when using AWS services. The document outlines a six-step framework recommended by the EDPB for assessing and managing international data transfers.

**Step 1: Know Your Transfers** - Customers must identify which data transfers occur through their use of AWS services. Since AWS is content-agnostic and has no visibility into customer data, only the customer can complete this step. AWS's European seller of record is Amazon Web Services EMEA SARL, based in Luxembourg. AWS will not transfer customer data outside the customer's selected AWS region unless necessary to provide/maintain services, comply with law, or prevent fraud. Customers select AWS regions in Europe including France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and the UK. Only a small number of AWS services (e.g., content delivery) involve third-country transfers, and customers can opt out of such transfers.

**Step 2: Identify Transfer Tools** - The Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) are incorporated into the AWS Service Terms and AWS Data Processing Addendum (DPA). Both Controller-to-Processor and Processor-to-Processor Clauses apply depending on the customer's role. AWS also offers UK and Switzerland addenda to the DPA for transfers from those countries.

**Step 3: Assess Laws/Practices of Recipient Countries** - Customers must assess whether the transfer tool provides effective protection. On July 10, 2023, the European Commission adopted its adequacy decision on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF), confirming the US ensures adequate protection for data transferred to DPF-certified companies. AWS reviews every law enforcement request individually and independently, challenges overbroad requests, and publishes regular Amazon Information Request Reports demonstrating that disclosures of customer data are very rare.

**Step 4: Adopt Supplementary Measures** - AWS offers three categories: (a) technical measures (encryption via AWS KMS with FIPS 140-2 certified HSMs, the AWS Nitro System which by design has no mechanism for AWS personnel to access customer data on Nitro hosts - independently affirmed by NCC Group); (b) organizational measures (internal processes for handling governmental requests, Information Request Reports); and (c) contractual protections (the AWS Supplementary Addendum, under which AWS commits to redirect governmental bodies to the customer, notify customers of requests when legally permitted, challenge overbroad requests, and disclose only minimum necessary data if compelled).

**Step 5: Procedural Steps** - No need to request supervisory authority authorization if supplementary measures don't contradict the SCCs and are sufficient to protect GDPR-level protection.

**Step 6: Re-evaluate** - Customers must continuously monitor developments in recipient countries; AWS will also monitor relevant developments.

Additional AWS assurances include adherence to the CISPE Data Protection Code of Conduct (validated by the EDPB and approved by the French DPA/CNIL), which goes beyond GDPR compliance by requiring cloud providers to offer EEA-exclusive storage/processing options (AWS initially declared 100 services under the CISPE Code).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: AWS Digital Sovereignty Pledge: Control without compromise | AWS Security Blog ---
URL: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/aws-digital-sovereignty-pledge-control-without-compromise

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an AWS Security Blog post announcing the "AWS Digital Sovereignty Pledge" — AWS's commitment to offering all customers the most advanced set of sovereignty controls and features available in the cloud. The pledge addresses customer concerns that they might have to choose between the full power of AWS and a feature-limited sovereign cloud solution.

Key points of the pledge include four commitment areas:

1. **Control over data location**: AWS commits to delivering more fine-grained data residency controls and transparency, including for operational data like identity and billing information. Currently, customers in Europe can deploy data across eight existing Regions.

2. **Verifiable control over data access**: The AWS Nitro System uses specialized hardware and software to protect data during processing on EC2, designed so that nobody—including anyone within AWS—can access customer workloads. AWS commits to additional access restrictions unless requested by the customer or a trusted partner.

3. **Encrypt everything everywhere**: All AWS services already support encryption, most with customer-managed keys inaccessible to AWS. AWS commits to additional sovereignty and encryption controls, with keys managed inside or outside the AWS Cloud (e.g., AWS KMS External Key Store).

4. **Cloud resilience**: AWS claims the highest network availability of any cloud provider. Each Region comprises multiple isolated Availability Zones (AZs), and AWS offers offline/remote capabilities for intermittently connected use cases.

The post highlights recent examples of sovereign-by-design work, including data residency guardrails added to AWS Control Tower (late 2021) and AWS services adhering to the CISPE Data Protection Code of Conduct (announced February 2022) for GDPR compliance. AWS also commits to transparency about data processing, challenging law enforcement requests for customer data, and working with local partners such as T-Systems (Deutsche Telekom) in Germany, which offers Data Protection as a Managed Service on AWS. The full content is also provided in French, German, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Spanish, and Arabic versions.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We firmly believe that customers shouldn't have to make this choice." (regarding choosing between full AWS power and feature-limited sovereign cloud solutions), "Our approach to delivering on this pledge is to continue to make the AWS Cloud sovereign-by-design—as it has been from day one.", "Currently, in Europe, customers have the choice to deploy their data into any of eight existing Regions.", "By providing a strong physical and logical security boundary, Nitro is designed to enforce restrictions so that nobody, including anyone in AWS, can access customer workloads on EC2.", "It is not possible to achieve digital sovereignty without resiliency and survivability."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Org Management account - AWS Prescriptive Guidance ---
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/privacy-reference-architecture/org-management-account.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is part of the AWS Privacy Reference Architecture (AWS PRA) documentation and describes the Org Management account, which is used to manage resource configuration drift for foundational privacy controls across all accounts in an AWS organization. The account enables consistent deployment of new member accounts with security and privacy controls. The page details three key AWS services configured in this account:

1. **AWS Artifact**: Provides on-demand downloads of AWS security and compliance documents for audits. Useful reports include the SOC 2 Type 2 Privacy report (demonstrating AWS controls for how personal data is collected, used, retained, disclosed, and disposed of), the Cloud Computing Compliance Controls Catalog (C5) report created by Germany's BSI, and the ISO/IEC 27701:2019 certification report (covering privacy information management systems/PIMS).

2. **AWS Control Tower**: Helps set up and govern a multi-account environment following prescriptive security practices. It automates deployment of proactive, preventative, and detective controls (guardrails) for data residency and sovereignty. There are more than 17 guardrails designed to control data residency (e.g., Disallow VPN connections, Disallow internet access for VPC instances, Deny access based on AWS Region). Sovereignty controls include requiring EBS volume encryption and restricting AWS KMS key policies. Mandatory controls protect logs (e.g., Disallow Deletion of Log Archive, Enable Integrity Validation for CloudTrail). Control Tower integrates with AWS Security Hub CSPM for detective controls to monitor configuration drift.

3. **AWS Organizations**: Used to centrally manage all accounts. Service control policies (SCPs) provide centralized control over maximum available permissions for IAM roles and users. SCPs can limit AWS Regions for data residency, and can restrict high-risk API calls such as enabling public access to S3 buckets, disabling Amazon GuardDuty, deleting AWS WAF data exfiltration rules, sharing EBS snapshots publicly, removing member accounts, and disassociating Amazon CodeGuru Reviewer. Management policies, particularly tag policies, help maintain consistent tags across the organization. Tags can distinguish resources handling personal data and support attribute-based access control (ABAC) policies. The page warns against placing personally identifiable information in tags (as tags are not encrypted and can be read by AWS services) and recommends making some tag values immutable to prevent circumvention of technical controls.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The Org Management account is primarily used to manage resource configuration drift for the foundational privacy controls across all of the accounts in your organization, which is managed by AWS Organizations."
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 3: Strategizing for global expansion - AWS Prescriptive Guidance ---
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/privacy-reference-architecture/global-expansion.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This AWS Prescriptive Guidance page provides strategies for global expansion when architecting for privacy and data sovereignty on AWS. It addresses common questions from AWS Security Assurance Services about data residency, operator access restriction, resiliency, and independence when expanding globally. The page emphasizes working closely with compliance and contract teams to confirm requirements for where, when, and how personal data can cross AWS Regions, including what qualifies as data transfer (moving, copying, or viewing), resiliency/data protection controls, cross-Region failover needs, and encryption requirements.

The page outlines three approaches for AWS multi-account strategy, in ascending order of infrastructure segregation:

1. **Central landing zone with managed Regions**: Uses an existing AWS Control Tower landing zone (MALZ) to manage additional Regions. Extends governance into new Regions while keeping personal data stores in managed Regions under a dedicated Personal Data OU. This is the most cost-effective option but requires additional consideration for controlling personal data flow across Regional boundaries (log redaction, VPC isolation, Transit Gateway design, and role/attribute-based access control).

2. **Regional landing zones**: Uses more than one MALZ to completely isolate workloads processing personal data. Simplifies centralized logging aggregation without needing log redaction exceptions. Allows separate security postures per Region (e.g., US and EU landing zones) and dedicated local cloud operations teams. Incurs additional costs and operational overhead for maintaining multiple MALZs.

3. **AWS European Sovereign Cloud**: A new independent cloud for Europe, physically and logically separate from existing AWS Regions, designed for stringent EEA sovereignty needs. Only AWS employees located in the EU control operations and support. All metadata (roles, permissions, resource labels, configurations) remains in the EU, with its own billing and usage metering. Deploys a dedicated MALZ for European customer services.

The page notes that privacy compliance extends beyond data sovereignty, referencing other challenges such as consent management, data subjects' requests, data governance, and AI bias covered elsewhere in the guide.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"For data residency requirements, different architecture deployments might work better for different organizations."
</key_excerpts>
