args.summary: This article from The HIPAA Journal (published December 29, 2023, by Steve Alder) addresses whether Google Cloud Platform (GCP) is HIPAA compliant. The answer is yes, but only for "covered products" provided they are configured to support HIPAA compliance and organizations accept Google's Business Associate Addendum terms. GCP is a leading cloud provider for healthcare due to easy integration with Google Workspace, strong data analytics, price competitiveness, and more open source integrations than competitors. Not all GCP products have adequate PHI protection capabilities, so Google separates compliant ones into "covered products" (including Cloud Storage, Compute Engine, Cloud SQL, App Engine, etc.). The HIPAA Compliance on Google Cloud page offers 28 best practice recommendations to help configure covered products. The GCP BAA is a Business Associate Addendum to the Google Cloud Terms of Service rather than a separate agreement, and must be requested from an account manager before any covered product is used to create, collect, store, or transmit PHI. The article also explains the Shared Responsibility Model: in most cases Google is responsible for security OF the cloud, while organizations are responsible for security IN the cloud, with responsibility divided by product type (IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS). The page includes extensive FAQ content covering HIPAA training requirements, breach notifications, business associate agreements, documentation retention (6 years), sanctions, transaction code monitoring, NPI usage, automatic logoff, password sharing, backup/disaster recovery, information access policies, security management processes, HIPAA Authorization Forms (§164.508), Notices of Privacy Practices (§164.520), patient access requests, minimum necessary standard, phishing/malware training, and covered entity vs. business associate distinctions. The page also promotes a free HIPAA Compliance Checklist and notes a 25% discount on HIPAA training courses (offer ends August 28, 2026).
args.key_excerpts: "Google Cloud Platform is HIPAA compliant for 'covered products', provided the products are configured to support HIPAA compliance and organizations accept the terms of Google's Business Associate Addendum – including those that relate to the Google Cloud Platform Shared Responsibility Model."

# Google reaffirms sovereign cloud solutions for EU

Aims to ease anxieties about trade tensions

![Preferred source](/static/img/google_preferred_source.172e670ec003.png)

Google has announced a series of additional security and sovereignty elements for its sovereign cloud in response to EU groups' concerns about trade tensions and the reliance on US tech companies.

First reported by the [Financial Times](https://www.ft.com/content/c9ee9f3b-8d9e-446d-a0f9-66d546b55fa3), and later detailed in a [blog post](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/google-advances-sovereignty-choice-and-security-in-the-cloud) from Google, the company is also looking to work more closely with its regional partners in France and Germany to help reassure customers that data will remain within country boundaries.

![Google logo](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/GettyImages-2159351659.width-358.jpg)

The move comes as European groups are raising concerns about the potential for the Trump administration to use reliance on US tech companies - such as Google, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, and others - as leverage for trade talks.

Local cloud providers have pointed to the White House's attacks on NATO, tariffs on the EU, and threats to invade Greenland as justification for moving off of US hyperscalers and onto local platforms.

The FT reports that, while not naming President Donald Trump specifically, Google's president of customer experience, Hayete Galott, said that global tensions were "creating anxiety in the world."

“Sovereignty used to be a very niche thing, that applied to very regulated industries, such as defence and intelligence,” Galott said. “And suddenly in the current environment, everybody is thinking about it.”

The blog post from Google notes that its updated sovereign cloud solution includes the Google Cloud Data Boundary, which enables customers to create a data boundary and control where data is stored and processed, including ensuring data processing is either in the US or EU and specifying the country where it is stored.

Newly announced today is the "User Data Shield," which adds Mandiant services to validate security for applications built on top of the data boundary.

In addition, through its Google Cloud Dedicated offering, Google's partnership with Thales in France to develop a "Trust Cloud by S3NS" is now available in preview, giving customers access to Google Cloud services with GPUs for AI workloads while being operated by S3NS, a standalone French company.

“For France to truly embrace digital sovereignty, it is essential to have a cloud solution that marries the immense power of hyperscale technology with the strictest local security and operational controls," said Christophe Salomon, EVP, Information Systems and Secured Communication, at Thales. "S3NS is committed to providing French organizations with access to advanced cloud services, including critical AI capabilities, all operated within France by a European operator to meet and exceed the rigorous SecNumCloud standards.”

The project with Thales has been ongoing since [2021](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/thales-and-google-form-new-joint-venture-for-french-sovereign-cloud-service/). The cloud giant has a similar offering being worked on in Germany with Deutsche's T-Systems since [2021](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/t-systems-and-google-partner-for-german-sovereign-cloud-project/).

The sovereign cloud is available as a "Supervised Cloud" offering, which is physically operated by T-Systems and kept separate from other Google Cloud infrastructure.

The reassurance from Google about its commitment to EU sovereignty comes just weeks after [Microsoft](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/microsoft-to-increase-european-data-center-capacity-by-40-percent-pledges-to-protect-local-customers-over-us-threats/) released a similar statement addressing EU customer anxiety, adding that it would increase its data center capacity in Europe by 40 percent over the next two years.

In a blog post, Microsoft president Brad Smith wrote: "Given recent geopolitical volatility, we recognize that European governments likely will consider additional options.

"Some of these may involve public financing to support European home-grown offerings. We recognize the importance of a diversified technology ecosystem, and we are committed to collaborating with European participants across the tech ecosystem."

# T-Systems Sovereign Cloud powered by Google Cloud

![Woman with glasses mood image](https://european.cloud/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/t-systems-gcp.png)

The **[T-Systems GCP Sovereign Cloud](https://www.t-systems.com/de/de/souveraene-cloud/loesungen/sovereign-cloud-powered-by-google-cloud)** is a cloud offering designed to deliver cloud services while simultaneously addressing stringent data sovereignty, compliance, and security requirements, primarily for organizations operating in regulated industries or in regions with strict data protection laws, such as the European Union (EU). This solution is a collaboration between **T-Systems**, a subsidiary of Deutsche Telekom, and **Google Cloud Platform (GCP)**, leveraging Google Cloud’s technologies with T-Systems’ expertise in meeting local compliance and regulatory demands.

## How the T-Systems GCP Sovereign Cloud works

With the T-Systems Sovereign Cloud powered by Google Cloud, GCP is transferring responsibility for sovereignty controls to T-Systems. The soverignty controls monitored and controlled by T-Systems are laid out in the diagram below.

![](https://european.cloud/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/gcp-sovereignty-controls-1024x522.png)

copyright T-Systems

T-Systems is monitoring the platform from outside in their own T-Systems Security Operations Center (SOC).

In the future, T-Systems and Google are planning to introduce two additional variants of the sovereign Google Cloud: The **Supervised Cloud by T-Systems** and the **Hosted Cloud by T-Systems**. The supervised cloud will be based on **Google Supervised Cloud** and the hosted cloud will be based on **Google Distributed Cloud**.

![](https://european.cloud/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/gcp-variants-1024x450.png)

copyright T-Systems

The **Supervised Cloud by T-Systems** is essentially a “semi-connected” variant of GCP, which is operated separately from other Google Cloud infrastructure by T-Systems.

The **Hosted Cloud by T-Systems** is a fully independent instance of GCP, fully air gapped, with it’s own IAM and no connection to global GCP. It is also operated by T-Systems but can be hosted in the customer’s data centre, if desired. This is similar to the model Oracle is offering with the [sovereign variants of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure](https://european.cloud/sovereign-cloud/oracle-sovereign-cloud/).

## Available Services

The T-Systems Sovereign Cloud, powered by Google Cloud, essentially operates as the standard Google Cloud Platform (GCP), with T-Systems overseeing and managing the sovereignty controls. While all GCP services are technically accessible, not all are fully supported by the sovereignty control mechanisms. A list of services that are supported and managed under T-Systems’ sovereignty framework is:

* Artifact Registry
* BigQuery
* Cloud Bigtable
* Cloud Composer
* Cloud DNS

Source: [Scope of Sovereign Controls by Partners Solutions](https://cloud.google.com/terms/in-scope-sovereign-cloud).

## Sovereign GCP Regions

The Sovereign Controls are implemented on a service level, rather than on a region level. Therefore, all GCP regions can be used with T-Systems controlling and supervising sovereignty.

The **Supervised Cloud by T-Systems** is going to be hosted by T-Systems. Here, the question about data centres becomes relevant. Details about that variant have yet to be announced. However, it is fair to assume that it is going to be hosted in the same regions as [Open Telekom Cloud](https://european.cloud/open-telekom-cloud/), namely all or one of the twin-core regions

* Biere and Magdeburg in Germany
* Almere and Aalsmeer in the Netherlands
* Zollikofen and Bern in Switzerland

Check the [Data Centre map](https://european.cloud/data-centres/) to see where these are geographically.

## Conclusion

The approach of Google is similar to the Microsoft Cloud for Sovereignty in the sense that sovereignty controls are built into the platform. The difference is that supervision of these controls is outsourced to T-Systems. With the announced variants of sovereign GCP, T-Systems and Google will be offering a range of options for sovereign GCP. It remains to be seen how successful those models are going to be and if the right lessons were learned from the failure of the [Microsoft Cloud Germany, operated by T-Systems](https://european.cloud/sovereign-cloud/microsoft-cloud-for-sovereignity/).

The T-Systems Sovereign Cloud powered by Google Cloud is a collaborative cloud offering between T-Systems (a Deutsche Telekom subsidiary) and Google Cloud Platform (GCP) designed to address data sovereignty, compliance, and security requirements for organizations in regulated industries or regions with strict data protection laws, such as the EU. GCP transfers responsibility for sovereignty controls to T-Systems, which monitors the platform from its own Security Operations Center (SOC).

The solution currently operates as standard GCP with T-Systems managing sovereignty controls on a service level (not region level), meaning all GCP regions can be used. T-Systems and Google plan two additional future variants: the Supervised Cloud by T-Systems (a "semi-connected" variant of GCP operated separately from other Google Cloud infrastructure) and the Hosted Cloud by T-Systems (a fully independent, air-gapped GCP instance with its own IAM and no connection to global GCP, which can be hosted in the customer's data centre — similar to Oracle's sovereign OCI model).

Supported services under the sovereignty framework include: Artifact Registry, BigQuery, Cloud Bigtable, Cloud Composer, Cloud DNS, Cloud EKM, Cloud KMS, Cloud HSM, Cloud Interconnect, Cloud Load Balancing, Cloud Logging, Cloud NAT, Cloud Router, Cloud Spanner, Cloud SQL, Cloud Storage, Cloud VPN, Compute Engine, Dataflow, Dataproc, Google Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy, Google Kubernetes Engine, IAM, Network Connectivity Center, Persistent Disk, Pub/Sub, Service Directory, Virtual Private Cloud, and VPC Service Controls.

The Supervised Cloud is expected to be hosted by T-Systems, likely in the same twin-core regions as Open Telekom Cloud: Biere and Magdeburg (Germany), Almere and Aalsmeer (Netherlands), and Zollikofen and Bern (Switzerland). The approach is similar to Microsoft Cloud for Sovereignty, but with sovereignty control supervision outsourced to T-Systems, and the article notes uncertainty about whether lessons were learned from the earlier Microsoft Cloud Germany operated by T-Systems.

This webpage is the Google Workspace customer stories page, showcasing how organizations of all sizes (from small businesses to Fortune 500 corporations) use Google Workspace to improve collaboration, productivity, and innovation. The page highlights several featured resources including the "Champions of Change" video series, the "User Love" series, and customer story blog posts.

**Key featured metrics:**
- Equifax migrated global teams from an on-premises solution to Workspace in 48 hours, achieving a mindset of "ruthless collaboration"
- One customer reduced time spent on product descriptions from 30-40 hours per month to just 1 hour using Duet AI/Gemini
- Incubeta achieved a 50% ROI improvement for short-term campaigns using Gemini to curate proactive and context-driven insights

**Featured customer stories include:** Equifax (185 real-world gen AI use cases), 3v3 tecnologia (Gemini in Google Sheets for Brazilian farmers), ACB Securities, ACDC Express, Adore Me, Airbus, Ajax Systems, All Nippon Airways, ATB Financial, BBVA, Colgate-Palmolive, Compass, DocuSign, Geotab, Globe Telecom (80% adoption of Google Workspace with Gemini), Humana AB (migrated 13,000 employees and 22 TB of data in four months), Mercer International ($3 million per year in productivity gains), and many others.

**Notable statistics across customer stories:**
- Mercer International unlocked $3 million a year in productivity gains using Google Workspace with Gemini
- Humana AB migrated 13k employees and 22 TB of data to Google Workspace in four months
- Globe Telecom reached 80% adoption of Google Workspace with Gemini
- Dezerv increased efficiency by 80% with Google Workspace and Gemini
- Ippen Digital onboarded employees 34% faster with Google Workspace
- MERGE improved customer turnaround time by 33% with Google Workspace with Gemini
- Maryland saved $400k and months of development time with Google AI
- LenDenClub cut project timelines in half across departments with Gemini
- Just Commit Foundation sped up educational resource development by 50-75% with Google Workspace with Gemini
- Google Workspace customers experience 40% fewer email security incidents than average (per At-Bay)

The page also includes navigation links to all Google Workspace products (Gmail, Drive, Meet, Chat, Calendar, Tasks, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Forms, Sites, Keep, Voice, Gemini app, Gemini Notebook, Studio, Vids, Pics, AppSheet), industry solutions (Financial Services, Healthcare, Retail, Manufacturing, Government, Professional Services, Technology), and resources (blog, training, customer stories, events, partners, and marketplace).

# Google Cloud Platform Customer Success Stories

## ResponsiBLUE

ResponsiBLUE is a multi-platform (web, iOS, and Android) app that supports the university’s policies related to COVID-19 safety based on the CDC guidelines. The app informs people of their latest compliance statuses for daily health screening check, quarantine & isolation, testing, and vaccinations.

Google Cloud Platform provides a complete serverless solution for ResponsiBLUE: hosting, storage, analytics, database, and authentication. Its scalability meets the needs of about 35,000 active daily users of the app while staying within the project’s monthly budget goals.

Due to its industry adoption and platform maturity, training and documentation are readily available to support developers’ work. With a relatively low learning-curve, the functional app team members, including designers and managers, have been able to utilize Google Cloud Platform products via the Firebase console for app content updates, metrics analysis, and testing.

Cloud Firestore, a scalable NoSQL database, is capable of delivering critical and time-sensitive information in realtime for the entire U-M population. Combined with Google Cloud Storage, it allows cross-organizational collaboration and the data to be shared with the U-M Data Warehouse to generate public dashboards to leadership reports.

The existing relationship between U-M and Google added a level of assurance in the Google Cloud Platform for ResponsiBLUE. And the ease of Information Assurance auditing further added to the confidence in the platform having met compliance requirements.

“The results have been a successful partnership between positive user experience design and the appropriate use of technology. It’s proven that we chose the appropriate platform to use for ResponsiBLUE.”

— ResponsiBLUE app team

## ORION Network Telescope

"The ORION Network Telescope consists of networking instrumentation that receives and records unsolicited Internet traffic destined to an unused, but routed, Internet address space. This traffic, usually referred to as Internet Background Radiation or Darknet traffic, mostly consists of malicious activity originating from malware that try to propagate to infect more Internet-accessible machines or nefarious users that sequentially scan the whole Internet to identify and exploit vulnerabilities. Monitoring and analyzing Darknet traffic is thus critical for understanding macroscopic Internet threats and defending critical infrastructure.

"The ORION Network Telescope is operated by researchers at Merit Network and at the University of Michigan and is partially funded by the National Science Foundation. One of its critical infrastructure components is the extraction of Darknet events on a near-real-time basis that are then exported to Google’s BigQuery for further analysis, visualizations and ease of data sharing. Our pipeline makes frequent use of other useful Google-cloud products, such as 1) storage buckets for exporting large amounts of analyzed Darknet data and 2) computing instances for data processing and exploration."

— Michael Kallitsis

## HITS DevOps

"The HITS DevOps team has migrated vendor applications (such as GitLab and Jira) as well as custom applications for Research and Education. The move to MCloud has allowed us to gain locality to solve complex problems efficiently. Using a combination of Ansible and Terraform, we’ve been able to spin up full environments (including Networking, Load Balancing, Compute, Container Orchestration, Identity and Access Management, and a Google-managed Database) in under 30 minutes. We’ve been able to leverage Google Kubernetes Engine’s self-healing and auto-scaling capabilities and greatly improve reliability and recovery targets. With the help of ITS, we’ve been approved to host ePHI. The move has also been cost-effective — moving our Atlassian apps from vendor-hosting to GKE hosting resulted in a ~65% cost reduction — and upgrades are actually easier now compared to when the vendor was doing them for us."

— Shanelle Boluyt

# Helpful Google Cloud customer success stories and cost optimization advice

[Edwin Kuss](https://hystax.com/autors/edwin-kuss-director-of-global-sales-at-hystax/)

While no one will be surprised by today’s growth in the cloud and the investment and the costs businesses are putting toward cloud usage, the statistics are telling.

A [newly released report](https://www.reportlinker.com/p06306033/?utm_source=GNW), “Cloud Computing Market Research Report by Workload, Service Model, Infrastructure, Solution, Organization Size, Industry, Deployment model, Region” conducted a global forecast through to 2027, keeping the impact of COVID-19 in mind. It found that while the Global Cloud Computing market size was estimated at $396.18 billion USD in 2021 and was expected to tally up to $456.05 billion USD in 2022, it is now projected to grow at a CAGR of 15.14% to reach $923.46 billion USD by 2027.

While the need for the cloud and an effective multi-cloud strategy at most companies is inarguable, the amount being spent warrants a hard look at how companies are looking at the cloud, as well as maintaining cloud cost optimization.

Business leaders are actively looking for strategies to implement within their FinOps teams. There is greater pressure and awareness of how to best manage cloud infrastructure today, as well as how to help enhance IT infrastructure usage in order to reduce monthly cloud bills.

![Google Cloud customer finops stories and cost optimization advice](https://hystax.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/Google-Cloud-customer-finops-stories-cost-optimization-advice.png)

While we’ve previously covered customer success stories on both [Microsoft Azure](https://hystax.com/get-inspired-cost-optimization-stories-of-ms-azure-customers/) and [Amazon Web Services (AWS)](https://hystax.com/how-aws-customers-are-seeing-cloud-cost-optimization/), it’s rare that today’s companies are only leveraging one of these platforms. The [Google Cloud Platform](https://cloud.google.com/gcp?utm_source=google&utm_medium=cpc&utm_campaign=emea-il-all-en-bkws-all-all-trial-e-gcp-1011340&utm_content=text-ad-none-any-DEV_c-CRE_500236788696-ADGP_Hybrid+%7C+BKWS+-+EXA+%7C+Txt+~+GCP+~+General%23v1-KWID_43700060384861723-kwd-87853815-userloc_1008006&utm_term=KW_gcp-NET_g-PLAC_&gclid=Cj0KCQjw08aYBhDlARIsAA_gb0cdUOiTUSctE7KwO0kuZOOkDOtvdSpwMlk_49H7x_CU84GeCcASB80aAuJ2EALw_wcB&gclsrc=aw.ds) (GCP) is widely used by today’s businesses.

Google prides itself in its core infrastructure, data analytics, and machine learning to set it apart from other providers out there. Users are privy to capabilities, including app and data protection “with the same security technology Google uses,” as well as the ability to avoid vendor lock-in in order to have apps running via open source solutions.

## How Google Cloud Platform entices users

GCP offers new customers enticing benefits. They can start running IT workloads free of charge, as well as receive [$300 in free credits](https://console.cloud.google.com/freetrial/) to run, test and deploy their workloads. Additionally, new customers receive complimentary access to [25+ products](https://cloud.google.com/free/docs/gcp-free-tier#free-tier) within their monthly usage limits.

Google also offers the ability to leverage a platform with easy-to-use tools and APIs which it says are made for developers with a deep understanding of their needs. Google also offers helpful courses and labs which to learn from.

Additionally, like other platforms out there and with cost optimization being a key focus of today’s FinOps teams, Google also offers a [pricing calculator](https://cloud.google.com/products/calculator). This calculator helps users determine their projected costs based on different workloads, locations and other factors.

However, while these tools and free capabilities are enticing to Google Cloud Platform users, there are usually case studies and customer success stories that offer them the most learnings.

## Google Cloud Platform success stories

![Google Cloud customer finops stories and cost optimization advice](https://hystax.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/Google-Cloud-customer-success-finops-stories-cost-optimization-advice.png)

The GCP site offers [an entire page](https://cloud.google.com/customers/) dedicated to customer success stories and helpful case study materials. GCP is used by the likes of Twitter, The Home Depot, Deutsche Bank, P&G, Airbus, Etsy, UPS, and the list goes on. [Google Cloud Platform](/google-cloud-platform-strengths-and-weaknesses/) has no shortage of notable users and businesses, as well as companies that span a variety of different industries with different needs and use cases.

Here are some highlights of how well-known companies are using GCP today and seeing results.

### Target’s usage of GCP for customer satisfaction

Target is using Google Cloud to implement storewide design and logistical solutions without sacrificing internal or external experiences. Their leaders are able to solve business problems by looking at data on their impact on customers, sales representatives, and their IT teams.

Target uses GCP to help manage its cloud efforts across 1,800 stores, 350,000 team members, and a website and app audience which totals 100 million visitors per month. Target leaders use GCP to help with geolocation efforts, inventory management, and online commerce experiences.

“We want to be a positive force behind millions of people, every day,” said Krishnan Srinivasan, Vice President of Cloud and Compute Infrastructure Platforms, Target. “If we’re going to keep doing that, we need a cloud technology that focuses on experiences. That’s elegant, simple, and adaptive. That doesn’t lock us in.”

Google Cloud Solutions are helpful for the retail market in that they can present a cost-efficient way to understand and track [customer loyalty](https://cloud.google.com/customers/featured/target), as well as make for an easy [shopping environment](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y0KNFWBsJ_U&feature=emb_imp_woyt) that offers consumers a best-in-class experience.

With mobile apps to help with checkout, among many other cloud uses, Target’s developers are benefiting from open source software, CI/CD, as well as contactless delivery. All in all, Target has designed a one-stop-shop to design, release and manage its apps and run them efficiently on Google Cloud.

eBay, L.L. Bean, and Zulily are other well-known retailers using GCP to scale and optimize their cloud efforts, with everything from modernizing page loads to leaning on more big data and analytics. GCP provides retailers with multiple locations or eCommerce experiences to have a secure, scalable environment to manage everything they need.

### How Etsy is scaling its business & cutting costs with GCP

Etsy, a well-known consumer marketplace for gifts, personalized items, and much more has seen incredible success since moving its data center and eCommerce platform to the cloud. Etsy hosts the offerings of more than 2.8 million businesses with 66 million items being sold. Etsy’s leaders have been using Google Workspace’s helpful collaboration tools to scale and meet the needs of its sellers and consumers.

The top line results are dramatic. Etsy has seen a savings of more than 50 percent in compute energy with GCP.  It’s also turned to discounts and other available optimizations to have compute costs reduced by 42 percent. The platform migrated 5.5 petabytes of data. Etsy has removed the efforts and costs attributed to keeping on-premises data centers running afloat. As a result, the team at Etsy has been able to focus more on enhancing its user capabilities, seller platform functionality, and search options.

Etsy leans heavily on the cloud to manage all of its eCommerce efforts, and ensure its platform continues to run seamlessly during high sales times, such as the holidays. Prior to the onboarding with GCP, Etsy’s leaders knew they needed a more effective collaboration method and data tracking tools to help employees work effectively and so that they could communicate with their sellers more easily.

![cost optimization, ML resource management](https://hystax.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/cost-optimization-ML-resource-management.png)

### Free cloud cost optimization & enhanced ML/AI resource management for a lifetime

[Sign up](https://my.optscale.com/register)

After mapping out Etsy’s on-premises architecture, its senior engineers and leadership created a footprint and point system to decide on and onboard an effective cloud provider. Apparently, Google Cloud came in above other platforms being considered by more than 10 percent.

With Google Cloud Platform, Etsy has been able to scale its efforts on demand, have access to data centers that help with planning and forecasting, conduct provisioning, and much more at a much quicker rate. Etsy has also turned to GCP to help with its sustainability efforts. With GCP, Etsy has been able to optimize its energy usage and track its carbon footprint more effectively. 

Cost optimization and FinOps are a priority in managing cloud infrastructure today because it helps enhance IT infrastructure usage and reduce cloud bills.

## Helpful tools for GCP users to optimize GCP costs

![GCP customer success stories and cost optimization advice](https://hystax.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/GCP-customer-success-stories-cost-optimization-advice.png)

Google Cloud Platform users can greatly benefit not just from the use of the platform itself, but from tools that help them track their overall cloud spending and optimize cloud costs. Hystax OptScale is one partner which can greatly help them widen the capabilities of native tools, plus give them an opportunity to manage their multi-cloud IT infrastructure more effectively, as most users are not running on GCP alone.

FinOps teams looking for cloud cost management tools and [ways to achieve GCP cost optimization](/first-steps-towards-gcp-cost-optimization-understanding-the-google-cloud-platform-billing-concepts/) can greatly benefit from turning to Hystax OptScale.

The cloud cost management platform is all about offering users more flexible provisioning scenarios and efficient cloud bill control.

From pool transparency to offering a breakdown of cloud usage and cloud consumption across multiple business units, users, projects, and individual cloud services, the platform can be a huge help for any GCP and multi-cloud user. Customers can set limits to prevent overspends and reduce cloud costs with greater visibility.

Hystax also offers the ability to optimize and cut cloud costs with multi-cloud asset provisioning workflows via a dashboard or API. OptScale’s dashboard can help users manage hybrid clouds with virtual machines, volumes, and network settings. The platform also offers custom and mandatory tagging, including TTL rules which can be drafted to clear out IT workloads in line with specific users’ needs.

Additionally, Hystax OptScale’s alerts and notifications are a true game changer for any cloud user. Having an alert sent to you immediately on unusual behavior, or notifying you of workload volume increases, forecasts overdrafts, and additional occurrences which seem out of whack, can be invaluable.

All [GCP users and companies](/gcp-cost-optimization-success-stories-2024-2025/) investing in multi-cloud strategies can benefit from OptScale’s hybrid cloud migration tools. With cross-cloud disaster recovery happening in a matter of seconds and minutes, users can rest assured. --- SOURCE 1: Does Azure OpenAI Services provide HIPAA compliance and BAA - Microsoft Q&A ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/2258799/does-azure-openai-services-provide-hipaa-complianc

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Microsoft Q&A forum thread (dated April 2025) addressing whether Azure OpenAI Services provides HIPAA compliance and a Business Associate Agreement (BAA). A moderator (Pavankumar Purilla) confirmed that Azure OpenAI Service IS HIPAA-eligible and that Microsoft provides a BAA through the Microsoft Online Services Data Protection Addendum (DPA). Key points: (1) Customers do NOT need to sign a separate BAA for each agreement — the BAA is included by default in eligible Microsoft licensing agreements (e.g., Enterprise Agreements or Cloud Solution Provider agreements); (2) Applicable legal terms including the DPA and BAA can be found on the Microsoft Licensing Terms portal at https://www.microsoft.com/licensing/terms; (3) No additional steps are needed to enable HIPAA compliance or BAA coverage as long as the organization uses Azure OpenAI under a valid licensing agreement and follows HIPAA-compliant practices (hosting data in appropriate U.S. regions, implementing encryption, and maintaining proper access controls). A follow-up comment (March 2026) from user Jason Johndrow raised concerns that the generic Azure HIPAA documentation does not mention Azure OpenAI, and questioned whether Azure OpenAI Agents deployed in a shared Azure cluster can be managed or monitored for HIPAA compliance — suggesting that deploying agents to one's own cluster communicating with a compliant OpenAI instance may be necessary.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Yes, Azure OpenAI Service is HIPAA-eligible, and Microsoft provides a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) through the Microsoft Online Services Data Protection Addendum (DPA). Customers are not required to sign a separate BAA for each agreement, as the BAA is already included by default in the standard terms of eligible Microsoft licensing agreements such as Enterprise Agreements or those through a Cloud Solution Provider."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Tenant and BAA setup for mycompany.com (Azure OpenAI / HIPAA , also other Cloud ) - Microsoft Q&A ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-ie/answers/questions/5920476/tenant-and-baa-setup-for-mycompany-com-(azure-open

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Microsoft Q&A forum post where a user (Kamran Iqbal) asks for guidance on setting up a Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) tenant for their company (mycompany.com) with HIPAA BAA coverage so they can use Azure OpenAI with Protected Health Information (PHI). The user wants full control over the tenant with their own Global Administrator accounts, wants to attach Azure subscriptions (dev and prod) for HIPAA-relevant workloads (Azure OpenAI, Key Vault, App Service), ensure DPA/HIPAA BAA coverage, and avoid unnecessary Microsoft 365 licenses. They explicitly want to avoid CSP involvement to retain full billing and licensing control.

The thread contains two answers (one from Microsoft moderator Shubham Sharma, one AI-generated):

**Answer 1 (Moderator - Shubham Sharma):**
- Provision the tenant directly via the Azure Portal using the organization's domain, signing up for Pay-As-You-Go or Enterprise Agreement directly with Microsoft, avoiding CSP for full control.
- Steps: Go to Azure Portal > Create a resource > Identity > Microsoft Entra ID > enter organization details with mycompany.com domain > assign yourself as Global Administrator.
- Microsoft's Online Services DPA includes the HIPAA BAA; when purchasing Azure services directly from Microsoft (not via CSP), the tenant is automatically covered by DPA/BAA as part of Microsoft Online Services Terms.
- Confirm coverage via the Microsoft Licensing Agreements Portal or by contacting Microsoft support/account manager.
- Azure OpenAI is listed as a HIPAA-eligible service under Microsoft's DPA/BAA.
- No Microsoft 365 licenses are needed for Azure and Entra ID workloads.
- If using a CSP, request tenant ownership and admin rights, confirmation of DPA/BAA inclusion, and documentation on transitioning to direct billing without losing compliance.

**Answer 2 (AI-generated):**
- A Microsoft Entra tenant can have many Azure subscriptions but only one tenant per subscription is trusted at a time; use direct Azure subscription (pay-as-you-go or Microsoft Customer Agreement) rather than CSP.
- The initial `*.onmicrosoft.com` domain must be globally unique and cannot be changed; custom domains like mycompany.com can be added and verified.
- Microsoft offers a HIPAA BAA as part of Microsoft Product Terms for covered entities/business associates for in-scope Azure services; Azure has enabled HIPAA/HITECH safeguards and aligns with NIST CSF and ISO/IEC 27001.
- The BAA provides contractual assurances about data safeguarding, breach notifications, and data access per HIPAA/HITECH.
- For CSP scenarios, ensure the tenant is created for mycompany.com, organization admins hold Global Administrator role, and Azure subscriptions are associated with that tenant.
- Azure Lighthouse supports delegation at subscription/resource group scopes allowing partners to manage resources without owning the tenant.
- BAA coverage follows the customer's agreement and in-scope services rather than a specific CSP; changes in billing model/partner should be coordinated to ensure continuity.

The user also reported difficulties: attempting to sign up with a work email required creating a Microsoft account, which rejected work/study emails; creating an Outlook email didn't allow tenant creation, showing a paid account error despite adding a card for Pay-As-You-Go. The moderator asked for an update via private message to proceed further.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"To ensure full Global Admin and Owner control, provision your tenant directly via the Azure Portal using your organization's domain (mycompany.com). Sign up for a Pay-As-You-Go or an Enterprise Agreement directly with Microsoft. Avoid CSP if you want exclusive control over billing, licensing, and tenant management." — Shubham Sharma, Microsoft moderator
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Azure AI BAA/HIPAA Compliance - Microsoft Q&A ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/2265200/azure-ai-baa-hipaa-compliance

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Microsoft Q&A forum thread (dated May 2025) addressing HIPAA compliance for Azure AI services. The original question from Neil Sanghavi asks how to ensure patient data confidentiality and HIPAA compliance when using Azure AI tools like OpenAI, including specific configurations, agreements (BAA), and best practices.

**Key answers from moderators (Sina Salam and Manas R Mohanty):**

1. **HIPAA Requirements on Azure:** Microsoft Azure supports HIPAA and HITRUST standards, but using the platform alone doesn't make organizations compliant—they must proactively configure and manage environments to meet security controls.

2. **Business Associate Agreement (BAA):** Microsoft provides a BAA through the Microsoft Online Services Data Protection Addendum (DPA), automatically included for customers under qualifying licensing models such as Enterprise Agreements, Microsoft 365, CSP arrangements, and Microsoft Customer Agreements. No separate BAA needs to be signed if already using Azure under a qualifying agreement. Confirmation documents can be downloaded from the Microsoft Service Trust Portal.

3. **HIPAA-Eligible Azure AI Services:**
   - Azure OpenAI: HIPAA-eligible for **text-based inputs only**; image inputs (DALL·E) and voice inputs are not covered by default
   - Azure Cognitive Services: Text Analytics, LUIS, Speech Services, and Translator are HIPAA-eligible; Computer Vision and Face API are **not** HIPAA-eligible by default
   - Azure Machine Learning: HIPAA-eligible with proper configurations
   - Azure Bot Services and Functions: Can be HIPAA-compliant when integrated with other compliant services

4. **Key Configuration Areas:**
   - Data Security: Encryption at rest and in transit; Azure Key Vault for customer-managed keys
   - Access Management: RBAC, Azure Active Directory, Conditional Access, and MFA

**Key Points:**

**NERC Overview:** NERC is a not-for-profit regulatory authority ensuring reliability of the North American bulk power system, subject to oversight by the US FERC and Canadian authorities. FERC granted NERC the Electric Reliability Organization (ERO) designation in 2006 under the Energy Policy Act of 2005. NERC develops and enforces CIP reliability standards (first approved by FERC in 2007).

**Azure vs. Azure Government:** Both provide multi-tenant cloud platforms with logical isolation for customer data. Azure Government is a US government community cloud, physically separated from Azure, available only in the US to US-based registered entities, with contractual commitments limiting access to screened US persons. Azure is available to NERC entities in both the US and Canada. Both are suitable for registered entities deploying certain NERC CIP-compliant workloads.

**NERC CIP Data Categorization:** CIP standards apply to the Bulk Electric System (BES) (generally 100 kV and above; 20MVA+ generating units; 75MVA+ generating plants; Control Centers), not to distribution (with exceptions like UFLS, UVLS, Blackstart Resources). Key definitions include Cyber Asset, BES Cyber Asset (BCA), BES Cyber System (BCS), Electronic Security Perimeter (ESP), Protected Cyber Asset (PCA), Electronic Access Point (EAP), Electronic Access Control or Monitoring Systems (EACMS), and Control Center. Current NERC CIP definitions emphasize physical assets ("in those devices") and lack provisions for cloud concepts like virtualization and multi-tenancy. Workloads not subject to the 15-minute rule include transmission planning, SCADA historical data, AI/analytics, IoT monitoring, and NERC CIP audit evidence. BES Cyber System Information (BCSI) can be deployed in cloud if proper security controls are in place.

**Compliance Audits:** Azure and Azure Government maintain three relevant independent third-party audits: CSA STAR Certification and Attestation, AICPA SOC 2 Type 2 Attestation, and FedRAMP High P-ATOs (issued by the JAB) plus over 250 Moderate and High ATOs. NERC reviewed Azure controls and FedRAMP evidence for CIP-004-6 and CIP-011-2 (applicable to BCSI), concluding no extra guidance is needed for cloud BCSI deployment.

Microsoft engineers have no default access to customer data. Azure Government requires US persons verification for operations personnel.

**Additional Considerations:** Nuclear electric utilities may face DoE 10 CFR Part 810 export control requirements. Registered entities are ultimately responsible for NERC CIP compliance. Microsoft offers a "Cloud implementation guide for NERC audits" (downloadable under NDA from the Service Trust Portal) with pre-filled Reliability Standard Audit Worksheets (RSAWs) narratives and control mappings between NERC CIP standards and FedRAMP Moderate baseline.

--- SOURCE 1: Breach Notification - Microsoft GDPR | Microsoft Learn ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/compliance/regulatory/gdpr-breach-notification

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Microsoft Learn documentation page on GDPR Breach Notification. It outlines Microsoft's approach to complying with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) regarding personal data breach notifications for organizations offering goods/services to EU residents or collecting/analyzing EU resident data.

**Key definitions**: A personal data breach is "a breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to, personal data transmitted, stored, or otherwise processed." Personal data refers to any information that can identify an individual directly or indirectly.

**Microsoft's breach notification obligations**: As a data processor, Microsoft ensures service customers can meet GDPR breach notification requirements as data controllers. Microsoft notifies customers of any personal data breach, except where personal data is confirmed unintelligible (e.g., encrypted data with confirmed key integrity). Initial notifications include a description of the breach's nature, approximate user impact, and mitigation steps. Data controllers are responsible for assessing privacy risks and determining whether a breach requires notification of their DPA.

**Product-specific breach notification details**:
1. **Office 365**: Microsoft invests in systems, processes, and personnel to reduce breach likelihood and mitigate consequences. Customers can contact Microsoft Support to report suspected breaches.
2. **Azure and Dynamics 365**: Microsoft operates a global 24x7 incident response service. Azure employs a shared responsibility model — Microsoft doesn't monitor security incidents within the customer's realm of responsibility. Microsoft determines breach priority/severity by investigating functional impact, recoverability, and information impact, working with global legal advisors. Customer notifications are delivered within 72 hours of breach declaration, except when notification would increase risk to other customers or when the 72-hour timeline limits available incident details.
3. **Microsoft Support and Professional Services**: Some data protection incidents may fall within the customer's realm of responsibility; Microsoft follows a documented industry-standard response plan.
4. **Windows**: The Windows diagnostic data processor configuration uses cloud infrastructure and built-in security features, backed by Microsoft's 24x7 global incident response service.

**Admin tools**: Tenant Administrators can set their organization's privacy contact via the Microsoft Entra admin center. The page also links to the Microsoft Trust Center for more GDPR information. Page last updated 2026-05-05.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Microsoft Support and Professional Services and Breach Notification Under the GDPR - Microsoft GDPR | Microsoft Learn ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/regulatory/gdpr-breach-microsoft-support-professional-services

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Microsoft Learn documentation page titled "Microsoft Support and Professional Services and Breach Notification Under the GDPR." It describes how Microsoft Professional Services (a team of over 21,000 consultants, Digital Advisors, engineers, and sales professionals across 191 countries and regions, supporting 46 languages) handles data protection incidents and GDPR breach notification requirements.

Key points covered:

- **Data protection incident definition**: A breach of security leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to Personal Data or Professional Services Data while processed by Microsoft.
- **Scope and limits**: Microsoft only responds to incidents within its realm of responsibility. Customer-driven incidents (e.g., customers inadvertently sending passwords, fraud against customers) are classified as "events" rather than Microsoft data protection incidents, though Microsoft will inform and assist customers.
- **Incident types**: The response team has identified various scenarios, from misdirected emails (requiring little investigation) to malicious personnel activity (requiring full forensic investigation).
- **Incident response process**: A triage process involving assessing the event, determining scope, assessing maliciousness, preliminary investigation with severity assignment, and stakeholder coordination. Detection methods include automated alerts, customer reports, external reports, anomaly observation, and malicious activity indicators.
- **Training and drills**: Annual data protection incident response drills are conducted with security, legal, and communications teams. All personnel must complete mandatory training on privacy fundamentals and GDPR regulations.
- **Notification requirements**: Microsoft targets notification to customers within 72 hours of declaring a data protection incident. Initial notifications may not include complete details, and some details may be withheld if disclosure would increase risk to others or interfere with law enforcement. Microsoft recognizes that customers, as data processors, are responsible for notifying Data Protection Authorities and their own data subjects.
- **Notification contents**: Nature of the breach, mitigation measures, product/service involved, exposure duration, volume of affected records, and sub-processor/supplier details (if known and applicable).
- **Post-mortems**: Internal post-mortems are conducted for higher-severity incidents, are highly confidential, and are reviewed by external auditors. Commercial customers with Unified Support or ISD should refer to the Microsoft Products and Services Data Protection Addendum (DPA).

The page notes that access requires authorization and was last updated on 2026-05-05. Additional resources link to Microsoft Professional Services trust information at https://aka.ms/pstrust.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Microsoft Learn documentation page explains Office 365's breach notification obligations and practices under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). As a data processor, Microsoft commits to: (1) allowing customers to designate a dedicated privacy contact via the Privacy reader role in Message Center; (2) notifying customers of personal data breaches within 72 hours of a breach being declared, published to Message Center and accessible through the Microsoft 365 admin center; and (3) including in the initial notification the nature of the breach, an approximation of user impact, and applicable mitigation steps. Microsoft notifies customers of any personal data breach except those where personal data is confirmed to be unintelligible (e.g., encrypted data with verified key integrity).

The page details Office 365's investments in data security, including: access control systems with a "zero-standing access" policy and least-privilege principles; real-time security monitoring systems with automatic threat resolution and red-team penetration testing exercises; and personnel/processes including a detailed privacy breach Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) shared across teams, plus regular training on data classification and personal data handling.

In the event of a breach, customers can expect a consistent incident response lifecycle, consistent notification criteria (focusing on confidentiality, integrity, and availability of customer data), and consistent notification details (timing of breach and awareness, approximate number of users impacted, type of user data breached, and mitigation actions needed). Office 365, as a data processor, does not determine breach risk — data controllers must assess breach severity, decide whether users need notification, whether regulators (DPAs) need notification, and what mitigation steps the controller should take. Customers wishing to notify Microsoft should contact Microsoft Support, which interfaces with engineering teams. Microsoft recommends customers designate Message Center Privacy readers through the Microsoft 365 admin center to receive breach notifications. The page was last updated on May 5, 2026.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: Azure, Dynamics 365, and Power Platform breach ... ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/regulatory/gdpr-breach-azure-dynamics

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Microsoft Learn documentation page describes how Microsoft Azure, Dynamics 365, and Power Platform handle data breach notification under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). 

**Key Topics:**

**Security Approach:** Microsoft uses a "assume breach" security strategy built on defense-in-depth, incorporating privacy-by-design and privacy-by-default via the Security Development Lifecycle. Microsoft has a dedicated global, 24/7 incident response service, with data center protections including video monitoring, smart cards, and biometric controls.

**Shared Responsibility Model:** Microsoft doesn't monitor or respond to security incidents within the customer's realm of responsibility. A customer-only security compromise isn't a Microsoft security incident. Customers can use services like Microsoft Defender for Cloud for their own incident response.

**Five-Stage Incident Response Process:**
1. **Detect** - First indication of a potential incident
2. **Assess** - Incident response team member evaluates impact and severity
3. **Diagnose** - Technical/forensic investigation; if customer data may be exposed, Customer Incident Notification begins in parallel
4. **Stabilize and Recover** - Recovery plan created; crisis containment (e.g., quarantining systems) may happen immediately
5. **Close and Post-mortem** - Post-mortem created to revise policies and prevent recurrence

**Detection Triggers:** Automated system alerts, first-party reports, MSRC vulnerability reports, customer reports via support portals, Red Team/Blue Team security activity, and escalations by Microsoft service operators.

**Incident Classifications:** False positive, Security event, Security Incident/Customer Reportable Security/Privacy Incident (CRSPI), Privacy Event, and Privacy Incident/CRSPI. A CRSPI is declared when unauthorized access to customer data happened or likely happened, or when legal/contractual commitments require notification.

**Customer Notification:** Microsoft notifies impacted customers and regulatory authorities without undue delay, and in no more than 72 hours from declaring a breach, except in limited circumstances (e.g., notification might increase risk to other customers, or details are not yet available). Notifications are delivered via the Azure service health notifications blade (as Security Advisory), and/or email to Azure Subscription Administrators/Owners, Microsoft Entra Global Tenant Administrators, and Microsoft Entra tenant Technical Contacts. For Dynamics 365 and Power Platform, notifications go through the Microsoft 365 admin center Message Center with a Data Privacy tag.

**Dynamics 365/Power Platform:** These services follow the same technical and organizational measures as Azure for breach security, with built-in features covering secure identity, data protection, role-based security, and threat management.

**Important recommendation:** Microsoft recommends using roles with the fewest permissions, and minimizing the number of users with Global Administrator role to improve security.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Microsoft delivers customer notices without undue delay, and in any event in no more than 72 hours from the time it declared a breach except in some limited circumstances."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 11: Azure AI Foundry: Modified Abuse Monitoring, EU data residency, retention, and least-privilege RBAC for runtime agent - Microsoft Q&A ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/5966351/azure-ai-foundry-modified-abuse-monitoring-eu-data

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Microsoft Q&A forum post from a nonprofit organization (using an Azure Nonprofit Sponsorship subscription) asking for guidance on configuring Azure AI Foundry / Azure OpenAI with Microsoft Entra ID authentication and RBAC (no API keys) for a runtime-only agent identity. The question covers four areas, and a detailed moderator answer (by Manish Deshpande, Microsoft External Staff) addresses each:

**1. European Data Zone Processing (answered first as it changes priorities):** The Global Standard deployment is the issue. Data residency documentation states that global deployment types may process data in any Azure region, while Data Zone types (EU, US, APAC) process only within the specified zone, and Standard single-region types process in the deployment region. The EU Data Zone follows the Azure EU Data Boundary, which can include EFTA countries like Switzerland. However, an EU Data Zone deployment does not keep processing in Switzerland specifically — if Swiss residency is required, a single-region Standard in Switzerland North would be needed (with narrower model availability). A documented caveat notes that Global deployments may process prompts/completions outside the EU even for EU-based resources. Recommended action: apply Azure Policy to disable global deployments, verify the deployment SKU reads DataZoneStandard, and confirm the parent Foundry resource is in an EU region.

**2. Data Retention, Storage, and Human Review:** Data storage applies only to the abuse-monitoring path; automated path prompts/completions are not stored or used for training. The abuse-monitoring store is logically separated per customer and located in the Azure geography of the Foundry resource. Human review occurs only when automated review fails confidence thresholds or is unavailable, accessed via Secure Access Workstations (SAWs) with Just-In-Time (JIT) approval. For models sold by Azure in the EEA, authorized reviewers are located in the EEA. The moderator explicitly refused to give a default retention number, noting that while a "30 days" figure circulates in forums, it is absent from the current authoritative documentation and should not be used in compliance files without a written contractual answer under the Microsoft Products and Services Data Protection Addendum. After Modified Abuse Monitoring approval: "the data storage and human review process described above is not performed. However, automated review may still be conducted."

**3. Modified Abuse Monitoring:** Being a nonprofit does not itself qualify — eligibility is limited to customers managed by a Microsoft account team or under an eligible program. However, non-managed customers are invited to apply anyway via the same forms. Review time is 5-10 business days. The form is linked from the Abuse monitoring and Limited access pages. Caveats: approval is per model class (not blanket), and disabling human review may make abuse detection less accurate. Verification after approval: check the Foundry resource JSON view or run `az cognitiveservices account show` and look for `{"name":"ContentLogging","value":"false"}` in Capabilities — absence of the property means storage is still on.

**4. Least-Privilege RBAC:** The moderator explicitly says NOT to use Cognitive Services OpenAI User or Azure AI Developer roles for Foundry scenarios (these are for direct AI Services resource access). The recommended role is **Foundry Agent Consumer** — the least-privilege role for principals that only interact with agents, with exactly one of eight capabilities (interact with agent endpoints). GUIDs should be used instead of display names due to recent role renames. Scope should be narrowed to a single agent. However, Foundry Agent Consumer doesn't grant access to Agent Applications — Foundry User or a custom role would be needed if the agent is published as an Agent Application. Notably, Owner and Contributor roles cannot interact with agent endpoints at all (ARM control-plane only). The moderator also emphasized that role-based enforcement only works if key-based authentication is disabled (set disableLocalAuth on the Foundry account), since API keys bypass role assignments entirely.

A second, shorter answer by user "Nithin" suggests somewhat different guidance: using Modified Abuse Monitoring to disable "30-day human review data retention," provisioning resources in EU regions (Sweden Central or France Central), and assigning the Cognitive Services OpenAI User role at resource group level — though this conflicts with the moderator's explicit guidance against that role for Foundry scenarios.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Data residency for all deployment types: Data stored at rest remains in the designated Azure geography. However, inferencing data is processed as follows: Global types: May be processed in any Azure region. Data Zone types: The service processes data only within the Microsoft-specified data zone (US, EU, or Asia Pacific (APAC)). Standard (single region) types: The service processes data in the deployment region."

--- SOURCE 13: What is the EU Data Boundary? - Microsoft Privacy | Microsoft Learn ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/privacy/eudb/eu-data-boundary-learn

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Microsoft Learn documentation defines the **EU Data Boundary** — a geographically defined boundary within which Microsoft commits to store and process Customer Data and personal data for its enterprise online services, including Azure, Dynamics 365, Power Platform, and Microsoft 365. Professional Services Data will be stored at rest for these services. These commitments are subject to limited circumstances where data continues to be transferred outside the EU Data Boundary.

**Key definitions:**
- **Customer Data**: All data (including text, sound, video, image files, and software) provided to Microsoft by or on behalf of a Customer through use of the Online Service. It excludes Professional Services Data and configuration information (technical settings, resource names).
- **Personal data in system-generated logs**: Microsoft online services create system-generated logs as part of regular operation. Some logs contain fields that identify or can identify specific persons (e.g., product and service usage data, user activity logs).
- **Pseudonymization**: Per GDPR Article 4(5), pseudonymization replaces personally identifiable information with artificial identifiers/pseudonyms. Microsoft requires all personal data in system-generated logs to be pseudonymized using techniques including encryption, masking, tokenization, and data blurring. This enables authorized Microsoft personnel to work (e.g., DevOps identifying service issues across regions) without identifying or reidentifying users. Anonymization is not used because it would permanently alter data and compromise Microsoft's ability to ensure quality, reliability, and security of services.
- **Security controls for system-generated logs** include: data minimization via minimum retention policies, regular checks and scrubbing, limited usage solely for service operations, and access controls limiting rehydration/reidentification of personal data.
- **Professional Services Data**: All data provided to Microsoft through an engagement to obtain Professional Services (consulting services and technical support services).

**EU Data Boundary countries and datacenter locations:**
- Consists of EU countries (Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden) and EFTA countries (Liechtenstein, Iceland, Norway, Switzerland).
- Uses Microsoft datacenters announced/operating in Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland. Additional datacenters may be established in the future.

**How to configure services:**
- **Azure**: Regional services deployed in an EU Data Boundary region are in-scope. Non-regional services require configuration via Azure Resource Manager.
- **Dynamics 365 and Power Platform**: Requires BOTH (1) provisioning the tenant and all environments in the "European Union (EU) and European Free Trade Association (EFTA)" Macro Region Geography, AND (2) maintaining a billing address in an EU Data Boundary country. Meeting only one requirement doesn't place environments within the boundary.
- **Microsoft 365**: Customers with a sign-up location in an EU or EFTA country are in-scope; however, customers with Multi-Geo Capabilities are not in-scope even if their tenant is in an EU/EFTA country.

The documentation was last updated February 26, 2025, and reflects the current state of the EU Data Boundary as of the publication date.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The EU Data Boundary is a geographically defined boundary within which Microsoft has committed to store and process Customer Data and personal data for our Microsoft enterprise online services, including Azure, Dynamics 365, Power Platform, and Microsoft 365.
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Microsoft Q&A forum thread titled "Inquiry on Data Residency, Compliance, and Security for Microsoft Azure OpenAI Subscription." The original poster, Nikhil Bhatia, asked four questions about: (1) whether data/prompts submitted to Azure OpenAI via API remain in Switzerland, (2) how Microsoft handles data requests from US or foreign authorities, (3) what AI subscriptions are commonly used by law firms and how data is secured against training usage, and (4) Microsoft's GDPR/FDAP compliance framework and list of sub-processors.

Key answers provided across the thread:

**Data Residency in Switzerland:** Azure OpenAI Service is available in the Switzerland North region, allowing data residency within Switzerland when configured with regional deployment. However, for 'Global' deployment types, prompts and responses may be processed in any geography where the relevant model is deployed. For 'DataZone' deployments, data may be processed within the specified data zone. A Microsoft moderator (Manas R Mohanty) clarified that with Global Standard deployments, data at rest remains in the designated geography (e.g., Europe) but inference calls may route to any global location. DataZone deployments keep data at rest in the designated geography (e.g., Switzerland North) while inference may occur anywhere within that data zone.

**Government Data Requests:** Microsoft only responds to government or foreign authority data requests under applicable laws, following a rigorous legal review. Microsoft does not provide governments direct access to customer data, attempts to redirect requests to customers where legally possible, and notifies customers unless prohibited. Microsoft's process includes legal review, customer notification, challenging unlawful requests, transparency reports, escalation to legal/compliance teams, and documentation in the Data Protection Addendum (DPA).

**Service Provider Entity:** For EU customers, including Ireland, the service provider is Microsoft Ireland Operations Limited (MIOL), operating under Irish law. However, Microsoft remains a US-headquartered company subject to US legal obligations such as the CLOUD Act. US authorities can issue data requests, but Microsoft will challenge non-EU government requests and only comply if legally required under EU law, notifying customers where permissible. The DPA includes clauses on Data Transfers referencing the 2021 Standard Contractual Clauses, GDPR Article 46 safeguards, and Article 30(2) documentation.

**Law Firm Subscriptions:** Law firms typically use Standard, PTU (Provisioned Throughput Unit), or Batch API subscriptions for legal drafting, contract analysis, and e-discovery. EA (Enterprise Agreement) subscriptions offer higher quota and support. Azure OpenAI models are stateless—no prompts or completions are stored in the model, and they are not used to train, retrain, or improve base models by default. Data is encrypted at rest by default.

**Compliance:** Azure OpenAI is GDPR- and FDAP-compliant, offering encryption in transit and at rest, Customer-Managed Keys, and pseudonymization. Microsoft publishes a list of sub-processors through the Microsoft Trust Center. Compliance offerings for EMEA include EU Cloud CoC, EU GDPR, EU Model Clauses, Germany C5, and others. Microsoft offers Sovereign Cloud options and features like Data Guardian (Europe-based access approval) and External Key Management for maximum sovereignty.
</summary>

"Microsoft Azure OpenAI provides robust support for data residency, including the option to host and process data entirely within Switzerland. The Azure OpenAI Service is available in the Switzerland North region, allowing organizations to ensure that all data—including prompts, completions, and embeddings remain within Swiss borders when configured appropriately."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/regulatory/gdpr-breach-office365

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Microsoft Learn documentation page explains Office 365's breach notification obligations and practices under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). As a data processor, Microsoft commits to: (1) allowing customers to designate a dedicated privacy contact via the Privacy reader role in Message Center; (2) notifying customers of personal data breaches within 72 hours of a breach being declared, published to Message Center and accessible through the Microsoft 365 admin center; and (3) including in the initial notification the nature of the breach, an approximation of user impact, and applicable mitigation steps. Microsoft notifies customers of any personal data breach except those where personal data is confirmed to be unintelligible (e.g., encrypted data with verified key integrity).

The page details Office 365's investments in data security, including: access control systems with a "zero-standing access" policy and least-privilege principles; real-time security monitoring systems with automatic threat resolution and red-team penetration testing exercises; and personnel/processes including a detailed privacy breach Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) shared across teams, plus regular training on data classification and personal data handling.

In the event of a breach, customers can expect a consistent incident response lifecycle, consistent notification criteria (focusing on confidentiality, integrity, and availability of customer data), and consistent notification details (timing of breach and awareness, approximate number of users impacted, type of user data breached, and mitigation actions needed). Office 365, as a data processor, does not determine breach risk — data controllers must assess breach severity, decide whether users need notification, whether regulators (DPAs) need notification, and what mitigation steps the controller should take. Customers wishing to notify Microsoft should contact Microsoft Support, which interfaces with engineering teams. Microsoft recommends customers designate Message Center Privacy readers through the Microsoft 365 admin center to receive breach notifications. The page was last updated on May 5, 2026.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 11: Microsoft completes landmark EU Data Boundary, offering enhanced data residency and transparency - Microsoft On the Issues ---
URL: https://blogs.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2025/02/26/microsoft-completes-landmark-eu-data-boundary-offering-enhanced-data-residency-and-transparency

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Microsoft announced the completion of the EU Data Boundary for the Microsoft Cloud in February 2025, an industry-leading solution that stores and processes public sector and commercial customer data within the EU and European Free Trade Association (EFTA) regions. This milestone, announced by Julie Brill (Corporate Vice President and Chief Privacy Officer) and Paul Lorimer (Corporate Vice President, Microsoft 365), enables European commercial and public sector customers to store and process customer data and pseudonymized personal data for Microsoft core cloud services—including Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, Power Platform, and most Azure services—within the EU and EFTA regions. Additionally, professional services data from technical support interactions for core cloud services is now stored within these regions.

The EU Data Boundary was delivered in three phases:
- Phase 1 (January 2023): Enabled storage and processing of customer data for core services including Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, Power Platform, and Azure.
- Phase 2 (January 2024): Expanded scope to include pseudonymized personal data.
- Phase 3 (February 2025): Ensured professional services data (customer logs and Microsoft-generated support case notes) for Microsoft 365, Power Platform, and Dynamics 365 support interactions are stored within EU/EFTA regions. Certain Azure services may require additional customer action for this commitment.

Microsoft's commitment to Europe spans more than 40 years, with over $20 billion invested in AI and cloud infrastructure across the continent over the past 16 months. Additional offerings include Microsoft 365 Advanced Data Residency for granular data location controls, Microsoft Cloud for Sovereignty for public sector customers, and the European Cloud Principles for transparency and accountability. Microsoft also highlighted its Secure Future Initiative (SFI) for cybersecurity, noting that in limited security instances requiring coordinated global response, essential data may be transferred with robust protections including encryption, strict access controls, and other security measures, with transparent information provided to customers.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Microsoft Q&A forum thread titled "Request for Clarification on Azure OpenAI Global Standard Deployment – Data Residency & Processing." The original poster, Zoey Azimi (from a Germany-based company), asks about data residency and processing for Azure OpenAI Service's Global Standard deployment mode, given strict GDPR and EU AI Act compliance requirements.

Key questions raised by the poster:
1. Which countries/data centers may process data (prompts, completions, telemetry, logs) in Global Standard mode for core model inference, abuse detection, and telemetry/moderation.
2. Whether any Microsoft or third-party services outside the EU/US (e.g., Asia, Latin America, Africa) are involved in data routing, logging, abuse monitoring, health monitoring, or diagnostics.
3. Whether Microsoft provides a detailed Data Flow Diagram or Architecture Document.
4. What contractual safeguards (SCCs, DPA, BAA) apply for GDPR compliance.
5. Whether logging/abuse monitoring can be opted out of, or additional protections like Azure Private Link or customer-managed keys can be used.

Community responses provided the following clarifications:
- In Global Standard mode, core model inference occurs in the selected Azure region (e.g., EU or US), but prompts and completions may be processed in any geography where the relevant Azure OpenAI model is deployed.
- Abuse detection samples are stored in the Azure geography where the customer's resource is deployed.
- Azure OpenAI models are deployed across various global regions including Australia East, Japan East, South India, and Sweden Central, among others.
- Microsoft relies on Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) and the Data Protection Addendum (DPA) for GDPR compliance and data transfers outside the EU/US.
- Abuse monitoring can be turned off upon approval, verifiable via the ContentLogging flag.
- Data is not shared with OpenAI or used for model training, which is important for GDPR alignment.
- Specific documentation on data flow diagrams, third-party vendor involvement in non-EU/US locations, and specific regional processing lists were not fully detailed; the responder suggested contacting Microsoft directly for precise details.
- A reference link to Microsoft's data privacy documentation was provided: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/legal/cognitive-services/openai/data-privacy?tabs=azure-portal

The thread contains follow-up exchanges (March 25 – April 7, 2025) where the poster acknowledged some clarity was achieved and raised final remaining questions about specific non-EU/US regions, third-party vendor involvement, and explicit legal bases for data transfers. The thread includes unanswered follow-up requests from the responder asking whether a resolution was reached.

--- SOURCE 13: What are Azure Availability Zones? ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/reliability/availability-zones-overview

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an official Microsoft Learn documentation page explaining Azure availability zones. Availability zones are separated groups of datacenters within an Azure region, each with independent power, cooling, and networking infrastructure, so that if one zone experiences an outage, regional services and high availability are supported by remaining zones. An availability zone is a logical grouping of one or more physically separate datacenters, typically separated by several kilometers but within about 100 kilometers of each other, providing low-latency connectivity while reducing the impact of local outages or weather events.

The page describes three types of availability zone support for Azure services: (1) Zone-redundant resources, which are replicated or distributed across multiple zones by the service (with Microsoft managing spreading requests and data replication, and automatic failover in the event of an outage); (2) Zonal resources, which are deployed to a single zone selected by the user and do not automatically provide resiliency (users must design multi-zone architectures themselves and are responsible for failover); and (3) Nonzonal/regional deployments, where resources are not configured to use zones and Azure may place them across any zones, potentially causing downtime if an affected zone experiences an outage. A resource is considered "zone-resilient" if it uses two or more zones.

Key technical details include: physical zones are mapped to logical zones per-subscription with potentially different mapping orders (determinable via Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, or Azure Resource Manager APIs such as List Locations and Check Zone Peers); Microsoft aims to deploy updates to a single zone at a time to reduce workload impact; inter-zone networking within a region targets round-trip latency of less than approximately 2 milliseconds; and Azure does not charge for data transfer between availability zones in the same region.

Architectural guidance recommends that production workloads use multiple availability zones if supported by the region, and that mission-critical workloads consider both multiregion and multi-zone solutions. For single-region workloads constrained by data residency, multi-zone deployment is the primary recommended way to maximize availability. Availability zones do not protect against full-region outages.

The page includes a table listing regions supporting availability zones across the Americas (e.g., Brazil South, Canada Central, Central US, East US, East US 2, Mexico Central, South Central US, West US 2, West US 3), Europe (e.g., Austria East, Belgium Central, Denmark East, France Central, Germany West Central, Italy North, North Europe, Norway East, Poland Central, Spain Central, Sweden Central, Switzerland North, UK South, West Europe), Middle East (Israel Central, Qatar Central, UAE North), Africa (South Africa North), and Asia Pacific (Australia East, Central India, East Asia, India South Central, Indonesia Central, Japan East, Japan West, Korea Central, Malaysia West, New Zealand North, Southeast Asia). The page was last updated on 2026-06-26.
</summary>

"Many Azure regions provide availability zones, which are separated groups of datacenters within a region. Each availability zone has independent power, cooling, and networking infrastructure, so that if one zone experiences an outage, then regional services, capacity, and high availability are supported by the remaining zones."
