--- SOURCE 2: AWS Security Incident Response: The customer’s journey to accelerating the incident response lifecycle | AWS Security Blog ---
URL: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/aws-security-incident-response-the-customers-journey-to-accelerating-the-incident-response-lifecycle

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This AWS Security Blog post (republished August 1, 2024, to remove incorrect references to AWS WAF and Shield) describes how AWS Security Incident Response—a Tier 1 AWS-native service launched in December 2024—accelerates the incident response lifecycle. The post walks through a real-world scenario to demonstrate the service's capabilities.

KEY STATISTICS AND CONTEXT:
- Over 50% of security alerts go unaddressed due to resource constraints and alert fatigue; false positives consume 30% of investigation time.
- Organizations take an average of 258 days to identify and contain security events (2024 IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report).
- Nearly half of SOC teams report increased detection/response times over the past two years; 80% say manual threat investigation significantly impacts response times.
- Organizations with mature incident response capabilities achieve 50% reduction in mean time to resolution (MTTR) and cost savings of up to 58% per incident.

SERVICE CAPABILITIES:
- Addresses three challenges: alert fatigue (via automated monitoring and intelligent triage), fragmented access/communications, and security skills gaps (via 24/7 access to AWS CIRT experts).
- Integrates with GuardDuty and Security Hub (detection), Systems Manager (management/governance), and third-party solutions through Security Hub integrations and the AWS Security Incident Response Partner Specialization program.
- Provides expert knowledge from AWS Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT), tools via APIs and console, and streamlined processes.

SETUP REQUIREMENTS:
- Configure IAM permissions (AWSSecurityIncidentResponseFullAccess for admins; AWSSecurityIncidentResponseCaseFullAccess and AWSSecurityIncidentResponseReadOnlyAccess for role-based access in dev/test environments).
- Establish incident response team contacts and notification channels.
- Optionally enable GuardDuty and Security Hub, and deploy CloudFormation StackSets for automated containment actions.

WALKTHROUGH SCENARIO (incident at 2:00 AM):
1. DETECTION: GuardDuty detects anomalous IAM behavior, unusual API calls from unknown IPs, and a surge of EC2 instance creations with SSH keys and internet-accessible security groups—matching known threat behaviors via GuardDuty Extended Threat Detection.
2. TRIAGE: The service automatically analyzes GuardDuty findings (including historical baseline, finding types, correlation patterns) and opens an AWS Security Incident Response case when a true positive is identified, notifying the configured team. It correlates disparate events (e.g., CloudTrail log deletion, unauthorized access key creation, suspicious S3 object access) and maps signals to MITRE ATT&CK tactics/techniques/procedures, revealing a potential ransomware threat.
3. AWS CIRT ENGAGEMENT: The team opens a one-click escalation to AWS CIRT through the incident case, with a 15-minute acknowledgement timeframe. AWS CIRT provides conference bridge calls, advanced artifact analysis, technical guidance, and recommendations—even in environments with limited logging.
4. RESOURCE TAGGING: The team tags affected resources using the incident case ID as the primary tag key, enabling targeted access controls, containment measures, cost tracking, and post-incident analysis.
5. CONTAINMENT (via Systems Manager): Using pre-deployed CloudFormation StackSets, the service performs three-step containment: Isolate (remove instances from security groups), Preserve (create snapshots), and Investigate (collect system info via Systems Manager). Actions are reversible.
6. RESOLUTION: Verification of containment, threat alleviation, service restoration, and access control normalization. The service compiles a comprehensive incident timeline for reporting to executives, regulators, and cyber insurance providers.

LESSONS LEARNED AND LONG-TERM IMPROVEMENTS: Enhanced logging based on AWS CIRT recommendations, updated security controls, and improved incident response processes.

ADDITIONAL RESOURCES: AWS Customer Playbook Framework, Assisted Log Enabler, Athena Security Analytics Bootstrap, and five publicly available AWS CIRT workshops.

The post concludes that AWS Security Incident Response delivers measurable benefits through continuous threat monitoring, reduced response times, enhanced investigation via AWS CIRT collaboration, streamlined containment, and comprehensive documentation—with cost savings up to 58% per incident.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Organizations with mature incident response capabilities demonstrate a 50 percent reduction in mean time to resolution (MTTR) and achieve cost savings of up to 58 percent per incident."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: DPA - AWS Data Processing Addendum - awsstatic.com ---
URL: https://d1.awsstatic.com/legal/aws-gdpr/aws-gdpr-dpa-online.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the AWS Data Processing Addendum (DPA), a legal document that supplements the AWS Customer Agreement and governs how AWS processes Customer Data on behalf of its customers. The DPA establishes AWS as a data processor and the Customer as either a controller or processor of Customer Data.

Key provisions include:
- **Data Processing Roles**: AWS acts as processor; Customer acts as controller or processor. The subject matter is Customer Data, with duration determined by the Customer.
- **Customer Instructions**: The DPA and Agreement constitute documented instructions for AWS's processing. Additional instructions require prior written agreement.
- **Confidentiality**: AWS will not access, use, or disclose Customer Data except as necessary to provide Services or comply with law/governmental orders. AWS will redirect governmental demands to Customer where possible.
- **Security Measures**: AWS maintains technical and organizational measures including network security, physical security of facilities, access controls for personnel, and regular testing/evaluation per the AWS Security Standards (Annex 1).
- **Sub-processors**: AWS has general authorization to use sub-processors, which are listed at https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/sub-processors/. AWS must notify Customers at least 30 days before engaging a new sub-processor and remains responsible for sub-processor compliance.
- **Data Subject Requests**: AWS assists via Service Controls and forwards data subject requests to Customer promptly.
- **Security Incidents**: AWS must notify Customer without undue delay after becoming aware of a Security Incident. Unsuccessful incidents (e.g., port scans, failed logins, denial of service attacks) are excluded.
- **Certifications and Audits**: AWS holds ISO 27001, 27017, 27018, and 27701 certifications and SOC 1, 2, and 3 reports. External audits are performed at least annually per ISO 27001 standards.
- **Data Transfers**: Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) apply to GDPR-protected data transferred to Third Countries. Controller-to-Processor Clauses apply when Customer is a controller; Processor-to-Processor Clauses apply when Customer is a processor. SCCs do not apply if AWS has adopted Binding Corporate Rules or alternative compliance standards.
- **Return/Deletion**: AWS returns or deletes Customer Data upon request up to 90 days post-termination, after which Customer must close all AWS accounts.
- **Termination**: The DPA remains in force until the Agreement terminates. In case of conflict, the DPA controls over the Agreement, except Service Terms control over the DPA.

The document also includes Annex 1 (AWS Security Standards) detailing the information security program, network security controls (firewalls, authentication), physical security measures (nondescript facilities, photo-ID badges, video surveillance, intrusion detection), limited employee/contractor access, and continued security evaluation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This DPA applies when Customer Data is processed by AWS. In this context, AWS will act as processor to Customer, who can act either as controller or processor of Customer Data.", "At least 30 days before AWS engages a Sub-processor, AWS will update the applicable website and provide Customer with a mechanism to obtain notice of that update.", "AWS will (a) notify Customer of a Security Incident without undue delay after becoming aware of the Security Incident, and (b) take appropriate measures to address the Security Incident, including measures to mitigate any adverse effects resulting from the Security Incident.", "The Standard Contractual Clauses will only apply to Customer Data subject to the GDPR that is transferred, either directly or via onward transfer, to any Third Country.", "At any time up to the Termination Date, and for 90 days following the Termination Date, subject to the terms and conditions of the Agreement, AWS will return or delete Customer Data when Customer uses the Service Controls to request such return or deletion."

URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/navigating-gdpr-compliance/aws-data-processing-addendum-dpa.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage describes AWS's Data Processing Addendum (DPA), which is designed to help AWS customers comply with GDPR contractual obligations. Key points include:

- The AWS DPA is incorporated into the AWS Service Terms and applies automatically to all customers globally whenever they use AWS services to process customer data, regardless of applicable data protection laws.
- AWS uses Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) as a data transfer tool for transfers of customer data outside the EU to countries not recognized by the European Commission as providing adequate protection. The SCCs are part of AWS Service Terms, incorporated by reference into the AWS DPA, and apply automatically.
- In February 2021, AWS adopted strengthened contractual commitments for protecting customer data through a Supplementary Addendum to the AWS DPA, which applies to all customer data processed by AWS, regardless of whether it is transferred outside the EEA. No additional customer action is required.
- Key commitments in the Supplementary Addendum include: redirecting governmental requests for customer data directly to customers whenever possible; promptly notifying customers if AWS is compelled to disclose customer data (unless prohibited by law); actively challenging overly broad or inappropriate governmental requests that conflict with EU laws; and disclosing only minimal necessary customer data when legally compelled.
- AWS outlines a structured framework clarifying division of responsibilities under a shared responsibility model: customers assess and implement technical/organizational measures to secure data transfers, while AWS maintains contractual and infrastructure-level safeguards.
- A practical six-step process based on European Data Protection Board (EDPB) guidance helps customers: (1) map data transfers; (2) identify the legal transfer mechanism (such as SCCs); (3) assess destination country laws and practices; (4) implement supplementary safeguards where necessary; (5) document procedural steps; and (6) reassess risk periodically.
- AWS offers safeguards including encryption, data residency controls, and legal commitments to resist overreaching governmental requests.
</summary>

The Global AWS DPA is designed to help customers satisfy requirements under data protection laws worldwide without creating separate country-specific data processing agreements, simplifying contracting procedures and reducing time spent assessing data privacy requirements on a country-by-country basis. Customers who have already signed the previous AWS GDPR DPA do not need to take any action and can continue relying on that addendum. The announcement was authored by Chad Woolf, who joined Amazon in 2010 and built the AWS compliance functions from the ground up, including audit and certifications, privacy, contract compliance, control automation engineering, and security process monitoring. The post directs readers to AWS's Data Protection & Privacy and GDPR Center resources for more information.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage describes AWS's Data Processing Addendum (DPA), which is designed to help AWS customers comply with GDPR contractual obligations. Key points include:

- The AWS DPA is incorporated into the AWS Service Terms and applies automatically to all customers globally whenever they use AWS services to process customer data, regardless of applicable data protection laws.
- AWS uses Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) as a data transfer tool for transfers of customer data outside the EU to countries not recognized by the European Commission as providing adequate protection. The SCCs are part of AWS Service Terms, incorporated by reference into the AWS DPA, and apply automatically.

- AWS offers safeguards including encryption, data residency controls, and legal commitments to resist overreaching governmental requests.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: In detail - Navigating GDPR Compliance on AWS ---
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/navigating-gdpr-compliance/in-detail.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This AWS whitepaper provides a detailed guide for AWS customers on how to conduct a Data Transfer Assessment (DTA) as part of their GDPR compliance obligations when using AWS services. The document outlines a six-step framework recommended by the EDPB for assessing and managing international data transfers.

**Step 1: Know Your Transfers** - Customers must identify which data transfers occur through their use of AWS services. Since AWS is content-agnostic and has no visibility into customer data, only the customer can complete this step. AWS's European seller of record is Amazon Web Services EMEA SARL, based in Luxembourg. AWS will not transfer customer data outside the customer's selected AWS region unless necessary to provide/maintain services, comply with law, or prevent fraud. Customers select AWS regions in Europe including France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and the UK. Only a small number of AWS services (e.g., content delivery) involve third-country transfers, and customers can opt out of such transfers.

**Step 2: Identify Transfer Tools** - The Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) are incorporated into the AWS Service Terms and AWS Data Processing Addendum (DPA). Both Controller-to-Processor and Processor-to-Processor Clauses apply depending on the customer's role. AWS also offers UK and Switzerland addenda to the DPA for transfers from those countries.

**Step 3: Assess Laws/Practices of Recipient Countries** - Customers must assess whether the transfer tool provides effective protection. On July 10, 2023, the European Commission adopted its adequacy decision on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF), confirming the US ensures adequate protection for data transferred to DPF-certified companies. AWS reviews every law enforcement request individually and independently, challenges overbroad requests, and publishes regular Amazon Information Request Reports demonstrating that disclosures of customer data are very rare.

**Step 4: Adopt Supplementary Measures** - AWS offers three categories: (a) technical measures (encryption via AWS KMS with FIPS 140-2 certified HSMs, the AWS Nitro System which by design has no mechanism for AWS personnel to access customer data on Nitro hosts - independently affirmed by NCC Group); (b) organizational measures (internal processes for handling governmental requests, Information Request Reports); and (c) contractual protections (the AWS Supplementary Addendum, under which AWS commits to redirect governmental bodies to the customer, notify customers of requests when legally permitted, challenge overbroad requests, and disclose only minimum necessary data if compelled).

**Step 5: Procedural Steps** - No need to request supervisory authority authorization if supplementary measures don't contradict the SCCs and are sufficient to protect GDPR-level protection.

**Step 6: Re-evaluate** - Customers must continuously monitor developments in recipient countries; AWS will also monitor relevant developments.

Additional AWS assurances include adherence to the CISPE Data Protection Code of Conduct (validated by the EDPB and approved by the French DPA/CNIL), which goes beyond GDPR compliance by requiring cloud providers to offer EEA-exclusive storage/processing options (AWS initially declared 100 services under the CISPE Code).
</summary>

"As set out in the AWS DPA, AWS will not transfer customer data outside the customer's selected AWS region unless it is necessary to provide or maintain the AWS services initiated by the customer, or as necessary to comply with the law or a valid and binding order."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: AWS Digital Sovereignty Pledge: Control without compromise | AWS Security Blog ---
URL: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/aws-digital-sovereignty-pledge-control-without-compromise

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an AWS Security Blog post announcing the "AWS Digital Sovereignty Pledge" — AWS's commitment to offering all customers the most advanced set of sovereignty controls and features available in the cloud. The pledge addresses customer concerns that they might have to choose between the full power of AWS and a feature-limited sovereign cloud solution.

Key points of the pledge include four commitment areas:

1. **Control over data location**: AWS commits to delivering more fine-grained data residency controls and transparency, including for operational data like identity and billing information. Currently, customers in Europe can deploy data across eight existing Regions.

2. **Verifiable control over data access**: The AWS Nitro System uses specialized hardware and software to protect data during processing on EC2, designed so that nobody—including anyone within AWS—can access customer workloads. AWS commits to additional access restrictions unless requested by the customer or a trusted partner.

3. **Encrypt everything everywhere**: All AWS services already support encryption, most with customer-managed keys inaccessible to AWS. AWS commits to additional sovereignty and encryption controls, with keys managed inside or outside the AWS Cloud (e.g., AWS KMS External Key Store).

4. **Cloud resilience**: AWS claims the highest network availability of any cloud provider. Each Region comprises multiple isolated Availability Zones (AZs), and AWS offers offline/remote capabilities for intermittently connected use cases.

The post highlights recent examples of sovereign-by-design work, including data residency guardrails added to AWS Control Tower (late 2021) and AWS services adhering to the CISPE Data Protection Code of Conduct (announced February 2022) for GDPR compliance. AWS also commits to transparency about data processing, challenging law enforcement requests for customer data, and working with local partners such as T-Systems (Deutsche Telekom) in Germany, which offers Data Protection as a Managed Service on AWS. The full content is also provided in French, German, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Spanish, and Arabic versions.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We firmly believe that customers shouldn't have to make this choice." (regarding choosing between full AWS power and feature-limited sovereign cloud solutions), "Our approach to delivering on this pledge is to continue to make the AWS Cloud sovereign-by-design—as it has been from day one.", "Currently, in Europe, customers have the choice to deploy their data into any of eight existing Regions.", "By providing a strong physical and logical security boundary, Nitro is designed to enforce restrictions so that nobody, including anyone in AWS, can access customer workloads on EC2.", "It is not possible to achieve digital sovereignty without resiliency and survivability."

--- SOURCE 2: Org Management account - AWS Prescriptive Guidance ---
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/privacy-reference-architecture/org-management-account.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is part of the AWS Privacy Reference Architecture (AWS PRA) documentation and describes the Org Management account, which is used to manage resource configuration drift for foundational privacy controls across all accounts in an AWS organization. The account enables consistent deployment of new member accounts with security and privacy controls. The page details three key AWS services configured in this account:

1. **AWS Artifact**: Provides on-demand downloads of AWS security and compliance documents for audits. Useful reports include the SOC 2 Type 2 Privacy report (demonstrating AWS controls for how personal data is collected, used, retained, disclosed, and disposed of), the Cloud Computing Compliance Controls Catalog (C5) report created by Germany's BSI, and the ISO/IEC 27701:2019 certification report (covering privacy information management systems/PIMS).

2. **AWS Control Tower**: Helps set up and govern a multi-account environment following prescriptive security practices. It automates deployment of proactive, preventative, and detective controls (guardrails) for data residency and sovereignty. Sovereignty controls include requiring EBS volume encryption and restricting AWS KMS key policies. Mandatory controls protect logs (e.g., Disallow Deletion of Log Archive, Enable Integrity Validation for CloudTrail). Control Tower integrates with AWS Security Hub CSPM for detective controls to monitor configuration drift.

3. **AWS Organizations**: Used to centrally manage all accounts. Service control policies (SCPs) provide centralized control over maximum available permissions for IAM roles and users. SCPs can limit AWS Regions for data residency, and can restrict high-risk API calls such as enabling public access to S3 buckets, disabling Amazon GuardDuty, deleting AWS WAF data exfiltration rules, sharing EBS snapshots publicly, removing member accounts, and disassociating Amazon CodeGuru Reviewer. Management policies, particularly tag policies, help maintain consistent tags across the organization. Tags can distinguish resources handling personal data and support attribute-based access control (ABAC) policies. The page warns against placing personally identifiable information in tags (as tags are not encrypted and can be read by AWS services) and recommends making some tag values immutable to prevent circumvention of technical controls.

<summary>
This AWS webpage defines and explains data sovereignty, which refers to data being subject to the laws and regulations of its physical location—whether in storage, processing, or transmission. The page details the AWS Digital Sovereignty Pledge, which commits AWS to offering the most advanced set of sovereignty controls in the cloud across four key areas: (1) control over where data resides (via AWS Regions, Local Zones, Dedicated Local Zones, Outposts, and Wavelength), (2) control over data access (e.g., the AWS Nitro System preventing unauthorized access to EC2 workloads), (3) data encryption capabilities (encryption in transit, at rest, and in memory, with customer-managed keys), and (4) cloud resilience (multiple Availability Zones per Region for high availability).

Implementation guidance includes: planning for data localization compliance by researching applicable regulations and partnering with compliance consultants; implementing fine-grained access controls using AWS IAM, AWS Control Tower, and digital sovereignty controls; building resilience for mission-critical systems by distributing data across multiple Availability Zones and using AWS Outposts or Amazon EKS Anywhere for on-premises workloads; and finding a cloud partner providing transparency and assurances.

Best practices include sorting and securing sensitive data, choosing data residency according to applicable laws, choosing a trusted cloud provider, and keeping up to date with compliance obligations.

The page also addresses challenges, noting that jurisdictions vary widely and may overlap (e.g., EU countries must comply with both national and EU laws), highly regulated industries have different regulations, and extraterritorial business creates complexity (e.g., Australian companies must comply with GDPR for EU citizens' data). AWS Cloud WAN is a managed wide-area networking (WAN) service that uses a centralized control plane and declarative JSON network policies to create a global network spanning multiple locations, eliminating the need to manually configure different networks using different technologies. The service uses Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) to automatically create a global network across AWS Regions and provides a unified dashboard for monitoring network health, security, and performance.

Key details from the post:
- AWS Cloud WAN supports connecting VPCs, Transit Gateways, and on-premises locations via AWS Site-to-Site VPN, AWS Direct Connect, or third-party SD-WAN products.

Key capabilities covered:
1. Policy-based networking with version control (each policy change creates a new version with rollback capabilities for audit trails).
2. Service insertion for security inspection (integrates AWS Network Firewall and third-party appliances via Gateway Load Balancer, supporting east-west, north-south, and hybrid traffic inspection; relevant for TIC 3.0 compliance).
3. Dynamic routing for cross-Region connectivity (automatic BGP peering between Core Network Edges, plus Routing Policy for fine-grained route filtering, summarization, and BGP path manipulation).
4. Hybrid connectivity with Direct Connect (through Transit Gateway attachments).
5. Tunnel-less Connect for SD-WAN (third-party appliances can peer with BGP, delivering up to 100 Gbps per Availability Zone without specialized tunneling protocols).
6. Centralized network management (unified topology, health, performance, and security posture dashboard).
7. Regional segment confinement (segments can be scoped to specific Regions for data residency requirements, such as ITAR workloads).

Configuration follows the same workflow as commercial Regions, using AWS Management Console, CLI, JSON policy, APIs, CloudFormation, or Terraform. The post includes a full example JSON policy (version 2025.11) defining Prod, Dev, and Hybrid segments with edge locations in both GovCloud Regions.

The post concludes that AWS Cloud WAN enables policy-driven network automation for government organizations and regulated industries, supporting disaster recovery across both GovCloud Regions, hybrid connectivity, and SD-WAN extension while maintaining compliance boundaries. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This AWS blog post addresses how Healthcare and Life Sciences (HCLS) organizations can deploy generative AI solutions while maintaining HIPAA compliance. The article demystifies healthcare compliance requirements, clarifies the division of responsibilities between AWS and customers, and provides actionable best practices for secure, compliant generative AI deployments.

**Shared Responsibility Model**: AWS operates, manages, and controls security of the cloud, while customers own responsibility for security in the cloud. Generative AI adds another layer of shared responsibility involving AWS, customers, third-party model providers, and those running agents within systems.

**HIPAA Eligible vs. HIPAA Compliant**: AWS offers over 166 HIPAA eligible services. Customers do not automatically inherit compliance by using these services—they must configure and implement controls. Non-HIPAA-eligible services (e.g., Amazon Q Developer, resource tags) can be used only if they don't process, store, or transmit ePHI.

**HITRUST CSF**: AWS offers over 177 HITRUST CSF certified services, third-party attested, incorporating frameworks like ISO27001 and NIST 800-53. HITRUST certificates are typically updated annually, which may create overhead.

**Key Compliance Considerations**:
- **AWS BAA**: Customers must execute a standardized Business Associate Addendum (BAA) to use HIPAA eligible services for ePHI.
- **VPC Configurations**: Use private/public subnets, Zero Trust network security, security groups, ACLs, and VPC endpoints. Use encrypted connections like Site-to-Site VPN or Direct Connect.
- **Secure Access Controls**: IAM best practices including least privilege, MFA, role-based access; use IAM Identity Center for SSO.
- **Encryption at Rest**: Strongly recommended (not explicitly required by current regulation) for ePHI; stored via S3, RDS, DynamoDB, Bedrock Knowledge Bases, EFS, FSx. Proposed HIPAA updates may increase encryption requirements.
- **Key Management**: Use AWS-managed keys or AWS KMS for customer-managed keys with centralized control over lifecycle and permissions.
- **Encryption in Transit**: Use TLS, HTTPS; traffic between AWS data centers is physically encrypted; Amazon Bedrock only allows encrypted connections.
- **Logging/Auditing**: Use CloudWatch, CloudTrail, encrypt log data, avoid ePHI in logs, use Amazon Macie for PII/ePHI scanning.
- **Resiliency/Backup**: Multi-AZ and multi-Region features, cross-Region replication for SageMaker, AWS Backup.
- **LLM Model Restrictions**: Verify terms and acceptable use policies for models (e.g., Anthropic's high-risk use case requirements, human-in-the-loop needs).
- **LLM Training**: Remove PII/ePHI from training data or implement guardrails; consider AWS Nitro Enclaves for inference over confidential data.
- **RAG Data Sources**: Apply guardrails on ePHI-containing RAG data; use Bedrock sensitive information filters.
- **Prompt Engineering/Guardrails**: Use SageMaker AI and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter ePHI and prevent jailbreaking/prompt injection.
- **Agentic AI**: Options include Amazon Bedrock Agents (fully managed with built-in compliance controls) or open-source Strands Agents SDK; data protection, access management, and audit logging remain key focus areas.
- **Response Validation**: Use guardrails, human-in-the-loop approaches, Amazon Comprehend for PII detection, and Automated Reasoning checks to prevent hallucinations.
- **Responsible AI**: Establish AI policies, use AWS AI Service Cards and foundation model cards, conduct risk assessments, use SageMaker Clarify for bias detection and model explainability, and SageMaker Model Monitor for production metrics.
- **Design Review**: Use AWS Well-Architected Tool, AWS Professional Services, or AWS generative AI Competency Partners.

The article concludes that leveraging AWS services like Amazon SageMaker AI and Amazon Bedrock allows healthcare companies to confidently deploy secure, scalable, and compliant generative AI applications by understanding the Shared Responsibility model and implementing robust security measures.

This AWS video tutorial (posted February 1, 2022, with 5,357 views) demonstrates how to enable data residency controls using AWS Control Tower guardrails. Key points covered:

**What is FedRAMP?** FedRAMP is a US government-wide program that standardizes security assessment, certification, and continuous monitoring for cloud products and services used by federal agencies. It is governed by the FedRAMP Board, Program Management Office (PMO), Technical Advisory Group (TAG), and Federal Secure Cloud Advisory Committee (FSCAC). CSPs must demonstrate FedRAMP compliance using NIST SP 800 series and complete an independent security assessment by a FedRAMP Recognized Independent Assessment Service (formerly 3PAO), compliant with FISMA 2002.

**Why FedRAMP matters:** Established in response to the federal government's Cloud First Policy (now Cloud Smart Strategy) via the OMB FedRAMP Policy Memo, FedRAMP is mandatory for all US federal agencies and cloud services.

**FedRAMP 20x Initiative:** The PMO, industry stakeholders, and agency experts are redesigning the FedRAMP assessment process to streamline and enhance compliance.

**FedRAMP Consolidated Rules for 2026 (CR26):** These published regulations modernize how CSPs communicate changes and maintain ongoing compliance. Key changes include:
- Significant Change Notifications (SCN) for communicating reportable changes to agency customers
- Collaborative Continuous Monitoring (CCM) for ongoing compliance reporting
- "FedRAMP Authorized" renamed to "FedRAMP Certified"

**AWS FedRAMP Certification details:**
- AWS has achieved FedRAMP Certification for AWS GovCloud (US) as Class D (formerly High baseline) and AWS US East-West as Class C (formerly Moderate baseline)
- No increase in AWS service costs due to FedRAMP compliance
- FedRAMP IDs: AWS US East-West = AGENCYAMAZONEW; AWS GovCloud (US) = F1603047866
- AWS maintains continuous monitoring through quarterly Ongoing Certification Reports (OCR) and Quarterly Review briefings
- AWS supports high-impact workloads on AWS GovCloud (US), which is authorized for high impact level

**Key distinctions:**
- FedRAMP Certification is issued by the FedRAMP PMO (congressionally mandated under the FedRAMP Authorization Act)
- The JAB Provisional Authority to Operate (P-ATO) previously issued to AWS is a legacy designation superseded by FedRAMP Certification
- Agencies must issue their own ATO through the Risk Management Framework (RMF) for systems incorporating FedRAMP Certified services
- FedRAMP is the process for CSPs; RMF is the process for agencies authorizing their IT systems

--- SOURCE 2: Understanding the GDPR breach notification timeline ---
URL: https://www.thoropass.com/blog/gdpr-breach-notification-timeline

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Thoropass blog post provides a step-by-step guide to understanding the GDPR breach notification timeline, with the 72-hour rule as the central requirement. Key content includes:

**Breach Definition under GDPR**: A personal data breach includes unauthorized access to personal data, as well as accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, or disclosure of personal data records. Breaches unrelated to personal data are not required to be reported under GDPR, regardless of severity.

**The 72-Hour Rule**: Organizations must notify relevant supervisory authorities of a personal data breach within 72 hours of becoming aware of it (when the IT security team discovers the breach). Failure to adhere may result in fines up to €10 million or 2% of the company's global annual revenue. Exceptions apply when breached data is encrypted with uncompromised encryption keys, or when the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms.

**Breach Identification and Risk Assessment**: Organizations should recognize indicators (sudden file changes, abnormal system behavior) and common causes (weak/stolen credentials, application vulnerabilities, malware, third-party risks). Risk assessment categorizes breaches as no risk, risk, or high risk, considering outcomes like identity theft, fraud, physical danger, distress, and public exposure.

**Reporting to Supervisory Authorities**: Organizations must select the appropriate authority based on the location of their main establishment within an EU member state. Required notification information includes: categories of data involved, approximate count of affected data records, details about the breach, likely consequences, measures taken or proposed, and DPO contact information.

**Notifying Affected Data Subjects**: Individual notification is required when a breach is likely to result in high risk to individuals' rights and freedoms. Notification must include breach details, consequences, and corrective measures, delivered clearly and simply. Breaches involving medical/financial information or sensitive data (psychological, ethnic) necessitate individual notification.

**Breach Response Plan Components**: A comprehensive plan should define roles (incident manager, information security team leader, communications lead, documentation lead), include pre-planning exercises, establish response teams, and be regularly reviewed and updated to maintain GDPR compliance.

The article concludes with Thoropass's promotional content describing its 5-step GDPR compliance approach (Kick-off, Onboarding, Implementation, GDPR assessment and reporting, and ongoing compliance) and a FAQ section addressing common questions about notification timelines, who to notify, and breach definitions.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In the case of a personal data breach, the controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority competent in accordance with Article 55, unless the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons." – GDPR
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Data Breach Notification Laws: Requirements by State and Global Regulations ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Data Breach Notification Laws: Requirements by State and Global Regulations

This article, published January 7, 2025, by Juan H. of Prey (a data security company), provides a comprehensive overview of data breach notification laws in the United States and globally.

### Key Context and Statistics
- A cyberattack occurs every 39 seconds worldwide; in 2023 alone, over 353 million people were impacted by data breaches in the U.S. (with 422 million affected globally according to the Identity Theft Resource Center).
- All 50 U.S. states have enacted data breach notification laws, each with unique criteria, timelines, thresholds, and penalties.

### What Data Breach Notification Laws Require
- Organizations must promptly notify affected individuals (and often regulators) when sensitive personal data is compromised (e.g., Social Security numbers, financial records, health information, login credentials).
- Notifications must include: description of the breach, data involved, steps taken to mitigate, actionable guidance for individuals, and contact details.
- System outages or failed phishing attempts typically do not trigger notification requirements.

### Global Regulatory Landscape
- **GDPR (EU)**: The global benchmark since 2018. Requires regulator notification within 72 hours; fines up to €20 million or 4% of global annual revenue. Meta was fined €1.2 billion in 2023 for data transfer violations.
- **California (CCPA/CPRA)**: Among the most comprehensive U.S. state laws; fines up to $7,500 per violation. As of 2024, 12 U.S. states have comprehensive privacy laws.
- **Canada (PIPEDA)**: Requires reporting breaches posing "real risk of significant harm"; fines up to CAD $10 million.
- **Australia (Privacy Act)**: Updated 2022; fines up to AUD $50 million.
- **Japan (APPI)** and **South Korea (PIPA)**: Fines up to 3% of global revenue for violations.
- **India (Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023)**: Emerging framework focusing on breach notifications and user rights.

### State-by-State Highlights (Top 25 States)
Key examples include:
- **California**: "Without unreasonable delay"; $7,500/violation; AG notification for 500+ affected.
- **New York (SHIELD Act)**: "Without unreasonable delay"; includes biometric/login data; up to $250,000 penalties.
- **Texas**: 60 days; credit agencies notified for 10,000+ affected; up to $100,000/violation.
- **Florida**: 30 days; $500,000 for delays.
- **Minnesota**: 48 hours (for government entities).
- **Connecticut**: 90 days (longest timeline listed).
- **Washington, Colorado, South Carolina**: 30 days.
- **Alabama, Arizona, North Carolina, Tennessee, Kentucky**: 45 days.
- Most other states use "without unreasonable delay" or "most expedient time possible."

### Compliance Challenges
- Multi-jurisdictional complexity (no federal standard in the U.S.)
- Varying definitions of personal data across states
- Significant direct and indirect costs of notification

### Best Practices
1. Establish a proactive data breach response plan with clearly defined roles
2. Conduct regular cybersecurity audits (at least annually)
3. Leverage automation and detection tools for real-time monitoring
4. Maintain breach logs and appoint a Data Protection Officer (under GDPR)

### Company Promotion
The article promotes Prey's data security solutions, including remote wipe capabilities, real-time monitoring, and threat detection tools, positioning them as aids for breach detection and compliance.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: EU-US Data Privacy Framework: Compliance for US Companies - GDPR Local ---
URL: https://gdprlocal.com/eu-us-data-privacy-framework

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from GDPRLocal provides a comprehensive guide to the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF) compliance for US companies, updated July 2026. The DPF is a self-certification scheme that allows US companies to legally receive personal data from the European Union without extra safeguards. It began on 10 July 2023 and replaced the Privacy Shield, which was struck down by courts following the Schrems II ruling in 2020.

Key points covered:
- The framework has three linked parts: EU-US DPF (covers EU member states), UK Extension (covers UK and Gibraltar), and Swiss-US DPF (covers Switzerland under Swiss FADP).
- The European Commission adopted the adequacy decision on 10 July 2023, determining certified US companies meet EU data protection standards.
- The Department of Commerce administers the framework through its International Trade Administration and maintains the public Data Privacy Framework List.
- Legal foundations include Executive Order 14086 (stronger limits on US intelligence activities), the Data Protection Review Court (allows EU individuals to challenge US government data access), and the essential equivalence standard.
- Benefits include: legal certainty (eliminates transfer assessments), market access to EU markets worth over $7 trillion in GDP, competitive advantage, and risk mitigation (avoids GDPR penalties up to 4% of global annual revenue).
- Comparison table shows DPF offers optimal balance: 2-4 weeks implementation, high legal certainty, annual re-certification, medium cost (vs. BCRs at 12-18 months, SCCs requiring assessments, consent with limited scope).

Certification process (3 steps):
1. Assess eligibility: data audit, transfer mapping, category assessment, resource evaluation.
2. Self-certify with Department of Commerce: submit commitments to DPF Principles, update privacy policies, designate recourse mechanism, appear on the public list.
3. Maintain compliance: annual re-certification, policy maintenance, vendor management, dispute resolution.

DPF Principles include: notice/transparency, choice mechanisms, accountability for onward transfers, security safeguards, access rights, and recourse/enforcement procedures.

Common mistakes: assuming coverage through certified vendors (only companies on the DPF List get adequacy protection), missing annual re-certification (loss of protection is immediate), and weak onward transfer protection.

The FTC can enforce DPF obligations under Section 5 for unfair or deceptive practices, including consent orders and penalties. The FAQ clarifies that companies can use alternatives like SCCs (with transfer impact assessments), must stop claiming participation if removed from the list (but still apply DPF Principles to held data), and need not participate in all three frameworks simultaneously (UK Extension requires EU-US DPF participation first).

The article is written by Ana Mishova, Sales & Business Development Consultant at GDPRLocal, a UK B2B compliance partner. GDPRLocal also offers services including AI Act compliance, GDPR Art. 27 EU/UK Rep services, Swiss Representative services, audits, breach management, and vendor assessments.
</summary>

"The EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF) is a self-certification scheme that lets US companies legally receive personal data from the European Union without extra safeguards. It started in July 2023 and replaced the Privacy Shield, which the courts struck down."

--- SOURCE 7: EU-US Data Privacy Framework: Key Insights, Updates and Resources ---
URL: https://www.data-privacy-framework.com

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides a comprehensive overview of the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF), the adequacy decision mechanism governing personal data transfers from the European Union to the United States.

**Background & Legal Foundation:**
- On July 10, 2023, the European Commission adopted an adequacy decision determining that the US provides an adequate and comparable level of protection for personal data transferred from the EU to US companies participating in the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework.
- The decision was preceded by the US issuance of Executive Order 14086 ("Enhancing Safeguards for US Signals Intelligence Activities") on October 7, 2022, which introduced binding safeguards addressing concerns raised in the Court of Justice of the European Union's Schrems II decision (July 2020), including the concepts of necessity and proportionality in US signals intelligence and a new redress mechanism.

**Key Updates (Chronological):**

1. **November 4, 2024** – The EDPB adopted its first report under the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework. Key findings included: the US Department of Commerce implemented the certification process; the multi-layered redress system was updated; the EDPB encouraged increased ex officio investigations by US authorities; called for practical guidance on the Accountability for Onward Transfer Principle and clarification of "HR Data"; noted the Data Protection Review Court was appointed with eight judges and two special advocates; raised concerns about the re-authorization of Section 702 of FISA (definition of "electronic communication service provider" not meeting requirements of clear, precise and accessible law); and recommended the next review occur within less than four years.

2. **September 3, 2025** – The General Court of the EU dismissed an action for annulment of the new framework, confirming the US ensured an adequate level of protection on the date of adoption of the contested decision. (Appeals limited to points of law could be brought within two months and ten days.)

3. **January 15, 2026** – EDPB published FAQ for European individuals (Version 2.0), explaining the DPF as a self-certification mechanism allowing free data transfers to US certified companies without further safeguards. Individuals have rights to be informed, access, correct, and delete their data. Complaints can be lodged with EEA national data protection authorities.

4. **July 2, 2026** – The US Supreme Court's ruling in Trump v. Slaughter confirmed the President possesses broader authority to remove FTC Commissioners. This raised legal questions about the assumptions underlying the adequacy decision, which had relied on FTC independence as a key safeguard. The ruling does not by itself invalidate the Framework but invites renewed scrutiny of whether the Framework's description of FTC independence remains legally accurate.

**Redress Mechanism:**
A two-layer redress mechanism was established for complaints about US intelligence collection: (1) the Civil Liberties Protection Officer of the US intelligence community investigates complaints; (2) individuals can appeal to the Data Protection Review Court (DPRC), an independent body whose members can only be dismissed for cause and cannot receive government instructions. Special advocates represent complainants' interests. Complaints can be submitted through national DPAs and transmitted via the EDPB.

**Adequacy Decisions Generally:**
The Commission may adopt adequacy decisions under Article 45 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679. The process involves a Commission proposal, EDPB opinion, approval of EU country representatives, and adoption by the Commission. Countries recognized as providing adequate protection include: Andorra, Argentina, Canada (commercial organisations), Faroe Islands, Guernsey, Israel, Isle of Man, Japan, Jersey, New Zealand, Republic of Korea, Switzerland, the UK (under GDPR and LED), the US (commercial organisations under DPF), and Uruguay.

**Commission Implementing Decision Key Provisions:**
- Article 1: US ensures adequate protection for personal data transferred to organizations on the DPF List maintained by the US Department of Commerce.
- Article 2: Member States must inform the Commission of powers exercised regarding data transfers.
- Article 3: The Commission shall continuously monitor the framework, evaluate findings after one year and periodically thereafter, and may suspend, amend, or repeal the decision if adequate protection is no longer ensured.

The website is maintained by Cyber Risk GmbH under the professional responsibility of George Lekatis, specializing in risk management and regulatory compliance support.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 11: Navigating common use cases spanning AWS GovCloud (US) and standard AWS | AWS Public Sector Blog ---
URL: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/publicsector/navigating-common-use-cases-spanning-aws-govcloud-us-standard-aws

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This AWS Public Sector Blog post (authored by Kirk Horne, Natti Swaminathan, and Rajdeep Saha) explores use cases where customers must orchestrate actions spanning AWS GovCloud (US) and standard AWS partitions. The post explains that an AWS partition logically and physically separates groups of AWS Regions, providing data, network, and machine isolation, and that a Region cannot be part of two partitions.

The post covers why AWS GovCloud (US) exists: it supports customers who must adhere to US ITAR regulations, FedRAMP requirements, DFARS, DoD Cloud Computing Security Requirements Guide (SRG) Impact Levels 2, 4, and 5, and other security/compliance requirements. Workloads not requiring these compliance standards can be deployed in the standard AWS partition.

Security considerations common to all use cases include storing credentials (IAM access keys) in AWS Secrets Manager (both as key/value secrets and plaintext/JSON), using Site-to-Site VPN connectivity between partitions, and adhering to the Shared Responsibility Model.

Three specific use cases are detailed:
1. **Calling Amazon SES in standard AWS from AWS GovCloud (US):** An API Gateway publishes customer data to Amazon SNS, Amazon SQS subscribes and queues messages, and a Lambda function in AWS GovCloud (US) retrieves the message, reads access keys from Secrets Manager, and invokes the Amazon SES SendEmail API in the standard AWS account to send confirmation emails.
2. **Event-driven architecture between partitions:** Common business logic is hosted in the standard AWS account. Lambda functions in AWS GovCloud (US) act as dispatchers, retrieving IAM access keys from Secrets Manager and invoking compute services (Lambda or Amazon EKS via Application Load Balancer) in the standard AWS account. This pattern is interchangeable between partitions and enables centralized deployment of business logic.
3. **Extending AWS Budget actions to AWS GovCloud (US):** Since AWS GovCloud (US) does not support budget actions, customers can use AWS Budgets in a standard AWS account to trigger an SNS topic and Lambda function when a budget threshold is exceeded. The Lambda retrieves AWS GovCloud (US) management account credentials from Secrets Manager and invokes the AWS Organizations AttachPolicy API to attach a restrictive Service Control Policy (SCP) that prevents new EC2 and RDS instances from being launched. When the budget resets, DetachPolicy is called to restore normal operations.

The post concludes by noting these design patterns can be extended to other AWS services and references two additional related posts about moving data in/out of AWS GovCloud (US) via Amazon S3 and sharing AWS Direct Connect between partitions.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The common reasons customers may need to invoke Amazon Web Services (AWS) services in a standard account from an AWS GovCloud (US) account (or vice versa) include: cross-domain applications, feature parity, and if the AWS service doesn't exist in AWS GovCloud (US)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 12: Case Study - Logical Separation on AWS ---
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/logical-separation/case-study.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This AWS whitepaper case study describes how the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) accepted a logical storage separation approach for sensitive unclassified workloads (Impact Level 5 systems). In December 2011, the U.S. Federal Chief Information Officer established FedRAMP (Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program), which maintains three standardized security baselines — Low, Moderate, and High impact — based on FIPS 199 categorizations. While the DoD established reciprocity with the FedRAMP Moderate baseline, it did not do so with the High baseline, instead developing a "FedRAMP plus" set of controls via the DoD Cloud Computing Security Requirements Guide (SRG).

The SRG requires separation between DoD and Federal government tenants via physical or logical means, and specifically requires physical separation (dedicated infrastructure) from non-DoD/non-Federal Government tenants for Impact Level 5 (IL5) systems. However, the SRG acknowledged that CSPs may offer alternate solutions providing equivalent security, with approval assessed case-by-case during the Provisional Authorization (PA) process. Through this accreditation process, AWS demonstrated that logical separation combined with dedicated tenancy could satisfy the intent behind the requirement for dedicated, physically isolated infrastructure for IL5 workloads. AWS argues that multi-tenant logically separated environments meeting robust security controls can provide security superior to dedicated private cloud deployments, with advantages in availability, scalability, and lower cost.

The whitepaper also details the IL5 location and separation requirements: only DoD private, DoD community, or Federal Government community clouds are eligible for IL5; virtual/logical separation between DoD and Federal tenants is permitted and minimally required between tenant/mission systems; and physical separation from non-DoD/non-Federal Government tenants is required. The note reiterates that CSPs can offer alternate solutions with equivalent security, subject to case-by-case PA assessment approval.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"CSPs must provide evidence of strong virtual separation controls and monitoring, and the ability to meet 'search and seizure' requests without the release of DoD information and data."

URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/govcloud-us/latest/UserGuide/govcloud-compliance.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from AWS documentation describes the compliance capabilities of AWS GovCloud (US), a cloud environment designed for US government customers and their partners. The page outlines the various compliance frameworks and standards that AWS GovCloud (US) supports, including:

- **FedRAMP High baseline**: AWS supports the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program for federal agencies processing, storing, and transmitting federal government data.
- **DoD CC SRG**: Supports the Department of Defense Cloud Computing Security Requirements Guide for Impact Levels 2, 4, and 5, enabling defense organizations to process, maintain, and store DoD data.
- **CMMC**: The Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification program protects sensitive unclassified information shared by the DoD with contractors and subcontractors.
- **ITAR**: AWS GovCloud (US) supports compliance with US International Traffic in Arms Regulations by providing an environment physically located in the US, with access by AWS personnel limited to US Persons.
- **CJIS**: Supports the FBI's Criminal Justice Information Services Security Policy, which protects the full lifecycle of Criminal Justice Information (CJI) at rest and in transit.
- **IRS 1075**: AWS aligns its implementations of NIST 800-53 and FedRAMP security controls with IRS Publication 1075 requirements for protecting Federal Tax Information (FTI).
- **FIPS 140-3**: Supports the Federal Information Processing Standard specifying security requirements for cryptographic modules.
- **ATO on AWS**: A program helping AWS Partners meet authorization needs for workloads supporting government organizations (FedRAMP, FISMA, RMF, and CMMC).

Each section links to more detailed AWS compliance documentation. The page also notes that JavaScript must be enabled to use the AWS Documentation.

U.S. Data Privacy Framework as Alternative Transfer Solutions to legitimize​ ​ certain transfers subject to the UK version of the GDPR (UK GDPR) and the applicable​ ​ Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection Act (Swiss FADP) respectively.​ ​ ●​ ​ This paper explains the basic requirements for European data transfers and how the​ ​ solutions adopted by Google enable and simplify lawful transfers.​ ​ Introduction​ ​ This paper outlines the rules for data transfers under the EU GDPR, the UK GDPR and the​ ​ Swiss FADP (“European Data Protection Law”) and explains how Google complies with them​ ​ using Alternative Transfer Solutions, while relying on SCCs in limited circumstances.​ ​ This paper is intended to help customers using Google Cloud Platform (GCP), Google​ ​ Workspace including Google Workspace for Education, Looker (original), SecOps Services,​ ​ Implementation Services and other Google Cloud services understand how their Customer​ ​ Data is protected when transferred to third countries that have not been approved as​ ​ providing adequate protection by the European Commission, the UK Secretary of State, or​ ​ any other relevant authority, as applicable.​ ​ 2​​ The EU GDPR, UK GDPR and Swiss FADP , as well as Section 4 (Data Transfers) of the European terms in​ ​ Appendix 3 (Specific Privacy Laws) of the CDPA, all apply to “Customer Personal Data”. However, for the sake of​ ​ brevity, this paper uses the term “Customer Data” throughout, including to refer to “Partner Data” and “Partner​ ​ Personal Data” (as those terms are defined in the Partner CDPA).​ ​ 1​​ A​​ partner version of the CDPA​​ applies to partners​​ reselling GCP , Looker (original) and SecOps Services, but this​ ​ paper uses the term “customers” to refer to both customers and partners.​ ​ 3​ ​ Note that this paper is intended for informational purposes only, and not as legal advice. Any​ ​ customer needing legal advice relating to Google Cloud services should consult a lawyer.​ ​ Outline of Legal Rules​ ​ a.​ ​ Transfers to third countries​ ​ The EU GDPR protects the personal data of identified or identifiable natural persons (“data​ ​ subjects”) in the “home territory” of the​​ European​​ Economic Area​​ (EEA). It governs any​ ​ processing of their data “in the context of the activities of an establishment of a controller or​ ​ a processor”​ ​ 3​​ in that home territory, and any processing​​ by a controller or processor located​ ​ outside the home territory if the processing relates to the offering of goods or services to​ ​ individuals in the territory or to the monitoring of their behaviour within the territory​ ​ 4​​ .​ ​ Under the EU GDPR, personal data relating to EEA individuals can only be transferred to a​ ​ country outside the EEA (a “third country”) if an appropriate level of data protection is​ ​ ensured in that country as specifically contemplated by Chapter V of the EU GDPR​ ​ 5​​ . The UK​ ​ GDPR and Swiss FADP impose similar restrictions, with their respective home territories​ ​ being the UK and Switzerland. However, if data is shared between two entities (e.g. a​ ​ controller and processor), both in the same home territory, no transfer solution is required​ ​ because applicable European Data Protection Law will bind both entities such that​ ​ appropriate protection can be assumed.​ ​ b.​ ​ Transfers to adequate countries​ ​ One type of transfer solution permitted by European Data Protection Law is a formal decision​ ​ by the relevant authority​ ​ 6​​ that a third country ensures​​ an adequate level of protection.​ ​ As of the publication date of this paper:​ ​ ●​ ​ those countries approved as adequate under the EU GDPR are listed​​ here​ , and include​ ​ the UK, Switzerland, Israel, Japan, South Korea, New Zealand, Argentina, Uruguay and​ ​ Canada (commercial organisations only);​ ​ 6​​ Such decisions are adopted by the European Commission (in the EU), the UK, the Secretary of State (in the UK),​ ​ and the​​ S​ ​ wiss Federal Data Protection and Information​​ Commissione​ ​ r​​ (in Switzerland).​ ​ 5​​ The EU GDPR also provides for a limited number of​​ exceptions, which apply in narrow use cases.​ ​ 4​​ Article 3(2) of the EU GDPR states “​ ​ This Regulation​​ applies to the processing of personal data of data subjects​ ​ who are in the Union by a controller or processor not established in the Union, where the processing activities are​ ​ related to: (a) the offering of goods or services, irrespective of whether a payment of the data subject is required, to​ ​ such data subjects in the Union; or (b) the monitoring of their behaviour as far as their behaviour takes place within​ ​ the Union.​ ​ ”​ ​ 3​​ Article 3(1) of the EU GDPR states “​ ​ This Regulation applies to the processing of personal data in the context of the​ ​ activities of an establishment of a controller or a processor in the Union, regardless of whether the processing takes​ ​ place in the Union or not.​ ​ ”​ ​ 4​ ​ ●​ ​ those countries approved as adequate under the UK GDPR are listed​​ here​​ and include​ ​ the EEA, Switzerland and the countries identified above as adequate for EU GDPR​ ​ purposes; and​ ​ ●​ ​ those countries approved as adequate under the Swiss FADP are listed​​ here​​ (see​ ​ those countries in the “List of countries” with an “X” in the “Niveau adéquat pour des​ ​ personnes physiques” column) and include the EEA and the UK.​ ​ If personal data is transferred to a third country deemed adequate under the relevant​ ​ European Data Protection Law, no additional transfer solution is needed, as the transfer will​ ​ already comply with applicable transfer requirements.​ ​ Moreover, where an adequacy assessment has been made by the relevant authority (as​ ​ reflected in an adequacy decision), there is no requirement under European Data Protection​ ​ Law for customers (or Google) to complete such assessments themselves.​ ​ c.​ ​ Other transfers based on adequacy​ ​ Another type of transfer solution permitted by European Data Protection Law is a formal​ ​ decision by the relevant authority that an adequate level of protection is ensured by an opt-in​ ​ compliance regime within a third country, as applies in the case of the​​ DPF​ .​ ​ The DPF is an opt-in certification scheme for U.S. organisations, enforced by the U.S. Federal​ ​ Trade Commission and Department of Transportation, and administered by the Department​ ​ of Commerce. It includes a set of enforceable principles and requirements that must be​ ​ certified to, and complied with, in order for U.S. organisations to join the DPF. These​ ​ principles take the form of commitments to data protection and govern how participating​ ​ organizations can use, collect and disclose personal data. They include the​​ Accountability​ ​ 5​ ​ for Onward Transfer Principle​​ which permits onward transfers of personal data by​ ​ participating organizations subject to compliance with the conditions specified.​ ​ The DPF has been operative since July 2023, when the European Commission​​ decided​​ that​ ​ an adequate level of protection was maintained by the DPF for EEA personal data. The DPF​ ​ has also been upheld by the General Court of the European Union, which in September 2025​ ​ dismissed a challenge to its validity​ ​ 7​​ .​ ​ Similarly:​ ​ ●​ ​ the UK Extension to the DPF has been operative since September 2023, when the UK​ ​ Government​​ decided​​ that an adequate level of protection​​ was maintained by the DPF​ ​ for UK personal data; and​ ​ ●​ ​ the Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework has been operative since August 2024, when​ ​ the Swiss Federal Council​​ decided​​ that an adequate​​ level of protection was​ ​ maintained by that Framework for Swiss personal data.​ ​ Where an adequacy assessment has been made by the relevant authority (as reflected in an​ ​ adequacy decision), there is no requirement under European Data Protection Law for​ ​ customers (or Google) to repeat such assessment.​ ​ d.​ ​ Transfers based on SCCs​ ​ SCCs are a means of ensuring appropriate safeguards for EEA/UK/Swiss personal data​ ​ transferred to third countries, where those countries (or organisations within those​ ​ countries) are​​ not​​ considered adequate under applicable​​ European Data Protection Law​ ​ 8​​ .​ ​ To serve their intended purpose, SCCs must be used without modification​ ​ 9​​ and entered by:​ ​ ●​ ​ one party (the “data exporter”) who is located in a home territory or otherwise​ ​ responsible under applicable European Data Protection Law for the transfer of​ ​ personal data to the “non-adequate” third country; and​ ​ ●​ ​ another party (the “data importer”) who is located in the non-adequate third country​ ​ and receives the transferred data from the data exporter.​ ​ Different modules of SCCs may be used, depending on whether each of the data exporter​ ​ and data importer is a controller or processor of the data being transferred. For​ ​ example, depending on the module used, SCCs may require both parties to complete transfer​ ​ impact assessments. They may also require the data exporter to implement “supplementary​ ​ measures” (a term derived from the decision of the Court of Justice of the European Union in​ ​ the so-called “Schrems II” case​ ​ 10​​ , and used to refer​​ to certain contractual, technical or​ ​ organisational safeguards), depending on the outcome of the data exporter’s transfer impact​ ​ assessment.​ ​ Google Cloud’s Approach​ ​ Google retains various modules of the EU SCCs in the​​ CDPA​ ​ , as well as UK and Swiss​ ​ versions of those SCCs, but Google Cloud’s SCCs only apply to transfers of EEA/UK/Swiss​ ​ Customer Data that are​​ not​​ covered by Alternative​​ Transfer Solutions. and​ ​ 10​​ See​​ Case C‑311/18, Data Protection Commissioner v​​ Facebook Ireland and Maximillian Schrems​ ​ .​ ​ 7​ ​ ●​ ​ the Swiss - U.S. Data Privacy Framework as an Alternative Transfer Solution for Swiss​ ​ Customer Data transferred to or onwards from the U.S., in reliance on Google LLC’s​ ​ certification to that framework.​ ​ b.​ ​ SCC coverage​ ​ Given the Alternative Transfer Solutions adopted as described above, and Google LLC’s​ ​ central role in engaging Google Cloud subprocessors, as of the publication date of this paper​ ​ Google Cloud’s SCCs apply​​ only​​ in the following two​​ scenarios:​ ​ ●​ ​ where the customer is located​ ​ 11​​ in the Middle East (including Turkey, excluding Israel)​ ​ or Africa and contracts with Google Cloud EMEA Limited (GCEMEA) as its service​ ​ provider:​ ​ ○​ ​ in this scenario, European Data Protection Law obliges GCEMEA to use the EU​ ​ P2C SCCs when transferring Customer Data to the customer, regardless of​ ​ whether the data relates to European data subjects, and the CDPA​ ​ automatically applies those SCCs; This whitepaper (November 2025) from Google Cloud explains the company's approach to European data transfers under EU GDPR, UK GDPR, and the Swiss FADP. Google offers customers protection via either an "Alternative Transfer Solution" or Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) through its Cloud Data Processing Addendum (CDPA).

Key legal framework points:
- European Data Protection Law restricts transfers of personal data to "third countries" unless an adequate level of protection is ensured. Adequacy decisions by relevant authorities (European Commission, UK Secretary of State, Swiss Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner) cover countries including the UK, Switzerland, Israel, Japan, South Korea, New Zealand, Argentina, Uruguay, and Canada (EU GDPR); the EEA, Switzerland, and the above (UK GDPR); and the EEA and UK (Swiss FADP).
- The Data Privacy Framework (DPF) is an opt-in certification scheme for U.S. organizations, enforced by the U.S. FTC and Department of Transportation, administered by the Department of Commerce. It has been operative since July 2023 (EU adequacy decision), upheld by the EU General Court in September 2025 (Case T-553/23, Latombe v Commission).
- The UK Extension to the DPF has been operative since September 2023; the Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework since August 2024.
- SCCs are used for transfers to non-adequate third countries and come in various modules (C2C, C2P, P2P, P2C). C2C SCCs have never been relevant for Google Cloud since Google is not a controller of Customer Data.

Google's approach:
- Since September 2023, Google adopted the DPF as an Alternative Transfer Solution for EEA Customer Data transferred to/from the U.S. (Google LLC is certified to the DPF).
- Since September 2024, Google adopted the UK Extension to the DPF and the Swiss-U.S. DPF for UK and Swiss Customer Data respectively.
- Google Cloud's SCCs now apply only in two scenarios: (1) customers located in the Middle East (excluding Israel) or Africa contracting with Google Cloud EMEA Limited (where EU P2C SCCs automatically apply), and (2) customers contracting with a non-Google LLC service provider in a non-adequate country whose processing is subject to European Data Protection Law (requiring customer certification where required).
- For all other scenarios (including all customers in the EEA, UK, Switzerland, and the U.S.), a combination of adequacy decisions and Alternative Transfer Solutions means Google Cloud's SCCs do not apply.
- Certification requirement: GCP, Google Workspace, and Cloud Identity customers located outside EMEA whose use is subject to European Data Protection Law must certify via the admin console and identify their competent European data protection authorities. Customers using other Google Cloud products or located in EMEA are not required to certify.

The conclusion states that Google's adoption of Alternative Transfer Solutions simplifies compliance for most customers and means customers in the EEA, UK, and Switzerland—as well as U.S. and other customers whose provider is Google LLC—no longer rely on SCCs for transfers under European Data Protection Law, including relief from transfer impact assessment and supplementary measure obligations.

# An update on Google Cloud’s commitments to E.U. businesses in light of the new E.U.-U.S. data transfer framework

##### Marc Crandall

Director and Global Head of Privacy, Google Cloud

##### Nathaly Rey

Director, Global Regulatory Affairs, Google Cloud

Last week, the European Commission and U.S. Government [agreed](https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/03/25/united-states-and-european-commission-joint-statement-on-trans-atlantic-data-privacy-framework/) on a new E.U.-U.S. data transfer framework. Earlier today, Google shared that it [welcomes](https://blog.google/outreach-initiatives/public-policy/trans-atlantic-data-privacy-framework-building-long-term/) these efforts by the U.S. government to enhance privacy protections for E.U. data and facilitate trusted transatlantic data flows. For our Google Cloud customers, we intend to make the protections offered by this new framework available once it is implemented.

Last year, we [reaffirmed](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/compliance/how-google-cloud-helps-customers-stay-current-with-gdpr) our commitment to E.U. businesses after the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) issued its Recommendations on Supplementary Measures, following Europe’s top court ruling invalidating the E.U.-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework and upholding the E.U. Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs).

Since then, we've continued to help our customers meet stringent data protection requirements by offering industry-leading technical controls, contractual commitments, and risk assessment resources. We've also continued our [advocacy](https://blog.google/around-the-globe/google-europe/its-time-for-a-new-eu-us-data-transfer-framework/) to create more legal certainty around transatlantic data flows.

Today, we would like to provide an update to our customers on this work.

### A customer-controlled cloud

Google Cloud1 continues to be a leading provider of technical and security controls to help meet customers’ data protection requirements, as well as their increasing data sovereignty expectations.

We are [committed to building our Cloud on Europe's terms](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/helping-build-the-digital-future-on-europes-terms), including by offering customer-managed encryption and data localization for a growing list of key products and collaborating with local partners to provide the highest levels of sovereignty, all while enabling the next wave of growth and transformation for Europe’s businesses and organizations.

### Google Cloud Platform

We recently [announced](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/meet-data-sovereignty-requirements-with-assured-workloads-for-eu-on-google-cloud?utm_source=POLITICO.EU&utm_campaign=17703213dd-EMAIL_CAMPAIGN_2022_02_03_06_07&utm_medium=email&utm_term=0_10959edeb5-17703213dd-190629740) the general availability of [Assured Workloads for the E.U.](https://cloud.google.com/assured-workloads) This product helps Google Cloud Platform (GCP) customers protect their data by allowing them to:

Store their data in their choice of E.U. Google Cloud region(s)

Ensure that only E.U. persons – located in the E.U. – have access to the data and provide customer support

Deploy cryptographic control for data access, including [customer-managed encryption keys](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/cmek?hl=en)

Cloud External Key Manager (EKM) enables customers to encrypt data in a variety of services with keys that are stored and managed in a third-party key management system deployed outside of Google’s infrastructure. Google Cloud continues to be the only cloud provider to enable customers to store and manage encryption keys for cloud-resident data outside the provider's infrastructure with customer’s control over decryption based on specific justifications, including government access requests.

[Key Access Justifications](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/control-access-to-gcp-data-with-key-access-justifications) greatly advances the control that GCP customers have over their data by giving customers a justification every time their externally hosted keys have to be used to decrypt data. [Signed Access Approval](https://cloud.google.com/cloud-provider-access-management/access-approval/docs/overview) (SAA) adds a layer of extra assurance that requires explicit customer consent for any administrative access to customer data or configurations.

Google Cloud’s [Confidential Computing portfolio](https://cloud.google.com/confidential-computing) is a breakthrough technology that allows customers to encrypt their most sensitive data in the cloud while in-use. [Ubiquitous Data Encryption](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/ubiquitous-data-encryption-on-google-cloud) further extends data protection by providing cryptographic protection for this data at-rest, in-transit, and in-use. The keys used to encrypt customer data outside of GCP using Cloud EKM are securely shared with applications operating within Confidential environments.

### Google Workspace

Our Google Workspace (including Workspace for Education) customers can choose to store their [covered data](https://support.google.com/a/answer/9223653?visit_id=637419430042474071-3052712775&rd=1) in Europe. Additionally, with Client-Side Encryption, we [offer](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/workspace/new-google-workspace-security-features) customers direct control of encryption keys and the identity service they choose to access those keys. With Client-Side Encryption, customer data is indecipherable to Google, while users can continue to take advantage of Google’s native web-based collaboration, access content on mobile devices, and share encrypted files externally. Client-Side Encryption is currently available in Public Beta for [Google Drive](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/workspace/new-google-workspace-security-features), Docs, Sheets, and Slides, and we plan to extend it to Gmail, Calendar and Meet. Additionally, customers can also benefit by choosing third party solutions that offer similar encryption capabilities with select Google Workspace services.

### Legal Basis for International Data Transfers

We [updated](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/compliance/google-cloud-approach-to-implementing-eu-sccs) our data processing terms for [GCP](https://cloud.google.com/terms/data-processing-terms) and [Google Workspace and Cloud Identity](https://workspace.google.com/terms/dpa_terms.html) to reflect various modules of the new [E.U. Standard Contractual Clauses](https://cloud.google.com/terms/sccs) (SCCs) approved by the European Commission on June 4, 2021, as well as separate U.K. SCCs.

Google Cloud plans to adopt the new E.U.-U.S. data transfer framework and offer it as a transfer solution to our cloud customers, as further detailed in our data processing terms.

### Advocacy and Additional Helpful Resources

We have adopted the [Trusted Cloud Principles](https://trustedcloudprinciples.com/principles/) with industry peers to demonstrate our commitments to protect the rights of our Google Cloud customers. We will continue to support the ongoing work of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development on government access to data and the negotiation of CLOUD Act Agreements — including between the U.S. and E.U. — as vehicles for surveillance reform.

We will continue to publish additional materials on our [Cloud Privacy Resource Center](https://cloud.google.com/privacy), such as our [whitepaper](https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/safeguards_for_international_data_transfers_with_google_cloud.pdf) on safeguards for international data transfers with Google Cloud.

Millions of organizations with users in Europe rely on our cloud services to run their businesses every day, and we remain steadfastly committed to helping them meet their regulatory requirements by maintaining a diverse set of compliance tools.

*1. Google Cloud: [Google Workspace](https://workspace.google.com/) (including [Google Workspace for Education](https://edu.google.com/intl/ALL_us/products/workspace-for-education/)) and [Google Cloud Platform](https://cloud.google.com/) (GCP)*
