# Department of Justice Issues a FedRAMP High ATO for Azure Government

![](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/azuregov/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/letter-avatar/5025aa712e85db6a2366225fedb3df79.svg)

[Matt Rathbun](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/azuregov/author/matt-rathbun)

The Department of Justice (DOJ) Justice Management Division (JMD) has issued two FedRAMP High ATOs for Azure Government. The DOJ performs critical services for U.S. Citizens with the [mission](https://www.justice.gov/about) “[t]o enforce the law and defend the interests of the United States according to the law; to ensure public safety against threats foreign and domestic; to provide federal leadership in preventing and controlling crime; to seek just punishment for those guilty of unlawful behavior; and to ensure fair and impartial administration of justice for all Americans.”

JMD is the principal organizational unit responsible for management and administrative support in the Department of Justice. Much of the work of this Division is internal facing and works to make sure that the infrastructure is in place so that all other components of the Department can complete the more visible Departmental work. Under the direction of the Assistant Attorney General for Administration (AAG/A), JMD provides Department-wide policy guidance to the Department’s offices, boards, divisions and, to a limited extent, its bureaus. The Division has four key areas of responsibility:

* Fiscal responsibility
* Human resources management
* Information resources and management
* Policy, management and planning

The authorizations will allow DOJ to take advantage of cloud-based core networking and application hosting environments to standardize cloud implementations for application owners within the organization. Having consistent implementations for individual mission owners within DOJ will streamline cloud adoption practices and security authorizations for future DOJ systems moving to Azure Government cloud.

By issuing the Azure Government ATO, DOJ can also take advantage of the cloud benefits provided by IaaS and PaaS capabilities. [Azure Site Recovery](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/services/site-recovery/) (ASR) allows streamlined migration options for customers migrating from on-premises datacenters to Azure Government. ASR automates the replication of virtual machines for disaster recovery scenarios, cloud migration, and replication for hybrid environments.

In addition to an Agency FedRAMP High ATO from DOJ, [Microsoft Azure Government](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/overview/clouds/government/) has also received a [FedRAMP High P-ATO](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/blog/azure-government-extends-lead-in-the-cloud-another-leap-in-fedramp-coverage/) from the Joint Authorization Board (JAB). [Microsoft Azure Government](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/overview/clouds/government/) leads the industry with 32 FedRAMP-approved services spanning both infrastructure-as-a-service and platform-as-a-service offerings. A complete list of the Azure services covered under the Azure Government FedRAMP High ATO can be found by visiting the [Microsoft Trust Center](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/TrustCenter/Compliance/FedRAMP).

Microsoft is committed to providing the most trusted, comprehensive cloud for mission-critical workloads so that our nearly 6 million government users across 7,000-plus federal, state and local organizations can achieve more in carrying out their mission-critical workloads. Please visit:

* [Microsoft](https://info.microsoft.com/GovernmentContactMe.html) to learn more
* [Azure Government](https://azuregov.microsoft.com/trial/azuregovtrial) to request a free trial
* [Check the facts: Not all clouds are created equal](https://enterprise.microsoft.com/en-us/industries/government/check-the-facts/)

To experience the power of Azure Government for your organization, sign up for an [Azure Government Trial](https://azuregov.microsoft.com/trial/azuregovtrial).

# Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP)

## FedRAMP overview

The US Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) was established in December 2011 to provide a standardized approach for assessing, monitoring, and authorizing cloud computing products and services under the Federal Information Security Management Act (FISMA), and to accelerate the adoption of secure cloud solutions by US federal agencies. Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) desiring to sell services to a federal agency can take three paths to demonstrate FedRAMP compliance:

* Earn a Provisional Authorization to Operate (P-ATO) from the FedRAMP Joint Authorization Board (JAB).
* Receive an Authorization to Operate (ATO) from a federal agency.
* Work independently to develop a CSP Supplied Package that meets program requirements.

Each of these paths requires an assessment by an independent third-party assessment organization (3PAO) that is accredited by the program and a stringent technical review by the FedRAMP Program Management Office (PMO).

FedRAMP is based on the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) [SP 800-53](https://csrc.nist.gov/Projects/risk-management/sp800-53-controls/release-search#/800-53) standard, augmented by FedRAMP controls and control enhancements. FedRAMP authorizations are granted at three impact levels based on the NIST [FIPS 199](https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/fips/199/final) guidelines — Low, Moderate, and High. These levels rank the impact that the loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability could have on an organization — Low (limited effect), Moderate (serious adverse effect), and High (severe or catastrophic effect). The number of controls in the corresponding baseline increases as the impact level increases, for example, FedRAMP Moderate baseline has 325 controls whereas FedRAMP High baseline has 421 controls.

The FedRAMP High authorization represents the highest bar for FedRAMP compliance. The FedRAMP Joint Authorization Board (JAB) is the primary governance and decision-making body for FedRAMP. Representatives from the Department of Defense (DoD), Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and General Services Administration (GSA) serve on the board. The board grants a P-ATO to cloud service offerings (CSO) that have demonstrated FedRAMP compliance. Once a P-ATO is granted, a CSP still requires an authorization (an ATO) from any government agency it works with. A government agency can use an existing P-ATO in its own security authorization process and rely on it as the basis for issuing an agency ATO that also meets FedRAMP requirements.

Note

FedRAMP is not a point-in-time certification or accreditation but an assessment and authorization program that comes with provisions for continuous monitoring to ensure that deployed security controls in a CSO remain effective in an evolving threat landscape and changes that occur in the system environment.

## Azure and FedRAMP

Both Azure and Azure Government maintain [FedRAMP High P-ATOs](https://marketplace.fedramp.gov/#!/product/azure-commercial-cloud/versus/azure-government-includes-dynamics-365) issued by the JAB in addition to more than 400 Moderate and High ATOs issued by individual federal agencies for the in-scope services. And while FedRAMP High authorization in the Azure public cloud will meet the needs of many US government customers, Azure Government provides additional customer assurances through controls that limit potential access to systems processing customer data to [screened US persons](/en-us/azure/azure-government/documentation-government-plan-security#screening).

For extra customer assistance, Microsoft provides the Azure Policy regulatory compliance built-in initiatives for Azure and Azure Government, which map to FedRAMP **compliance domains** and **controls**:

* Azure
  + [FedRAMP High Azure regulatory compliance built-in initiative](/en-us/azure/governance/policy/samples/fedramp-high)
  + [FedRAMP Moderate Azure regulatory compliance built-in initiative](/en-us/azure/governance/policy/samples/fedramp-moderate)
* Azure Government
  + [FedRAMP High Azure Government regulatory compliance built-in initiative](/en-us/azure/governance/policy/samples/gov-fedramp-high)
  + [FedRAMP Moderate Azure Government regulatory compliance built-in initiative](/en-us/azure/governance/policy/samples/gov-fedramp-moderate)

Regulatory compliance in Azure Policy provides built-in initiative definitions to view a list of controls and compliance domains based on responsibility – customer, Microsoft, or shared. For Microsoft-responsible controls, we provide extra audit result details based on third-party attestations and our control implementation details to achieve that compliance. Each FedRAMP control is associated with one or more Azure Policy definitions. These policies may help you [assess compliance](/en-us/azure/governance/policy/how-to/get-compliance-data) with the control; however, compliance in Azure Policy is only a partial view of your overall compliance status. Azure Policy helps to enforce organizational standards and assess compliance at scale. Through its compliance dashboard, it provides an aggregated view to evaluate the overall state of the environment, with the ability to drill down to more granular status.

## Applicability

* Azure
* Azure Government

## Services in scope

For a list of Microsoft online services in scope for the FedRAMP High P-ATO in Azure and Azure Government, see [Cloud services in audit scope](cloud-services-in-audit-scope).

## Office 365 and FedRAMP

For more information about Office 365 compliance, see [Office 365 FedRAMP documentation](/en-us/compliance/regulatory/offering-fedramp).

## Attestation documents

You can request Azure and Azure Government FedRAMP documentation directly from the [FedRAMP Marketplace](https://marketplace.fedramp.gov/#!/product/azure-commercial-cloud/versus/azure-government-includes-dynamics-365) by submitting a package access request form. You must have a .gov or .mil email address to access a FedRAMP security package directly from the FedRAMP Marketplace.

Azure Commercial System Security Plan (SSP) is available from the Service Trust Portal (STP) [FedRAMP reports](https://servicetrust.microsoft.com/viewpage/FedRAMP) section. You must sign in to access audit reports on the STP. You must have an existing subscription or free trial account in [Azure](https://azure.microsoft.com/free/) or [Azure Government](https://azure.microsoft.com/global-infrastructure/government/request/) to download audit documents. For more information, see [Get started with Microsoft Service Trust Portal](https://aka.ms/stphelp).

Select Azure and Azure Government FedRAMP documentation, including the System Security Plan (SSP), continuous monitoring reports, Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M), and so on, are available under NDA and pending access authorization from a restricted Service Trust Portal (STP) [FedRAMP reports](https://servicetrust.microsoft.com/viewpage/FedRAMP) section. Contact your Microsoft account representative for assistance.

## Azure penetration test reports

An independent third-party assessment organization (3PAO) that is accredited by FedRAMP conducts Azure penetration tests annually. The resulting reports are typically due in September for submission to the FedRAMP Joint Authorization Board (JAB). Once reviewed and approved by the FedRAMP JAB, penetration test reports are uploaded to the Service Trust Portal (STP) [Pen Tests and Security Assessments](https://servicetrust.microsoft.com/viewpage/PenTest) section. This process can take several months from report submission. Therefore, if you can't locate the Azure penetration test report for the current year, it's most likely still under review and pending approval. We aim to upload penetration test reports to the STP by December or shortly thereafter; however, this timeline can vary.

If any vulnerabilities are identified in penetration test reports, their resolution can be tracked via Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) submissions. Contact your Microsoft account representative for assistance with access to a restricted section of the STP from where you can download select FedRAMP documentation, including the POA&M files.

For penetration testing that Microsoft conducts routinely on the Azure cloud services platform, see *Live-site penetration testing* in [Security assurance processes and practices](/en-us/azure/azure-government/azure-secure-isolation-guidance#security-assurance-processes-and-practices). For penetration testing that you can conduct on your own cloud applications, see [Penetration testing](/en-us/azure/security/fundamentals/pen-testing).

## Frequently asked questions

**Which Azure regions are in scope for the FedRAMP High P-ATO?**   
 All Azure public regions in the United States are in scope for the Azure FedRAMP High P-ATO. Azure regions outside the United States aren't formally authorized by the FedRAMP JAB, and aren't in the FedRAMP High P-ATO scope. However, Azure security controls and operational processes are the same everywhere Azure runs. FedRAMP is based on the NIST SP 800-53 control baselines. All NIST SP 800-53 controls that support the Azure FedRAMP High P-ATO in the United States are also operational in other Azure regions outside the United States. Therefore, Azure customers outside the United States can count on the same control implementation details that pertain to the NIST SP 800-53 High control baseline.

**Which Azure Government regions are in scope for the FedRAMP High P-ATO?**   
 Azure Government regions US Gov Arizona, US Gov Texas, and US Gov Virginia are in scope for the Azure Government FedRAMP High P-ATO.

**Does Azure comply with the Federal Information Security Management Act (FISMA)?**   
 FISMA is a US federal law that requires US federal agencies and their partners to procure information systems and services only from organizations that adhere to FISMA requirements. Most agencies and their vendors that indicate that they are FISMA-compliant are referring to how they meet the controls identified in NIST SP 800-53. The FISMA process (but not the underlying standards) was replaced by FedRAMP in 2011. FedRAMP provides a standardized approach for security assessment, authorization, and continuous monitoring of cloud services.

**To whom does FedRAMP apply?**   
 FedRAMP is mandatory for federal agency cloud deployments and service models at the low, moderate, and high-risk impact levels. Any federal agency that wants to engage a CSP may be required to meet FedRAMP specifications. In addition, companies that employ cloud technologies in products or services used by the federal government may be required to obtain an ATO.

**Where does my agency start its own compliance effort?**   
 For an overview of the steps federal agencies must take to successfully navigate FedRAMP and meet its requirements, go to [Get Authorized: Agency Authorization](https://www.fedramp.gov/agency-authorization/).

**Can I use Azure FedRAMP compliance in my agency’s authorization process?**   
 Yes. You may use Azure or Azure Government FedRAMP High P-ATO as the foundation for any program or initiative that requires an ATO from a federal government agency. However, you need to achieve your own authorizations for components outside these services.

**Where can I get the Azure FedRAMP documentation?**   
 For links to audit documentation, see [Attestation documents](#attestation-documents). You must sign in to access audit reports on the Service Trust Portal (STP). For more information, see [Get started with Microsoft Service Trust Portal](https://aka.ms/stphelp). You must have an existing subscription or free trial account in [Azure](https://azure.microsoft.com/free/) or [Azure Government](https://azure.microsoft.com/global-infrastructure/government/request/) to download audit reports from the STP.

**What was the resolution of identified vulnerabilities and where is the latest Azure penetration test report?**   
 See [Azure penetration test reports](#azure-penetration-test-reports) for more information.

**What Azure Government services are covered by FedRAMP High P-ATO and in what regions?**   
 To find out what services are available in Azure Government, see [Products available by region](https://azure.microsoft.com/global-infrastructure/services/?products=all&regions=usgov-non-regional,us-dod-central,us-dod-east,usgov-arizona,usgov-texas,usgov-virginia&rar=true). For a list of services in scope for the FedRAMP High P-ATO, see [Cloud services in audit scope](cloud-services-in-audit-scope).

# Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP)

## FedRAMP overview

The US Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) was established in December 2011 to provide a standardized approach for assessing, monitoring, and authorizing cloud computing products and services under the Federal Information Security Management Act (FISMA), and to accelerate the adoption of secure cloud solutions by US federal agencies. Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) desiring to sell services to a federal agency can take three paths to demonstrate FedRAMP compliance:

* Earn a Provisional Authorization to Operate (P-ATO) from the FedRAMP Joint Authorization Board (JAB).
* Receive an Authorization to Operate (ATO) from a federal agency.
* Work independently to develop a CSP Supplied Package that meets program requirements.

Each of these paths requires an assessment by an independent third-party assessment organization (3PAO) that is accredited by the program and a stringent technical review by the FedRAMP Program Management Office (PMO).

FedRAMP is based on the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) [SP 800-53](https://csrc.nist.gov/Projects/risk-management/sp800-53-controls/release-search#/800-53) standard, augmented by FedRAMP controls and control enhancements. FedRAMP authorizations are granted at three impact levels based on the NIST [FIPS 199](https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/fips/199/final) guidelines — Low, Moderate, and High. These levels rank the impact that the loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability could have on an organization — Low (limited effect), Moderate (serious adverse effect), and High (severe or catastrophic effect). The number of controls in the corresponding baseline increases as the impact level increases, for example, FedRAMP Moderate baseline has 325 controls whereas FedRAMP High baseline has 421 controls.

The FedRAMP High authorization represents the highest bar for FedRAMP compliance. The FedRAMP Joint Authorization Board (JAB) is the primary governance and decision-making body for FedRAMP. Representatives from the Department of Defense (DoD), Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and General Services Administration (GSA) serve on the board. The board grants a P-ATO to cloud service offerings (CSO) that have demonstrated FedRAMP compliance. Once a P-ATO is granted, a CSP still requires an authorization (an ATO) from any government agency it works with. A government agency can use an existing P-ATO in its own security authorization process and rely on it as the basis for issuing an agency ATO that also meets FedRAMP requirements.

Note

FedRAMP is not a point-in-time certification or accreditation but an assessment and authorization program that comes with provisions for continuous monitoring to ensure that deployed security controls in a CSO remain effective in an evolving threat landscape and changes that occur in the system environment.

## Azure and FedRAMP

Both Azure and Azure Government maintain [FedRAMP High P-ATOs](https://marketplace.fedramp.gov/#!/product/azure-commercial-cloud/versus/azure-government-includes-dynamics-365) issued by the JAB in addition to more than 400 Moderate and High ATOs issued by individual federal agencies for the in-scope services. And while FedRAMP High authorization in the Azure public cloud will meet the needs of many US government customers, Azure Government provides additional customer assurances through controls that limit potential access to systems processing customer data to [screened US persons](/en-us/azure/azure-government/documentation-government-plan-security#screening).

For extra customer assistance, Microsoft provides the Azure Policy regulatory compliance built-in initiatives for Azure and Azure Government, which map to FedRAMP **compliance domains** and **controls**:

* Azure
  + [FedRAMP High Azure regulatory compliance built-in initiative](/en-us/azure/governance/policy/samples/fedramp-high)
  + [FedRAMP Moderate Azure regulatory compliance built-in initiative](/en-us/azure/governance/policy/samples/fedramp-moderate)
* Azure Government
  + [FedRAMP High Azure Government regulatory compliance built-in initiative](/en-us/azure/governance/policy/samples/gov-fedramp-high)
  + [FedRAMP Moderate Azure Government regulatory compliance built-in initiative](/en-us/azure/governance/policy/samples/gov-fedramp-moderate)

Regulatory compliance in Azure Policy provides built-in initiative definitions to view a list of controls and compliance domains based on responsibility – customer, Microsoft, or shared. For Microsoft-responsible controls, we provide extra audit result details based on third-party attestations and our control implementation details to achieve that compliance. Each FedRAMP control is associated with one or more Azure Policy definitions. These policies may help you [assess compliance](/en-us/azure/governance/policy/how-to/get-compliance-data) with the control; however, compliance in Azure Policy is only a partial view of your overall compliance status. Azure Policy helps to enforce organizational standards and assess compliance at scale. Through its compliance dashboard, it provides an aggregated view to evaluate the overall state of the environment, with the ability to drill down to more granular status.

## Applicability

* Azure
* Azure Government

## Services in scope

For a list of Microsoft online services in scope for the FedRAMP High P-ATO in Azure and Azure Government, see [Cloud services in audit scope](cloud-services-in-audit-scope).

## Office 365 and FedRAMP

For more information about Office 365 compliance, see [Office 365 FedRAMP documentation](/en-us/compliance/regulatory/offering-fedramp).

## Attestation documents

You can request Azure and Azure Government FedRAMP documentation directly from the [FedRAMP Marketplace](https://marketplace.fedramp.gov/#!/product/azure-commercial-cloud/versus/azure-government-includes-dynamics-365) by submitting a package access request form. You must have a .gov or .mil email address to access a FedRAMP security package directly from the FedRAMP Marketplace.

Azure Commercial System Security Plan (SSP) is available from the Service Trust Portal (STP) [FedRAMP reports](https://servicetrust.microsoft.com/viewpage/FedRAMP) section. You must sign in to access audit reports on the STP. You must have an existing subscription or free trial account in [Azure](https://azure.microsoft.com/free/) or [Azure Government](https://azure.microsoft.com/global-infrastructure/government/request/) to download audit documents. For more information, see [Get started with Microsoft Service Trust Portal](https://aka.ms/stphelp).

Select Azure and Azure Government FedRAMP documentation, including the System Security Plan (SSP), continuous monitoring reports, Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M), and so on, are available under NDA and pending access authorization from a restricted Service Trust Portal (STP) [FedRAMP reports](https://servicetrust.microsoft.com/viewpage/FedRAMP) section. Contact your Microsoft account representative for assistance.

## Azure penetration test reports

An independent third-party assessment organization (3PAO) that is accredited by FedRAMP conducts Azure penetration tests annually. The resulting reports are typically due in September for submission to the FedRAMP Joint Authorization Board (JAB). Once reviewed and approved by the FedRAMP JAB, penetration test reports are uploaded to the Service Trust Portal (STP) [Pen Tests and Security Assessments](https://servicetrust.microsoft.com/viewpage/PenTest) section. This process can take several months from report submission. Therefore, if you can't locate the Azure penetration test report for the current year, it's most likely still under review and pending approval. We aim to upload penetration test reports to the STP by December or shortly thereafter; however, this timeline can vary.

If any vulnerabilities are identified in penetration test reports, their resolution can be tracked via Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) submissions. Contact your Microsoft account representative for assistance with access to a restricted section of the STP from where you can download select FedRAMP documentation, including the POA&M files.

For penetration testing that Microsoft conducts routinely on the Azure cloud services platform, see *Live-site penetration testing* in [Security assurance processes and practices](/en-us/azure/azure-government/azure-secure-isolation-guidance#security-assurance-processes-and-practices). For penetration testing that you can conduct on your own cloud applications, see [Penetration testing](/en-us/azure/security/fundamentals/pen-testing).

## Frequently asked questions

**Which Azure regions are in scope for the FedRAMP High P-ATO?**   
 All Azure public regions in the United States are in scope for the Azure FedRAMP High P-ATO. Azure regions outside the United States aren't formally authorized by the FedRAMP JAB, and aren't in the FedRAMP High P-ATO scope. However, Azure security controls and operational processes are the same everywhere Azure runs. FedRAMP is based on the NIST SP 800-53 control baselines. All NIST SP 800-53 controls that support the Azure FedRAMP High P-ATO in the United States are also operational in other Azure regions outside the United States. Therefore, Azure customers outside the United States can count on the same control implementation details that pertain to the NIST SP 800-53 High control baseline.

**Which Azure Government regions are in scope for the FedRAMP High P-ATO?**   
 Azure Government regions US Gov Arizona, US Gov Texas, and US Gov Virginia are in scope for the Azure Government FedRAMP High P-ATO.

**Does Azure comply with the Federal Information Security Management Act (FISMA)?**   
 FISMA is a US federal law that requires US federal agencies and their partners to procure information systems and services only from organizations that adhere to FISMA requirements. Most agencies and their vendors that indicate that they are FISMA-compliant are referring to how they meet the controls identified in NIST SP 800-53. The FISMA process (but not the underlying standards) was replaced by FedRAMP in 2011. FedRAMP provides a standardized approach for security assessment, authorization, and continuous monitoring of cloud services.

**To whom does FedRAMP apply?**   
 FedRAMP is mandatory for federal agency cloud deployments and service models at the low, moderate, and high-risk impact levels. Any federal agency that wants to engage a CSP may be required to meet FedRAMP specifications. In addition, companies that employ cloud technologies in products or services used by the federal government may be required to obtain an ATO.

**Where does my agency start its own compliance effort?**   
 For an overview of the steps federal agencies must take to successfully navigate FedRAMP and meet its requirements, go to [Get Authorized: Agency Authorization](https://www.fedramp.gov/agency-authorization/).

**Can I use Azure FedRAMP compliance in my agency’s authorization process?**   
 Yes. You may use Azure or Azure Government FedRAMP High P-ATO as the foundation for any program or initiative that requires an ATO from a federal government agency. However, you need to achieve your own authorizations for components outside these services.

**Where can I get the Azure FedRAMP documentation?**   
 For links to audit documentation, see [Attestation documents](#attestation-documents). You must sign in to access audit reports on the Service Trust Portal (STP). For more information, see [Get started with Microsoft Service Trust Portal](https://aka.ms/stphelp). You must have an existing subscription or free trial account in [Azure](https://azure.microsoft.com/free/) or [Azure Government](https://azure.microsoft.com/global-infrastructure/government/request/) to download audit reports from the STP.

**What was the resolution of identified vulnerabilities and where is the latest Azure penetration test report?**   
 See [Azure penetration test reports](#azure-penetration-test-reports) for more information.

**What Azure Government services are covered by FedRAMP High P-ATO and in what regions?**   
 To find out what services are available in Azure Government, see [Products available by region](https://azure.microsoft.com/global-infrastructure/services/?products=all&regions=usgov-non-regional,us-dod-central,us-dod-east,usgov-arizona,usgov-texas,usgov-virginia&rar=true). For a list of services in scope for the FedRAMP High P-ATO, see [Cloud services in audit scope](cloud-services-in-audit-scope).

## Resources

* [Azure compliance documentation](/en-us/azure/compliance/)
* [Azure enables a world of compliance](https://azure.microsoft.com/resources/azure-enables-a-world-of-compliance/)
* [Microsoft 365 compliance offerings](/en-us/compliance/regulatory/offering-home)
* [Compliance on the Microsoft Trust Center](https://www.microsoft.com/trust-center/compliance/compliance-overview)
* [What is Azure Government](/en-us/azure/azure-government/documentation-government-welcome)?
* [Explore Azure Government](https://azure.microsoft.com/global-infrastructure/government/)
* [Microsoft government solutions](https://www.microsoft.com/industry/government)
* [FedRAMP documents and templates](https://www.fedramp.gov/documents-templates/)
* [NIST SP 800-53](https://csrc.nist.gov/Projects/risk-management/sp800-53-controls/release-search#/800-53) *Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations*

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Google Cloud documentation page provides a comprehensive guide to HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) compliance on Google Cloud. The guide is intended for security officers, compliance officers, IT administrators, and employees responsible for HIPAA implementation on Google Cloud, and covers HIPAA compliance for Google Cloud (with Google Workspace covered separately).

Key points:
- There is no official certification recognized by the US HHS for HIPAA compliance; compliance is a shared responsibility between the customer and Google.
- HIPAA requires compliance with the Security Rule, Privacy Rule, and Breach Notification Rule.
- Google will enter into Business Associate Agreements (BAAs) with customers as necessary under HIPAA.
- Customers must determine whether they are a Covered Entity or a Business Associate and whether they require a BAA with Google.
- While Google provides secure infrastructure for storing and processing Protected Health Information (PHI), customers are responsible for properly configuring and securing the environment and applications they build on top of Google Cloud.
- The Google Cloud BAA covers Google Cloud's entire infrastructure (all regions, zones, network paths, and points of presence) and a listed set of covered products.
- A unique feature is that the HIPAA BAA covers the entire infrastructure, not a set-aside portion, meaning customers are not restricted to a specific region—enabling multi-regional redundancy, scalability, and use of Preemptible VMs to reduce costs.
- Google Cloud offers HIPAA-compliant products at the same pricing available to all customers, including sustained use discounts (unlike other public clouds that charge more for HIPAA compliance).
- The guide includes a disclaimer stating it is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice.
- The page was last updated 2026-08-11 UTC.

All federal agency cloud deployments (except certain on-premises private clouds) must meet FedRAMP requirements at Low, Moderate, or High risk impact levels.

It implements a Software Defined Community Cloud rather than physical separation.

Google Workspace Business and Enterprise editions have built-in security controls for FedRAMP High compliance. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Google Cloud documentation page provides implementation guidance for FedRAMP (Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program) compliance on Google Cloud. The document is designed for security, compliance, and IT personnel responsible for FedRAMP implementation and compliance.

**Key Points:**

1. **About FedRAMP**: FedRAMP is a US federal program established to standardize security assessment, authorization, and continuous monitoring of cloud products across government agencies. Congress codified it in 2022. In 2025, FedRAMP launched the "FedRAMP 20x" initiative to adopt automated monitoring and move away from manually compiled documentation. FedRAMP is based on NIST SP 800-53, with impact levels (Low, Moderate, High). The FedRAMP Moderate baseline has 325 controls, while the High baseline has 421 controls.

2. **Google Cloud FedRAMP Authorization**: The FedRAMP Board (formerly JAB, including CIOs from DoD, DHS, and GSA) has issued a FedRAMP High Provisional Authority to Operate (P-ATO) to Google Cloud and its underlying Google Common Infrastructure (GCI). Following FedRAMP 20x improvements, the GSA became the authorizing agency for Google Cloud. The FedRAMP Moderate baseline is a subset of High, so High authorization covers all Moderate requirements.

3. **Services in Audit Scope**: Google Cloud's FedRAMP High P-ATO covers more than 150 cloud services, including ML/AI services (Generative AI on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Model Garden with 200+ LLMs). Individual LLMs are not independently FedRAMP-authorized; the cloud services hosting them are. Google-managed models (Gemini family, Anthropic partners) support Provisioned Throughput in FedRAMP High environments.

4. **Achieving FedRAMP ATO**: The path is the Rev. 5 Agency ATO, requiring collaboration with Google and a third-party assessment organization (3PAO). For FedRAMP High compliance, users must use Data Boundary for FedRAMP High via Assured Workloads. Google provides a Customer Responsibility Matrix (CRM) and System Security Plan (SSP) under NDA.

5. **Guidance and Automation**: Google provides service-specific Control Mapping Guides (CMGs) for services including BigQuery, Compute Engine, IAM, Cloud Logging, and Generative AI on Agent Platform. FedRAMP High implementation guides cover service-specific APIs for Apigee, GKE, Cloud Storage, Cloud KMS, and others—all under NDA.

6. **Data Residency and SA-9(5)**: Data residency requirements apply only to FedRAMP High baseline. Google offers data residency contractual commitments for regional services, ensuring FedRAMP High data stays in US regions. In July 2020, FedRAMP updated the SA-9(5) control restricting high-impact data to the US. Some Google Cloud services were flagged in the FedRAMP Marketplace with an asterisk as not meeting SA-9(5); Google is actively pursuing resubmission to remove these clarifications.

7. **Digital Sovereignty and Encryption**: Google emphasizes digital sovereignty via Assured Workloads and software-defined community cloud. Recommended mitigations include customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) via Cloud KMS, Cloud External Key Manager (Cloud EKM), Cloud HSM (FIPS 140 validated), envelope encryption, and data encryption in transit (MACsec at Layer 2, TLS at application layer, Cloud VPN for on-premises connections). FIPS 140 validation is required for FedRAMP authorization (SC-13 control).

8. **Key Assurances**: Google personnel cannot access unencrypted customer key material; decrypted key material can't be exported or viewed; HSMs are FIPS 140 validated; Google system operators are prevented from accessing customer key material.

The document concludes with a comprehensive "What's next" section linking to FedRAMP and DoD compliance scope, network configuration guides, the FedRAMP Marketplace entry (FR1805751477), FedRAMP 20x initiative, and NIST standards. Last reviewed 2026-02-10 UTC.
</summary>

- **Data Subject Rights:** Google will enable Customer to access, rectify, restrict processing, and export Customer Data. Google's Cloud Data Protection Team will refer data subject requests to Customer and not respond without authorization.

- **Subprocessors:** Customer authorizes Google's engagement of Subprocessors. --- SOURCE 15: Last updated January 2023 ---
URL: https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/abs_googlecloud_mapping

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is Google Cloud's mapping of its security and compliance controls against the Monetary Authority of Singapore's (MAS) "Guideline on Outsourcing" control objectives, organized into three categories: A) Govern the Cloud, B) Design and Secure the Cloud, and C) Run the Cloud. It is last updated January 2023.

The document presents a table format pairing MAS guideline control objectives with Google Cloud's corresponding controls and notes whether each requirement is primarily the customer's responsibility or is satisfied by Google.

KEY POINTS BY CATEGORY:

**A) Govern the Cloud**
- Most governance requirements (oversight of cloud outsourcing, accountability, staff skills, empowered interface, compliance, testing, remediation, billing) are primarily customer responsibilities.
- Google provides: external security documentation and whitepapers, an internal ISMS certified under ISO 27001, SLAs publicly available, audits/access commitments under the Cloud Data Processing Addendum and Financial Services Addendum (FSCMA), an incident management process, Cloud Console for resource management/diagnostics, and cost management tools (cloud.google.com/cost-management).
- Google Cloud holds third-party certifications including MTCS Singapore Standard 584 Tier 3, ISO 27001, ISO 27017, ISO 27018, and SOC 1/2/3 (SSAE 16/ISAE 3402 Type II).

**B) Design and Secure the Cloud**
- Google offers financial services-specific solutions (cloud.google.com/solutions/financial-services/).
- Data isolation: Google logically isolates each customer's data; data centers use electronic card key access linked to system alarms with logged access attempts.
- Code development follows a structured, peer-reviewed release process with purpose-built code analysis tools and continuous post-production testing.
- Redundancy is embedded in architecture; essential hardware is hot swappable; status dashboards at status.cloud.google.com.
- IAM tools (Cloud IAM, Identity) provide centralized access management; defense-in-depth techniques documented.
- Encryption: Google maintains encryption at rest for customer data and security measures for data in transit; provides encryption whitepapers (Encryption in Transit, Encryption at Rest, G Suite Encryption).
- Key management: Google provides controls to manage encryption keys through their lifecycle; capabilities to manage keys on behalf of tenants.
- Third-party audits: SOC 1/2/3, ISO 27001, ISO 27017/27018, PCI-DSS, HIPAA; Access Transparency provides audit logs for GCP.
- Physical security: formal access procedures, 2-factor authentication for all production resources, need-to-know access restrictions, asset tracking via barcodes/asset tags from acquisition to destruction.
- Data retention: customers manage their own policies using storage features or Google Vault (G Suite).
- Penetration testing: Google performs fuzz testing, penetration testing, and vulnerability scanning; maintains a Vulnerability Rewards Program.
- Incident management: network and host-based detection tools, automated log collection, rigorous incident response process; Data Incident Response Whitepaper available.

**C) Run the Cloud**
- Change management: structured peer-reviewed code development and release process; customers can bring their own change/configuration management tools.
- Event management: rigorous incident management process prioritizing events that directly impact customers.
- Intrusion detection involves: (1) tightly controlling attack surface, (2) intelligent detection at data entry points, (3) automated remediation of dangerous situations.
- Patching: Google operates a homogeneous machine environment with custom software to minimize exposure; patches as quickly as vulnerabilities are addressed rather than on a scheduled basis.
- Capacity management: budget approvals and internal SLAs govern provisioning; customers can monitor service consumption.
- Disaster recovery: Google replicates data over multiple systems, maintains a Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Plan aligned with Alphabet Inc.'s plans, provides uptime metrics and certifications (ISO 27001, ISO 27018).

Across nearly all control objectives, the document emphasizes that it is "Primarily customer responsibility to satisfy this requirement" for configuration, compliance with jurisdiction-specific requirements, data retention, access management, and change management, while Google provides the underlying infrastructure, certifications, documentation, and tools.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Google provides comprehensive external documentation and whitepapers detailing our security infrastructure and operational model. Google also maintains an internal ISMS and evidence of its effectiveness is provided via ISO 27001 certification."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: How to Implement GDPR Data Processing Compliance Controls in Google Cloud ---
URL: https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-17-how-to-implement-gdpr-data-processing-compliance-controls-in-google-cloud/view

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a technical blog post from OneUptime (an open-source observability platform) providing a practical guide to implementing GDPR data processing compliance controls on Google Cloud. Published by Nawaz Dhandala on Feb 17, 2026, and technically validated on May 28, 2026.

The article covers the following key areas:

**Google's Data Processing Agreement (DPA):** A prerequisite before processing EU personal data on Google Cloud. Covers Google as data processor, sub-processor transparency, data deletion upon contract termination, and assistance with data subject requests. Accepted through Google Cloud Console under Organization Settings.

**Data Residency and Location Controls:** While GDPR doesn't strictly require EU data residency, many organizations choose it as a compliance simplification. The guide provides CLI commands for creating resources in EU regions (Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Cloud SQL) and enforcing EU-only locations via Organization Policies using the constraint `gcp.resourceLocations` with allowed value `in:eu-locations`.

**Personal Data Classification with Cloud DLP:** Use Cloud DLP inspection jobs to identify personal data (PERSON_NAME, EMAIL_ADDRESS, PHONE_NUMBER, DATE_OF_BIRTH, STREET_ADDRESS, IP_ADDRESS, CREDIT_CARD_NUMBER, IBAN_CODE, VAT_NUMBER) across data stores, including reusable inspection templates.

**Data Subject Rights Implementation:**
- Article 15 (Right of Access): Python code to export all personal data for a user across multiple BigQuery tables to GCS.
- Article 17 (Right to Erasure): Python/BigQuery code to delete user data across tables, with audit logging and consideration of crypto-shredding for large-scale data.
- Article 20 (Data Portability): Export data in machine-readable formats (CSV/JSON) using `bq extract` and query-based exports.

**Consent Management:** BigQuery schema for tracking consent records (consent_type, consent_given, timestamps, source, version, IP address) and SQL queries to verify active consent before processing.

**Data Retention:** Automated retention policies using BigQuery partition expiration (e.g., 730 days) and scheduled cleanup queries.

**Breach Detection:** Enable Event Threat Detection via SCC, create high-priority monitoring alerts for unusual data access (BigQuery scanned_bytes > 10GB threshold), and SCC notifications for DATA_EXFILTRATION and ANOMALOUS_ACCESS findings.

**DPIA Support:** Export Cloud Asset Inventory, IAM policies, and data flow logs (BigQuery InsertJob activity) for Data Protection Impact Assessment documentation.

**Terraform Infrastructure:** Terraform configuration for GDPR-compliant infrastructure including EU-only location org policies, EU-located BigQuery datasets with KMS encryption and partition expiration.

The article concludes that GDPR compliance requires both technical controls (well-supported by Google Cloud) and organizational processes (consent management, data subject request handling, DPIA workflows). It recommends starting with data classification to understand where personal data lives.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"GDPR compliance on Google Cloud requires a combination of technical controls and organizational processes. The technical side - encryption, access controls, data residency, and logging - is well-supported by Google Cloud services. The organizational side - consent management, data subject request handling, and DPIA processes - requires building workflows on top of those services. Start with data classification to understand what personal data you have and where it lives, then layer on the controls from there."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: GDPR Data Breach Notification: The 72-Hour Rule | ISpectra ---
URL: https://ispectratechnologies.com/hub/gdpr/gdpr-data-breach-notification.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a GDPR educational guide published by ISpectra Technologies (a cybersecurity and compliance firm serving 200+ enterprises) focusing on the GDPR Data Breach Notification 72-Hour Rule. The guide explains that a qualifying personal data breach must be reported to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of it (not after investigation is complete), unless the breach is unlikely to pose a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms.

Key content points:
- A personal data breach is broader than a hack, defined as a security breach leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, or unauthorized disclosure/access to personal data (e.g., lost laptops, missent emails, ransomware, unauthorized employee access).
- Three breach types: confidentiality (unauthorized disclosure/access), integrity (unauthorized alteration), and availability (loss of access/destruction); a single incident can involve multiple types (e.g., ransomware is often both availability and confidentiality).
- When risk to individuals is high, affected persons must be notified without undue delay in clear language (e.g., advise password changes, fraud awareness).
- Regulator notification must describe: nature of breach, categories and approximate number of affected individuals/records, likely consequences, measures taken/proposed, and a contact point (e.g., DPO).
- Phased notification is permitted — report what you know within 72 hours and provide further details as available.
- Processors must notify controllers without undue delay; the controller meets the 72-hour deadline.
- Every breach must be documented in a breach register (facts, effects, action taken), regardless of notifiability.
- Risk assessment determines whether to notify regulator, individuals, both, or neither; decisions not to notify must be justifiable.
- The 72-hour clock starts upon "awareness" — interpreted broadly once there is reasonable certainty a security incident compromised personal data, not when investigation completes.
- Common breach mistakes: failing to recognize an incident as a breach, starting the clock too late, missing the window while investigating, failing to notify individuals at high risk, and not documenting non-notified breaches.
- ISpectra offers services to build breach response plans, set up detection/escalation, prepare notification templates, run tabletop exercises, and maintain breach registers. The page includes an FAQ section and links to other GDPR Hub resources (complete guide, requirements, fines, ongoing compliance, controller vs processor, RoPA).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"When personal data is compromised, GDPR imposes one of its most time-pressured obligations: a qualifying breach must be reported to your supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of it."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Data Breach Notification Clause: Timelines & Drafting ---
URL: https://www.contractken.com/glossary/data-breach-notification-clause

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a comprehensive glossary entry on "Data Breach Notification Clause" from ContractKen's Contract Clauses Central repository, aimed at legal professionals reviewing and drafting contracts.

**Definition and Core Elements:**
A data breach notification clause is the contractual mechanism allocating the obligation to report, investigate, and coordinate response to security incidents affecting personal data. It typically appears in data processing agreements (controller-processor), master services agreements, or cybersecurity addenda. The clause addresses four core elements: (1) definition of a reportable incident, (2) notification trigger and timeline, (3) minimum content and method of notification, and (4) allocation of cooperation obligations.

**Key Regulatory Frameworks:**
- GDPR Article 33 requires controllers to notify supervisory authorities within 72 hours of awareness; Article 34 requires individual notification for high-risk breaches
- HIPAA Breach Notification Rule (45 CFR 164.400-414) requires 60-day notice to individuals, HHS, and media (for breaches affecting 500+ residents)
- All 50 U.S. states, DC, and Puerto Rico have breach notification statutes, with timelines ranging from 30 days (Texas) to 90 days (several states)

**Why It Matters:**
- The Identity Theft Resource Center reported 3,205 publicly disclosed data compromises in 2023 (78% increase over 2022), affecting over 353 million victim notices
- IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2024: global average cost USD 4.88 million; U.S. average USD 9.36 million; healthcare at USD 9.77 million; financial services at USD 6.08 million
- Notification-related costs alone average 35-40% of total breach costs
- CCPA/CPRA private right of action provides statutory damages of USD 100-750 per consumer

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Google Cloud documentation page (last updated June 2026) explains Google's Data Incident Response Process for protecting customer data in Google Cloud. It defines a data incident per the Cloud Data Processing Addendum as "a breach of Google's security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to, Customer Data on systems managed by or otherwise controlled by Google." Unsuccessful login attempts, pings, port scans, and denial of service attacks do not qualify as data incidents.

The incident response program involves expert teams including specialized incident response teams (including a machine-learning incident response team), product engineering, site reliability engineering, cloud security, digital forensics, detection and response, legal counsel, security response operations, privacy and trust response, trust and safety, and Cloud Customer Care. An incident commander is designated to coordinate response and assembles a response team.

The response process follows seven main steps: (1) Identification - detection via automated network/system log analysis, behavioral anomaly detection, penetration tests, internal code reviews, privileged access monitoring, and Google's vulnerability reward program, with AI-powered smart alert triaging; (2) Reporting; (3) Coordination/Triage - severity assessment based on potential harm, nature of incident, data type affected, service impact, and incident status; (4) Response team engagement; (5) Resolution - investigation, containment and recovery, and communication (including customer notification); (6) Closure - lessons learned and post-mortem analysis; and (7) Continuous improvement - program development and prevention.

AI is used throughout the process: machine-learning models analyze alert signals and correlate events during identification; AI agents suggest resolutions during investigation (strictly limited to suggestions); and during resolution, AI models are prohibited from executing commands directly—they generate structured action payloads requiring human-in-the-loop confirmation. All AI actions are recorded in immutable audit logs.

Customer notifications are sent via Essential Contacts and the Google Admin console, using @google.com email addresses from various senders. Notifications include affected services/projects, incident description, detection time, unique incident identifier, and links to resources. Customers should configure incident response group emails, grant the Advisory Notifications Viewer (roles/advisorynotifications.viewer) IAM role, and create Cloud Monitoring alerts.

Google aligns its incident response with regulatory frameworks including EU's Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) and Network and Information Systems Directive 2.0 (NIS2), and products undergo certification for ISO-27017, ISO-27018, ISO-27001, PCI-DSS, SOC 2, and FedRAMP. --- SOURCE 14: Overview of Assured Workloads ---
URL: https://docs.cloud.google.com/assured-workloads/docs/overview

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Google Cloud documentation page provides an overview of Assured Workloads, a service that enables organizations in the private and public sectors to configure a sovereign data and access boundary with residency, access, and personnel controls for sensitive workloads in the cloud. The service allows users to apply predefined control packages to folders to simplify management and configuration of regulated workloads while maintaining the scale, cost, and service availability benefits of commercial cloud infrastructure.

**Use cases:** Organizations with strict regulations for data storage, key management, and access (financial services, healthcare, governmental bodies); organizations that must store data within certain regions/countries; and organizations that must control Google Cloud personnel access to their data.

**Key capabilities:**
- **Control packages** (foundation for compliance enforcement) available in three types: regional data boundaries, regulatory data boundaries, and Sovereign Controls by Partners.
- **Regional data boundaries** restrict resource storage to specified geographic regions (e.g., EU Data Boundary restricts to EU-only regions).
- **Regulatory data boundaries** address specific compliance requirements including CJIS, FedRAMP Moderate/High, Healthcare and Life Sciences Controls (HIPAA/HITRUST), IL2/IL4/IL5, ITAR, and IRS Publication 1075.
- **Sovereign Controls by Partners** lets users use a local, trusted partner to manage encryption keys, access justification, and audits.
- **Personnel access control** via Assured Support (available with Enhanced or Premium Support), requiring Google support personnel to adhere to geographical and background check requirements (e.g., FedRAMP High requires US-located personnel with enhanced background checks).
- **Key management** controls vary by package — ITAR requires customer-managed encryption keys (CMEKs) with separate key management projects; support also includes Google-owned/managed keys (FIPS-140-2), Cloud EKM, and key import.
- **Workload updates** allow evaluation and maintenance of control package configurations, applying upgrades when newer versions are available.
- **Violation monitoring** tracks organization policy constraint violations and resource violations, with email notification options.

**Related access control services:** Access Approval (customer approval before Google personnel access), Access Transparency (logs of Google personnel activity), and Key Access Justifications (approve/deny key access requests).

**Control package renaming notice (effective June 2025):** Control package names in the console and APIs changed as of June 2025, reflected in the ComplianceRegime enums used in the Assured Workloads API. Only names changed, not underlying functionality. Examples include: "EU Data Boundary" became "EU Regions," "US Data Boundary" became "US Regions," "Data Boundary for ITAR" became "International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR)," and various "Regions" names replaced previous naming conventions. A complete mapping table of old to new names is provided.

The page also links to pricing information, available control packages, supported products, a free trial program, and Audit Manager for environment auditing. Last updated 2026-07-17 UTC.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Assured Workloads enables organizations in the private and public sectors to configure a sovereign data and access boundary with residency, access, and personnel controls for sensitive workloads in the cloud."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 15: Assured Workloads in Google Cloud Platform ---
URL: https://www.rkon.com/articles/assured-workloads-in-google-cloud-platform

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from RKON (a Chicago-based technology and IT services company) provides a comprehensive overview of Google Cloud Platform's (GCP) Assured Workloads service, which applies control packages to GCP folders to support regulatory, compliance, or data residency requirements. The service restricts folders and projects to only approved GCP products and regions, monitors resources, and alerts when something becomes non-compliant.

Key compliance control packages offered include CJIS, FedRAMP High and Moderate, HIPAA (Preview), HITRUST (Preview), DOD IL 2, 4, and 5, and ITAR. Country/region-specific data residency options include Australia, Brazil, Canada, Chile, EU, India, Indonesia, Israel, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, Saudi Arabia, Switzerland (Preview), Taiwan, UK, and US.

Two primary use cases are highlighted: (1) residency requirements—ensuring data stays within a specific region or country (e.g., the Australia control package restricts to ~45 products hosted in Australian data centers), and (2) compliance requirements—ensuring only authorized services are used (e.g., FedRAMP-authorized services only for government cloud purchases).

The implementation process involves 6 steps: analyzing pros/cons, designing architecture (Assured Workloads cannot be applied to existing folders), creating the Assured Workload folder (which automatically enables Access Transparency), creating sub-folders/projects, deploying the application, and configuring monitoring for violation notifications.

Pros: ensures only approved services run, ensures data residency, free unless Assured Support is needed, simpler architecture for regulated services, and automated monitoring of violations. Cons: many GCP products unavailable in Assured Workload folders, Assured Support requires Premium Tier (adds 20% to service costs), and migration difficulty since it must be applied at folder creation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Google Cloud Platform's (GCP) Assured Workloads provides a way for control packages to be applied to support meeting regulatory, compliance or data residency requirements.

--- SOURCE 1: HIPAA - Compliance | Google Cloud ---
URL: https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/hipaa-compliance

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Google Cloud compliance documentation page about HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996). The page explains that HIPAA is a federal law establishing data privacy and security requirements for organizations safeguarding protected health information (PHI), including "covered entities" and "business associates."

Key points covered:
- Customers subject to HIPAA who want to use Google Cloud products with PHI must review and accept Google's Business Associate Agreement (BAA).
- The Google Cloud BAA covers Google Cloud's entire infrastructure (all regions, zones, network paths, and points of presence) and aligns with Google's ISO/IEC 27001, 27017, and 27018 certifications and SOC 2 report.
- Google Cloud services in scope for HIPAA include: Google Cloud (with Assured Workloads Healthcare & Life Sciences offerings), Google Workspace, Chronicle, and Looker (original).
- Related documentation includes the Google Cloud HIPAA overview guide, HIPAA-aligned project solution guides, and the Google Workspace and Cloud Identity HIPAA Implementation Guide.

FAQ highlights:
1. The BAA allows covered entities and business associates to enter into an agreement governing PHI processing through Google Cloud; organizations should contact their account managers to execute a BAA.
2. Having a BAA is NOT sufficient for full HIPAA compliance — the covered entity is responsible for building a HIPAA compliant solution using approved Google Cloud services and implementing compliance controls.
3. The BAA is not subject to modification.

The page also links to relevant HIPAA rules (Privacy Rule, Security Rule, Breach Notification Rule) and related compliance offerings (ISO/IEC 27001, 27017, 27018, SOC 2).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) is a federal law that establishes data privacy and security requirements for organizations that are charged with safeguarding individuals' protected health information (PHI)."

--- SOURCE 2: HIPAA Compliance on Google Cloud | GCP Security ---
URL: https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/hipaa

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Google Cloud documentation page provides a comprehensive guide to HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) compliance on Google Cloud. The guide is intended for security officers, compliance officers, IT administrators, and employees responsible for HIPAA implementation on Google Cloud, and covers HIPAA compliance for Google Cloud (with Google Workspace covered separately).

Key points:
- There is no official certification recognized by the US HHS for HIPAA compliance; compliance is a shared responsibility between the customer and Google.
- HIPAA requires compliance with the Security Rule, Privacy Rule, and Breach Notification Rule.
- Google will enter into Business Associate Agreements (BAAs) with customers as necessary under HIPAA.
- Customers must determine whether they are a Covered Entity or a Business Associate and whether they require a BAA with Google.
- While Google provides secure infrastructure for storing and processing Protected Health Information (PHI), customers are responsible for properly configuring and securing the environment and applications they build on top of Google Cloud.
- The Google Cloud BAA covers Google Cloud's entire infrastructure (all regions, zones, network paths, and points of presence) and a listed set of covered products.
- A unique feature is that the HIPAA BAA covers the entire infrastructure, not a set-aside portion, meaning customers are not restricted to a specific region—enabling multi-regional redundancy, scalability, and use of Preemptible VMs to reduce costs.
- Google Cloud offers HIPAA-compliant products at the same pricing available to all customers, including sustained use discounts (unlike other public clouds that charge more for HIPAA compliance).
- The guide includes a disclaimer stating it is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice.
- The page was last updated 2026-08-11 UTC.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Using Google Cloud in GxP Systems ---
URL: https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/gxp_systems_gcp_whitepaper

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Google Cloud whitepaper (January 2023) titled "Using Google Cloud in GxP Systems" that explains how life science organizations can use Google Cloud to build GxP-aligned IT environments and comply with FDA electronic records requirements under 21 CFR Part 11 and its global equivalents.

**Key Topics Covered:**

**GxP Background:** GxP refers to "good practice" regulations covering medical products. In the US, these include GMP (21 CFR Parts 210/211 for drugs), QSR (21 CFR Part 820 for medical devices), GLP (21 CFR Part 58), GCP, and GDP. The paper focuses on how Google Cloud can serve as an element of customers' GxP compliance systems.

**Shared Responsibility Model:** Google is responsible for securing infrastructure; customers are responsible for securing their data. Responsibilities vary based on whether customers use IaaS (Compute Engine), PaaS (App Engine), or SaaS (G Suite) services.

**Electronic Records Requirements (Part 11 Compliance):** The paper details how Google Cloud supports electronic record and signature requirements across five key areas:
- **Data Retention:** Cloud Object Lifecycle Management, Nearline/Coldline storage options, BigQuery and Cloud Bigtable expiration automation
- **Identity & Access Management:** Cloud IAM, credential rotation, MFA/2-step verification, Cloud Key Management Service
- **Data Security & Audit Trail:** Cloud Audit Logs (immutable logs for Admin Activity, Data Access, System Events), Cloud Logging, encryption by default for data at rest, custom encryption key management
- **Data Ownership:** Customers own their data; Google accesses it only for contractual/legal obligations; least-privilege access for Google employees
- **Physical/Network/Application Security:** Layered data center security (biometrics, laser intrusion detection, fewer than 1% of Google employees enter data centers), VPC Service Controls, Shared VPC networks, Web Security Scanner, Cloud Endpoints, Apigee

**Validation and Infrastructure Qualification:** Cloud resources can be provisioned via Cloud Console, Cloud Deployment Manager, Hashicorp Terraform, or RESTful APIs. Deployment Manager Manifests document requirements and actual builds to support infrastructure qualification. Change management can be controlled through Cloud IAM, Security Command Center, and the operations suite. Incident response follows four phases: Identification, Coordination, Resolution, and Continuous improvement.

**Satisfying GxP Requirements:** The paper maps Google Cloud capabilities to GMP/QS requirements including management responsibilities (Cloud IAM, VPC Service Controls, Identity-Aware Proxy), personnel training (Google Cloud trainings and certifications), records and reports (Cloud Audit Logs, Cloud Logging), quality audits (operations suite, Forseti Security), purchasing controls, and supplier evaluations.

**Certifications & Compliance:** Google Cloud undergoes independent third-party audits against ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27017, ISO/IEC 27018, SOC 2 and SOC 3, plus participates in FedRAMP, HITRUST CSF, BSI C5, and MTCS frameworks. For FDA regulatory submissions, Google provides publicly-available documentation; confidential documentation can be marked as confidential under 21 CFR Part 20.

**HIPAA Compliance:** Customers subject to HIPAA must review and accept Google's Business Associate Agreement (BAA). HHS does not recognize formal HIPAA certification, but Google undergoes independent audits based on global standards encompassing HIPAA requirements. HIPAA compliance is a shared responsibility.

**Conclusion:** Life science organizations can leverage Google Cloud to streamline product development, execute and track quality manufacturing processes, and enable a robust software development lifecycle as part of compliance efforts.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"While the responsibility for GxP compliance ultimately lies with our life science customers, our shared responsibility model helps customers allocate resources more effectively by reducing the amount of effort needed to develop and maintain an IT environment."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/soc-1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Google Cloud documents the SOC 1 (Service and Organization Controls) compliance framework for Google Cloud and Google Workspace services. SOC 1 reports are based on the AICPA's SSAE 18 standard, which evaluates a service organization's internal controls relevant to financial reporting. Google Cloud undergoes regular third-party audits conducted by independent auditors Ernst & Young LLP and Coalfire.

Key details include:
- SOC 1 reports are available via the Compliance Reports Manager and are issued quarterly (Type II reports) for core Google Cloud and Google Workspace services.
- Google Cloud only issues SOC 1 Type II reports (covering design and operating effectiveness over a period of time), not Type I reports (which cover design at a specific point in time).
- Additional SOC 1 Type II reports for a small subset of products (Bare Metal Solution, BigQuery Omni, Google Cloud NetApp Volumes, and Google Cloud VMware Engine) are issued semi-annually or annually and obtained via sales or support.
- Bridge letters, which attest to material changes or issues in the internal control environment between the end of the most recent SOC report and a customer's period end date, are issued monthly and available on Compliance Reports Manager for core reports. Bridge letters cover look-back periods such as November 1 to December 31 to extend a report ending October 31.

The page provides an extensive list of Google Cloud services in scope for SOC 1, organized by category: AI/ML, API Management, Compute, Data Analytics, Databases, Developer Tools, Healthcare and Life Sciences, Hybrid and Multi-cloud, Management Tools, Media and Gaming, Migration, Networking, Operations, Security and Identity, Storage, Firebase, and Other (including Cloud Billing, Earth Engine, Google Cloud Marketplace, and Google Cloud VMware Engine). Also included are Google Workspace products (Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, Google Meet, Google Chat, Google Docs, and more), various APIs and developer offerings, and Google Workspace Admin SDK APIs.

Customers can request SOC 1 reports via the Compliance Reports Manager, and potential customers can contact sales for more information.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Google Cloud regularly undergoes third-party audits for our products, systems, and infrastructure related to this standard. The SOC 1 reports are generated by an objective third party attesting to a set of assertions made by Google Cloud about its controls."

--- SOURCE 1: How to Enforce Data Sovereignty with Google Cloud Regions ---
URL: https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-17-how-to-enforce-data-sovereignty-with-google-cloud-regions-and-organization-policies/view

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a OneUptime blog post (by Nawaz Dhandala, Feb 17, 2026, technically validated May 28, 2026) titled "How to Enforce Data Sovereignty with Google Cloud Regions." It provides a comprehensive guide for enforcing data sovereignty requirements on Google Cloud using organization policies, resource location constraints, and monitoring.

Key content:
- Data sovereignty laws (GDPR, LGPD, India, Russia) require data to stay within specific geographic boundaries.
- GCP resources exist in regions/zones; a resource's location reflects where its data is stored.
- Step-by-step guide:
  1. Define location requirements by mapping regulatory needs to GCP regions (e.g., EU Customer PII → europe-west1/3/4 for GDPR; US Financial Data → us-central1/us-east1/us-east4 for SOX).
  2. Apply resource location restrictions using the `gcp.resourceLocations` organization policy constraint (at organization, folder, or project level), using listPolicy with allowedValues like "in:eu-locations" or specific regions.
  3. Restrict service-specific locations for BigQuery (--location=EU), Cloud Storage (e.g., europe-west1, with retention policies), and Cloud SQL (--region=europe-west1).
  4. Prevent data replication to wrong regions via resource location constraints and service-specific configs (e.g., Spanner EU-only multi-region config `eur3`).
  5. Set up custom organization policies for specific controls (e.g., custom.bigquery.requireEuLocation constraint requiring BigQuery datasets in EU multi-region).
  6. Monitor for compliance violations using Google Cloud Asset Inventory (SearchAllResourcesRequest) to scan compute, storage, BigQuery, and SQL resources outside allowed regions.
  7. Automate remediation via Cloud Asset Inventory Pub/Sub notifications that tag non-compliant resources and alert security teams.
- For stronger guarantees, use Assured Workloads with EU compliance regime (`eu-regions-and-support`) and sovereign controls enabled.
- Conclusion: Data sovereignty requires defense-in-depth—organization policies for prevention, asset inventory scans for detection, and automated remediation for response.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Data sovereignty laws are getting stricter around the world. Whether it is GDPR in Europe, LGPD in Brazil, or data localization requirements in India and Russia, the mandate is clear: certain data must stay within specific geographic boundaries."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Data Residency and Processing Reference | F5 Distributed Cloud Technical Knowledge ---
URL: https://docs.cloud.f5.com/docs-v2/platform/reference/data-residency-locations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is F5's official reference on Data Residency and Processing for F5 Distributed Cloud Services, published April 5, 2023 and last updated June 16, 2026. It details where customer data is persistently stored and non-persistently processed for each supported F5 service, along with the sub-processors used.

KEY DEFINITIONS:
- Non-Persistent Storage Location: Data stored in memory for immediate/imminent processing, cleared or overwritten after processing completes (e.g., WAF processing an HTTP request in main memory).
- Persistent Storage Location: Data stored for processing necessary to provide subscribed services but may not be immediate/imminent (e.g., storing customer data for 30 days for queries or reports).
- Acronyms: TAM (Technical Account Manager) and SOC (Security Operations Center).

SERVICE DATA LOCATIONS:
- Bot Defense (Standard, SSD, Aggregator): Persistent storage in US, Canada, EU, Sydney, São Paulo. Bot Defense Standard has four scrubbing center regions (EMEA: Frankfurt, Ireland, Bahrain, Stockholm; APAC: Singapore, Sydney, Mumbai, Tokyo, Hong Kong, Jakarta; US: North Virginia, Oregon; LATAM: São Paulo). Customer's scrubbing center choice is independent of persistent storage location.
- Data Intelligence: Persistent storage in US, EU, Canada, Indonesia, Australia. Non-persistent processing in US, Canada, Israel, Singapore. All data transmitted to customers transits the United States.
- Client-Side Defense: Persistent storage in US; non-persistent in US and Israel.
- Application Traffic Insight: Persistent storage in US, EU, Canada, Indonesia, Japan, Australia; non-persistent in US and Israel.
- F5 Distributed Cloud L7 DDoS, WAF, API Protection, CDN, App Connect: Persistent storage in India, EU, US, Canada. CDN logs also exported to EU. Flow Anomaly logs only supported in EU. All data transfers encrypted over TLS; storage uses industry standard block encryption. Non-persistent processing in 25 global locations (Atlanta, Dallas, Washington DC, New York, San Jose, São Paulo, Toronto, Seattle, Chennai, Hong Kong, Melbourne, Sydney, Osaka, Tokyo, Singapore, Amsterdam, Frankfurt, Lisbon, London, Madrid, Paris, Stockholm, Montreal, Dubai, Mumbai, Chicago).
- F5 Distributed Cloud L3/L4 DDoS: Persistent storage in US only.
- F5 AI Guardrails and F5 AI Red Team: Persistent and non-persistent storage in US only.
- NGINX One Console: Persistent and non-persistent storage in US.
- NGINXaaS: Persistent and non-persistent processing in 17 countries (Australia, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, Finland, Germany, India, Ireland, Japan, Netherlands, Poland, Singapore, South Korea, Sweden, UK, US) to support data sovereignty requirements.
- TAM Locations: 43 countries worldwide.
- SOC Locations: US, Poland, Mexico, India, Singapore.

SUB-PROCESSORS:
- F5 Distributed Cloud (DDoS Protection, CDN, WAAP, AI Assistant): AWS, Google, C-Serv Global Ltd, Stripe, Databricks, Microsoft, GitLab, ZenDesk (decommissioned Dec 2024), Salesforce Service Cloud, Kentik Technologies, Microsoft Azure, MongoDB, Tines Security Services.
- Bot Defense, Data Intelligence, Application Traffic Insight, Client-Side Defense: AWS, Okta, Google Cloud, Microsoft, ZenDesk (decommissioned Dec 2024), Salesforce Service Cloud, Accenture (US & India), CommVault Systems, Tines Security Services.
- NGINXaaS: Salesforce Service Cloud, AWS, Google, Microsoft, ClickHouse, Okta.
- NGINX One Console: Salesforce Service Cloud, AWS, ClickHouse.
- F5 AI Guardrails / AI Red Team: AWS only.
- F5 Affiliates: 40+ entities across countries including US, UK, India, Brazil, Japan, Germany, Singapore, and many more.

DATA RETENTION POLICY:
- Bot Defense: Customer data retained up to one year after contract termination or upon deletion request.
- Data Intelligence: Customer data retained up to one year after contract termination or upon deletion request.

The document notes that the scope covers where and who processes data, not what type of data is processed (covered separately in F5 Privacy Statements). Users can subscribe to RSS feeds for updates on processing and sub-processing information.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Non-Persistent Storage Location is a location where data is stored in memory for the purpose of immediate or imminent processing, and is cleared or overwritten from the memory after the processing is complete."
</key_excerpts>
